name: Existence of injective envelopes
text: every module over any ring has an injective envelope, an injective module containing it as an essential submodule, and one is found inside any injective module containing it (Eckmann–Schopf 1953; Lam, *Lectures on Modules and Rings*, Thm 3.29).

name: Newman's Tauberian theorem
text: if f is bounded on [0, ∞) and its Laplace transform G(z) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^{−zt} dt extends holomorphically to a neighbourhood of Re z ≥ 0, then ∫₀^∞ f(t) dt converges to G(0) (Newman 1980; Zagier, *Newman's short proof of the prime number theorem*, 1997).

name: The Milnor exact sequence
text: for a tower of complexes of modules C₀ ← C₁ ← ⋯ with surjective transition maps, or Mittag-Leffler in each degree, 0 → lim¹ Hᵢ(Cₙ) → Hⱼ(lim Cₙ) → lim Hⱼ(Cₙ) → 0 is exact for consecutive degrees i, j (Weibel, *An Introduction to Homological Algebra*, Thm 3.5.8).

name: Schur's theorem
text: for a torsion-free metric connection on a connected manifold of dimension at least three, if the sectional curvature at each point is the same on every tangent two-plane, then it is constant (Kobayashi–Nomizu, *Foundations of Differential Geometry* I, Ch. V Thm 2.2).

name: The global norm index theorem
text: for a finite abelian extension L/K of number fields, the norm group N_{L/K}(C_L) has index exactly [L : K] in the idele class group C_K (Milne, *Class Field Theory*, Ch. VII; Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, VI §5).

name: Conformal invariance of the Weyl tensor
text: for a Riemannian metric g and smooth f > 0 in dimension n ≠ 2, the Weyl tensor of fg is f·W^g, so the (1,3) Weyl tensor is conformally invariant; the Schouten tensor transforms by the standard Hessian formula (Besse, *Einstein Manifolds*, Thm 1.159).

name: Finiteness of classes of binary quadratic forms
text: for every nonsquare discriminant D, now including indefinite D > 0, the primitive integral forms of discriminant D fall into finitely many proper classes, each containing a form with |b| ≤ |a| ≤ |c|, so 3|ac| ≤ |D| (Lagrange 1773; Buell, *Binary Quadratic Forms*, Ch. 3).

name: Classification of odd unimodular forms over ℤ₂
text: two odd unimodular symmetric bilinear forms over the 2-adic integers of the same rank are isometric exactly when their determinants differ by a square and their oddities, the norms of characteristic vectors modulo 8, agree (Conway–Sloane, *Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups*, Ch. 15 §7).

name: The center of U_q(sl₂)
text: for q nonzero and not a root of unity, the center of U_q(sl₂) is the polynomial algebra ℂ[Ω] on the Casimir element Ω = FE + (qK + q⁻¹K⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹)² (Kassel, *Quantum Groups*, Thm VI.4.8).

name: Compactness in L¹_loc for functions of bounded variation
text: on an open Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ, a family of functions with ∫_Ω |u| ≤ M and |Du|(Ω) ≤ M is relatively compact in L¹(K) for every compact K ⊆ Ω (Ambrosio–Fusco–Pallara, *Functions of Bounded Variation and Free Discontinuity Problems*, Thm 3.23).

name: The Leech lattice
text: K ∪ (s + K), with K the Construction B lattice of the binary Golay code and s = (−3/2, 1/2, …, 1/2): a positive definite even unimodular lattice of rank 24 with minimum norm 4, so rootless (Conway–Sloane, *Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups*, Ch. 4 §11).

name: The Hopf algebroid (L, LB) of formal group laws
text: the coproduct and conjugation on LB = L[b₁, b₂, …] over the Lazard ring L, satisfying all the Hopf algebroid identities, so that (L, LB) corepresents the groupoid of formal group laws and strict isomorphisms (Ravenel, *Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres*, A2.1).

name: Symmetric spectra
text: the sphere symmetric sequence n ↦ (S¹)^∧n of pointed simplicial sets is a commutative monoid for Day convolution, and symmetric spectra are defined as the modules over it (Hovey–Shipley–Smith, *Symmetric spectra*, 2000, §§1.2, 2.2).

name: Semianalytic sets
text: subsets of a real normed space that near every point are finite Boolean combinations of sets f = 0 and f > 0 with f real analytic; a Boolean algebra stable under analytic preimages, containing the semialgebraic sets (Bierstone–Milman, *Semianalytic and subanalytic sets*, §2).

name: The Slodowy slice
text: for an sl₂-triple (h, e, f), the affine subspace e + ker(ad f), with the contracting action c ↦ c² Ad(λ(c⁻¹)) of Kˣ, which fixes e, preserves the slice, and has weights at least 2 on its direction (Slodowy, *Simple Singularities and Simple Algebraic Groups*, §7.4).

name: Hypersurfaces of contact type
text: a hypersurface in a symplectic manifold (M, ω) near which ω = dα with a Liouville vector field transverse to it; the unit cosphere bundle of a Riemannian manifold is of restricted contact type in T*M (Weinstein 1979; McDuff–Salamon, *Introduction to Symplectic Topology*, Ch. 3).

name: The noncentral beta distribution
text: the law of U/(U + V) for independent U ∼ noncentral χ²(2a; λ) and V ∼ χ²(2b), equal to the Poisson mixture Σⱼ e^{−λ/2}(λ/2)^j/j! · Beta(a + j, b); then (b/a)X/(1 − X) is noncentral F(2a, 2b; λ) (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan, *Continuous Univariate Distributions* 2, Ch. 30).

name: The modular Artin induction theorem
text: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic p, every class x in the Grothendieck group G₀(k[G]) of finitely generated modules has a positive multiple, |G|·x in fact, in the subgroup generated by the classes induced from cyclic subgroups of order prime to p; it rests on [Artin's identity |G|·1 = Σ_C a_C|C|·Ind_C 1 in G₀(k[G])](https://cbirkbeck.github.io/tauceti-reviewed-by-test/#/d/TauCeti.natCard_nsmul_one_eq_sum_artinCoeff_indK0), the characteristic-zero Artin induction announced earlier now holding over every field (Neukirch–Schmidt–Wingberg, 7.3.4; Milne, *Arithmetic Duality Theorems*, I 2.10).

name: Pinsker's inequality
text: for probability measures μ, ν on any measurable space, ‖μ − ν‖² ≤ 2·KL(μ‖ν), where ‖·‖ is the total variation of the signed measure μ − ν (twice the usual d_TV, so d_TV² ≤ KL/2), and [2(μ(s) − ν(s))² ≤ KL(μ‖ν) for every measurable s](https://cbirkbeck.github.io/tauceti-reviewed-by-test/#/d/TauCeti.two_mul_sq_measureReal_sub_le_klDiv); no absolute continuity is assumed and infinite entropy is allowed; proved from the Donsker–Varadhan bound and Hoeffding's lemma (Csiszár–Körner, *Information Theory*).

name: The Calderón–Zygmund theorem: singular integrals are bounded on Lᵖ, 1 < p < ∞
text: for T bounded on L²(ℝⁿ) (Hilbert-space valued) whose kernel satisfies Hörmander's condition, [‖Tf‖ₚ ≤ C(p, n, ‖T‖, B)·‖f‖ₚ for 1 < p < 2](https://cbirkbeck.github.io/tauceti-reviewed-by-test/#/d/ContinuousLinearMap.eLpNorm_le_of_hormander) by Marcinkiewicz interpolation from the weak (1, 1) bound announced earlier, and [for 2 < p < ∞](https://cbirkbeck.github.io/tauceti-reviewed-by-test/#/d/ContinuousLinearMap.eLpNorm_le_of_hormander_adjoint) by duality when the adjoint satisfies the same cancellation condition; the estimates are proved for f ∈ L² ∩ Lᵖ, and the extension of T to all of Lᵖ by density is still to come (Stein, *Singular Integrals*, II §2; Grafakos §5.3).

name: Hilbert reciprocity over ℚ
text: for a, b ∈ ℚˣ the Hilbert symbols (a, b)_v over all primes and the real place, written additively in ℤ/2, sum to zero; over a number field the law is proved whenever √b lies in a cyclotomic extension (Serre, *A Course in Arithmetic*, III §2).

Correctly stated: the equality case of the isodiametric inequality for nonempty closed bounded sets (Schneider, Convex Bodies, Thm 7.1.1 via the difference body); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Stacks Definition 10.157.1 (031P), depth M_p ≥ min(n, dim Supp M_p) at every prime; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: Stacks Lemma 10.157.3 (031R), reduced iff (R_0) and (S_1) for a Noetherian ring; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the von Mises law with density e^{κ cos(θ−m)}/I₀(κ) against normalised Haar measure (Mardia–Jupp, Directional Statistics §3.5.4); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the wrapped Cauchy law as the circle image of the centred Cauchy law of scale γ shifted by m (Mardia–Jupp §3.5.7); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the law of (Z+δ)/√(V/ν) with Z standard Gaussian and V an independent χ²(ν) (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 31); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Puiseux field as an algebraic closure of K((X)) for K algebraically closed of characteristic zero (Newton–Puiseux theorem in the Wikipedia form); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: algebraic closedness of the Puiseux field over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: Rudin, Functional Analysis, Thm 3.31 (Dunford), weak holomorphy on an open set implies holomorphy into a complex Banach space; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Clarkson's first inequality for 2 ≤ p < ∞ (Brezis Thm 4.10 proof), for norms satisfying the parallelogram law; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: uniform convexity of Lᵖ for 2 ≤ p < ∞, the range the docstring names; the range 1 < p < 2 is a separate statement; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the residue field of a regular local ring has projective dimension dim R (Matsumura Thm 19.2 via a regular system of parameters); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: every module over a regular ring of dimension ≤ n has projective dimension ≤ n (Stacks §10.110), finitely generated or not; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the local case of the global-dimension bound for regular rings (Matsumura §19); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: pd M ≤ dim R over a regular ring, the unconditional form; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem, cat(M) ≤ #Crit(f) in the unnormalised count convention, for every smooth f on a compact boundaryless manifold (Cornea–Lupton–Oprea–Tanré Ch. 1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated as labelled: Etingof–Nikshych–Ostrik nonvanishing for pivotal fusion categories in characteristic zero (ENO Thm 2.3); the pivotal hypothesis is stated in name and docstring, the general fusion case being a separate statement; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: ∑ leftDim S ≫ leftDim Sᘁ over simple classes, EGNO §7.21; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: Sanov's theorem, [[1,2],[0,1]] and [[1,0],[2,1]] freely generate a free subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) (de la Harpe II.B); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: every free group of countable rank embeds in SL(2,ℤ); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: Hatcher Thm 2.27 for the ordered simplicial chains of an ordered abstract simplicial complex and the singular homology of its realization; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the Hall inner product on degree-n symmetric polynomials with the Schur polynomials orthonormal (Macdonald I §4), finite alphabet; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the Frobenius characteristic is an isometry from the character pairing of S_n to the Hall inner product (Macdonald I §7); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Stacks 062F, acyclicity of the Koszul complex of a weakly regular sequence in positive degrees; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Markov trace of the Jones representation equals δ times the normalised Kauffman bracket of the closure (Jones 1987, Kauffman 1987), over every commutative ring; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Fredholm alternative for completely continuous operators over a complete nonarchimedean field (Serre 1962 §§2–3), invertibility iff injectivity; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the BV Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality on bounded convex sets with the explicit constant (Evans–Gariepy §5.6, Gilbarg–Trudinger Lemma 7.16); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Cartan–Killing classification over ℚ, every irreducible reduced crystallographic finite root system isomorphic to the model of exactly one Dynkin type (Humphreys §11, Bourbaki VI §4); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the Gromov–Prokhorov distance of Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter, Def. 5.1, with the disjoint union as common space; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

name: The Cartan–Killing classification of root systems
text: every irreducible reduced crystallographic root system over ℚ is isomorphic to the model root system of exactly one Dynkin type, now independently of the chosen base and with every type realised by a model (Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras*, §11).

name: Brenier's polar factorization theorem
text: a map U : (Ω, m) → ℝⁿ with absolutely continuous law and finite quadratic cost to an absolutely continuous P factors as U = ∇u ∘ s, u convex, s of law P, s unique and minimising ∫‖s′ − U‖² among maps of law P (Brenier, CPAM 44 (1991), Thm 1.2).

name: The global dimension of a regular local ring is its Krull dimension
text: over a regular local ring of dimension d every module, finitely generated or not, has projective dimension at most d, and the residue field has projective dimension exactly d (Matsumura, *Commutative Ring Theory*, Thm 19.2).

name: The trace theorem on Lipschitz domains
text: for a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω and 1 ≤ p < ∞ there is a unique bounded linear trace W^{1,p}(Ω) → Lᵖ(∂Ω, 𝓗ⁿ⁻¹) sending every function continuous up to the boundary to its restriction to ∂Ω (Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, §5.5 Thm 1).

name: The Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem
text: a smooth function on a compact manifold without boundary has at least as many critical points, degenerate ones included, as the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of the manifold (Cornea–Lupton–Oprea–Tanré, *Lusternik–Schnirelmann Category*, Ch. 1).

name: Simplicial homology is singular homology
text: for an ordered abstract simplicial complex K and any coefficient ring, the homology of its ordered simplicial chain complex is the singular homology of the realization |K|, through the cellular chains of its CW structure (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Thm 2.27).

name: The homology of a classifying space is group homology
text: for every group G and commutative ring k, Hₙ(BG; k) of Milnor's classifying space is the group homology Hₙ(G, k) of the trivial module, in every degree (Brown, *Cohomology of Groups*, II.4).

name: Bombieri–Vaaler's theorem
text: an integer p × n matrix A of rank p has n − p independent primitive integer kernel vectors x₁, …, x_{n−p} with ∏ ‖xₗ‖_∞ ≤ √det(AAᵀ) / g, g the gcd of the p × p minors of A (Bombieri–Vaaler, Invent. Math. 73 (1983), Thm 2).

name: The Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion for potential good reduction
text: an elliptic curve over a nonarchimedean local field has potential good reduction exactly when inertia acts on its ℓ-adic Tate module through a finite quotient, ℓ prime to the residue characteristic (Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*, VII.7.3).

name: The Cohen–Hewitt factorization theorem
text: if a Banach algebra A with a left approximate identity bounded by C acts boundedly on a Banach space E, every x in the closed span of A·E is a·y with ‖a‖ ≤ C and y ∈ closure(A·x) arbitrarily close to x (Dales, *Banach Algebras and Automatic Continuity*, Thm 2.9.24).

name: The Koszul complex of a regular sequence is acyclic
text: for a weakly regular sequence x₁, …, xₙ in a commutative ring R, the Koszul complex K(x) has vanishing homology in positive degrees, so it is a finite free resolution of R/(x₁, …, xₙ) (Stacks, Tag 062F).

name: The disc theorem in a manifold
text: two smooth embeddings of ℝⁿ into a boundaryless n-manifold with the same centre and derivatives there of the same orientation are smoothly isotopic through embeddings fixing the centre (Hirsch, *Differential Topology*, Ch. 4 Thm 6.6).

name: The cohomology of a classifying space is group cohomology
text: for every group G and module M over a commutative ring, Hⁿ(BG; M) of Milnor's classifying space is the group cohomology Hⁿ(G, M) of the trivial module M (Brown, *Cohomology of Groups*, III.1).

name: The Fredholm alternative for completely continuous operators
text: on a Banach space over a complete nonarchimedean field, 1 − u is Fredholm of index zero for every completely continuous u, so it is invertible exactly when injective, exactly when surjective (Serre, *Endomorphismes complètement continus des espaces de Banach p-adiques*, 1962).

name: Roby's representability theorem
text: for modules M, N over a commutative ring, composition with the universal law γ_d is a linear equivalence between linear maps Γ^d(M) → N out of the degree-d divided power module and homogeneous polynomial laws M → N of degree d (Roby, Ann. ENS 1963, Thm IV.1).

name: Equality in the isodiametric inequality
text: a nonempty closed bounded set s ⊆ ℝⁿ has the volume of a ball of radius diam(s)/2 exactly when it is such a ball, and a bounded measurable set exactly when it agrees with one almost everywhere (Schneider, *Convex Bodies*, Thm 7.1.1).

name: The Hall inner product, and the Frobenius characteristic is an isometry
text: the bilinear form on degree-n symmetric polynomials in which the Schur polynomials are orthonormal, with ⟨h_μ, m_ν⟩ = δ_{μν} and ⟨p_ρ, p_σ⟩ = z_ρ δ_{ρσ}, and the Frobenius characteristic carries the character pairing of Sₙ to it (Macdonald, *Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials*, I §4, §7).

name: Dunford's theorem: weak holomorphy implies holomorphy
text: a function from an open subset of ℂ into a complex Banach space is holomorphic as soon as its composite with every continuous linear functional is holomorphic (Rudin, *Functional Analysis*, Thm 3.31).

name: Central extensions of the formal loop algebra are classified by invariant forms
text: for a simple Lie algebra 𝔤 over an algebraically closed field K of characteristic zero, Φ ↦ [Res(f dg) Φ(x, y)] is a linear isomorphism from invariant symmetric forms on 𝔤 onto H²_cont(𝔤((t)), K) (Frenkel, *Langlands Correspondence for Loop Groups*, §1.3).

name: The braid and diagram routes to the Jones polynomial agree
text: for any braid word w, the writhe-normalised Markov trace of the Jones representation of its braid equals −(a² + a⁻²) times the writhe-normalised Kauffman bracket of the closure of w, so both routes give the Jones polynomial (Jones, Ann. of Math. 126 (1987)).

name: The Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality for BV functions
text: for a bounded convex open Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ, S ⊆ Ω of positive measure and u ∈ L¹(Ω), ∫_Ω |u − ⨍_S u| ≤ |B(0,1)| (diam Ω)^{n+1}/|S| · |Du|(Ω), now with the total variation of any integrable u in place of ‖∇u‖ (Evans–Gariepy, *Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions*, §5.6).

name: Linear groups over Noetherian rings are equationally Noetherian
text: for a commutative Noetherian ring R, every system of group equations in finitely many variables over GLₙ(R), hence over any subgroup of it, has a finite subsystem with the same solutions (Baumslag–Myasnikov–Remeslennikov, *Algebraic geometry over groups I*, Thm B1).

name: Sanov's theorem
text: the matrices [[1, 2], [0, 1]] and [[1, 0], [2, 1]] freely generate a free subgroup of SL₂(ℤ), so every free group of countable rank embeds in SL₂(ℤ) (de la Harpe, *Topics in Geometric Group Theory*, II.B).

name: Free cumulants with products as arguments
text: grouping consecutive letters of a word a₁⋯aₙ into products A₁⋯Aₘ, κₘ(A₁, …, Aₘ) = Σ κ_π(a₁, …, aₙ) over the noncrossing partitions π of n whose join with the grouping partition is the one-block partition (Nica–Speicher, *Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability*, Thm 11.12).

name: A plane domain is simply connected exactly when it has no holes
text: a connected open U ⊆ ℂ is simply connected if and only if every connected component of ℂ ∖ U is unbounded (Rudin, *Real and Complex Analysis*, Thm 13.11).

name: Serre's conditions (Sₙ) and (Rₙ)
text: (Sₙ) asks depth M_𝔭 ≥ min(n, dim M_𝔭) at every prime 𝔭, (Rₙ) that R_𝔭 be regular whenever ht 𝔭 ≤ n; a Noetherian ring is reduced exactly when it satisfies (R₀) and (S₁) (Stacks, Tag 031R).

name: The height of a formal group law
text: for a formal group law F over a field of characteristic p, the h with [p]_F(T) = cT^{p^h} + ⋯, c ≠ 0, or ∞ when [p]_F = 0; invariant under field extension, with 𝔾ₐ of height ∞ and 𝔾ₘ of height 1 (Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*, IV.7).

name: The Pontryagin product
text: for a topological monoid G, the product H_p(G; R) ⊗ H_q(G; R) → H_{p+q}(G; R) given by the homology cross product followed by the multiplication of G; it is associative and, for commutative G, graded commutative (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, §3.C).

name: Regular ring maps
text: a ring map R → B is regular when B is flat over R and every fibre κ(𝔭) ⊗_R B is geometrically regular over κ(𝔭); smooth maps and localizations are regular (Stacks, Definition 15.42.1).

name: The Gromov–Prokhorov distance
text: for measures on two extended pseudometric spaces, the infimum over metric couplings of the Lévy–Prokhorov distance of the two measures in the glued disjoint union; symmetric, satisfying the triangle inequality and invariant under isometries (Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter, PTRF 145 (2009), Def. 5.1).

name: The Cotton tensor
text: C(X, Y, Z) = (∇_Z P)(X, Y) − (∇_Y P)(X, Z) for the Schouten tensor P of a Riemannian manifold, antisymmetric in Y, Z, cyclically summing to zero, and vanishing in constant sectional curvature (Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds*, Ch. 7).

name: The von Mises distribution
text: the law on the circle with density e^{κ cos(θ − m)}/I₀(κ) against normalised Haar measure, κ ≥ 0, with Fourier moments E[e^{inθ}] = e^{inm} I_{|n|}(κ)/I₀(κ) and mean resultant length I₁(κ)/I₀(κ) (Mardia–Jupp, *Directional Statistics*, §3.5.4).

name: The noncentral t distribution
text: the law of (Z + δ)/√(V/ν) for Z standard Gaussian and V an independent χ² with ν degrees of freedom, absolutely continuous, reducing to Student's t at δ = 0 and squaring to the noncentral F(1, ν; δ²) (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan, *Continuous Univariate Distributions* 2, Ch. 31).

name: The wrapped Cauchy distribution
text: the law on the circle of a Cauchy variable of scale γ reduced modulo 2π and shifted to m, with Fourier moments e^{inm}e^{−γ|n|}, mean resultant length e^{−γ}, and convolutions adding locations and scales (Mardia–Jupp, *Directional Statistics*, §3.5.7).

The declaration is as intended. `cyclicCohomology` is Connes' cyclic cohomology: the cohomology of the cyclically invariant cochains. Over a ground ring containing ℚ it agrees with the cohomology of the cyclic bicomplex (Loday's HC). Over other rings the two can differ, and that is what the 𝔽₂ example shows. So the definition is the usual one in Mathlib's style, stated for any ring, and under the usual hypothesis, ℚ ⊆ R (Connes worked over ℂ), it is HCⁿ(A).

The module documentation already said this. [TauCeti#21174](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/pull/21174) adds the same caveat to the declaration's own docstring.

The predicate is as intended: it holds the two test-function inequalities, and convexity of `u` is a separate hypothesis. Every result built on it assumes `ConvexOn ℝ Ω u`: `isMongeAmpereViscositySolution_of_mongeAmpereMeasure_eq`, `isMongeAmpereViscositySolution_iff_forall_det_eq`, and both bridges from the Monge–Ampère measure. The example u = 1 − ‖x‖² is strictly concave, the vacuous case that hypothesis excludes. With the hypothesis, this is the standard notion of a convex viscosity solution.

[TauCeti#21171](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/pull/21171) says so in the docstring.

The instance is correct as stated. `MixedHodgeStructureCat` puts no finiteness condition on its carriers, so it is larger than Deligne's category, whose objects have a finitely generated integral (or finite-dimensional rational) carrier. Deligne's category is the full subcategory of the finitely generated ones, and the larger category is abelian, which is what this instance proves. The generality is in Mathlib's style; restricted to finitely generated carriers, it is the usual category.

[TauCeti#21175](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/pull/21175) records the generality in the structure's docstring.

The two carry the same data. Mathlib gives `ProbabilityMeasure α` the Giry σ-algebra restricted to probability measures (`inferInstanceAs <| MeasurableSpace (Subtype _)`). So a measurable `ν : Ω → ProbabilityMeasure α` is exactly a Markov kernel from `Ω` to `α`: compose with the coercion to `Measure α`, and conversely `Measurable.subtype_mk` turns a Markov kernel into such a map.

The definition uses the `ProbabilityMeasure`-valued form because it treats `ν` as a random element and constrains the joint law of `(ν, block)`. The left side pushes `μ` forward along `ω ↦ (ν ω, block ω)`, and the right side has the Dirac mass `δ_{ν ω}`, so `ν ω` has to be a point of a measurable space. The de Finetti results built on it are statements about the law of `ν`, the mixing law, a measure on `ProbabilityMeasure α` (`MixedIID.existsUnique_mixingLaw`, `conditionallyIID_ae_unique`; see the module docs of `TauCeti.Probability.DeFinetti.Theorem`). With a `κ : Kernel Ω α` in its place, `κ ω` would play the same role as a point of `Measure α`, and the mixing law would live on `Measure α`, concentrated on probability measures. That is the same strength in different notation; `ProbabilityMeasure` just carries the "probability" part in the type.

If a `Kernel` view would serve users better, the natural fix is a pair of lemmas converting between `ConditionallyIIDWith μ X ν` and the same statement for a Markov kernel, rather than a change to the definition.

This theorem has no problem, as the review itself says: it proves the uniqueness half of Gabriel's theorem as stated. Correctly stated at Tau Ceti commit `271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a`.

I read the site's signature, docstring and definition value, and the [source at that commit](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a/TauCeti/NumberTheory/NumberField/DirichletDensityBounds.lean#L81). The site's declaration data contained no prior review records when I selected it.

**Intended mathematics.** [ArithmeticDirichletSeries, Layer 7.1](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/8888d45eea61a0573e32d9b39a00c833f844fc44/Completed/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/README.md#L289) explicitly requests epsilon-style upper *bounds* on Mathlib's ratio, without assuming the ratio has a limit. For `R_S(s) = (sum over S of N(p)^(-s))/(sum over all nonzero primes of N(p)^(-s))`, this definition says: for every epsilon > 0, eventually as s tends to 1 from above, R_S(s) < delta + epsilon. This is equivalent to limsup R_S <= delta, rather than equality with delta.

For an independent comparison, [Kedlaya, MIT 18.785 (2007), section 2, p. 1](https://kskedlaya.org/18.785/dirichlet.pdf#page=1) uses the limsup of the corresponding ratio for upper Dirichlet density; [Sutherland, MIT 18.785 (2021), Problem Set 9, Problem 4, p. 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_pset9.pdf#page=6) gives precisely this absolute-norm/all-prime ratio for number fields. I proved in Lean that the declaration is equivalent to `Filter.limsup R_S (nhdsWithin 1 (Set.Ioi 1)) <= delta`, using the existing bounds 0 <= R_S <= 1. The full reproducible checks are below.

**Axes checked.** Object/convention: the carrier is nonzero prime ideals of the ring of integers of an arbitrary number field; the absolute norm, denominator, approach from the right, and direction of the bound agree. Edge cases: Lean checks show that the empty set, and every finite prime set, admit exactly the bounds delta >= 0; all primes admit exactly the bounds delta >= 1. Negative bounds are impossible for any S, while every delta >= 1 is a valid bound. Thus the strict epsilon inequality permits sharp endpoints and the predicate is deliberately not restricted to density values in [0,1]. Junk/vacuity: for s > 1, [the prime series is summable](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a/TauCeti/NumberTheory/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/Convergence.lean#L110) and [the denominator is positive](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a/TauCeti/NumberTheory/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/Convergence.lean#L180). Values at s <= 1 therefore do not affect this right-hand limit; Lean also supplies a nontrivial right-neighborhood filter in the limsup proof. Choice/generality/naming: the declaration adds no arbitrary chosen density or convergence hypothesis, accepts arbitrary prime sets, and correctly calls its possibly nonunique delta a bound.

**Roadmap Checks.** The relevant check is [Worked examples and rejection tests, item 3](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/8888d45eea61a0573e32d9b39a00c833f844fc44/Completed/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/README.md#L394). The roadmap's Suggested.lean explicitly identifies its two named witnesses:

- Finite prime sets have density zero: **passes**, [NumberField.Set.hasDirichletDensity_of_finite](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a/TauCeti/NumberTheory/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/DirichletDensity/Negligible.lean#L94). The additional `finite_iff` check below applies this to the upper-bound predicate.
- Finite changes preserve density: **passes**, [NumberField.Set.hasDirichletDensity_iff_of_finite_symmDiff](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a/TauCeti/NumberTheory/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/DirichletDensity/Negligible.lean#L159). The directly relevant upper-bound version also **passes**: [NumberField.Set.isUpperDirichletDensityBound_iff_of_finite_symmDiff](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/271e1af4dd54c50b9192cf3e213b7686843a0b3a/TauCeti/NumberTheory/ArithmeticDirichletSeries/DirichletDensity/Negligible.lean#L229).

All three witnesses are present at the site's commit and contain no sorry. I built their module and the definition's module, and ran the checks below with Lean v4.36.0-rc1 and the pinned Mathlib commit `2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055`. The inspected proof axioms are only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

**Limits.** This reviews the stated meaning of this one definition. I did not audit every transitive proof, the logarithm-normalization development in Layer 7.2, the other layers' checks, or extensions beyond number fields. The file's Serre and Neukirch book references were identified but not consulted; the independent comparisons above use accessible primary course notes. import TauCeti.NumberTheory.ArithmeticDirichletSeries.DirichletDensity.Negligible
import Mathlib.Order.LiminfLimsup

open Filter IsDedekindDomain NumberField NumberField.Set
open scoped Topology symmDiff

namespace ReviewChecks

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [NumberField K]

noncomputable def ratio (S : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) (s : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  S.primeIdealZetaSum s /
    NumberField.Set.primeIdealZetaSum (Set.univ : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) s

/-- Independent comparison with the classical limsup formulation. -/
theorem upperBound_iff_limsup_le (S : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) (δ : ℝ) :
    IsUpperDirichletDensityBound S δ ↔ limsup (ratio S) (𝓝[>] 1) ≤ δ := by
  have hlo : (𝓝[>] (1 : ℝ)).IsCoboundedUnder (· ≤ ·) (ratio S) :=
    isCoboundedUnder_le_of_le _ fun s => primeIdealZetaSum_div_univ_nonneg S s
  have hhi : (𝓝[>] (1 : ℝ)).IsBoundedUnder (· ≤ ·) (ratio S) :=
    isBoundedUnder_of_eventually_le
      (Eventually.of_forall fun s => primeIdealZetaSum_div_univ_le_one S s)
  rw [isUpperDirichletDensityBound_iff, Filter.limsup_le_iff hlo hhi]
  constructor
  · intro h y hy
    simpa only [ratio, add_sub_cancel] using h (y - δ) (sub_pos.mpr hy)
  · intro h ε hε
    exact h (δ + ε) (lt_add_of_pos_right δ hε)

/-- Strict epsilon inequalities must still admit the sharp endpoint zero. -/
theorem empty_iff (δ : ℝ) :
    IsUpperDirichletDensityBound (∅ : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) δ ↔ 0 ≤ δ := by
  constructor
  · exact IsUpperDirichletDensityBound.nonneg
  · intro hδ
    exact (hasDirichletDensity_empty.isUpperDirichletDensityBound).mono hδ

/-- Negative bounds are impossible, including for the empty set. -/
theorem negative_rejected (S : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) {δ : ℝ} (hδ : δ < 0) :
    ¬ IsUpperDirichletDensityBound S δ := by
  intro h
  exact (not_le_of_gt hδ) h.nonneg

/-- Bounds above one remain legitimate bounds, rather than being rejected as non-densities. -/
theorem above_one (S : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) {δ : ℝ} (hδ : 1 ≤ δ) :
    IsUpperDirichletDensityBound S δ :=
  (isUpperDirichletDensityBound_one S).mono hδ

/-- A matching lower bound recovers actual convergence. -/
example (S : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) (δ : ℝ) :
    S.HasDirichletDensity δ ↔
      IsUpperDirichletDensityBound S δ ∧ IsLowerDirichletDensityBound S δ :=
  hasDirichletDensity_iff_bounds

/-- The full prime set has sharp upper bound one, never zero. -/
theorem all_primes_iff (δ : ℝ) :
    IsUpperDirichletDensityBound (Set.univ : Set (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))) δ ↔ 1 ≤ δ := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact hasDirichletDensity_univ.isLowerDirichletDensityBound.le_of_isUpperDirichletDensityBound h
  · intro hδ
    exact (isUpperDirichletDensityBound_one Set.univ).mono hδ

text: on a nonzero affinoid algebra over a complete nonarchimedean field, every element attains its supremum seminorm at a maximal ideal: |f(x)| = |f|_sup for some x (Bosch–Güntzer–Remmert, *Non-Archimedean Analysis*, §6.2.1).

name: Weierstrass preparation for overconvergent power series
text: a series in the Monsky–Washnitzer algebra K⟨X, Y⟩† that is distinguished of degree s in Y factors uniquely as an overconvergent unit times a monic polynomial of degree s over K⟨X⟩†, extending the Tate-algebra case (Grosse-Klönne, *Rigid analytic spaces with overconvergent structure sheaf*, §1.3).

name: Pivotal structures correspond to twists on a braided rigid category
text: on a braided rigid monoidal category, pivotal structures and balanced structures are in bijection, the twist of a pivotal structure being θ_X = φ_X ∘ u_X⁻¹ with u the Drinfeld isomorphism (Etingof–Gelaki–Nikshych–Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, §8.10).

name: Weierstrass preparation for entire series, normalised form
text: over a complete ultrametric normed ring, an entire series with constant term 1 that is distinguished of degree d at radius c is uniquely a degree-d polynomial with constant term 1 times an entire series with constant term 1 invertible on the disc of radius c (Coleman, *p-adic Banach spaces and families of modular forms*, App. A3).

name: The going-down theorem for torsion-free integral algebras
text: going down holds for an integral algebra over an integrally closed domain as soon as the algebra is torsion-free as a module; Mathlib has the case where the algebra is a domain (Stacks Project, Tag 00H8).

name: Dehn filling
text: a filling of a knot exterior along a slope, recorded as a decomposition of the filled space into the exterior and a solid torus glued along the boundary torus; the filling along the meridian is the ambient space and 0-surgery on the unknot gives S¹ × S² (Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Ch. 9).

name: G-topologies
text: admissible opens and admissible covers on a space, with their coverage and Grothendieck topology, whose sheaves are the presheaves with unique gluing on admissible covers; ordinary open covers give Mathlib's open-set site (Bosch–Güntzer–Remmert, *Non-Archimedean Analysis*, §9.1.1).

name: The negative hypergeometric distribution
text: the law of the number of failures drawn without replacement from N objects with K successes before the r-th success, with its mass function, moment generating function, mean r(N − K)/(K + 1) and variance (Johnson–Kemp–Kotz, *Univariate Discrete Distributions*, §6.2.2).

name: Real closed fields via an algebraically closed quadratic extension
text: a field F is real closed exactly when −1 is not a square in F and a quadratic extension of F, equivalently F(√−1), is algebraically closed; also being formalised in mathlib4#41911 (Lang, *Algebra*, XI §2).

name: Guba's theorem: free groups are equationally Noetherian
text: every system of equations in finitely many variables with coefficients in a free group of countable rank has the same solutions as one of its finite subsystems (Guba 1986).

name: Explicit 2-descent: the étale-algebra description of the 2-Selmer group
text: for an elliptic curve y² = f(x) over the fraction field K of a Dedekind domain, such as a number field, the Galois-cohomological 2-Selmer group is isomorphic, through the descent map, to the explicit 2-Selmer group inside (K[X]/(f))ˣ/squares (Schaefer 1995).

name: A wedge of circles is a K(F, 1)
text: for any set S, the wedge of S circles is an Eilenberg–MacLane space for the free group on S, the loop around the i-th circle being the generator i (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, §1.B).

name: The Hecke eigenvalue of a newform at a bad prime where its character is ramified
text: for a newform of weight k, level N and character χ, and a prime p ∣ N with χ not defined modulo N/p, |a_p| = p^((k−1)/2); with the earlier cases this completes Miyake's Theorem 4.6.17 (Li 1975, Thm 3).

name: The Banach space BV(Ω)
text: the integrable functions on an open set Ω with finite total variation |Du|(Ω), modulo null sets, with the norm ‖u‖₁ + |Du|(Ω), for which it is complete (Ambrosio–Fusco–Pallara, §3.1).

name: The Kronecker symbol
text: the extension (a/n) of the Jacobi symbol to every integer denominator, and, for a discriminant D ≡ 0, 1 (mod 4), the quadratic Dirichlet character (D/·) of modulus |D| (Cohen, *A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory*, §1.4).

name: G-rings
text: the Noetherian rings whose local ring at every prime has geometrically regular formal fibres, so that its completion map is regular; the first half of quasi-excellence (Stacks, Definition 15.51.1).

Correctly stated; I compared it with Frenkel §1.3 (Lemma 1.3.2) and the A1 target of TauCetiRoadmap/AffineLieAlgebras, which lists no tagged Check for this declaration. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean, saying why the Lean statement is the classical one.

**The hypotheses are "𝔤 simple".** `[LieAlgebra.IsKilling K L]` is Mathlib's way of saying the Killing form is nondegenerate (its radical is zero), and `[LieModule.IsIrreducible K L L]` says the adjoint representation is irreducible, which includes `L ≠ 0`. Together these force `L` to be simple, and conversely every simple Lie algebra in characteristic zero satisfies both (Cartan's criterion), so no generality is lost or gained. Square-bracket hypotheses are not inputs a user chooses; Lean finds them automatically from the structure of `L`.

**The two sides.** `invariantForms K L L` is the `K`-subspace of symmetric bilinear forms `Φ` on `L` with `Φ([x,y],z) = −Φ(y,[x,z])`; the `↥` in front only turns that subspace into a set of elements. `currentAlgebra K L` is `K⸨X⸩ ⊗ L`, where `K⸨X⸩` is Mathlib's `LaurentSeries`: formal series with finitely many negative powers and possibly infinitely many positive ones, so for finite-dimensional `L` this is exactly `𝔤((t))`. `TrivialLieModule K (currentAlgebra K L) K` is just the field `K` with the zero action, and `continuousSecondCohomology` is the quotient of continuous 2-cocycles by coboundaries of continuous 1-cochains, "continuous" meaning for the `t`-adic topology on `𝔤((t))` with `K` discrete, as in Frenkel. So the right side is `H²_cont(𝔤((t)), K)`.

**`≃ₗ[K]` says more than "isomorphic".** A `LinearEquiv` is a specific `K`-linear bijection, not merely the existence of one, which here would be empty content since both sides are one-dimensional. Which map it is can be read off the `_apply` lemma just below it in the file: the forward map sends `Φ` to the class of `(f ⊗ x, g ⊗ y) ↦ Res(f dg) Φ(x, y)`, proved by `rfl`, meaning the map is that one by definition. Frenkel's cocycle carries the opposite sign; negating a form is an automorphism of both sides, so the classification is unaffected.

**No junk values.** The statement involves no division, subtraction of naturals or limit that Lean would assign a default value to: the residue is the coefficient of `t⁻¹`, a genuine linear functional, and `dg` is the formal derivative. Nothing is vacuous: `sl₂(K)` satisfies every hypothesis.

Correctly stated; compared with Weibel, *An Introduction to Homological Algebra*, §5.6, and McCleary, Theorem 2.15, the file's references. The roadmap lists no tagged Check for it (DerivedModuleAlgebra §S.1's `DoubleComplex.spectralSequence` is a different, cohomological target).

**It is a construction whose content is pinned by its neighbours.** An `abbrev` only names the general filtered-complex spectral sequence applied to the row filtration; what makes it the spectral sequence of the bicomplex are the isomorphisms proved beside it: the first page is the homology of the rows ([L426](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L426)), the abutment in degree `-n` is `H_n` of the total complex ([L476](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L476)), and each position stabilises after finitely many pages to the corresponding graded piece of the abutment ([L497](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L497)), which is what "converges" means for a filtration finite in each degree.

**Hypotheses.** `[Abelian C]` is the abelian category. `HomologicalComplex₂ C (down ℕ) (down ℕ)` is a chain complex of chain complexes indexed by `ℕ × ℕ`, so "first quadrant" is built into the index type and both differentials lower degree. Mathlib's bicomplexes have commuting differentials; the sign sits in the total differential `d₁ + (-1)^p d₂` (the `TotalComplexShape` instance of `ComplexShapeSigns`), which is Weibel's anticommuting convention after changing the sign of the vertical differential on alternate columns, so the total complex and its homology are the classical ones.

**Indexing.** Row `q` is `⋯ → (K.X 1).X q → (K.X 0).X q` with the horizontal differentials. `rowFiltration q` is the subcomplex spanned by the rows `< q`, zero for `q ≤ 0` ([L366](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L366)) and increasing. Mathlib's `coreE₂Cohomological` numbers the first page `2` and is cohomological: the total complex is read with chain degree `n` in cochain degree `-n`, and the shape `up' (r, 1 - r)` in the type says `d_r` goes from `(p, q)` to `(p + r, q - r + 1)`. Translating, the object at `(p, q)` is `H_k(row q)` with `p + 2q + k = 0`, and `d_2` lowers the row by one keeping `k`: it is the map induced on horizontal homology by the vertical differential, Weibel's `d¹` on `E¹ = H^h(rows)`; page `r` here is Weibel's `E^{r-1}`. Rows `q < 0` and positions with `p + 2q > 0` carry zero ([L454](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L454), [L465](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L465)), the first-quadrant support.

**No junk, not vacuous.** No value is supplied by a default: every term is a kernel, cokernel or homology object. The tensor product double complex of two projective resolutions, whose row spectral sequence Weibel uses in §5.6 to balance Tor, satisfies every hypothesis; a bicomplex with one nonzero row collapses to `E_2 = H(row 0) = H(Tot)`.

Correctly stated; compared with Hall, *Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations*, Ch. 3 (the Lie algebra homomorphism `φ_*` induced by a Lie group homomorphism, with `φ(e^X) = e^{φ_* X}`) and with "The functor on morphisms" in Layer 3 of TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/LieGroups, which lists no tagged Check for it.

**The hypotheses say "G, G' are finite-dimensional real Lie groups and φ a smooth homomorphism".** `[LieGroup I ∞ G]` means multiplication and inversion are `C^∞` for the charts of `G`; the `(↑⊤)` printed in the signature is Mathlib's `∞` (smooth), not `ω` (analytic). `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]` makes the model space, hence `G`, finite-dimensional. A `ModelWithCorners` may in general have boundary, but a group manifold with `C¹` multiplication has only interior points (`ContMDiffMul.isInteriorPoint` in `TauCeti/Geometry/Lie/Interior.lean`), so no generality is hidden. Hausdorffness is not assumed because it is automatic for Lie groups (`t2Space_of_lieGroup`). `ContMDiffMonoidMorphism I I' ∞ G G'` is a monoid homomorphism (for groups, a group homomorphism) bundled with a proof that it is `C^∞`. No connectedness is assumed, and none is needed for this definition.

**The objects.** `LeftInvariantDerivation I G` is Mathlib's model of the Lie algebra 𝔤: derivations of `C^∞(G)` that commute with left translations, with bracket the commutator of derivations (verified in Mathlib's `LeftInvariantDerivation.lean`); this is the usual "left-invariant vector fields" description. `→ₗ⁅ℝ⁆` is a `LieHom`: an `ℝ`-linear map that preserves brackets.

**Which map it is.** Since this is a definition, its content is the formula, pinned by the lemma `leftInvariantDerivationLieEquivGroupLieAlgebra_lieMap` directly below it: identifying 𝔤 with the tangent space `T₁G` by evaluating a derivation at the identity (the Lie-algebra isomorphism `leftInvariantDerivationLieEquivGroupLieAlgebra`, where `T₁G` carries Mathlib's bracket of invariant vector fields), `lieMap φ` becomes `mfderiv I I' φ 1`, the differential of `φ` at the identity. So `lieMap φ = dφ_e`, as Hall defines `φ_*`. Mathlib's `mfderiv` is `0` where a map is not differentiable, but `φ` is smooth, so here it is the genuine differential. The bracket-preservation is a theorem proved inside the definition, not an assumption.

**The functor laws and naturality are separate theorems**, `lieMap_id`, `lieMap_comp` (`lieMap (ψ ∘ φ) = lieMap ψ ∘ lieMap φ`) and `map_lieExp` (`φ (exp X) = exp (lieMap φ X)`), so Voyager's announcement matches the file.

**Not vacuous.** The units of a finite-dimensional real normed algebra, e.g. `GL_n(ℝ)`, are a Lie group in Mathlib (`Instances/UnitsOfNormedAlgebra.lean`), and any smooth homomorphism between such groups, the identity included, is a valid `φ`; classically `lieMap det = tr`.

Correctly stated; compared with O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C (Theorem 91:9, Jordan splittings of a lattice on a regular quadratic space over a local field). The roadmap has no target naming it and lists no tagged Check.

**The hypotheses say "R is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser π, M a finitely generated R-module, B a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on M".** `[IsDomain R] [IsDiscreteValuationRing R]` is Mathlib's DVR: a local principal ideal domain that is not a field. `Irreducible π` is, in a DVR, exactly "π generates the maximal ideal" (`irreducible_iff_uniformizer`), so `π` is any uniformiser, e.g. `p` in `ℤ_p`. `hB : B.IsSymm` is `B x y = B y x`. `hnd : B.Nondegenerate` is Mathlib's "separating on both sides": `B x y = 0` for all `y` forces `x = 0` (and symmetrically). This is weaker than unimodularity, and is the right reading of O'Meara's "lattice on a regular space": for a free module it says the Gram determinant is nonzero, i.e. `B` is nondegenerate after tensoring with the fraction field. Nondegeneracy over a domain kills torsion (`r x = 0` with `r ≠ 0` gives `r B x y = 0`, so `x = 0`), hence `M` is free of finite rank, which the proof uses; no freeness hypothesis is needed.

**The conclusion.** `B.IsJordanSplitting π N` for a family `N : ℕ → Submodule R M` is (by its definition in the same file): `M` is the internal direct sum of the `N i` (`DirectSum.IsInternal`: the summation map `⊕ N i → M` is bijective), distinct `N i`, `N j` are orthogonal for `B`, and the restriction of `B` to `N i` is `π ^ i`-modular, where `IsModular B a` means `B = a • C` for a perfect pairing `C` (`C` induces bijections `N i ≅ (N i)^*` on both sides). So each `N i` is `π^i` times a unimodular lattice: O'Meara's `π^i`-modular component. Only nonnegative exponents occur because `B` takes values in `R`; constituents may be zero (the zero module is `a`-modular for every `a`), and only finitely many are nonzero (`IsJordanSplitting.hasFiniteSupport`). The theorem asserts existence (`∃ N`), not uniqueness; the invariance of the ranks is a separate result in the file.

**Dyadic case and generality.** No hypothesis excludes residue characteristic 2, so `R = ℤ_2` is included, where O'Meara's components need not be diagonalisable. The statement is in fact more general than O'Meara: it allows DVRs of equal characteristic 2 such as `𝔽₂[[t]]`, where symmetric bilinear forms, not quadratic forms, are the object, which is what the Lean statement is about.

**Not vacuous.** `R = ℤ_p`, `M = ℤ_p²` with Gram matrix `diag(1, p)`: `N 0 = ℤ_p e₁`, `N 1 = ℤ_p e₂`, all other `N i = 0`; or `ℤ_2` with the hyperbolic plane `[[0,1],[1,0]]`, where `N 0 = M`.

**Hypotheses.** `K` is a number field and `𝓞 K` its ring of integers; `P` is a maximal ideal of `𝓞 K` (`[P.IsMaximal]`, so `𝓞 K ⧸ P` is a finite field); `n ≥ 1` (`[NeZero n]`); and `[HasEnoughRootsOfUnity (𝓞 K) n]` says `𝓞 K` contains a primitive `n`-th root of unity and its `n`-th roots of unity form a cyclic group, the second part automatic in a domain, so this is just "`μ_n ⊂ K`". Square-bracket hypotheses are found by Lean automatically.

**The object.** `MulChar (𝓞 K ⧸ P) (𝓞 K)` is Mathlib's multiplicative character: a monoid homomorphism from the residue field to `𝓞 K` that is `0` on every non-unit, here only at `0`. So the symbol is a map on the residue field, with `(0/P)_n = 0`, as Ireland–Rosen prescribe.

**The value.** When `gcd(N P, n) = 1` — equivalent to Ireland–Rosen's `n ∉ P`, since `N P` is a power of the residue characteristic — the definition sends a unit `x` to `x^{(N P − 1)/n}`, which is an `n`-th root of unity of the residue field because `n ∣ N P − 1` (`dvd_absNorm_sub_one`), then lifts it through the inverse of reduction `μ_n(𝓞 K) ≅ μ_n(𝓞 K ⧸ P)` (`rootsOfUnityEquivQuot`, a group isomorphism under this hypothesis) and reads the result in `𝓞 K`. That is exactly "the unique `n`-th root of unity congruent to `x^{(N P−1)/n}` mod `P`", and `powerResidueSymbol_eq_iff` states that characterisation. `absNorm P` is the index of `P`, i.e. `|𝓞 K ⧸ P|`; the natural-number subtraction `N P − 1` is not truncated since `N P ≥ 2` for a maximal ideal, and the natural-number division is exact by the divisibility above, so no junk value enters.

**Outside the classical domain.** When `gcd(N P, n) ≠ 1` the symbol is the trivial character (`1` on units, `0` at `0`), by the convention the roadmap pins; every lemma describing values carries the coprimality hypothesis, so this choice is never used as a formula, Mathlib's usual style for total definitions.

**Not vacuous.** `K = ℚ`, `n = 2`, `P = (p)` with `p` odd: the symbol is the Legendre symbol `(·/p)`, read as a character of `𝔽_p` with values `±1, 0` in `ℤ`. `K = ℚ(i)`, `n = 4`, `P = (2 + i)` of norm `5`: `(i/P)_4 = i^{(5−1)/4} = i`, a genuine fourth root of unity, not a sign. `orderOf_powerResidueSymbol` confirms the character has order exactly `n`.

The literature keeps this as a standing assumption rather than a clause (Sturm states the consequences of `CD(K, ∞)` for `supp m`), and the docstring says so: a reference measure without full support is passed to `M.supportSpace`, again complete and separable. A reader should know that `m = 0` on a nonempty space fails `CD(K, ∞)` here.

**The convexity clause is Sturm's.** `WassersteinSpace 2 X` is `P₂(X)`, the laws of finite second moment, with distance `W₂` (`WassersteinSpace.dist_def`). `IsGeodesicSegment γ μ₀ μ₁` is a curve with endpoints `μ₀`, `μ₁` and `W₂(γ s, γ t) = |s - t| W₂(μ₀, μ₁)` on `[0, 1]`: a constant-speed `W₂`-geodesic; values outside `[0, 1]` are irrelevant. `ConvexAlong K φ γ` is `φ(γ t) ≤ (1 - t) φ(μ₀) + t φ(μ₁) - (K/2) t(1 - t) W₂(μ₀, μ₁)²` for `t ∈ [0, 1]`, with Sturm's `K/2`.

**The entropy and its extended values.** `boltzmannEntropy m μ` is `Ent_m(μ) ∈ [-∞, ∞]`: `+∞` unless `μ ≪ m`, otherwise `∫ ρ log ρ dm` as the integral of the positive part minus that of the negative part, `+∞` if the former diverges, `-∞` if only the latter does. Mathlib's Radon–Nikodym derivative is genuine here: `m` is σ-finite (`sigmaFinite_of_locallyFinite`), `μ` a probability. The endpoint hypotheses `≠ ⊤` are Sturm's effective domain and admit `Ent = -∞`; the inequality is read in `[-∞, ∞]` with the rules checked in Mathlib's source: a positive real times `-∞` is `-∞`, `-∞ + x = -∞`, `0 · (-∞) = 0`. So an endpoint of entropy `-∞` forces `-∞` along the open geodesic, and at `t = 0, 1` the inequality is an equality. No `+∞` can appear on the right, so no `∞ - ∞` arises.

**The input is a quasi-coherent graded 𝒪_X-algebra.** `X` is any scheme, with no Noetherian or finiteness hypothesis. `A : CommMon (GradedObject ℕ X.Modules)` is a commutative monoid object in the symmetric monoidal category of `ℕ`-graded sheaves of `𝒪_X`-modules: a family `A₀, A₁, …` of `𝒪_X`-modules with a unit `𝒪_X → A₀` and multiplications `Aᵢ ⊗ Aⱼ → Aᵢ₊ⱼ` that are associative, unital and commutative. The tensor product of graded objects in Mathlib is the Day convolution `(A ⊗ B)ₙ = ⨁_{i+j=n} Aᵢ ⊗ Bⱼ`, with unit `𝒪_X` placed in degree `0`, so this is precisely a graded `𝒪_X`-algebra. Mathlib's braiding on graded objects is the braiding of `𝒪_X`-modules degree by degree, with no Koszul sign, so "commutative" is the plain `ab = ba` of Stacks, not graded-commutativity. The bracketed hypothesis `[∀ n, IsQuasicoherent (A.X n)]` asks each homogeneous piece to be quasi-coherent in Mathlib's sense (locally a cokernel of a map between free modules), which is Stacks' "quasi-coherent graded `𝒪_S`-algebra". `A₀` need not be `𝒪_X`, and no generation in degree one is assumed, as in Stacks.

Gluing is a colimit, determined only up to isomorphism; what pins it to the classical notion is `isPullback_relativeProjCover`: the restriction of `relativeProjToBase : Proj_X(A) → X` over each affine open `U` is `Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) → U`. Stacks Lemma 27.15.4 says this property characterises the relative Proj up to unique isomorphism over `X`.

**No defaults, not vacuous.** The definition is total under its hypotheses and assigns no junk value. For `X = Spec k` and `A = k[T₀, T₁]` graded by degree, `Proj_X(A) = ℙ¹_k`; for `A = 𝒪_X` in degree zero it is empty.

**The field.** `NontriviallyNormedField K` (an instance argument, found automatically) is a field with a multiplicative absolute value that is not the trivial one (some `|x| > 1`), `IsUltrametricDist K` is the strong triangle inequality `|x + y| ≤ max(|x|, |y|)`, and `CompleteSpace K` is completeness. So `K` is any complete nonarchimedean nontrivially valued field: `ℚ_p`, `ℂ_p`, `𝔽_p((t))`. Serre assumes a discrete valuation; the statement is more general.

**The model spaces.** `I` and `J` are index sets: the pair `TopologicalSpace`/`DiscreteTopology` only says "a set", `DecidableEq J` is bookkeeping. `C₀(J, K)` is Mathlib's space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity; on a discrete set every function is continuous and "vanishing at infinity" is convergence to `0` along the cofinite filter (`Filter.cocompact_eq_cofinite`): for every `ε` only finitely many `|x_j| ≥ ε`. With the sup norm this is Serre's `c(J)`. `→L[K]` is a continuous `K`-linear map.

**Row compactness.** `matrixCoeff i j` is the `i`-th coordinate of `u(e_j)`, `rowNorm i = ⨆ j, ‖a_ij‖`, and `IsRowCompact` asks for a uniform bound on the entries together with `Tendsto rowNorm cofinite (𝓝 0)`: for every `ε`, only finitely many rows have `sup_j |a_ij| ≥ ε`, Serre's "`sup_j |a_ij| → 0` as `i → ∞`". A junk value lurks here: Mathlib's real supremum of an unbounded family is `0` (`ciSup_of_not_bddAbove`, `Real.sSup_empty`), which is why the bound is part of the definition. Over a field it is automatic, `|a_ij| ≤ ‖u‖` (`norm_matrixCoeff_le`, a nontrivially normed field being Tate), so the condition is exactly the classical one.

**Complete continuity.** `IsCompletelyContinuous` says that for every `ε > 0` there is a continuous linear `v` of finite rank (range inside a finitely generated submodule, over a field a finite-dimensional subspace) with `‖u x − v x‖ ≤ ε ‖x‖` for all `x`, that is `‖u − v‖ ≤ ε`: `u` is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators, Serre's definition.

**The conclusion.** `↔` asserts the two properties are equivalent for every bounded `u` (the braces around `u` only mean Lean infers it when the theorem is used). Not vacuous: over `ℚ_p` with `I = J = ℕ`, the diagonal operator with entries `pⁱ` has both properties, the identity has neither (`not_isRowCompact_id`, `isCompletelyContinuous_id_iff`), and for finite `I` every operator has both.

Correctly stated; compared with Le Gouic–Loubes, *Existence and consistency of Wasserstein barycenters*, Theorem 8 (the finitely supported case), Agueh–Carlier §2 for the objective, and item 3 of Layer 12 of TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport, which lists no tagged Check for it.

The exponent `p` is an extended real: `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]` is the hypothesis `1 ≤ p` passed as an instance, and `hp_top` excludes `∞`, so `1 ≤ p < ∞`. The weights are nonnegative reals summing to `1`; zero weights are allowed, and the sum forces `J` nonempty. Each `μ j` is a point of `WassersteinSpace p X`, i.e. `P_p(X)`, a probability law on `X` of finite `p`-th moment.

**The objects.** `∑ j, w j • Measure.dirac (μ j)` is the law `Σ w_j δ_{μ_j}` on `P_p(X)`, a measure on a space of measures. `IsFrechetBarycenter p Λ ν` says the `p`-Fréchet radius `(∫ d(ν, y)^p dΛ(y))^{1/p}` is finite at `ν` and no point has a smaller one; the finiteness clause only excludes the degenerate case of an identically infinite radius. The distance on `P_p(X)` is `W_p` (`WassersteinSpace.edist_def`), so the radius to the `p`-th power is `Σ w_j W_p(ν, μ_j)^p`, finite on `P_p(X)`: `isFrechetBarycenter_sum_smul_dirac_iff_isMinOn` proves the conclusion is exactly "some `ν ∈ P_p(X)` minimises `Σ w_j W_p(ν, μ_j)^p` over `P_p(X)`", the Wasserstein barycenter of the literature.

This is one reason `p ≠ ∞` is needed.

**Minimising over `P_p(X)` loses nothing.** Laws outside `P_p(X)` have infinite cost against any `μ_j` with positive weight, so a minimiser over `P_p(X)` minimises over all probability laws (`isMinOn_sum_mul_wassersteinEDist_rpow_of_isFrechetBarycenter`). `^ p.toReal` is the real exponent of the finite `p`; no division, truncation or default value occurs.

**Not vacuous.** `X = ℝ²`, `p = 2`, `μ = (δ_a, δ_b)` with weights `½, ½`: the barycenter is `δ_{(a+b)/2}`. The theorem is not a restatement of compactness of `P_p(X)`, which is not proper; the file obtains the barycenter from an optimal multi-coupling and a measurable choice of pointwise barycenters.

Correctly stated; compared with Conway, *A Course in Functional Analysis*, VIII.3.11, Reed–Simon I, Theorem VI.10, and milestone PD-B26 of TauCetiRoadmap/OperatorTheory/PolarDecomposition, which lists no tagged Check for it. The site shows no earlier review.

**Hypotheses.** `RCLike 𝕜` means `𝕜` is `ℝ` or `ℂ`. `E` and `F` are Hilbert spaces over `𝕜`: normed groups with a compatible inner product, complete. All are instance arguments, found automatically. No separability or dimension restriction; the zero space is allowed, where everything is `0`. `T` is any bounded operator `E → F`.

**The modulus.** `T.modulus` is `|T| = √(T*T)`, the square root of the continuous functional calculus. Mathlib's `CFC.sqrt` returns the junk value `0` when its argument is not a positive element, but `T*T` is positive, and `eq_modulus_iff` pins `|T|` as the unique positive operator with `|T|² = T*T`, so no junk is in play. The square root is taken for the real-algebra structure obtained by restricting scalars along `ℝ → 𝕜`; `modulus_eq_sqrt` shows any compatible choice gives the same operator.

**The polar factor is a specific operator, not "some partial isometry".** `T.polarFactor` is `T.factorThru |T|`: on the closure of the range of `|T|` it is the continuous extension of the rule `|T| x ↦ T x`, which is well defined and isometric because `‖|T| x‖ = ‖T x‖` (`norm_modulus_apply`), and it is `0` on the orthogonal complement, which is `ker T` (`orthogonal_range_modulus`). That is Conway's `W`, with initial space `(ker T)^⊥`. The general `factorThru` warns its value is unspecified without a bound `‖T x‖ ≤ C ‖A x‖`; here `C = 1` holds, so the construction is the classical one.

**The conclusion.** `∘L` is composition of bounded operators and `=` is equality of operators, so the statement is `U (|T| x) = T x` for every `x`: the polar decomposition `T = U |T|`. That `U` is a partial isometry, `ker U = ker T`, its final space is the closure of the range of `T`, and the uniqueness of `U` among operators vanishing on `ker T` are the neighbouring declarations `isPartialIsometry_polarFactor`, `ker_polarFactor`, `range_polarFactor`, `eq_polarFactor_iff`; this declaration is the factorisation itself, for that canonical `U`; this is what gives it content beyond mere existence of a factorisation.

**Not vacuous.** For `T = 0` both sides are `0` (`polarFactor_zero`). For the unilateral shift `S` on `ℓ²`, `S*S = 1`, so `|S| = 1` and `U = S`. For the rank-one `T = ⟨·, e⟩ f` with unit vectors `e, f`, `|T|` is the projection onto `e` and `U` sends `e` to `f`.

Correctly stated; compared with Fortet, *Résolution d'un système d'équations de M. Schrödinger* (1940), Nutz, *Introduction to Entropic Optimal Transport*, Theorem 2.1 (the product form of the Schrödinger density), and item 3 of Layer 13A of TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport, which lists no tagged Check for it.

**Hypotheses.** `X`, `Y` are arbitrary measurable spaces, with no topology: the bounded case needs none. `μ`, `ν` are finite measures (`IsFiniteMeasure`: total mass `< ∞`) of equal total mass, `μ univ = ν univ`, an equality in `[0, ∞]` of two finite values; they need not be probabilities. `g : X × Y → ℝ` is measurable for the product σ-algebra and bounded everywhere by `M` (`|g z| ≤ M` for all `z`, not merely almost everywhere); if `M < 0` the hypothesis is unsatisfiable on a nonempty product, so nothing is claimed. Compared with Nutz, `g = -c/ε` for a bounded cost `c` and temperature `ε`.

**What is asserted.** There are measurable potentials `φ` on `X` and `ψ` on `Y`, bounded by a common constant `C`, such that the measure `π` on `X × Y` with density `exp(φ(x) + ψ(y) + g(x, y))` against the product measure `μ ⊗ ν` is a coupling of `μ` and `ν`. `Measure.prod` is the product measure, `withDensity f` the measure `s ↦ ∫_s f d(μ ⊗ ν)`, and `IsCoupling π μ ν` says the pushforwards of `π` under the two projections (`Measure.fst`, `Measure.snd`) are `μ` and `ν`. The density is given in `[0, ∞]` as `ENNReal.ofReal (exp …)`; `ofReal` sends negatives to `0`, but `exp > 0`, so it is the honest value. So `P` is exactly a Sinkhorn–Knopp scaling of `K` with marginals `(a, b)`; equal total mass is not assumed separately because it follows (`HasMarginals.sum_eq`). `u₀ > 0` is the arbitrary starting row vector.

**The iteration.** `sinkhornStep K a b u = a / (K (b / (Kᵀ u)))`, a column update followed by a row update (the file's [definition](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Data/Matrix/Sinkhorn/Basic.lean#L163)); `f^[n]` is the `n`-fold iterate (`f^[0] = id`). `sinkhornPlan K a b u` is the matrix `(step u)_i · K i j · (b / Kᵀu)_j`, the scaled matrix after a full sweep, whose row sums are exactly `a`. This is Peyré–Cuturi's iteration `u ← a/(Kv)`, `v ← b/(Kᵀu)`, paired so each plan is row-normalised; starting from row factors rather than `v⁽⁰⁾ = 𝟙` changes nothing, since any positive start is allowed.

**Conclusion.** `Filter.Tendsto (…) atTop (𝓝 P)` says the plans `Pₙ → P` as `n → ∞`. Mathlib's topology on `Matrix ι κ ℝ` is the product topology on `ι → κ → ℝ` (Mathlib, `Topology/Instances/Matrix.lean`), i.e. entrywise convergence, which for a finite matrix is convergence in any norm. The open Codex "problem" concerns how the operator was described; at the site's commit the docstring and `HeckeSlash/Operators.lean` say exactly what `heckeTCuspNat` is, and the statement is read below on that footing.

**Hypotheses.** `[NeZero N]` and `[NeZero n]`: the level and the index are positive (`n = 0` would make `diag(1, n)` collapse to the junk value `1`, hence the guard). `Nat.Coprime n N` is `gcd(n, N) = 1`. `k` is any integer weight; `f, g` are cusp forms of weight `k` for `Γ₁(N)` (bottom row `≡ (0, 1) mod N`), written as its image in `GL₂(ℝ)` because Mathlib indexes forms by real matrix groups.

**The operator.** `heckeTCuspNat k n` is the slash operator of the single double coset `Γ₁(N)·diag(1, n)·Γ₁(N)` on `S_k(Γ₁(N))`, with Mathlib's normalisation `(f ∣[k] γ)(τ) = (det γ)^{k−1}(cτ+d)^{−k} f(γτ)`, Diamond–Shurman's. For `n` coprime to `N` this is their `Tₙ` exactly when `n` is squarefree (every prime, in particular); at `n = p²` the classical `T_{p²}` exceeds it by `p^{k−2}⟨p⟩`, and the classical operator at every `n` lives elsewhere (`heckeTCompositeGamma0`). So the theorem is Diamond–Shurman 5.5.3 for squarefree `n` prime to `N`, and for all other `n` it is Shimura's adjoint formula for the one double coset: the adjoint of `[Γ₁(N)·α·Γ₁(N)]` is `[Γ₁(N)·α'·Γ₁(N)]` with `α' = n·α⁻¹ = diag(n, 1)`, and `Γ₁(N)·diag(n, 1)·Γ₁(N)` is `⟨n⟩⁻¹` composed with `Γ₁(N)·diag(1, n)·Γ₁(N)` (`trace_translate_adjugateGL_natDiagGL_eq_diamondOpCusp_heckeTCuspNat`).

**The diamond.** `ZMod.unitOfCoprime n hn` is the class of `n` in `(ℤ/N)ˣ`; the `⁻¹` inverts that unit, and `diamondOpCusp k d` is `⟨d⟩`, slashing by any element of `Γ₀(N)` with lower-right entry `≡ d` (`coe_diamondOpCusp`). Since `d ↦ ⟨d⟩` is a homomorphism, `⟨n⁻¹⟩ = ⟨n⟩⁻¹`, as in the source.

**The pairing.** `CuspForm.peterssonInnerCosets f g` is `∑_{γ ∈ Γ₁(N){±1}\SL₂(ℤ)} ∫_𝒟 \overline{(f∣γ⁻¹)} (g∣γ⁻¹) y^k dμ` over Mathlib's standard fundamental domain `𝒟`, i.e. the Petersson integral over a fundamental domain of `Γ₁(N)` (Petersson/FiniteIndex.lean). Two conventions differ harmlessly from Diamond–Shurman: there is no `1/V_Γ` factor, and the conjugate sits on the first argument rather than the second; a scalar and complex conjugation of both sides leave the adjoint relation `⟪Tf, g⟫ = ⟪f, T*g⟫` unchanged.

**Not vacuous.** `N = 1`, `n = 2`, `k = 12`, `f = g = Δ`: `⟨2⟩` is the identity at level one and the statement is the self-adjointness `⟪T₂Δ, Δ⟫ = ⟪Δ, T₂Δ⟫`; at `N = 5`, `n = 2`, the inverse diamond is `⟨3⟩`.

**It is a construction whose content is pinned by its neighbours.** An `abbrev` only names the general filtered-complex spectral sequence applied to the row filtration; what makes it the spectral sequence of the bicomplex are the isomorphisms proved beside it: the first page is the homology of the rows ([L426](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L426)), the abutment in degree `-n` is `H_n` of the total complex ([L476](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L476)), and each position stabilises after finitely many pages to the corresponding graded piece of the abutment ([L497](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L497)), which is what "converges" means for a filtration finite in each degree.

**Hypotheses.** `[Abelian C]` is the abelian category. `HomologicalComplex₂ C (down ℕ) (down ℕ)` is a chain complex of chain complexes indexed by `ℕ × ℕ`, so "first quadrant" is built into the index type and both differentials lower degree. Mathlib's bicomplexes have commuting differentials; the sign sits in the total differential `d₁ + (-1)^p d₂` (the `TotalComplexShape` instance of `ComplexShapeSigns`), which is Weibel's anticommuting convention after changing the sign of the vertical differential on alternate columns, so the total complex and its homology are the classical ones.

**Indexing.** Row `q` is `⋯ → (K.X 1).X q → (K.X 0).X q` with the horizontal differentials. `rowFiltration q` is the subcomplex spanned by the rows `< q`, zero for `q ≤ 0` ([L366](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L366)) and increasing. Mathlib's `coreE₂Cohomological` numbers the first page `2` and is cohomological: the total complex is read with chain degree `n` in cochain degree `-n`, and the shape `up' (r, 1 - r)` in the type says `d_r` goes from `(p, q)` to `(p + r, q - r + 1)`. Translating, the object at `(p, q)` is `H_k(row q)` with `p + 2q + k = 0`, and `d_2` lowers the row by one keeping `k`: it is the map induced on horizontal homology by the vertical differential, Weibel's `d¹` on `E¹ = H^h(rows)`; page `r` here is Weibel's `E^{r-1}`. Rows `q < 0` and positions with `p + 2q > 0` carry zero ([L454](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L454), [L465](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/SpectralSequence/Bicomplex.lean#L465)), the first-quadrant support.

**No junk, not vacuous.** No value is supplied by a default: every term is a kernel, cokernel or homology object. The tensor product double complex of two projective resolutions, whose row spectral sequence Weibel uses in §5.6 to balance Tor, satisfies every hypothesis; a bicomplex with one nonzero row collapses to `E_2 = H(row 0) = H(Tot)`.

Mathlib derives from this that the valuation is discrete and the residue field `𝓀[K]` (the signature shows it unfolded as the residue field of the valuation ring) is finite; so `ringChar 𝓀[K]` is the residue characteristic, a prime `p`. Finite extensions of `ℚ_p` and `𝔽_q((t))` are instances; nothing is vacuous.

**The left side is `I_K/P_K`.** `Field.absoluteGaloisGroup K` is the automorphism group of Mathlib's `AlgebraicClosure K` over `K`, with the Krull topology (`krullTopology`). `inertiaSubgroup K` is the subgroup fixing the maximal unramified subextension, `wildInertiaSubgroup K` the subgroup fixing the maximal tame subextension `K^t`, defined by adjoining all `m`-th roots of nonzero elements of `K` for `p ∤ m` (which equals `K^ur(π^{1/m})`, `maximalTameExtension_eq_sup_adjoin`). `(wildInertiaSubgroup K).subgroupOf (inertiaSubgroup K)` is `P_K ∩ I_K` viewed as a subgroup of `I_K`; since `P_K ≤ I_K` (`wildInertiaSubgroup_le_inertiaSubgroup`) the quotient `⧸` is literally `I_K/P_K`, and Mathlib's instance `QuotientGroup.instTopologicalSpace` gives it the quotient topology. **The right side is `Ẑ^{(p')}(1)`.** `PrimeToPTateModule p E` is, for any commutative monoid `E`, the set of families `(ζ_m)` with `ζ_m` an `m`-th root of unity of `E`, indexed by `m ≠ 0` coprime to `p`, satisfying `ζ_m^{m/n} = ζ_n` whenever `n ∣ m`; the natural-number division `m / n` is exact there, so no truncation occurs. Its topology is induced from the product of the discrete levels, the inverse-limit topology, and for a field each level is finite, so it is profinite. Over `AlgebraicClosure K` with `p` the residue characteristic this is `lim_{p∤m} μ_m = Ẑ^{(p')}(1)`; prime-to-`p` roots of unity are separable, so using the algebraic rather than separable closure changes nothing.

The roadmap lists no tagged Check for it; its acceptance instantiations are already recorded in the Codex review. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses are exactly "a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field".** `[Field K]` is a commutative field of any characteristic (Lean's `Field` is nontrivial, so `K ≠ 0`); its convention `0⁻¹ = 0` plays no role since the statement contains no division. `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]` say `L` is a `K`-vector space with a bilinear bracket satisfying `[x,x] = 0` and the Jacobi identity; the axiom is `[x,x] = 0`, not mere antisymmetry, so characteristic 2 is handled in the correct way. `[FiniteDimensional K L]` is `Module.Finite K L`, "finitely generated as a `K`-module", which over a field is finite-dimensionality; no `finrank` (which would read `0` in infinite dimension) appears.

**What is asserted to exist.** The conclusion is an existential over a type `V` together with its additive group structure, `K`-vector-space structure and a finite-dimensionality proof: the representation space is part of what is asserted, as in the classical statement. `Module.End K V` is the space of `K`-linear maps `V → V`, and its Lie bracket here is the commutator `ST − TS`: the file installs Mathlib's `LieRing.ofAssociativeRing`, whose bracket is `x * y − y * x` by definition ([`of_associative_ring_bracket`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Algebra/Lie/OfAssociative.lean)). So `ρ : L →ₗ⁅K⁆ Module.End K V` is a `K`-linear map with `ρ[x,y] = ρx ρy − ρy ρx`, i.e. a representation of `L` on `V`, and `Function.Injective ρ` (equal images force equal arguments) is faithfulness: for a linear map this is `ker ρ = 0`. Nothing bounds `dim V`, and nothing is constructed: the theorem is a proposition, so no choice is being made.

**Universe bookkeeping.** `V` lives in `Type (max u v)` where the roadmap wrote `Type u`; a universe large enough to hold both `K` and `L` is the natural home of a space built from them, and the mathematical content is identical.

**Not vacuous, and not the adjoint representation in disguise.** The 3-dimensional Heisenberg algebra over any field, say `𝔽₂`, satisfies every hypothesis and has a one-dimensional centre, so `ad` is not faithful; the theorem still promises a faithful finite-dimensional representation (the strictly upper triangular `3 × 3` matrices give one). The zero Lie algebra is allowed and is trivially covered.

The right side says there is a matrix `Q` with nonnegative entries, with `Q i j = 0 ↔ K i j = 0`, that is with exactly the zero pattern of `K`, and with `HasMarginals Q a b`, which by its definition ([Basic.lean#L148](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Data/Matrix/Scaling/Basic.lean#L148)) is just the two equations "row sums `a`, column sums `b`". `↔` is logical equivalence.

**Hypotheses.** The only one is `0 ≤ K i j` for all entries. There is deliberately none on `a` and `b`: on either side the matrix in question is nonnegative, so `a ≥ 0`, `b ≥ 0`, and the total mass identity `∑ a_i = ∑ b_j` is automatic (`HasMarginals.sum_eq`). Left to right is immediate, since a scaling by positive factors vanishes exactly where `K` does; the content is the converse, and "exactly" matters, as the example below shows.

**Edge cases.** For `K = 0` both sides say `a = 0` and `b = 0`; a zero row of `K` forces `a_i = 0` on both sides; for empty `ι` both sides reduce to `b = 0`. No division or limit occurs in the statement.

**Not vacuous.** With `K = !![1, 1; 0, 1]` and `a = b = (1, 1)`, the only nonnegative matrix with these marginals vanishing at the `(1, 0)` entry is the identity, which also vanishes at `(0, 1)` where `K` does not, so neither side holds: `K` has no such scaling (the file header's example). With `K` the identity and the same marginals, `Q = K` and `u = v = (1, 1)` witness both sides. For strictly positive `K` and positive marginals of equal mass, `Q_ij = a_i b_j / ∑ a` witnesses the right side, giving Sinkhorn's theorem `Matrix.exists_sinkhorn_scaling`.

Mathlib's matrix inverse is `0` on singular matrices (`nonsing_inv_apply_not_isUnit`), but `S₂₂` is positive definite, hence invertible, so `S₂₂⁻¹` is the true inverse.

This is exactly the right notion: a regular conditional distribution is only determined up to a null set of conditioning values, so a pointwise equality would be meaningless, and a.e. equality under the law of `X₂` is how Anderson's "the conditional distribution of `X₁` given `X₂ = x₂` is `N(…)`" is made precise.

**Which volume.** `volume` on the right is the volume of `V` itself, not of `ℝ^ι`. `V` inherits an inner product (`Submodule.innerProductSpace`), is finite-dimensional, and carries the Borel σ-algebra of the subspace (`Subtype.borelSpace`); on such a space Mathlib's `volume` (`measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace`) is the Haar measure in which the parallelepiped spanned by an orthonormal basis has volume one (`Basis.addHaar_self`), that is, the intrinsic `k`-dimensional Lebesgue measure. On `ℝ` this agrees with the usual Lebesgue measure, so for `V = ℝ^ι` the right side is `2^{#ι}`, the volume of the cube.

**Edge cases, not vacuous.** For `V = 0` the section is `{0}`, of volume one in the zero-dimensional space, and the statement is `1 ≤ 1`. For the diagonal line in `ℝ²` the section is a segment of length `2√2 ≥ 2`, and for a coordinate `k`-plane it is a `k`-cube of volume exactly `2^k`, showing the constant is sharp.
