**The operator and its resolvent.** `X →ₗ.[ℝ] X` is a linear map defined on a subspace `A.domain` of the real Banach space `X` (Mathlib's `LinearPMap`), an unbounded operator with its domain. `A.resolventSet` is Tau Ceti's resolvent set for such operators (Mathlib's is only for elements of a Banach algebra): `λ` belongs to it when `λI − A : D(A) → X` has a bounded two-sided inverse (`IsResolventAt`), and `A.resolvent λ` is that inverse, which is unique (`IsResolventAt.unique`). Off the resolvent set `A.resolvent λ` is an unspecified bounded operator, but the theorem never looks there: `hpow` only speaks of `λ > ω`, and `hres` puts every such `λ` in the resolvent set. `A.resolvent λ ^ n` is the `n`-th power in the algebra of bounded operators, so `‖A.resolvent λ ^ n‖ ≤ M / (λ − ω) ^ n` is exactly `‖R(λ,A)ⁿ‖ ≤ M/(λ−ω)ⁿ`; the division is a genuine real division since `λ − ω > 0`, and `n ≥ 1` excludes the power `0`. `Dense ↑A.domain` is Mathlib's `Dense`: the closure of the domain is all of `X`.

**The conclusion.** `StronglyContinuousSemigroup X` is a structure: operators `S(t)`, `t ∈ ℝ≥0`, with `S(0) = I`, `S(s+t) = S(s)S(t)` and each orbit `t ↦ S(t)x` continuous at `0`; on a Banach space that is the C₀ condition (Engel–Nagel Prop. I.5.3). `S.generator` is `x ↦ lim_{t→0⁺}(S(t)x − x)/t` on the subspace where the limit exists; the limit is unique, so Lean's choice of it is the limit. `S.HasGrowthBound ω M` unfolds to `1 ≤ M` and `‖S.realOperator t‖ ≤ M e^{ωt}` for all `t ≥ 0`, where `realOperator t` is `S(t)` for `t ≥ 0` (its value for negative `t`, the identity, is never quantified over). So the conclusion is: some C₀-semigroup with `‖S(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt}` has `A`, domain included, as its generator.

**Generality.** `ω` is any real number, negative included, and `M ≥ 1` any real; `X` may be the zero space, where everything holds trivially.

**Not vacuous.** `X = ℝ`, `A x = a x` on all of `ℝ`: every `λ > a` is a resolvent point with `R(λ) = 1/(λ − a)`, so `hpow` holds with `M = 1`, `ω = a`, and the theorem produces a semigroup with generator `a`, necessarily `S(t) = e^{at}`, with `|S(t)| ≤ e^{at}`.

**The hypotheses.** `K` is a field complete for a multiplicative nonarchimedean absolute value (`NormedField`, `IsUltrametricDist`, `CompleteSpace`), possibly trivially valued. `A` is any commutative `K`-algebra, and `IsAffinoidAlgebra K A` says some `K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩ → A` is a surjective `K`-algebra homomorphism, with no norm or topology on `A`; that is BGR's definition 6.1.1/1. No nontriviality is asked and none is needed: the zero ring is affinoid (quotient by the unit ideal) and is Jacobson, its only ideal being the unit ideal.

**The conclusion.** Mathlib's `IsJacobsonRing A` says that for every radical ideal `I`, `I.jacobson = I`, where `Ideal.jacobson I` is the intersection (`sInf`) of the maximal ideals containing `I`. Mathlib's `Ideal.IsMaximal` excludes the unit ideal, and for `I = ⊤` the intersection is empty, hence `⊤`, so the edge case is consistent. By Mathlib's `isJacobsonRing_iff_prime_eq` this is the same as "every prime ideal is the intersection of the maximal ideals containing it", which is the docstring's and BGR's formulation; the two agree because a radical ideal is the intersection of the primes containing it.

**Why it has content.** The affinoid hypothesis is the whole point: the formal power series ring `K[[X]]` is local with the non-maximal prime `(0)`, so it is not Jacobson, while `K⟨X⟩` is, its maximal ideals being the points of the closed unit disc over finite extensions of `K`. The input is `TauCeti.MvPowerSeries.isJacobsonRing` for `Tₙ`; the descent to quotients is Mathlib's `isJacobsonRing_of_surjective`, so no further hypothesis (reducedness, a norm, a domain) is needed or present.

**Trivial absolute value.** Then `K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩ = K[X₁,…,Xₙ]`, affinoid algebras are the finitely generated `K`-algebras, and the statement specialises to the classical fact that these are Jacobson (Mathlib's `isJacobsonRing_MvPolynomial_fin` and quotients), so the extra generality is harmless.

**Not vacuous.** `A = ℚ_p⟨X⟩`, where the zero ideal is the intersection of the maximal ideals, one for each point of the closed unit disc over a finite extension; `A = ℚ_p⟨X⟩/(X² − p)`, a field; the nonreduced `K⟨X⟩/(X²)`, Artinian local, hence Jacobson, showing nilpotents are allowed.

What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses.** `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: `K` is a field of characteristic zero, not assumed algebraically closed. `sl (Fin 2) K` is Mathlib's `sl₂(K)`, the trace-zero `2 × 2` matrices with the commutator bracket. The instance arguments `AddCommGroup`, `Module K`, `LieRingModule`, `LieModule` together say that `M` is a representation of `sl₂(K)` on a `K`-vector space, and `FiniteDimensional K M` that it is finite-dimensional. `LieModule.IsIrreducible` is Mathlib's `IsSimpleOrder` on the lattice of `sl₂`-stable subspaces: `M ≠ 0` and its only stable subspaces are `0` and `M`. `IsTriangularizable K sl₂ M` says that for every `x ∈ sl₂` the generalized eigenspaces of `x` on `M` span `M`, i.e. every `x` acts with split characteristic polynomial. Over an algebraically closed field this holds for every finite-dimensional module (Mathlib's `instIsTriangularizableOfIsAlgClosed`), so over `ℂ` the statement is exactly Humphreys'.

**The right-hand side.** `Sl2Std K n` is `V(n)` ([Standard.lean#L180](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Lie/Sl2/Standard.lean#L180)): the coordinate space `K^{n+1}` with basis `v₀, …, vₙ` and the ladder action `e·vᵢ = i·vᵢ₋₁`, `f·vᵢ = (n − i)·vᵢ₊₁`, `h·vᵢ = (n − 2i)·vᵢ` for the standard triple `e = E₀₁`, `f = E₁₀`, `h = E₀₀ − E₁₁`. So `v₀` is a highest weight vector of weight `n`, the weights are `n, n − 2, …, −n`, and `dim V(n) = n + 1`. This differs from Humphreys' normalisation `vᵢ = fⁱv₀/i!` only by rescaling the basis, so it is the same module.

**The conclusion.** `∃! n : ℕ, Nonempty (M ≃ₗ⁅K,sl₂⁆ Sl2Std K n)` reads: there is exactly one natural number `n` for which there exists a `K`-linear bijection `M → V(n)` commuting with the `sl₂`-action. `Nonempty` asserts the existence of such an isomorphism without choosing one, which is what a classification says; uniqueness of `n` is forced by dimension. No junk value is in play: `n` ranges over all naturals, `n = 0` giving the trivial module `V(0) = K`.

**Not vacuous.** `K = ℂ`, `M = ℂ²` with matrices acting on column vectors satisfies every hypothesis (triangularizable because `ℂ` is algebraically closed; irreducible because no line is stable under both `e` and `f`), and the theorem returns `n = 1`.

Correctly stated; compared with the file header's account of Turaev §1 and Milnor §3 and with target N4 of TauCetiRoadmap/MorseNovikov, which lists no tagged Check for it. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The input.** `ChainComplex (ModuleCat F) ℤ` is a `ℤ`-graded chain complex of `F`-vector spaces, differential `d : C_{i+1} → C_i` (Mathlib keeps a map `d i j` for every pair, zero unless `i = j + 1`). `c i : Basis (Fin (n i)) F (C.X i)` is an ordered basis of `C_i` indexed by `{0, …, n i − 1}`, so each term is finite-dimensional of dimension `n i`, and the dimension function `n` is read off from the bases (it is an implicit argument). Nothing requires the complex to be bounded a priori; boundedness is tested inside the definition as "`n i ≠ 0` for only finitely many `i`", which for finite-dimensional terms is exactly "`C_i = 0` outside finitely many degrees". `C.Acyclic` is Mathlib's "exact at every degree", i.e. all homology vanishes.

**The value.** On a bounded acyclic complex it is the alternating product of brackets. The bracket in degree `j+1` is `det` in the basis `c (j+1)` of the family "basis of `B_{j+1} = im d` followed by lifts through `d` of a basis of `B_j`", which is a basis because `0 → B_{j+1} → C_{j+1} → B_j → 0` is exact (`torsionBracket_eq_det_append`; Mathlib's `Basis.det` is the determinant of the coordinate matrix, by `det_apply`). The auxiliary bases and lifts are picked by the axiom of choice (`finBasis`, `surjInv`), which is harmless because `reidemeisterTorsion_eq_finprod` shows any bases and lifts give the same product. The exponent is `(−1)^j` for the bracket of degree `j+1`, with `x ^ (−1 : ℤ) = x⁻¹`; since every bracket is a nonzero determinant (`torsionBracket_ne_zero`), the field convention `0⁻¹ = 0` never enters.

**Sign convention.** Walk through `F --a--> F` in degrees `1, 0`, bases `1`, `a ≠ 0`: `B_0 = F` with basis `a`, lift `1`; `B_1 = 0`. The degree-`0` bracket is `det(a) = a` with exponent `(−1)^{−1} = −1`; the degree-`1` bracket is `det(1) = 1`. So `τ = a⁻¹`, which is Turaev's normalization and the one N4 fixes. Milnor's exponent is `(−1)^i` on the degree-`i` bracket, the inverse; conventions in the literature differ by this inversion and the header says which is used.

**Outside the classical domain.** `∏ᶠ` is Mathlib's product over a finite support, `1` if the support is infinite; the definition never reaches that fallback, because the `if` returns `0` when the complex is unbounded or not acyclic. So `0` is the only junk value, deliberately, and `reidemeisterTorsion_eq_zero_iff` makes it the detector of non-acyclicity for bounded complexes. Only the chain bases are genuine inputs: this is based torsion, changing basis multiplies it by alternating determinants (`reidemeisterTorsion_eq_mul_finprod_det`).

**What a `Basis` is in Mathlib.** `Basis (ι →₀ ℕ) R U` is not a family of vectors that happen to be independent and spanning; it is a chosen `R`-linear bijection between `U(L)` and the free module on the index set (its `repr` field, in `Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Basis/Defs.lean`). So a term of this type is at once the statement "these elements are linearly independent and span `U(L)` over `R`" and the coordinate isomorphism. Here it is built by `Basis.mk` from a linear-independence proof and a spanning proof, and `Basis.mk_apply` guarantees the basis vector at `n` is the intended element, not some re-chosen one: by `pbwBasis_eq_prod_pow` it is `∏ ι(b i)^{n i}`, the product taken over the support of `n` in increasing order of `ι`, and `pbwBasis_zero` gives the empty product `1`.

**Indices and the order.** `ι →₀ ℕ` is the set of exponent vectors `n : ι → ℕ` with finitely many nonzero entries, exactly the multi-indices of ordered monomials `x_{i₁}^{n₁}⋯x_{i_r}^{n_r}` with `i₁ < ⋯ < i_r`; it needs no finiteness of `ι`. `[LinearOrder ι]` is a total order on the index set, the choice Humphreys makes once and for all; it is a hypothesis (any set admits one), and a different order gives a different, equally valid, basis.

**The objects.** `UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra R L` is Mathlib's quotient of the tensor algebra by the relation `xy − yx = [x, y]` for `x, y ∈ L` (`Rel.lie_compat`, written additively so as to use only the semiring structure), the standard `U(L)`; `ι` is the canonical map `L → U(L)`. `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra R L]` is a Lie algebra over `R` with the strong axiom `[x, x] = 0`, as in Bourbaki, so no characteristic restriction is smuggled in. `b : Basis ι R L` is the hypothesis "`L` is free as an `R`-module, with a chosen basis", which is what PBW over a commutative ring needs (Bourbaki states it for `L` free). The ring is any commutative ring, zero ring included; the conclusion is then the correct (degenerate) one, since all modules over it are zero.

**Not vacuous and no junk.** Take `R = ℤ` and `L = sl₂(ℤ)` with basis `e < h < f`: the statement says `e^a h^b f^c` is a `ℤ`-basis of `U(sl₂(ℤ))`. There is no division, cardinality or truncated subtraction anywhere; the only arithmetic is natural-number exponents.

**Dictionary.** Tau Ceti treats an affine group scheme over `R` through its coordinate ring: an object `H` of `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat R` is a commutative Hopf algebra that is finitely generated as an `R`-algebra, that is `G = Spec H` is an affine group scheme of finite type over `Spec R`. `MonoidAlgebra R X` is the group algebra `R[X]` of the abelian group `X` (written multiplicatively, `[CommGroup X]`), with Mathlib's Hopf structure `x ↦ x ⊗ x`; its spectrum is the diagonalizable group `D(X)`, and `X` may be any abelian group, finitely generated or not, so tori, `μ_n` and their products are covered. A bialgebra map `π : H →ₐc[R] R[X]` is the comorphism of a homomorphism `D(X) → G` (coordinate rings pull back). A Hopf ideal is an ideal `I` with `Δ(I) ⊆ I ⊗ H + H ⊗ I`, `ε(I) = 0`, `S(I) ⊆ I`, that is exactly a closed subgroup scheme `Spec (H/I)`; `quotient H I` is `H/I` as a finite-type Hopf algebra.

**Which subgroup.** `centralizerHopfIdeal π` is the ideal spanned by the coefficients of the conjugation defect `(g, t) ↦ g π(t) g⁻¹ − π(t)` written in `H ⊗ R[X]`. Its universal property, `centralizerHopfIdeal_le_ker_iff`, says an `A`-point of `G` factors through `Spec (H/I)` exactly when it commutes with every point of `D(X)` after every base change of `A`; this is the scheme-theoretic centralizer `Z_G(D(X))` of SGA 3, and `π` need not be injective.

**What "smooth" asserts.** `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty R` is, by `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty_iff`, Mathlib's `Algebra.Smooth R (H/I)`: formally smooth plus finitely presented. The hypothesis `[Algebra.Smooth R H]` says `G` is smooth, and `[IsNoetherianRing R]` is used only so that "finite type" implies "finitely presented"; the formally smooth part of the conclusion is proved in the same file for any formally smooth `H` over any commutative ring, with no finite-type, field, connectedness or reductivity assumption (`formallySmooth_quotient_centralizerHopfIdeal`).

**Not vacuous.** `G = SL₂` over `ℚ`, `X = ℤ`, `π` the comorphism of `t ↦ diag(t, t⁻¹)`: the centralizer is the diagonal torus, smooth as the theorem says. The trivial group `X = 1` gives `I = 0` and recovers `G` itself.

Correctly stated; compared with Fulton–Harris §11.2 and Humphreys §22 (Clebsch–Gordan: `V(m) ⊗ V(n) ≅ V(m+n) ⊕ V(m+n−2) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ V(|m−n|)`, each summand once) and with the "Clebsch-Gordan" item of Layer 0 in `TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/LieHighestWeight/README.md`, which lists no tagged Check for it. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses.** `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: a field of characteristic zero, with no algebraic closure assumed. `m n : ℕ` are arbitrary, `0` included.

**The objects.** `Sl2Std K m ⊗[K] Sl2Std K n` is `V(m) ⊗_K V(n)` with Mathlib's action of a Lie algebra on a tensor product, the Leibniz rule `x·(a ⊗ b) = (x·a) ⊗ b + a ⊗ (x·b)` (`TensorProduct.LieModule.lie_tmul_right`), the classical tensor product of representations. The index `k : Fin (min m n + 1)` runs over `0, 1, …, min(m, n)`. `cgSummand K m n k` ([ClebschGordan.lean#L220](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Lie/Sl2/ClebschGordan.lean#L220)) is the `sl₂`-submodule generated by the explicit vector `w_k = ∑_{j ≤ k} (−1)^j C(k, j) · v_{k−j} ⊗ u_j`, where `vᵢ`, `uⱼ` are the coordinate bases of `V(m)`, `V(n)` ([`cgVector`, #L100](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Lie/Sl2/ClebschGordan.lean#L100)); the `↑` in the signature views it as a mere subspace.

**The conclusion.** `DirectSum.IsInternal A`, for subspaces `A_k` of a vector space `V`, means that the canonical map `⨁_k A_k → V`, `(a_k) ↦ ∑_k a_k`, is bijective (Mathlib, `Mathlib/Algebra/DirectSum/Basic.lean`): the `A_k` are independent and span `V`. Since every `A_k` is `sl₂`-stable this is a decomposition of representations, and the companion theorem `nonempty_lieModuleEquiv_cgSummand` in the same file identifies the `k`-th piece with `V(m + n − 2k)`. Together they are the Clebsch–Gordan rule; the weights descend from `m + n` to `m + n − 2 min(m, n) = |m − n|`, the classical list.

**Conventions that do not bite.** The natural-number subtraction in `m + n − 2k` is never truncated, since `k ≤ min(m, n)` gives `2k ≤ m + n`. `basisVector K m (k − j)` is the `(k − j)`-th coordinate vector, extended by zero past index `m`, but with `j ≤ k ≤ m` the index is genuine. The binomial `C(k, j)` has `j ≤ k`, so Mathlib's `choose = 0` convention is never reached, and the coefficient `(−1)^j C(k, j)` cast into `K` is nonzero in characteristic zero.

**Not vacuous.** For `m = n = 1` over `ℚ`: `w₀ = v₀ ⊗ u₀` generates the symmetric square, a copy of `V(2)`, and `w₁ = v₁ ⊗ u₀ − v₀ ⊗ u₁` spans the antisymmetric line, a copy of `V(0)`; the theorem says `V(1) ⊗ V(1)` is their direct sum.

Correctly stated; compared with Fulton, *Introduction to Toric Varieties* §2.4 (and Cox–Little–Schenck, Theorem 3.4.1) and with Layer 5, item 4 of TauCetiRoadmap/AnalyticToricGeometry, which lists no tagged Check for it.

**What a `Fan i` is.** The data `i : N →+ V` with the field `lattice` of the structure is a lattice `N ≅ ℤⁿ` sitting inside `V = N ⊗ ℝ ≅ ℝⁿ` (`IsIntegralLattice`: `N` free and finitely generated over `ℤ`, `V` its base change to `ℝ`). A fan is a *finite* set of strongly convex rational polyhedral cones in `V` (`IsToricCone`: generated by finitely many lattice vectors and containing no line), closed under faces, any two meeting in a common face. Finiteness is part of the definition. `Φ.IsRegular` says each cone is smooth: its primitive ray generators extend to a `ℤ`-basis of `N`. `Nonempty Φ.cones` says the fan has at least one cone; closure under faces then forces the zero cone in, so this is exactly "not the empty fan".

**The left side.** `Φ.analyticRealization hΦ` is the topological space glued from the charts `U_σ = Hom_{ℂ-alg}(ℂ[S_σ], ℂ)`, `S_σ = σ^∨ ∩ M` the dual semigroup, each carrying the topology induced by evaluating at a finite generating set of monomials, i.e. the subspace topology from `ℂ^r`, which is independent of the generators chosen; charts are glued along `U_{σ∩τ}`. This is `X_Σ(ℂ)` with its classical topology. The `↑` turns the `TopCat` object into its underlying set. `CompactSpace` is Mathlib's "every open cover of the whole space has a finite subcover" and does not build in Hausdorffness; nothing is lost, since the realization is Hausdorff by the instance `t2Space_analyticRealization`, so the statement is compactness in the usual sense.

**The right side.** `Φ.IsComplete` is `support = univ`, the union of the cones being all of `V`.

**The nonemptiness hypothesis is genuinely needed, and the statement records it correctly.** The empty fan has empty, hence compact, realization (`isEmpty_analyticRealization_iff`) and empty support, so it is not complete; the roadmap's edge-case list names this case explicitly, and the sibling `compactSpace_analyticRealization_iff_isEmpty_or_isComplete` gives the unconditional form.

**Not vacuous.** The fan of `ℙ¹` (`projectiveLineFan`, proved regular and complete in `Algebraic/Examples/ProjectiveLine.lean`) satisfies every hypothesis and its realization is the Riemann sphere; the fan of a single smooth cone gives `ℂⁿ`, non-compact and non-complete, so both directions have content.

**Generality.** The theorem is stated for smooth fans only (so that the analytic realization exists as defined here); the classical statement holds for all fans, and the roadmap restricts to smooth fans by design.

**Hypotheses.** `[Field K]` and `[Invertible 2]`: the latter is an instance argument recording an inverse of `2` in `K`, so it is exactly "characteristic not 2" and is found automatically. `q : RegularFormClass K` is an isometry class of diagonal presentations `⟨a₁,…,aₙ⟩` (`aᵢ ∈ K^×`); with `2` invertible every regular quadratic form on a finite-dimensional space is diagonalisable, so this is the set of isometry classes of nondegenerate forms, rank `0` included.

**The two sides.** `q.hasseInvariant ∈ Br(K)` is `∏_{i<j} [(aᵢ,aⱼ)]`, where `(a,b)` is Mathlib's quaternion algebra `ℍ[K,a,b]` with `i² = a`, `j² = b`, `ij = −ji` (Mathlib, `Algebra/Quaternion.lean`): this is Lam's `s(q)`, not the Clifford invariant. It is well defined on the class by Witt's chain-equivalence theorem. `⟨q.hasseInvariant, ⋯⟩` packages it as an element of the subgroup `Br(K)[2]` (the kernel of squaring), the `⋯` being the proof `hasseInvariant_sq` that `s(q)² = 1`; `Additive.ofMul` only switches notation from multiplicative to additive so the group isomorphism can be written with `+`. `sw2Class q = ∑_{i<j} (aᵢ) ∪ (aⱼ)` in `H²_cont(G_K, 𝔽₂)`, with `(a)` the Kummer class of `a` in `H¹` and `G_K` the absolute Galois group `Gal(K^sep/K)`; the coefficients `trivialF2` are `ℤ/2` with trivial action (`ULift` is a universe bookkeeping device).

**The map.** `brauer2EquivH2 K : Br(K)[2] ≃+ H²(G_K, 𝔽₂)` is a specific group isomorphism, not merely an abstract one: it is characterised (`brauer2EquivH2_h2MuToUnits`) as the restriction to `2`-torsion of the comparison `Br(K) ≃ H²(G_K, K^{sep×})` that sends a crossed product to the class of its cocycle, read through the Kummer map `H²(μ₂) → H²(K^{sep×})`, with `μ₂ = {±1}` identified with `𝔽₂` (legitimate because `±1 ∈ K`, so the Galois action on `μ₂` is trivial). So the statement is the classical `ι(s(q)) = w₂(q)`, whose content is the termwise formula `ι[(a,b)] = (a) ∪ (b)` (`brauerCohomologyEquiv_quaternionClass`); as every class involved is `2`-torsion, sign conventions in the cup product cannot change the value.

**Edge cases and junk.** Rank `0` or `1` gives an empty product on the left and an empty sum on the right, both the identity; no division, casts or default values appear. `BrauerGroup.{u,u} K` is the Brauer group built from central simple algebras in the universe of `K`, the usual one.

**Not vacuous.** `K = ℚ`, `q = ⟨−1,−1⟩`: `s(q)` is the class of Hamilton's quaternions, nontrivial in `Br(ℚ)`, so the theorem says `w₂(q) = (−1) ∪ (−1) ≠ 0`.

Correctly stated; compared with Folland, *A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis*, Thm 4.18 with the transform of (4.17), and the Part C stretch goal ("an LCA group via Pontryagin duality") of TauCetiRoadmap/OneParameterSemigroups, which lists no tagged Check for it.

**The group.** `[AddCommGroup G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalAddGroup G] [LocallyCompactSpace G]` is an abelian topological group, written additively, in which every neighbourhood of a point contains a compact neighbourhood. Hausdorffness is not assumed, unlike Folland; that is harmless, since a continuous `φ` and every character are constant on cosets of the closure of `{0}`, so the statement for `G` is the statement for the Hausdorff LCA group `G/closure{0}`, which has the same dual. `Multiplicative G` is `G` with its law written multiplicatively (a relabelling, same elements), and `PontryaginDual (Multiplicative G)` is the group of continuous homomorphisms `G → Circle` (the unit circle in `ℂ`) with the compact-open topology, locally compact and Hausdorff; `[MeasurableSpace …] [BorelSpace …]` fixes its σ-algebra to be the Borel one.

**Positive definite.** `IsPositiveDefiniteSub φ` says that for every finite family `c₁,…,cₙ ∈ ℂ`, `v₁,…,vₙ ∈ G`, the sum `∑ cᵢ c̄ⱼ φ(vᵢ − vⱼ)` is `≥ 0` in Mathlib's partial order on `ℂ` (`Complex.le_def`: real part `≥ 0` and imaginary part `0`), i.e. a nonnegative real number: Folland's definition, with `n = 0` giving the empty sum `0 ≤ 0`. `Continuous φ` is continuity everywhere, as for Folland's class `P(G)`.

**The transform.** `μ.pontryaginMeasureTransform g = ∫ χ(g) dμ(χ)` over the dual (`pontryaginMeasureTransform_apply`): Folland's `μ̌`, no conjugate and no `2π`, characters already being circle valued. The integrand has modulus `1` and is continuous, so it is integrable against a finite measure and the integral is never Lean's default `0` for non-integrable functions.

**The measures and uniqueness.** `FiniteMeasure` is a positive measure of finite total mass; `μ.toMeasure.InnerRegular` is `μ(s) = sup{μ(K) : K ⊆ s compact}` for every Borel `s`. Folland's measures are finite Radon measures; on a locally compact Hausdorff space a finite Radon measure is inner regular on every Borel set (Folland Prop. 7.5), and a finite inner regular measure is outer regular by passing to complements, so the two classes coincide and `∃!` asserts exactly Folland's uniqueness: one representing measure within this class. Uniqueness is not claimed among arbitrary Borel measures.

**Not vacuous.** `G = ℝ`, `φ(x) = cos x`: continuous and positive definite, and with the dual identified with `ℝ` via `ξ ↦ (x ↦ e^{iξx})` its unique inner regular representing measure is `½(δ₁ + δ₋₁)`.

Correctly stated; compared with Collingwood–McGovern Theorem 3.4.10 as the file header reports it and with target N2.1 of TauCetiRoadmap/NilpotentOrbits, which lists no tagged Check for it (the site lists `TauCeti.expAdSubgroup_le_stabilizer`, passing). What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses.** `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: a field of characteristic zero, any one, not necessarily algebraically closed. `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L] [FiniteDimensional K L]`: a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over `K`; no semisimplicity or nondegenerate Killing form is asked (those enter Jacobson–Morozov, not this theorem). `IsSl2Triple h e f` is Mathlib's predicate `h ≠ 0`, `[e, f] = h`, `[h, e] = 2e`, `[h, f] = −2f`; the `2 •` is the integer multiple, so the relations are the usual ones. The two triples share their nilpositive element `e` by construction: `t'` is about `h', e, f'` with the same `e`.

**The `[LieAlgebra ℚ L]` hypothesis is not an extra assumption.** It is how Lean lets `exp (ad y) = Σ (ad y)ⁱ / i!` divide by factorials (Mathlib's `IsNilpotent.exp` is that finite sum). An additive group carries at most one `ℚ`-vector-space structure, and Mathlib records this (`Subsingleton (LieAlgebra ℚ L)`), so the hypothesis names a structure rather than choosing one, and no compatibility with `K` need be stated; over a characteristic-zero field it always exists (`TauCeti.ratLieAlgebra`). It therefore loses no generality and cannot make the statement vacuous.

**The conclusion.** `∃ φ : L ≃ₗ⁅K⁆ L` is a `K`-linear bijection of `L` with itself preserving brackets, i.e. an automorphism of the Lie algebra, with four properties: its underlying linear map lies in `expAdSubgroup K e`, the subgroup of `GL(L)` generated (`Subgroup.closure`, the smallest subgroup containing the set) by the `exp (ad y)` with `y ∈ ker(ad e) ∩ [e, L]` and `ad y` nilpotent, which by Jacobson's lemma is every such `y`; and `φ(e) = e`, `φ(h) = h'`, `φ(f) = f'`. The group is the one Kostant and Collingwood–McGovern use, and `φ e = e` is stated even though the subgroup already forces it. This is existence of a conjugating element, as in the source; no uniqueness is claimed and none holds.

**Not vacuous.** In `sl₂(ℚ)` with the standard `e`, `ker(ad e) ∩ [e, L]` is the line through `e`, and `(h + 2e, e, f − h − e)` is a second triple; `φ = exp(ad(−e))`, conjugation by the unipotent matrix with `−1` above the diagonal, fixes `e` and carries `h` to `h + 2e`, as the theorem asserts. The theorem is also consistent with Morozov's lemma: given `h'`, `f'` is forced, which is why only `h'` had to be moved.

**The fields.** `K` is complete for a multiplicative nonarchimedean absolute value. `L` is a normed field that is a `NormedAlgebra K L`: Mathlib asks only `‖k • x‖ ≤ ‖k‖ ‖x‖`, but since both norms are multiplicative with `‖1‖ = 1`, Mathlib's `norm_algebraMap'` gives `‖k·1_L‖ = ‖k‖`, so `L` is an isometric extension field of `K`, and it is automatically ultrametric (`IsUltrametricDist.of_normedAlgebra`), which is why no such hypothesis appears. `L = K` and `L = ℂ_p` over `K = ℚ_p` are both allowed; nothing asks `L` to be algebraic over `K`.

**The series.** `f.IsRestricted c` (Mathlib) is `‖aₙ‖ cⁿ → 0`: `f` converges on the closed disc of radius `c`. `IsDistinguished c s f` (Tau Ceti) says `‖a_s‖ c^s` equals the Gauss norm, Mathlib's `PowerSeries.gaussNorm`, the supremum of all `‖aₙ‖ cⁿ`, and that `‖aₘ‖ cᵐ` is strictly smaller for every `m > s`: `s` is the last index where the maximum is attained. This forces `f ≠ 0` (`IsDistinguished.ne_zero`), and for a nonzero restricted series at positive radius such an `s` exists and is unique (`exists_isDistinguished`, `IsDistinguished.unique`), so the hypothesis names an invariant of `f` rather than restricting `f`.

**Evaluation.** `f.evalAt x` is `∑' n, aₙ • xⁿ`, a `tsum`, which Mathlib sets to `0` when the series diverges. For `‖x‖ ≤ c` and `f` restricted at `c` the terms tend to `0`, and in a complete ultrametric field that suffices for convergence (`PowerSeries.IsRestricted.hasSum_evalAt`), so inside the disc `f.evalAt x = 0` means the honest value `f(x)` vanishes; the set is cut out by `‖x‖ ≤ c` first, so the junk value never enters.

**The count.** `Set.encard` takes values in `ℕ ∪ {∞}`, with `∞` for an infinite set, and `↑s` is `s` in that semiring; so `encard ≤ s` asserts the set of zeros of norm at most `c` is finite with at most `s` elements, with no collapse at infinity as `ncard` would have. Zeros are counted without multiplicity, as in Strassmann.

**Sharp and not vacuous.** `X^p − X` over `ℚ_p` at `c = 1` has `s = p` and exactly `p` zeros in `ℤ_p`; `X − a` with `‖a‖ ≤ 1` has `s = 1`; a unit series has `s = 0` and no zeros in the disc.

Correctly stated; compared with McCleary, *A User's Guide to Spectral Sequences*, Thm 2.6 and §2.2, and with DGFloer Layer 1, item 3 of the roadmap, which lists no tagged Check for it. Checks: the three named tests are as listed in the Codex review.

**What the input is.** `EInt` is Mathlib's `WithBotTop ℤ`, the integers with `−∞` and `+∞` adjoined, a category by its order. A functor `F : EInt ⥤ CochainComplex C ℤ` is thus a chain of cochain complexes `F_{−∞} → ⋯ → F_q → F_{q+1} → ⋯ → F_{+∞}` in an abelian category `C`. The classical input, an increasing filtration `F_q ⊆ K` by subcomplexes, is such a chain with `F_{−∞} = 0`, `F_{+∞} = K` and all maps inclusions (`filtrationFunctor`); when the maps are not injective, mapping cones replace quotients.

**What a `SpectralSequence` is here.** Mathlib's `CategoryTheory.SpectralSequence C c r₀` is a family of pages `E_r`, `r ≥ r₀`, each a complex with the shape `c r`, together with chosen isomorphisms `H(E_r) ≅ E_{r+1}`. Being a `def`, the declaration is a construction, and which one it is comes from Mathlib's recipe `coreE₂Cohomological` applied to the spectral object of `F` (the `H^n` of all cones `cone(F_i → F_j)` with their long exact sequences), and is pinned by the comparison lemmas next to it: `E_2^{p,q} = H^{p+q}(cone(F_q → F_{q+1}))`, which is `H^{p+q}(F_{q+1}/F_q)` for a filtration, and the page-`2` differential is the connecting map of `0 → F_q/F_{q−1} → F_{q+1}/F_{q−1} → F_{q+1}/F_q → 0`.

**Indexing conventions that look odd but change nothing.** The first page is numbered `2`, not `1`: the page classically called `E_r` is page `r+1` here. The shape `ComplexShape.up' (r, 1−r)` says `d_r` goes from `(p, q)` to `(p+r, q+1−r)`: total degree `p+q` rises by one and the filtration index `q` falls by `r−1`, which is exactly the classical `d_{r−1}` of an increasing filtration; and for a decreasing filtration `F^s = F_{−s}` the usual `E_1^{s,t}` is recovered with `s = −q−1`, `t = p+2q+1`.

**What is not in this declaration.** Convergence is separate: strong convergence for a finite filtration is a theorem in Convergence.lean about `filtrationFunctor`, and Voyager's phrase "converging strongly when `F` is globally finite" describes those, not a hypothesis or clause of this definition, which exists for every `F` with no hypothesis at all (Mathlib's `HasSpectralSequence` holds automatically here). Nothing is vacuous: the two-step filtration `0 ⊆ A ⊆ K` yields the long exact sequence of `A ⊆ K` as its page `2`.

Correctly stated; compared with Horn–Johnson, *Matrix Analysis* §0.8.7 (Cauchy–Binet) and the "Native Plücker heights" target of TauCetiRoadmap/DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §2.5, which asks for it under the name `plucker_cauchyBinet` "including p=0 and p>#ι". The target's Checks are untagged prose bullets, so the roadmap lists no tagged Check for it.

**Hypotheses.** `[CommRing R]` is any commutative ring (the zero ring included, harmlessly); `[Fintype ι]` says the column index set `ι` is finite; `[LinearOrder ι]` is a total order on the columns, used only to say in which order a minor's columns are taken. Any finite set can be so ordered, and the choice does not matter here: changing it permutes the `p`-subsets and multiplies both `plucker x s` and `plucker y s` by the same sign. 
**The two sides.** `x` and `y` are `p × ι` matrices, given as families of `p` row vectors indexed by `Fin p = {0,…,p−1}` (`Matrix.of x` is that matrix). By Mathlib's definitions of the product and transpose (`Matrix.mul_apply`, `Matrix.transpose`), `Matrix.of x * (Matrix.of y).transpose` is the `p × p` matrix with entries `∑ₖ x i k · y j k`, and `Matrix.det` is the Leibniz determinant (`Matrix.det_apply`). On the right, `Set.powersetCard ι p` is the set of finite subsets of `ι` with exactly `p` elements, and the sum runs over all of them. `plucker x s` is, by its definition and `ofFinEmbEquiv_symm_apply`, the determinant of the `p × p` matrix whose `j`-th column is the column of `x` at the `j`-th smallest element of `s` (`Finset.orderEmbOfFin`): the maximal minor on the columns `s`, in increasing order. So the statement reads `det(x yᵀ) = ∑_{|S| = p} det(x_S) det(y_S)`, which is Cauchy–Binet with `B = yᵀ`, since `det((y_S)ᵀ) = det(y_S)` and both minors use the same column order.

**Edge cases, no junk.** For `p = 0` the left side is the determinant of the empty matrix, `1` (`Matrix.det_isEmpty`), and the right side is one term, over `s = ∅`, with `plucker = 1` (`plucker_of_isEmpty`). For `p > #ι` there are no `p`-subsets, so the right side is the empty sum `0`, and the statement asserts the genuine fact that `x yᵀ` is singular, a product through fewer than `p` columns. Neither side is a default value: no division, natural subtraction or limit occurs.

**Not vacuous.** Over `ℤ` with a single row `x = y = (1, 2)` both sides are `5 = 1² + 2²`; over `ℂ` with `x = y = (1, i)` both are `0`, which is why the Hermitian version in the same file conjugates `y`.

**The hypotheses.** `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: a field of characteristic zero, not assumed algebraically closed. `L` is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over `K` with `IsKilling K L`, Mathlib's class saying the Killing form is nondegenerate, which in characteristic zero is semisimplicity. `H` is a Cartan subalgebra, and `IsTriangularizable K H L` says every element of `H` acts on `L` with split characteristic polynomial: `H` is a *splitting* Cartan subalgebra, so `(L, H)` is a split semisimple Lie algebra. `b : (rootSystem H).Base` is a base (a set of simple roots) of its root system, Mathlib's `RootPairing.Base`, whose `support` is the finite set of simple-root indices.

**The objects.** `Matrix.ToLieAlgebra K A` is Mathlib's Serre algebra of an integer matrix `A`: the free Lie algebra on generators `Hᵢ, Eᵢ, Fᵢ` modulo the six families of Serre relations (`Mathlib/Algebra/Lie/SerreConstruction.lean`); here `A` is the transposed Cartan matrix of the base, the index order the Codex review already discusses. `serreH K A i` is the image of the generator `Hᵢ` in that quotient. `(rootSystem H).coroot i` is Mathlib's coroot `αᵢ∨ ∈ H`, normalised by `αᵢ(αᵢ∨) = 2` (`IsKilling.root_apply_coroot`).

**The conclusion.** There is a Lie algebra homomorphism `φ` from the Serre algebra onto `L` (`Function.Surjective`) with `φ(Hᵢ) = αᵢ∨` for every simple root: `L` is a quotient of the Serre algebra of its own Cartan matrix by a map matching the Cartan generators with the simple coroots. Only the images of the `Hᵢ` are pinned; the proof sends `Eᵢ, Fᵢ` to root vectors in `L_{αᵢ}`, `L_{−αᵢ}` completing `αᵢ∨` to an `sl₂` triple ([`exists_isSerreSystem_of_base`, Killing.lean#L197](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Lie/Presentation/Serre/Killing.lean#L197)), but as stated the theorem claims less than Serre's theorem, not something different: injectivity (the isomorphism of Humphreys 18.3) is not asserted.

**Conventions that do not bite.** The higher relations use `(−A i j).toNat`, which truncates a negative integer to `0`; off the diagonal a Cartan matrix has entries `≤ 0`, so the exponent is honest, and on the diagonal `(−2).toNat = 0` makes the `i = j` relation `⁅Eᵢ, Eᵢ⁆ = 0`, trivially true.

**Not vacuous.** `sl₂(ℚ)` with `H` the diagonal matrices and the base `{α}` satisfies every hypothesis; the Serre algebra of the `1 × 1` matrix `(2)` then maps onto `sl₂(ℚ)` with `H₁ ↦ h`.

BGR work over a field at radius `1`; here `R` may be any such ring, e.g. a Tate algebra, and `c > 0` any radius. Mathlib's `IsRestricted c f` is `‖fₙ‖ cⁿ → 0` (a limit along the cofinite filter on `ℕ`, i.e. `n → ∞`): `f` converges on the closed disc of radius `c`. `IsDistinguished c s f` says the Gauss norm `supₙ ‖fₙ‖ cⁿ` is attained at `n = s` and every later term is strictly smaller. Mathlib sets a real supremum to `0` when unbounded, but restrictedness bounds the family and distinguishedness forces it positive, so no default value enters. That `fₛ` is a unit of `R` is BGR's "`gₛ` a unit of the coefficient ring"; over a field it is automatic, since a distinguished series has `fₛ ≠ 0`.

**What `∃!` asserts.** Exactly one pair `(e, ω)`, `e` in the subring of restricted series at `c` (the `↥` only turns that subring into a type) and `ω ∈ R[X]`, such that: `IsUnit e` holds *in that subring*, so the inverse of `e` is itself restricted, not merely a unit of `R⟦X⟧`; `ω.IsMonicOfDegree s` is Mathlib's "`natDegree = s` and leading coefficient `1`", so for `s = 0` it forces `ω = 1`; and `e · ω = f` after the `↑` coercions into `R⟦X⟧`. Uniqueness ranges over all monic `ω` of degree `s`, without BGR's normalisation `‖ω‖ = cˢ`; with a multiplicative norm that normalisation is automatic (`IsDistinguished.of_isUnit_mul` makes `ω` distinguished of degree `s`), so this is BGR's statement at a general radius with a slightly stronger uniqueness clause.

**Edge cases.** The trivial ring is a `NormedCommRing`, but no series over it is distinguished (its Gauss norm would have to be positive), so nothing false is claimed there.

Classically the formula is for the irreducible `L(λ)` with `λ` dominant integral; such an `M` is irreducible (docstring), and finite-dimensionality forces `lam` dominant integral (`IsHighestWeightVector.isDominantIntegral`, used in the proof), so no separate dominance hypothesis is needed and the class of modules is the classical one.

What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses are Humphreys's standing ones.** `K` is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero; `L` is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra whose Killing form is non-degenerate, which in characteristic zero is exactly semisimplicity; `H` is a Cartan subalgebra (nilpotent and self-normalising, splitting because `K` is algebraically closed); `b` is a base, i.e. a choice of simple roots, and "positive root" means positive height with respect to `b`. `M` is a finite-dimensional `L`-module, `v` a highest weight vector of weight `λ` (nonzero, `H` acts on it through `λ`, the positive nilradical `n⁺` kills it), and `hgen` says `v` generates `M` as an `L`-module. Such an `M` is irreducible, hence is `L(λ)`, and `λ` is automatically dominant integral, so nothing is lost against Humphreys's `L(λ)`. The square-bracket assumption that the Weyl group is finite always holds (`TauCeti.finite_weylGroup`), so it costs nothing.

**The two sides.** The left side is the dimension of the honest weight space `M_μ = {m : x·m = μ(x)m for all x ∈ H}` (Mathlib's `weightSpace`, an intersection of eigenspaces, not the generalized one), cast into `ℤ` so that it can equal a signed sum. The right side unfolds to `∑_{w ∈ W} sgn(w)·P(w⬝λ − μ)` with `w⬝λ = w(λ+ρ) − ρ`, so `w⬝λ − μ = w(λ+ρ) − (μ+ρ)`, Kostant's shifted difference; `ρ` is half the sum of the positive roots, `sgn(w) = (−1)^{#inversions}` is the usual sign character, and `P(ν)` counts the functions from the positive roots to `ℕ` writing `ν` as a sum of positive roots. That count is a genuine cardinality: finiteness is proved (`finite_setOf_isKostantPartition`) before `Nat.card` is taken, so no "infinite set has card 0" default is in play, and `P(ν) = 0` off the positive cone is the classical convention.

**Edge cases.** For `μ` not a weight both sides are `0`; the formula asserts this too, as Kostant's does. No division occurs: the inverse of the Weyl denominator enters only as a formal series paired against `ℤ[𝔥*]`.

**Not vacuous.** For `sl₂(ℂ)`, `M = V(n)`, `μ = n − 2k`: the identity term gives `P(kα) = 1` for `0 ≤ k`, the reflection term `P(−(n+1−k)α) = 1` only for `k ≥ n+1`, so the alternating sum is `1` for `0 ≤ k ≤ n` and `0` otherwise.

**The setting, in mathematical terms.** `G = Spec H` is an affine group scheme over a commutative ring `R`, given by its Hopf algebra `H`. `Bialgebra.CotangentSpace R H` is `I/I²` for the augmentation ideal `I = ker ε`, the cotangent space at the identity, and the Lie algebra of `G` is taken to be its `R`-dual `Module.Dual R (I/I²)` (the tangent space at the identity). The two instance hypotheses `[Module.Finite …] [Module.Projective …]` say `I/I²` is a finitely generated projective `R`-module; over a field this holds for every group of finite type, over a ring for smooth groups of finite type. `M` is an abstract abelian group written multiplicatively, `MonoidAlgebra R M = R[M]` its group algebra, whose spectrum is the diagonalizable group `D(M)` with character group `M`; a bialgebra map `π : H →ₐc[R] R[M]` is the comorphism of a homomorphism `D(M) → G`.

**The definition.** `adjointWeightSpace π α` is the `α`-weight space `𝔤_α`: the elements `x` of the Lie algebra whose adjoint coaction, pushed into `R[M]`, is `x ⊗ [α]`, equivalently on which every point of `D(M)` acts by the scalar `α`. `nontrivialAdjointWeights π` is the subset of `M` of those `α` with `α ≠ 1` and `𝔤_α ≠ ⊥`, where `⊥` is the zero submodule and `1` is the trivial character because `M` is written multiplicatively; in additive notation this reads "`α ≠ 0` and `𝔤_α ≠ 0`", Milne's definition verbatim. Finiteness (`finite_nontrivialAdjointWeights`) and the decomposition `𝔤 = 𝔤_1 ⊕ ⨁ 𝔤_α` (`isInternal_adjointWeightSpace`) are theorems, not parts of the definition, so no choice is built into the set.

**Generality and edge cases.** No hypothesis says `D(M) → G` is a closed immersion, that `D(M)` is a torus or maximal, or that `G` is reductive: the name says "nontrivial adjoint weights", and the docstring reserves "roots" for a split maximal torus in a reductive group, where it coincides with Milne's. Over a non-field base, `𝔤_α ≠ ⊥` is a global statement about an `R`-submodule. For `M = 1`, the trivial homomorphism, or `𝔤 = 0` the set is empty. No junk value is involved.

**Not vacuous.** For `SL_{r+1}` with its diagonal torus, the set is exactly the characters `t ↦ t_i/t_j`, `i ≠ j` (`SpecialLinear.range_ofAdd_diagonalRootDatum_root_eq_nontrivialAdjointWeights`, no `sorry` in that file).

**The Lie algebra and the module.** `Matrix (Fin N) (Fin N) K` is `𝔤𝔩_N(K)` with bracket `AB − BA` (the file switches on Mathlib's `LieRing.ofAssociativeRing`, whose bracket is `x * y - y * x` by definition). `glIrreducible N mu` is a concrete `𝔤𝔩_N`-module: the span of a chosen highest weight vector of weight `μ` in a trace-twisted exterior power of `K^N`, divided by a chosen maximal proper submodule. This is harmless: every statement about `L(μ)` carries `hmu`, and `nonempty_lieModuleEquiv_glIrreducible` identifies `L(μ)` with any irreducible carrying a highest weight vector of weight `μ`, so the choices are invisible up to isomorphism.

So this is the classical "L(μ) is a nonzero module whose only submodules are 0 and itself"; nonvanishing is part of the claim. With `isGlHighestWeightVector_glIrreducibleGenerator` (the class of the chosen vector is a highest weight vector of weight `μ`, "highest" for the upper-triangular Borel: `Eᵢᵢ` acts by `μᵢ`, `Eᵢⱼ` with `i < j` kills it), this is the existence half of the highest weight theorem.

Correctly stated; compared with Karp, *Finite-quantifier equivalence* (1965), cited in the file header, and with the `karp_theorem` entry of TauCetiRoadmap/InfinitaryLogic (README, "Carriers (Karp)"), which lists no tagged Check for it. What follows says why the Lean statement is the classical one for a reader who does not read Lean.

**Hypotheses.** `L` is any first-order language and `M`, `N` any two `L`-structures, of any cardinality and in independent universes; no countability appears. `[L.IsRelational]` is Mathlib's `∀ n, IsEmpty (L.Functions n)`: no function symbols and, since constants are 0-ary functions, no constants. Mathlib structures may be empty; two empty structures are potentially isomorphic (the empty partial map) and agree on every sentence, and an empty against a nonempty one fails both sides (`∃x, x = x` separates them), so the edge case is consistent.

**Left side.** `PotentialIso M N` is Karp's notion: a nonempty family `S` of partial isomorphisms between finitely generated substructures (Mathlib's `FGEquiv`; in a relational language these are finite) such that every member extends, *within* `S`, to one whose domain contains any given element of `M`, and to one whose range contains any given element of `N`; `f ≤ g` is "g extends f" (`PartialEquiv.le_def`). This is deliberately not Mathlib's `IsExtensionPair`, which asks every finite partial isomorphism to extend and fails for `(ℕ,<)` against itself.

**Right side.** `InfEquivW M N` says that for every type `κ` in the universe of `M ⊕ N`, each `L_{∞ω}` sentence whose infinite conjunctions and disjunctions are indexed by `κ` holds in `M` exactly when it holds in `N`. The syntax `BoundedFormulaInf` has atomic formulas, implication (hence negation and finite connectives), one universal quantifier at a time (so finitely many quantifiers per formula: the "ω"), and `iInf`/`iSup` over `κ`-indexed families, realised as "for all i" / "exists i". Conjunctions over a subset of `κ` are obtained by padding with a true formula, so "indexed by `κ`" loses nothing. This is `L_{∞ω}`-equivalence, with the usual caveat that "all sets" means the sets of the ambient universe.

**The iff.** The forward direction holds at every carrier (`PotentialIso.infEquivAt`); the converse needs only the carrier `M ⊕ N`, where the separating conjunctions range over the elements of the two structures, as in Karp's proof. No junk values: both sides are plain propositions without arithmetic.

**Not vacuous.** With one binary relation, `(ℚ,<)` and `(ℝ,<)` are potentially isomorphic (back-and-forth for dense orders without endpoints), hence `L_{∞ω}`-equivalent though not isomorphic; `(ℤ,<)` and `(ℤ ⊕ ℤ,<)` are elementarily equivalent but separated by the infinitary sentence "any two points are finitely far apart", so neither side is trivial.

Correctly stated; compared with Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter*, §12.1 (relative perimeter `P(E; A)`), Ambrosio–Fusco–Pallara Definition 3.4, and the perimeter convention of TauCetiRoadmap/GeometricMeasureTheory, which lists no tagged Check for it. A reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean follows.

**What is being defined.** `perimeter μ Ω s` is the total variation on `Ω` of the indicator of `s` (the function equal to `1` on `s` and `0` elsewhere). Unfolding `totalVariationOn` ([TotalVariation.lean#L92](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Analysis/BoundedVariation/TotalVariation.lean#L92)), it is the supremum of `ENNReal.ofReal (∫ div φ · 𝟙_s dμ)` over `φ ∈ 𝓓(Ω, E)` with `‖φ(x)‖ ≤ 1` for all `x`. `𝓓(Ω, E)` is Mathlib's space of smooth vector fields `E → E` with compact support contained in `Ω`, and `div φ` is the trace of the derivative. So this is `P(s; Ω) = sup { ∫_s div φ : φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω, ℝⁿ), |φ| ≤ 1 }`, De Giorgi's perimeter as in Maggi (12.1).

**Hypotheses.** `E` is any finite-dimensional real inner product space (`ℝⁿ` up to isometry) with a σ-algebra and a measure `μ`. Nothing ties `μ` or the σ-algebra to the topology: the definition is made in that generality, Mathlib-style, and the theorems needing Lebesgue measure assume `[BorelSpace E] [μ.IsAddHaarMeasure]` (`perimeter_compl`) or `[OpensMeasurableSpace E]` (lower semicontinuity). For `μ` Lebesgue measure it is exactly the textbook object. `Ω : Opens E` is an open set, `⊤` the whole space.

**Conventions that do not change the meaning.** (1) The integral is over all of `E`, not `Ω`, but `div φ` vanishes outside the support of `φ`, which lies in `Ω`. (2) `ENNReal.ofReal` sends a negative real to `0` (it is `Real.toNNReal`), so negative pairings are clipped; harmless, since `−φ` is admissible whenever `φ` is and `φ = 0` gives `0`, so clipping never lowers the supremum. (3) Maggi allows `C¹_c` fields; mollification keeps `|φ| ≤ 1` and converges in `C¹`, so the suprema over `C¹_c` and `C^∞_c` agree. (4) The value lies in `[0, ∞]`, which is the point: finite perimeter in `Ω` means the value is `< ∞`, with no finite-volume requirement. (5) Junk: for `s` not null-measurable, Mathlib's integral of a non-integrable function is `0`, so the value may be meaningless; the file header says so, and `perimeter_eq_iSup` and everything built on it assume `NullMeasurableSet s μ`, the roadmap's Lebesgue-measurability convention.

**Not vacuous.** In `ℝ` with Lebesgue measure `perimeter volume ⊤ (Ioo a b) = 2` (`TauCeti.Real.perimeter_Ioo`); in `ℝⁿ` a ball of radius `r` has perimeter `n r^{n−1} vol(B₁)` (`TauCeti.perimeter_ball`), the area of the sphere.

Correctly stated; compared with Kadeishvili 1988 and Keller §3.4 as cited in the file header, and with the Layer 8 item of TauCetiRoadmap/DGAInfinity ("the standard sufficient intrinsic-formality criterion `HH^{n,2-n}(H,H)=0` for every `n≥3`"). The roadmap lists no tagged Check for it. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses say "H is a graded algebra, and HH^{n,2−n}(H,H) = 0 for n ≥ 3".** `[Field K]` is the ground field and `A` any `K`-vector space, with no finite-dimensionality or boundedness of degrees. `ℋ` is an `A∞`-structure on `A`: an internal `ℤ`-grading, operations `m_n : A^{⊗n} → A` of degree `2 − n`, no unit, `m_0 = 0`, Stasheff relations. `hℋ` (`IsMinimal`, defined as `m₁ = 0`, [Minimal.lean#L62](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Minimal.lean#L62)) and `hm` (`m_n = 0` for `n ≥ 3`) together reduce `ℋ` to a graded associative algebra `H`: the arity-three Stasheff identity becomes associativity of `m₂`. `hHH` is the vanishing of the bigraded Hochschild cohomology, written on cochains: a cochain is a linear map `F` from the positive-length words on the suspension `sA` to `A`; `F ∘ lengthProj n = F` means `F` is supported on words of length exactly `n` (so it is an `n`-ary operation); "suspended degree one" is the degree a Taylor component of an `m_n` has, and the Hochschild differential is the Gerstenhaber bracket with the product. The argument `⟨n, by omega⟩` is just the proof that `n > 1`, needed so that `n − 1` is a positive word length; it carries no hypothesis.

**The conclusion is Kadeishvili's.** `IsIntrinsicallyFormal` ([IntrinsicFormality.lean#L80](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/IntrinsicFormality.lean#L80)) repeats that `ℋ` is a graded algebra and then says: for every `A∞`-algebra `𝒜` over `K` and every bijective strict morphism `ℋ → H*(𝒜)`, that is a degree-preserving linear bijection commuting with all operations, which here means an isomorphism of graded algebras `H ≅ H*(𝒜)`, the algebra `𝒜` is formal. `IsFormal` is the existence of an `A∞`-quasi-isomorphism `𝒜 → H*(𝒜)`, the cohomology carrying only its product. The direction of the arrow is immaterial over a field, and the file records the equivalent form "every minimal `A∞`-structure on `H` with the same `m₂` is `A∞`-isomorphic to `ℋ`" (`isIntrinsicallyFormal_iff_forall_exists_isIso`), which is how Kadeishvili states it. The criterion is sufficient, not necessary, and the statement claims nothing more.

**Conventions that do not change the meaning.** The algebra is nonunital and the Hochschild complex is the full one, not the normalised one; for a unital `H` both compute the same `HH`, so the hypothesis is the classical one, and the theorem covers nonunital `H` as well. The `A∞`-algebras quantified over have carriers in the universe of `A`; this is size bookkeeping only. No junk values occur: `n − 1` is taken for `n ≥ 3`, and there is no division or cardinality.

**Not vacuous.** Any associative algebra placed in degree `0`, say `K[x]` or `M₂(K)`, satisfies every hypothesis: a suspended-degree-one cochain on `n ≥ 3` letters would have internal degree `2 − n < 0`, so it is zero and bounds `0`; the conclusion is then the genuine statement that every `A∞`-algebra with cohomology concentrated in degree `0` is formal.

Correctly stated; compared with Tate–Oort, *Group schemes of prime order*, §1 (the theorem attributed to Deligne) and the ModularCurves roadmap, Layer 0 ("a finite locally free commutative group scheme of rank `N` is killed by `N`"), which lists no tagged Check for it. A reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean follows.

**The group scheme.** `[CommRing R] [CommRing H] [HopfAlgebra R H]` says `H` is a commutative Hopf algebra over the commutative ring `R`, so `G = Spec H` is an affine group scheme over `R`; Mathlib's `HopfAlgebra` requires the antipode axiom, not merely a bialgebra. `[Coalgebra.IsCocomm R H]` says the comultiplication is symmetric, i.e. `G` is a commutative group scheme. For a commutative `R`-algebra `A`, the set of `R`-algebra homomorphisms `H →ₐ[R] A` is `G(A)`; `WithConv` is a wrapper telling Lean to multiply them by convolution, `(x * y)(h) = Σ x(h₍₁₎) y(h₍₂₎)`, with unit `h ↦ ε(h)·1` and inverse via the antipode (`convMul_def`, `convOne_def`, `convGroup`). So `x ^ n = 1` is `[n](x) = 0` in the abstract group `G(A)`, not the `n`-th power of the ring map `x`. `A` is allowed to be a semiring; that only widens the statement.

**"Finite locally free of rank `n`."** `Module.Finite R H` is "finitely generated as an `R`-module" and `Module.Flat R H` is flatness; over an arbitrary ring, finite flat is weaker than finite projective. `Module.rankAtStalk H p` is the rank of the free `R_p`-module `H_p` (free by `free_of_flat_of_isLocalRing`, Stacks 00NZ), and `hn` asks it to equal `n` at every prime. A finitely generated flat module whose stalk rank is constant is finite locally free (`Module.Free.away_of_finite_of_flat_of_rankAtStalk_constant`), so the hypotheses are exactly "finite locally free of constant rank `n`", the classical form (a non-constant rank is handled by splitting `Spec R`). `rankAtStalk` is a `finrank`, which is `0` only for infinite rank, impossible here.

**Points with values anywhere.** The theorem quantifies over every commutative `R`-algebra `A` and every point `x`, which is what "the group scheme is killed by `n`" means (equivalently, `[n]` factors through the unit section); it is proved for the universal point, the identity of `H`, and then specialised.

**Not vacuous.** `R = ℤ`, `H = ℤ[t]/(tᴺ − 1)` with `Δt = t ⊗ t`, `ε(t) = 1`, `S(t) = t⁻¹` is `μ_N`, free of rank `N`; a point with values in `A` is an `N`-th root of unity `ζ ∈ A` and convolution is multiplication of roots of unity, so the theorem says `ζᴺ = 1`.

Correctly stated; compared with Conway, *A Course in Functional Analysis*, 2nd ed. (Toeplitz operators `T_φ = P M_φ|H²` on the circle), and target T2 of TauCetiRoadmap/OperatorTheory/ToeplitzOperators (its `Suggested.lean` form `hardySubspace.orthogonalProjectionOnto ∘L symbolMultiplier a ∘L hardySubspace.subtypeL` is the one used here), which lists no tagged Check for it. A reading guide for a mathematician follows.

**The objects.** The circle is `AddCircle 1 = ℝ/ℤ` with `AddCircle.haarAddCircle`, Mathlib's Haar measure normalised to total mass `1` (its source says so and registers it as a probability measure). `Lp ℂ ∞ haarAddCircle` is `L^∞` of the circle: classes of measurable functions equal almost everywhere, normed by the essential supremum (Mathlib's `eLpNorm` at exponent `∞` is `essSup ‖f‖`). `HardySpace` is the closed subspace `H²` of `L²` spanned by the modes `e_n(x) = exp(2πinx)`, `n ≥ 0`; `mem_hardySubmodule_iff` says its elements are exactly the `L²` functions whose negative Fourier coefficients vanish, which is the usual boundary `H²`. The `↥` only turns that subspace into a type.

**What is constructed.** `toeplitz` is a map of two arguments: a symbol `a ∈ L^∞` and then `f ∈ H²`. For fixed `a`, `toeplitz a` is the operator `P M_a ι`: include `H²` into `L²` (`subtypeL`), multiply pointwise by `a` (`Lp.multiplicationOperator`, which acts by `a·f` almost everywhere), and project orthogonally back onto `H²` (`orthogonalProjectionOnto`). `toeplitz_apply` pins this by `rfl`, so the map is that composite by definition, and `coe_toeplitz_apply` says `T_a f = P(af)` in `L²`. This is Conway's `T_a`.

**What `→L[ℂ] … →L[ℂ]` adds.** The inner arrow says each `T_a` is a bounded complex-linear operator on `H²`; the outer one says the symbol map `a ↦ T_a` is itself bounded and linear, with the bound `‖T_a‖ ≤ ‖a‖_∞` built in (`LinearMap.mkContinuous` with constant `1`). Both are standard facts (`T_{a+b} = T_a + T_b`, `‖T_a‖ ≤ ‖a‖_∞`), so bundling them changes nothing, and `norm_toeplitz` upgrades the bound to equality.

**Conventions in play.** Mathlib's inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot (`inner_smul_left`), the same as Conway, so the matrix entry `⟨e_i, T_a e_j⟩` is `â(i − j)` (`inner_hardyBasis_toeplitz_hardyBasis`) with `â(n) = ∫ e_{−n} a`, Mathlib's `fourierCoeff`. The `∞` in the signature is `⊤ : ℝ≥0∞`, Mathlib's name for the exponent `∞`. No junk values arise: there is no division, no truncation, and the adjoint `T_a^* = T_{ā}` (`adjoint_toeplitz`) uses `star a`, complex conjugation almost everywhere.

**Not vacuous.** For a constant symbol `c`, `toeplitz c = c · id` (`toeplitz_const`); for `a = e_1` it is the unilateral shift `e_n ↦ e_{n+1}`, whose matrix `â(i − j) = [i = j + 1]` the matrix formula confirms.

Correctly stated; compared with Keller §3.3, Theorem 3.3 ("the structure is unique up to (non-unique) isomorphism of `A∞`-algebras"), with Voyager's text and with the Layer 3 item of TauCetiRoadmap/DGAInfinity. The roadmap lists no tagged Check for it; Checks as listed in the Codex review. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses.** `[Field K]` is the ground field. `𝒜` is any `A∞`-algebra on a `K`-vector space `A` (nonunital, `m_0 = 0`, `m_n` of degree `2 − n`, no finiteness), and `ℬ` one on another vector space `B`, with `hℬ` saying `m₁ = 0` on `ℬ`. `f : AInfinityHom ℬ 𝒜` is an `A∞`-morphism, stored as a degree-zero coalgebra map of reduced bar constructions commuting with the bar differentials, which is the usual family `f_n : B^{⊗n} → A` of degree `1 − n` satisfying the morphism identities. `hf : f.IsQuasiIso` ([Hom/Cohomology.lean#L376](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Hom/Cohomology.lean#L376)) says the map `H(ℬ) → H(𝒜)` induced by `f₁` is bijective; it is stated on total cohomology, but `f₁` preserves degrees, so this is bijectivity in every degree. Since `ℬ` is minimal, `H(ℬ) = B`, and the hypothesis says that `b ↦ [f₁ b]` is a bijection `B → H(𝒜)`.

**The objects.** `𝒜.minimalModel` is the `A∞`-structure on `H(𝒜)` obtained by transfer along a contraction built from chosen homogeneous representatives, with `m₁ = 0` and `m₂` the cohomology product. `𝒜.minimalModelProjection` is the `A∞`-morphism `𝒜 → H(𝒜)` extending the projection of that contraction; its linear part sends a cycle to its class ([L598](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Transfer/Cohomology.lean#L598)), and it is a left inverse of the inclusion of the model. `comp g f` means "first `f`, then `g`" (its bar map is `g ∘ f`), so the composite in the statement is `ℬ → 𝒜 → H(𝒜)`.

**The conclusion.** `IsIso` ([Hom/Iso.lean#L199](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Hom/Iso.lean#L199)) is the existence of a two-sided inverse `A∞`-morphism: an isomorphism of `A∞`-algebras in the strict sense, not a quasi-isomorphism and not an inverse up to homotopy. So the theorem says: any minimal `A∞`-algebra that admits a quasi-isomorphism into `𝒜` is `A∞`-isomorphic to the minimal model, through the explicit composite. That is Keller's uniqueness clause; the isomorphism depends on `f` and on the chosen contraction, which is his "non-unique". The twin theorem just below, `isIso_comp_minimalModelInclusion`, handles quasi-isomorphisms out of `𝒜`, and with the existence half this is Theorem 3.3 in full.

**Conventions.** `A` and `B` may live in different universes; harmless. The field hypothesis is needed for the minimal model to exist (complements are chosen); the fact that a quasi-isomorphism between minimal algebras is an isomorphism (`isQuasiIso_iff_isIso`) holds over any commutative ring, but the statement is about the field-level object `minimalModel`. No junk values: nothing is divided, counted or truncated.

**Not vacuous.** For the Heisenberg cochain algebra `Λ(a, b, c)`, `dc = ab`, over `K`, `Transfer/Heisenberg.lean` builds by hand a minimal model with `m₃([a],[a],[b]) = [ac] ≠ 0` and its quasi-isomorphism into the algebra; the theorem makes that hand-built model `A∞`-isomorphic to the abstract `minimalModel`, as it must be. Taking `ℬ = 𝒜.minimalModel` and `f` its inclusion gives the identity, by `minimalModelProjection_comp_minimalModelInclusion`.

**The inputs.** `[CommRing R]` is any commutative ring, not necessarily a field, and `𝒜` any `A∞`-algebra on an `R`-module `A` (nonunital, `m_0 = 0`, `m_n` of degree `2 − n`). `𝒜.Cohomology` is `ker m₁ / im m₁` as a single `R`-module ([Cohomology.lean#L178](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Cohomology.lean#L178)), so `x, y, z` are cohomology classes that need not be homogeneous. Its product `x * y` is induced by `m₂` and is associative on cohomology thanks to `m₃` (the arity-three Stasheff identity).

**The value is a set, as it should be.** The declaration is a `def` whose value is a subset of the cohomology: the classical triple Massey product is multivalued, and the Lean object is the set of all its values, not a chosen one. An element is the class of the Massey cycle `m₂(u, c) − m₂(τa, v) + m₃(a, b, c)` of a defining system ([L92](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Massey.lean#L92)): cycles `a, b, c` representing `x, y, z`, and cochains `u, v` with `m₁u = m₂(a, b)`, `m₁v = m₂(b, c)`. Here `τ` (`koszulTwist 1`) multiplies a homogeneous element of degree `e` by `(−1)^e`, May's bar `ā`, extended linearly to inhomogeneous elements; the `m₃` term is absent in a DG algebra and is exactly what makes the cochain a cycle for a genuine `A∞`-algebra (`cycle_mem_cycles`). `Set.range` over a structure with no inhabitant is the empty set, so when `xy ≠ 0` or `yz ≠ 0` the product is `∅`, the honest rendering of "undefined"; there is no default element.

So on homogeneous classes the Lean set is May's product plus the translates obtained by changing `u, v` by cycles of other degrees; it is the same coset of the same indeterminacy, read inside total cohomology rather than one degree. May's product differs from the values here by a global sign `(−1)^{|y|+1}`, which does not change the set's role (it is a coset through a point, and `−1` preserves the indeterminacy).

**Conventions.** `noncomputable` only reflects the quotient; no choice of contraction or representative enters the definition, so the set is intrinsic to `𝒜`. No junk values: nothing is divided or counted. Over the zero ring everything is `0`, harmlessly.

**The hypotheses.** `[CommRing R]` is any commutative ring. `AA` is an `A∞`-algebra on `A` and `MM` a right `A∞`-module on `M`: a square-zero degree-one coderivation on the cofree bar comodule `sM ⊗ Tᶜ(sA)`, which is the usual family of operations `m_n(x, a₁, …, a_{n−1})` of degree `2 − n` with the module Stasheff identities; the operations are indexed with the module input first, so `MM.m 2 x ![e]` is `m₂(x, e)`, and `![e]` is just the one-entry tuple. `he : AA.StrictUnit e` ([Unit.lean#L44](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Algebra/Unit.lean#L44)) is Keller's strict unit: `e` has degree `0`, is a two-sided unit for `m₂`, and every `m_n` with `n ≠ 2` vanishes when an input is `e` (so `m₁ e = 0`). `hM` asks only that `e` be a right unit for the binary module operation; nothing is assumed about higher module operations with `e` among their inputs, so the module need not be strictly unital, which is weaker than Keller's standing assumption and is all the proof uses. The three types sit in one universe `u` because the morphism complex is formed in Mathlib's category of `R`-modules; this is bookkeeping only.

**The two complexes.** `AA.toRightModule` is `A` as the free right module of rank one over itself, with the algebra's own operations (`m_toRightModule`). `homComplex AA.toRightModule MM` is the morphism complex `Hom(A, M)` of the DG category of right `A∞`-modules: in degree `p`, the comodule maps `sA ⊗ Tᶜ(sA) → sM ⊗ Tᶜ(sA)` of degree `p`, which by cofreeness are the families `(a₀, a₁, …, aₙ) ↦ f_{n+1}(a₀, …, aₙ)` of all arities, with differential the graded commutator with the two bar differentials. Its degree-zero cocycles are the `A∞`-module morphisms, and its degree `−1` cochains bounding `f − g` are the homotopies. `MM.cochainComplex` is the underlying complex `(M, m₁)` with the module's grading ([Right/Cohomology.lean#L88](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Homology/AInfinity/Module/Right/Cohomology.lean#L88)).

**What the conclusion is.** Mathlib's `HomotopyEquiv` ([Homotopy.lean#L740](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97/Mathlib/Algebra/Homology/Homotopy.lean#L740)) is data: a chain map each way and homotopies from both composites to the identities. So the declaration does not merely say the two complexes are homotopy equivalent (which would be weak content), it says which maps: `hom` is evaluation at `e`, sending a cochain `F` to `f₁(e)`, and `inv` is the Yoneda map `x ↦ (a₁, …, aₙ) ↦ m_{n+1}(x, a₁, …, aₙ)` with Koszul signs. The composite `inv ≫ hom` is the identity on the nose, by `m₂(x, e) = x`, and `hom ≫ inv` is homotopic to the identity through the contracting homotopy "prepend `e`". In particular evaluation at `e` induces an isomorphism `H*(Hom(A, M)) ≅ H*(M)`, the Yoneda lemma proper (`quasiIso_yonedaEval` just below). It is not an isomorphism of complexes, unlike the DG case, because a morphism out of `A` has higher components not determined by its value at `e`; the statement claims exactly the homotopy equivalence.

**Conventions.** `≫` is diagrammatic composition; `Homotopy.ofEq` is the trivial homotopy of an equality. No junk values, no flatness, and no completeness: tensor words are finite, so every sum is finite, which is why any commutative ring is allowed.

**Not vacuous.** Any unital DG algebra over `R`, viewed as an `A∞`-algebra with `m_n = 0` for `n ≥ 3` and `e = 1`, with any DG module `M` over it (for instance `M = A`), satisfies every hypothesis.

**Where the field lives, and why "separable" is not written.** Mathlib's `SeparableClosure K` is the subfield of separable elements of an algebraic closure of `K`; it is separably closed and separable over `K`. An `IntermediateField K (SeparableClosure K)` is a subfield `L` with `K ⊆ L ⊆ K^sep`, and `↥L` just means "`L` regarded as a field". Any subfield of a separable extension is separable over `K` (`isSeparable_tower_bot`), which is why the name says `isSeparable` although no separability hypothesis appears in the text. Conversely every finite separable extension of `K` embeds into `K^sep`, so quantifying over subfields of `K^sep` loses nothing against the textbook form "some finite separable extension".

The size `n` is existential in the definition but forced to be `deg A = √dim_K A` for central simple `A` (`isSplittingField_iff_deg`). `FiniteDimensional K ↥L` is `[L:K] < ∞`, so the conclusion is exactly "a finite separable splitting field exists"; the theorem is pure existence, with no canonical or minimal choice.

**The hypotheses.** `[Field K]` is any field, perfect or not. `[DivisionRing D] [Algebra K D]` is a (possibly noncommutative) division algebra over `K`; `[FiniteDimensional K D]` is `dim_K D < ∞`; `[Algebra.IsCentral K D]` says the centre of `D` is contained in the image of `K`, which, since `K` is a field, means the centre is exactly `K`. A division ring is automatically a simple ring, so the square-dimension theorem applies to `D` without being assumed.

**The object produced.** `L : Subalgebra K D` is a `K`-subalgebra of `D`; `↥L` is it regarded as a ring. `IsField ↥L` is a proposition, not extra structure: `L` is commutative, has `0 ≠ 1`, and every nonzero element has an inverse in `L`. Inside a division ring this says `L` is a subfield in the ordinary sense. `Algebra.IsSeparable K ↥L` says every element of `L` has separable minimal polynomial over `K` (Mathlib: coprime to its derivative), i.e. `L/K` is a separable extension. `Module.finrank K ↥L = deg K D` says `[L:K] = deg D`, where `deg D` is the square root of `dim_K D`, meaningful by `deg_sq` since that dimension is a square.

**Why this is "maximal subfield".** The word maximal does not appear; the degree equality carries it. A subfield `L ⊆ D` with `[L:K] = deg D` admits no larger subfield of `D` (`bijective_of_finrank_eq_deg`), and conversely every maximal subfield of a central division algebra has degree `deg D` by the double centraliser theorem, so the statement is the textbook one. It is existence only: no canonical `L`, and nothing is said about other maximal subfields, which may be inseparable.

**No junk values.** `finrank` is `0` only for infinite-dimensional spaces, impossible for `L ⊆ D`; `deg` is a rounded square root, harmless here as the Codex review explains.

**Not vacuous.** `D = ℍ`, `K = ℝ`: `L = ℂ` is a separable subfield of degree `2 = deg ℍ`. `D = K` gives `L = K` with degree `1`. The content is in characteristic `p`: for a central division algebra over `K = 𝔽_p(t)` a purely inseparable maximal subfield may exist, and the theorem still produces a separable one, by Jacobson–Noether.

**The diagrams.** `BrauerDiagram k` is `PerfectMatching (Fin k ⊕ Fin k)`: a permutation `f` of the `2k` boundary points with `f (f a) = a` and `f a ≠ a`, i.e. a fixed-point-free involution, which is the same thing as a perfect matching of the `k` bottom points (`Sum.inl`) with the `k` top points (`Sum.inr`). A diagram is a matching and nothing more, as in the classical definition: no isotopy class or planar picture is part of the data, so crossings carry no information. `Fin k` is `{0, …, k−1}`, and its indices are only matched, never added, so no modular arithmetic is in play. There are `(2k−1)‼` diagrams (`card_brauerDiagram`, with an example checking `3` on two strands); `Nat.doubleFactorial` is defined by `0‼ = 1‼ = 1`, `(n+2)‼ = (n+2)·n‼`, the classical count.

**The algebra.** `BrauerDiagram k →₀ R` is Mathlib's finitely supported functions, the free `R`-module with the diagrams as basis, and `coeff` reads off coordinates. The product is `mulCoeff`, the bilinear extension of `D₁ · D₂ = δ^c · (D₁ ∘ D₂)`: `composeDiagram D₁ D₂` is the matching read off by following strands through the middle, and `middleLoopCount D₁ D₂` counts the closed middle loops by their least middle point, as `Set.ncard` of a subset of the finite set `Fin k`, so no infinite-set junk value can arise. `δ ^ c` is a natural-number power in `R` with `δ⁰ = 1`, so a loop-free stack is weighted by `1`. The unit is the identity diagram `permToBrauer 1`. Mathlib's `Algebra R` instance means `R` acts centrally, so `B_k(δ)` is an `R`-algebra in the ordinary sense; associativity and the unit laws are discharged by the combinatorial lemmas `composeDiagram_assoc` and `middleLoopCount_add_middleLoopCount_composeDiagram`. Permutation diagrams compose as permutations and close no loop (`composeDiagram_permToBrauer`, `middleLoopCount_permToBrauer_left`), which is why `R[S_k]` embeds (`ofPerm_injective`).

**The rank.** `finrank_eq_doubleFactorial` needs `[StrongRankCondition R]`, which holds for every nontrivial commutative ring; without it `Module.finrank` could read `0`, but the basis `basis R δ k` is there regardless.

The annotation `BrauerGroup.{u, u}` says the algebras have carriers in the same universe as `K`; every finite-dimensional `K`-algebra is isomorphic to one there (a subalgebra of a matrix algebra over `K`), so a reader may ignore it. `[Field K]` is any field, of any characteristic.

**The witness.** A `GaloisCocycle K` packages four things: an intermediate field `L` of `SeparableClosure K` (Mathlib's separable closure of `K` inside its algebraic closure, so `L/K` is separable algebraic with a fixed embedding into `Kˢ`); a proof of `FiniteDimensional K L`, i.e. `[L : K] < ∞`; a proof of `IsGalois K L`, which in Mathlib is "separable and normal"; and `cocycle : TwoCocycle K L`, a function `c : Gal(L/K) × Gal(L/K) → Lˣ` satisfying Mathlib's `groupCohomology.IsMulCocycle₂`, `c(στ, ρ)·c(σ, τ) = σ(c(τ, ρ))·c(σ, τρ)`, the inhomogeneous 2-cocycle identity of Gille–Szamuely and Serre. Here `L ≃ₐ[K] L` is the full automorphism group, which is `Gal(L/K)` because `L/K` is Galois.

**The conclusion.** `g.brauerClass` is by definition (`brauerClass_def`) the class of the crossed product of `c`: `⊕_σ L·u_σ` with `u_σ x = σ(x) u_σ` and `u_σ u_τ = c(σ, τ) u_{στ}` (`basis_mul_inc`, `basis_mul_basis`), proved central simple of dimension `[L : K]²` elsewhere so that it is an element of `CSA K`. `∃ g, g.brauerClass = x` is plain existence: some finite Galois `L ⊆ Kˢ` and some cocycle on it. No uniqueness and no control of `L` is asserted, and none holds: cohomologous cocycles (`crossedProductClass_eq_of_cohomologous`) and inflations to a larger Galois field (`crossedProductClass_comap`) give the same class. So the theorem is exactly "every element of `Br(K)` is a crossed-product class", i.e. `Br(K) = ⋃_L Br(L/K)` with each `Br(L/K)` covered by `H²(Gal(L/K), Lˣ)`.

**The conclusion.** There are `n` and a basis `b₀, …, b_{n−1}` of `M` (necessarily `n = dim M`) such that the coefficient matrix `(c_{ij})` of `ρ` in this basis, defined by `ρ(b_j) = Σ_i b_i ⊗ c_{ij}`, has `c_{ij} = 0` whenever `j < i` (Mathlib's `IsUpperTriangular` is `BlockTriangular id`, "entries below the diagonal vanish") and has diagonal entries that are group-like. A point `g ∈ G(A)` acts on `M ⊗ A` by the matrix `(g(c_{ij}))`, so the statement says: in a suitable basis every point of `G`, over every ring of values and not only `k`-points, acts by an upper triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the values of characters `χ_i : G → 𝔾ₘ`. This is Lie–Kolchin for the group scheme `G`, slightly stronger than Humphreys' statement about `G(k)`.

The sum is finite because `ad x_α` is nilpotent, and each `(ad x_α)ⁿ/n!` preserves `L_ℤ` (Kostant), so the operator is defined over `A` without dividing by `n!` in `A`. The zero weight contributes `x_0 = 1` (`adjointRootSubgroup_eq_one_of_isZero`), so the generators are the root subgroups of the nonzero roots only, as in Carter's `E(K) = ⟨x_r(t) : r ∈ Φ, t ∈ K⟩`.

Correctly stated; compared with Keller, *Introduction to A-infinity algebras and modules*, §3.1, and the "Cohomological grading and Koszul signs" convention and Layer 1 of TauCetiRoadmap/DGAInfinity, which lists no tagged Check for it (the site's four named tests pass).

**What the inputs are.** `R` is any commutative ring and `A` any associative unital ring that is an `R`-algebra. `𝒜 : ℤ → Submodule R A` is a family of `R`-submodules `A^p`, one for each integer, and `[GradedAlgebra 𝒜]` (Mathlib's `GradedRing` for submodules) is the hypothesis that they form an internal grading: `A` is the internal direct sum `⨁_p A^p` (`DirectSum.Decomposition` carries the decomposition map with its two-sided inverse, so every element has unique homogeneous components), `1 ∈ A^0` and `A^p · A^q ⊆ A^{p+q}` (`SetLike.GradedMonoid`). `d : A →ₗ[R] A` is a single `R`-linear endomorphism of the whole carrier rather than a family of maps `A^p → A^{p+1}`; the first axiom, `map_mem`, is what makes it homogeneous of degree `+1`, so the two presentations agree.

**What the predicate says.** `IsDGAlgebra` is a `structure … : Prop`, so it is a property of the triple `(A, 𝒜, d)` and involves no choice. Its three fields are exactly Keller's axioms: `d(A^p) ⊆ A^{p+1}`, `d² = 0`, and `d(ab) = d(a)b + (−1)^p a d(b)` for `a ∈ A^p`. The sign is `Int.negOnePow p = (−1)^p` as a unit of `ℤ`, defined for every integer `p` with `(−1)^p = (−1)^{|p|}`; a unit `u` acts on `A` by `u • x = (u : ℤ) • x` (`Units.smul_def`), so the term is `±(a d(b))` with no hidden factor. `d² = 0` is required for every `a`, not only homogeneous `a`; by linearity the two are equivalent.

**Hidden generality that is harmless.** Nothing bounds the grading above or below, `R` may be `ℤ` (so DG rings are included), and `A` may be the zero ring, which is a DG algebra under every convention. There is no separate axiom `d(1) = 0`, because it follows, as the file proves without dividing by `2`.

**Not vacuous.** Beyond the ground ring with zero differential, the Koszul complex of an element `r ∈ R` qualifies: `A = R[ε]/(ε²)` with `ε` in degree `−1`, `d(ε) = r`, `d(1) = 0`; the Leibniz rule for `a = b = ε` reads `0 = rε + (−1)^{−1} εr`, which holds.
