Correctly stated; compared with May, *Simplicial Objects in Algebraic Topology*, Chapter I §3, and with item 2 of Stage 8 of `TauCetiRoadmap/AlgebraicTopology/README.md`, which lists no tagged Check for this definition; the four named tests the site lists pass.

**The inputs.** `X : SSet` is any simplicial set, `x : X _⦋0⦌` one of its vertices (its `0`-simplices, written through the opposite simplex category), and `n` any natural number, including `0`. No Kan hypothesis is part of the definition; see below for why that is harmless.

**The objects classified.** A *pointed `n`-simplex* (Mathlib's `X.PtSimplex n x`, the type being quotiented) is a map `Δ[n] → X` agreeing on the boundary `∂Δ[n]` with the constant map at `x`; by Yoneda, an `n`-simplex all of whose faces are the degenerate simplex on `x`, May's spherical simplex. `Subcomplex.ofSimplex x` is the subcomplex generated by the vertex `x`, containing only its degeneracies, and `const` the constant map into it: this is "sending `∂Δ[n]` to `x`".

**The relation.** Two pointed simplices are identified when joined by a homotopy `Δ[n] × Δ[1] → X` constant at `x` on `∂Δ[n] × Δ[1]`; the type is a `Quot`, so the identification is the equivalence relation this generates. In a Kan complex with `n ≥ 1` no generation is needed: `mk_eq_mk_iff_nonempty_homotopy` says two classes agree exactly when one such homotopy exists, and `mk_eq_mk_iff` turns that into May's one-simplex condition, an `(n+1)`-simplex having the two simplices as adjacent faces and `x` on all others. Whichever adjacent pair of face positions a source uses, `PtSimplex.lean` proves all give the same relation in a Kan complex, so that is a convention. Every class comes from a pointed simplex (`mk_surjective`).

**What is, and is not, asserted.** `π n X x` is a *type* with a distinguished element `1`, the constant simplex. The group law of the classical `π_n`, `n ≥ 1`, is the separate instance `π.group`, available only under `[KanComplex X]`; the order in which it multiplies is a convention changing at most the group into its opposite, which inversion identifies with it. For `n = 0` the boundary `∂Δ[0]` is empty, so `π 0 X x` is the vertices modulo the relation generated by edges, the set of components, with `x` only marking one.

**Outside the classical domain.** May defines `π_n` only for Kan complexes. For non-Kan `X` the type exists but need not be the homotopy of the realisation: in `∂Δ[2]`, a simplicial circle, the only pointed `1`-simplex at a vertex is degenerate, so `π 1` has one element. This is Mathlib's style of total definition; every result using `π` as a homotopy group assumes `[KanComplex X]`.

**Not vacuous.** The singular simplicial set of a space `T` is a Kan complex (`TopCat.kanComplex_toSSet_obj`), and `TopCat.toSSetPiEquivHomotopyGroup` identifies its `π (n+1)` with the topological `π_{n+1}(T, t)`; for the circle, `ℤ` in degree one.

Correctly stated; compared with Hatcher §1.3 (covering spaces as permutation representations of `π₁`, and the classification theorem 1.38) and Stage 2, item 8 of TauCetiRoadmap/UniversalCovers ("alternative lens"), which lists no tagged Check for it; the named tests the site lists are not repeated here. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The hypotheses are Hatcher's three.** `[PathConnectedSpace X]` is Mathlib's class: `X` is nonempty and any two points are joined by a path. `[LocallyPathConnectedSpace X]` says every point has a neighbourhood basis of path-connected sets. `[SemilocallySimplyConnectedSpace X]` is Tau Ceti's own class (not yet in Mathlib): every point `x` has a neighbourhood `U` such that every loop in `U` based at `x` is null-homotopic in `X`, the null-homotopy being allowed to leave `U`; this is exactly Hatcher's "π₁(U,x) → π₁(X,x) is trivial". All three are square-bracket hypotheses, found by Lean automatically, and together they are the standing assumptions under which Hatcher proves the classification.

**The left side.** `ConnectedCoveringSpace X` is the category whose objects are covering maps `p : E → X` in Mathlib's sense (`IsCoveringMap`: each point of `X` has an open neighbourhood `U` with `p⁻¹(U)` homeomorphic over `U` to `U × (fibre)`, the fibre discrete) with `E` connected in Mathlib's sense, which includes `E ≠ ∅`; morphisms are continuous maps commuting with the projections. Mathlib's `IsCoveringMap` does not demand surjectivity, so a covering map may have empty fibres in general, but over a path-connected base a connected cover has every fibre nonempty (`nonempty_fiber`), so these are precisely Hatcher's connected covering spaces.

**The right side.** A `FundamentalGroupoid X ⥤ Type u` is a set `F(x)` for each point `x` and a bijection `F(x) → F(y)` for each homotopy class of paths from `x` to `y`, compatible with concatenation; a morphism is a natural transformation, i.e. a family of maps commuting with path transport. "Fibrewise transitive" adds that each `F(x)` is nonempty and `π₁(X,x)` acts transitively on it. Mathlib's `monodromyFunctor` sends a class `[γ]` to the map "endpoint of the lift of `γ` starting at `e`", so the forward functor is the usual monodromy representation.

**What `≌` asserts.** A `CategoryTheory.Equivalence` is a functor together with a quasi-inverse and natural isomorphisms unit and counit, so the statement is a genuine equivalence of categories, not merely a bijection on isomorphism classes; deck transformations therefore match automorphisms of the action. The quasi-inverse is produced from fully faithful plus essentially surjective (`asEquivalence`), hence is chosen, but it is unique up to unique natural isomorphism, and the content is in the forward functor, which `monodromyEquivalence_functor` pins to `transitiveMonodromyFunctor` by definition.

**Not vacuous.** The circle `S¹` satisfies all three hypotheses; its connected covers are `ℝ → S¹` and `z ↦ zⁿ` for `n ≥ 1`, and `π₁ = ℤ` has exactly the transitive sets `ℤ` and `ℤ/nℤ`, matched in that order.

**What "oriented" means here.** `o : HomologicalOrientation M E n` is a function assigning to each point `x` a *local orientation*: an element `o x` of the local homology group `Hₙ(M, M ∖ {x}; ℤ)` of which every class of that group is an integer multiple (`IsLocalOrientation`), such that transporting `o x` along any path class from `x` to `y` gives `o y`. Transport is computed through balls in charts, so this is Hatcher's local consistency condition, and in degree `n = dim E` the local group is a copy of `ℤ` (`singularHomologyComplSingletonFinrankIso`), so `o x` is one of its two generators. The side condition `hn : finrank ℝ E = n` cannot be dropped: where the local group is `0`, its zero element "generates" it, so an orientation in the wrong degree is a vacuous datum.

**The homology group.** `TopCat.toSSet.obj M` is the singular simplicial set of `M` (its `k`-simplices are the continuous maps from the standard `k`-simplex), and `SSet.homology … n` is the `n`-th homology of its alternating-face-map chain complex with coefficients in `ULift ℤ`, which is `ℤ` moved to another universe level; so the right side is ordinary singular homology `Hₙ(M; ℤ)`. The leading `↑` only turns the object of the category of `ℤ`-modules into the set of its elements. `ChartedSpace E M` is an atlas of homeomorphisms from open subsets of `M` onto open subsets of `E`, a manifold without boundary; no second countability is assumed and none is needed, compactness doing its work.

**What the conclusion asserts.** `ℤ ≃ₗ[ℤ] …` is a `ℤ`-linear bijection, that is an isomorphism of abelian groups, and a definite one: `fundamentalClassEquiv_apply` shows it is `c ↦ c • [M]`, where `[M] = o.fundamentalClass hn` is the unique class restricting to `o x` at every `x` (`eq_fundamentalClass`). So the statement is "the fundamental class freely generates `Hₙ(M; ℤ)`", not merely "`Hₙ(M; ℤ) ≅ ℤ`".

**Not vacuous.** The 2-sphere in `ℝ³` with Mathlib's chart structure over `ℝ²` is compact, connected, Hausdorff and simply connected, so `ofSimplyConnectedSpace` extends either generator at one point to an orientation, and the statement gives `H₂(S²; ℤ) ≅ ℤ`; the circle gives `H₁(S¹; ℤ) ≅ ℤ`. A non-orientable manifold such as `ℝP²` admits no `o`, so the statement is silent about it, in agreement with `H₂(ℝP²; ℤ) = 0`. The universe choices (`Type`, `ULift.{0}`) are implementation detail and carry no mathematical content.

**Hypotheses.** The three square-bracket classes are found automatically: `PathConnectedSpace` (nonempty, any two points joined by a path), `LocallyPathConnectedSpace` (a basis of path-connected neighbourhoods at every point), and Tau Ceti's `SemilocallySimplyConnectedSpace` (every point has a neighbourhood whose loops are null-homotopic in `X`). These are exactly the standing hypotheses under which the classification of covers holds, and the only ones.

**The group on the left, and its multiplication order.** Mathlib's `FundamentalGroup X x₀` is the vertex group of the fundamental groupoid at `x₀`: homotopy classes of loops at `x₀`. Its product is the categorical `End` product, `g * h = h ≫ g`, i.e. "`h` then `g`", the reverse of Hatcher's `[γ][δ] = γ·δ`. This reversal is harmless and in fact required: transport along "`h` then `g`" is transport along `g` after transport along `h`, so with this order monodromy is an honest left action, `(g * h) • e = g • (h • e)`, and no opposite group appears. The group `Aut` on the right multiplies by the same rule (`y` then `x`), so `≃*`, a bijection preserving products, is a group isomorphism in the ordinary sense; and as every group is isomorphic to its opposite by inversion, the abstract group is Hatcher's `π₁(X, x₀)` either way.

**The group on the right.** `fiberFunctor x₀` sends a covering space `p : E → X` (any cover in Mathlib's sense, connected or not, finite or not, including the empty cover and the trivial cover `X → X`) to the set `p⁻¹(x₀)`, and a map of covers to its restriction to fibres. `Aut (fiberFunctor x₀)` is the group of natural isomorphisms of this functor with itself: a bijection of `p⁻¹(x₀)` for every cover `p`, compatible with every map of covers. So the statement reads: `π₁(X, x₀)` is precisely the group of all such compatible families, a loop class acting by transporting each fibre along itself. On the empty and trivial covers every family acts trivially, which costs nothing.

**Not vacuous, with a check by two routes.** For `X = S¹`, `x₀ = 1`: `π₁ = ℤ`, and the statement says the compatible families of fibre bijections form `ℤ`, the generator translating the fibre `ℤ` of `exp : ℝ → S¹` by one and rotating the fibre `μₙ` of `z ↦ zⁿ` by `e^{2πi/n}`. Independently, by Tannaka duality a natural automorphism of the forgetful functor on `ℤ`-sets is determined by where it sends `0` in the regular `ℤ`-set, giving `ℤ` again. Restricting to finite covers would instead give `ẑ`, which is why the functor is taken on all covers.

**Hypotheses.** The three square-bracket classes are found automatically and mean: `PathConnectedSpace`, `X` is nonempty and any two points are joined by a path; `LocallyPathConnectedSpace`, every point has a basis of path-connected neighbourhoods; `SemilocallySimplyConnectedSpace` (Tau Ceti's class, Hatcher's definition), every point has a neighbourhood all of whose loops at that point are null-homotopic in `X`. They are the classical hypotheses, and nothing is assumed about the covers.

**The left side.** `CoveringSpace X` is the category of covering maps `p : E → X` in Mathlib's sense (`IsCoveringMap`: every point of `X` has an open neighbourhood `U` with `p⁻¹(U)` homeomorphic over `U` to `U × (fibre)`, the fibre discrete), with continuous maps over `X` as morphisms. Mathlib does not require surjectivity, so the empty cover, disconnected covers, and covers with fibres of different sizes over different points are all objects, as in Hatcher, who also permits an empty union of sheets. An isomorphism in this category is a homeomorphism over `X` (`isIso_iff_isHomeomorph_left`), so "equivalence" below means the usual isomorphism of covers.

**The right side.** `FundamentalGroupoid X` has the points of `X` as objects and homotopy classes of paths rel endpoints as morphisms, composed by concatenation. A functor to `Type u` is a set `F(x)` for every point and a bijection `F(x) → F(y)` for every path class, compatible with concatenation; a morphism is a family of maps commuting with transport. These are the "π₁-sets" of the classification with no basepoint chosen; nothing requires nonemptiness or transitivity, matching the left side.

**What `≌` says and which functor.** A `CategoryTheory.Equivalence` is a functor with a quasi-inverse and natural isomorphisms unit and counit, so this is an equivalence of categories, not just a bijection on isomorphism classes. The forward functor is Mathlib's `IsCoveringMap.monodromyFunctor`: a cover goes to `x ↦ p⁻¹(x)`, and a path class to "endpoint of the lift starting at `e`", well defined by homotopy lifting. The quasi-inverse is built from fully faithful plus essentially surjective (`asEquivalence`) and so is chosen, but any two choices are uniquely naturally isomorphic.

**Universes.** `Type u` is the universe of `X`'s points; the fibres of a cover of `X` live there, so no functor is excluded by size.

**Not vacuous.** For `X = S¹`, functors from its fundamental groupoid are, up to equivalence, `ℤ`-sets: `ℤ ⊔ ℤ/2` corresponds to the disconnected cover `ℝ ⊔ S¹ → S¹` (`exp` and `z ↦ z²`), the empty set to the empty cover, and a one-point set to `S¹ → S¹` itself.

Correctly stated; compared with Eilenberg–Zilber (1953), Weibel §8.5 (Theorem 8.5.1 and the Alexander–Whitney and shuffle formulas there) and item 1 of Stage 5 of `TauCetiRoadmap/AlgebraicTopology/README.md`, which lists no tagged Check; the two named degree-zero tests are as listed in the Codex review.

**The coefficient category.** The square-bracket hypotheses say: `C` is preadditive (Hom-sets are abelian groups, composition bilinear), has coproducts indexed by sets of the universe `w` (needed because `n`-chains are a coproduct of copies of the coefficient object, one per `n`-simplex), carries a tensor product that is additive in each variable (`MonoidalPreadditive`), and tensoring on either side preserves those coproducts, so that `C(K; R) ⊗ C(L; S)` is again a coproduct with one summand `R ⊗ S` per pair of simplices. Modules over a commutative ring `k` with `R = S = k` satisfy all of this, giving the textbook statement; nothing abelian or flat is assumed, so `R` and `S` are arbitrary objects.

**The two complexes.** `K ⊗ L` in `SSet` is the product simplicial set `K × L` (Mathlib's monoidal structure on simplicial sets is the cartesian one). `K.chainComplex R` is Mathlib's *unnormalised* simplicial chain complex: in degree `n` the coproduct of copies of `R` indexed by all `n`-simplices, degenerate ones included, with differential the alternating sum of the face maps (`ιChainComplex_d`). The tensor product of chain complexes is Mathlib's: degree `n` is the sum of `C_p ⊗ D_q` over `p + q = n`, with the Koszul sign `(−1)^p` on the second differential (the `TensorSigns` instance for `ComplexShape.down ℕ` is `ε' p = (−1)^p`), the standard convention.

**What is asserted, and which maps.** `HomotopyEquiv` is not a bare existence statement: it is a structure holding a chain map each way and two chain homotopies, `h` with `f − g = dh + hd`, between each composite and the identity. The forward map is pinned by `eilenbergZilberHomotopyEquiv_hom` to be the Alexander–Whitney map, which on a simplex `(x, y)` of `K × L` is `∑_{p+q=n} x|[0..p] ⊗ y|[p..n]`, front face tensor back face; the inverse is pinned by `eilenbergZilberHomotopyEquiv_inv` to be the shuffle map `x ⊗ y ↦ ∑ ± (s_ν x, s_μ y)` over `(p, q)`-shuffles, built there by a recursion on lattice paths with the usual shuffle sign. Composition `hom ≫ inv` is in diagrammatic order, so the first homotopy is `shuffle ∘ AW ≃ id` on chains of the product, as in Weibel.

**Not an isomorphism, and not vacuous.** For `K = L = Δ[1]` with integer coefficients, `Δ[1]` has `2` vertices and `3` one-simplices (the monotone maps `[1] → [1]`), so the product has `3 · 3 = 9` one-simplices while `(C ⊗ C)_1 = C_0 ⊗ C_1 ⊕ C_1 ⊗ C_0` has rank `2·3 + 3·2 = 12`: the two complexes differ already in degree `1`, so "homotopy equivalence" is the right strength, and the theorem is a genuine statement about these two different complexes. No junk values occur; the universes `w, v, u` are bookkeeping only.

Correctly stated; compared with May, *Simplicial Objects in Algebraic Topology*, Theorem 17.1 (and Definition 1.3 for the extension condition), Goerss–Jardine Lemma I.3.4, and the `simplicialGroupKan` item of Stage 8.2 of `TauCetiRoadmap/AlgebraicTopology/README.md`; Checks: as listed in the Codex review.

**How "simplicial group" is encoded.** The input is a simplicial set `X` together with two things. `[∀ n, Group (X.obj n)]` gives, for every object `n` of the opposite simplex category, that is for every degree, a group structure on the set `X_n` of `n`-simplices; the square brackets mean Lean finds it automatically, and it is data, not merely the existence of some group law. `hX` says that for every morphism `f` of the simplex category, so for every face, every degeneracy and every composite of them, the induced map `X.map f : X_m → X_n` is multiplicative (`ConcreteCategory.hom` is only the coercion of a morphism of sets to a function). This is an unbundled version of a functor `Δᵒᵖ → Grp`, and it is equivalent to one: the instance `kanComplex_comp_forget_grpCat` in the same file derives the Kan property of the underlying simplicial set of any Mathlib simplicial object in `GrpCat` from this theorem. So the hypothesis is exactly May's "group complex" and nothing weaker.

**What the conclusion asserts.** `X.KanComplex` is Mathlib's abbreviation for `IsFibrant X`: the map to the point has the right lifting property against every horn inclusion `Λ[n+1, i] ↪ Δ[n+1]`, `n ≥ 0`, `0 ≤ i ≤ n+1`. By `KanComplex.iff` this is May's extension condition: any family of `n`-simplices indexed by the faces `j ≠ i` whose faces match where they must (`horn.IsCompatible`) are the faces of some `(n+1)`-simplex. It is a proposition, so no filler is chosen or claimed unique, and all horns, inner and outer, are included.

**Generality.** No commutativity, finiteness, connectedness or further naturality is required, and the group structures in different degrees are tied together only through `hX`. The additive form `kanComplex_of_addGroup` covers simplicial abelian groups and modules by passing to `Multiplicative`.

**Not vacuous, and not trivial.** The constant simplicial set on a group satisfies the hypotheses, but a better instance is the free abelian group on a simplicial set that is not itself Kan: `Δ[1]` fails the extension condition for the horn `Λ[2, 0]` made of the edges `(0,1)` and `(0,0)` (a filler `a ≤ b ≤ c` would need `b = 1` and `c = 0`), while `ℤΔ[1]`, with `ℤ[X_n]` in degree `n` and the face and degeneracy maps extended linearly, is a simplicial abelian group, hence Kan by this theorem. The one-dimensional case `n = 0`, where a horn is a single vertex, is covered too, as the source shows.

**The hypotheses.** `F` is any topological space (no Hausdorff, compactness or CW condition) and `φ : F ≃ₜ F` a homeomorphism. Hatcher allows any continuous self-map; the quotient by a ℤ-action used here needs `φ` invertible, so this is Hatcher's case of a homeomorphism, as the docstring says. The coefficients `R` are an object of an abelian category `A` with coproducts indexed by sets as large as `F` (`[HasCoproducts A]`, `[Abelian A]`); `A` the abelian groups and `R = ℤ` gives ordinary integral singular homology.

**The spaces and complexes.** `MappingTorus φ` is `F × ℝ` modulo `(x, t) ∼ (φ x, t + 1)` (Hatcher's `(x, 0) ∼ (f x, 1)`, with `f = φ`). `singularChainComplexFunctor` applied to `R` and a space `X` (`↧X` packages `X` as an object of the category of spaces) is the complex whose degree-`n` term is the direct sum of copies of `R` indexed by continuous maps from the standard `n`-simplex to `X`, with the alternating-face differential; `homology … n` is its `n`-th homology. The three terms are `Hₙ(F)`, `Hₙ(F)`, `Hₙ(T_φ)`, for every `n ≥ 0`.

**The two maps.** `wangEndomorphism φ R` is the chain map `id − C(φ)`; on `Hₙ` it induces `1 − φ_*` (`homologyMap_wangEndomorphism`). `fibreInclusionChainMap` is induced by `x ↦ [(x, 0)]`, the fibre at height `0`.

**What `Exact` asserts.** `ShortComplex.mk f g _` is the pair of maps with the proof `g ∘ f = 0` (the `by simp` in the signature is only that proof). `ShortComplex.Exact` means the homology at the middle term vanishes: image of `1 − φ_*` equals kernel of the fibre inclusion (Mathlib's `moduleCat_exact_iff_range_eq_ker`; the file's `ker_homologyMap_fibreInclusionChainMap` restates the theorem that way). Exactness does not see the sign `1 − φ_*` versus `φ_* − 1`, both having the same image; the sign matters only for the connecting map, absent here.

**A concrete instance.** `F` the circle, `φ` complex conjugation, `R = ℤ`, `n = 1`: `T_φ` is the Klein bottle. `φ_* = −1` on `H₁(S¹) = ℤ`, so `1 − φ_*` is multiplication by `2`, image `2ℤ`. From `π₁ = ⟨a, t | t a t⁻¹ = a⁻¹⟩` with `a` the fibre loop, `H₁(K) = ℤ ⊕ ℤ/2` with the fibre class generating the `ℤ/2`, so the kernel of the fibre inclusion is `2ℤ` too. For `φ = id` (the torus) `1 − φ_*` is zero, so the fibre circle injects on `H₁`, as it does.

Its inputs are a topological space `B` (`[TopologicalSpace B]` is a hypothesis Lean fills in itself; no Hausdorff or other separation axiom is assumed, and the source assumes none), a point `b`, and a commutative ring `R` of coefficients (the source takes `R = ℤ`, but Definition 1.8 reads verbatim over any commutative ring). The rendered type `Type (max …)` is the type of objects; the category structure, with morphisms the degree-zero `R`-linear maps commuting with the action and the differentials, is an instance found automatically. The universe parameters are harmless.

**The coefficient algebra is the source's.** `loopChain_isDGAlgebra B b R` is the proof that `⨁ₙ C^□_n(Ω_b B; R)`, the normalized cubical chains of the Moore loop space with the Pontryagin product, is a DG algebra; its name is used as the token that pins the algebra, grading and differential. "Normalized" means chains modulo the degenerate cubes ([`NormalizedCubicalChain`](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/AlgebraicTopology/Singular/Cubical/Normalized.lean#L204)). **Module grading.** The module grading is a decomposition indexed by all of `ℤ`, with no boundedness imposed, matching the source's unqualified "chain complex `F_*`"; Tau Ceti's cohomological indexing (`C_n` in degree `−n`) is the usual relabelling and changes no sign.

The degree-zero objects are exactly the classical local systems (`classicalDGLocalSystemEquivalence` in `Classical/EssImage.lean`).

**What `GaloisCategory` asserts.** Mathlib's `GaloisCategory C` is a proposition: `C` has a terminal object and pullbacks (G1), finite coproducts and quotients by finite groups (G2; Mathlib phrases the quotient of an object by a finite group `G` as a colimit of shape `SingleObj G`, i.e. the coequaliser of a `G`-action), every monomorphism is an isomorphism onto a direct summand (G3), and *there exists* a functor `F : C ⥤ FintypeCat` to finite sets that preserves terminal objects and pullbacks (G4), finite coproducts, epimorphisms and finite quotients (G5), and reflects isomorphisms (G6). Since it is a proposition, this instance says only that some fibre functor exists; which one is the companion `instFiberFunctor`: the fibre over `x₀`. An `instance` is a fact Lean supplies automatically whenever the hypotheses hold.

**The category.** `FiniteCoveringSpace X` is the full subcategory of spaces over `X` whose objects are covering maps `p : E → X` with every fibre `p⁻¹{x}` finite, and whose morphisms are continuous maps over `X`. Mathlib's `IsCoveringMap p` is the classical notion: every point of `X` has an open neighbourhood `U` with `p⁻¹U ≅ U × I` over `U` for a discrete `I`. No surjectivity is required, so `I` may be empty; this is not a defect but what (G2) needs, since the initial object is the empty cover. `X : TopCat` is a bundled topological space, in the universe in which the finite sets of the fibre functor also live.

**The hypotheses are necessary, not conveniences.** `[PathConnectedSpace X]` is Mathlib's "nonempty, and any two points are joined by a path"; `[LocallyPathConnectedSpace X]`, "every point has a neighbourhood basis of path-connected sets"; `[SemilocallySimplyConnectedSpace X]` is Tau Ceti's class, "every point `x` has a neighbourhood `U` such that every loop at `x` inside `U` is null-homotopic in `X`" (Hatcher §1.3). These are the hypotheses of the classification of covering spaces, which the proof transports along, and the first cannot be dropped: for the two-point discrete space, finite covers are pairs of finite sets, the terminal object `1 = (pt, pt)` is the coproduct of `A = (pt, ∅)` and `B = (∅, pt)`, so by (G4), (G5) a fibre functor sends one of `A`, `B` to a singleton and the other to `∅`; then `A → 1` (say) is a monomorphism that `F` sends to a bijection without being an isomorphism, against (G6). So no fibre functor exists there.

**Not vacuous.** For `X = S¹`, the category is equivalent to finite `ℤ`-sets; the identity cover is the terminal object, and the connected `n`-fold cover `z ↦ zⁿ` has fibre the `n` roots of unity over `1`.

Correctly stated; compared with its docstring, Stage 4, item 14 of TauCetiRoadmap/UniversalCovers (recognition of `K(G, 1)` spaces, which tags no Check; the circle and torus examples are as listed in the Codex review) and Hatcher §1.B. A reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**What the predicate says.** `IsAspherical X x` is a property, not a structure carrying data: a topological space `X` with a chosen point `x` is aspherical when `X` is path-connected and `πₙ(X, x)` has exactly one element for every `n ≥ 2`. The quantifier `∀ n : ℕ, … (n + 2)` ranges over `2, 3, 4, …`, since Lean's naturals start at `0`; `π₁` and `π₀` are untouched.

**What `π_ n X x` is in Mathlib.** `HomotopyGroup (Fin n) X x` is the set of continuous maps from the cube `[0,1]ⁿ` to `X` sending the boundary of the cube to `x` (`GenLoop`), modulo homotopy relative to that boundary (`GenLoop.Homotopic`). Collapsing the boundary of the cube gives `Sⁿ`, so this is the classical `πₙ(X, x)`. Mathlib puts the group structure on it for `n ≥ 1` and proves commutativity for `n ≥ 2`, but the definition needs none of that: `Subsingleton` says the quotient has at most one element, and the constant map is always an element, so it says the group is trivial.

**Path-connected.** Mathlib's `PathConnectedSpace X` is "nonempty, and any two points are joined by a path"; nonemptiness is anyway forced by the point `x`.

**Based versus unbased, and which definition of "aspherical".** The textbook notion is unbased; a point enters only because `πₙ` needs one, and `IsAspherical.of_basepoint` shows the property holds at every point once it holds at one, so `IsAspherical X x` is "X is aspherical". Hatcher defines a `K(G, 1)` by a contractible universal cover; for CW complexes that is equivalent to the vanishing of `πₙ` for `n ≥ 2` by Whitehead's theorem, and in general it is stronger. The roadmap target asks for the homotopy-group form (a weakly contractible universal cover makes the space aspherical), and that is what is defined here, with no separation, CW or local-connectedness condition built in; results that need CW type assume it explicitly (`IsAspherical.exists_homotopyEquiv`).

**Not vacuous, not trivial.** The circle satisfies it (`AddCircle.isAspherical`: `πₙ(S¹) = 0` for `n ≥ 2` through the universal cover `ℝ`), with `π₁ ≅ ℤ`, and so does every contractible space. The 2-sphere does not, since `π₂(S²) ≅ ℤ`, so the predicate separates spaces.

**The objects.** Mathlib's `FundamentalGroupoid X` has the points of `X` as objects and, as morphisms `x → y`, homotopy classes rel endpoints of paths from `x` to `y`, with `p ≫ q` meaning "`p` then `q`". `Grpd` is the category of groupoids with functors as morphisms, so a colimit here is a colimit of groupoids, as in Brown. `CechIndex ι` is the set of nonempty finite subsets `s` of the index set, ordered by reverse inclusion (`s ≤ t` iff `t ⊆ s`), and `cechIntersection U s = ⋂_{i ∈ s} U i`; an arrow `s → t` is thus an inclusion of a smaller intersection into a larger one, and `cechDiagram U` sends it to the induced functor between fundamental groupoids. `cechCocone U` has vertex `π(X)` and legs the functors induced by the inclusions `U_s ⊆ X` (`cechInclusion`, which is `Opens.inclusion'`).

**The hypothesis.** `hU : IsOpenCover U` is Mathlib's `⨆ᵢ U i = ⊤`: the open sets cover `X`. Nothing else: `X` is any topological space, and no member or intersection is asked to be connected, nonempty or anything else.

**What `IsColimit` asserts.** It is the universal property, held as data: for every groupoid `Γ` and every family of functors `F_s : π(U_s) → Γ` compatible with the inclusions (`F_s = F_t ∘ incl` whenever `U_s ⊆ U_t` in the diagram), there is exactly one functor `F : π(X) → Γ` with `F ∘ incl_s = F_s` for all `s`. That is precisely "`π(X)` is the colimit of the `π(U_s)`", Brown's form of van Kampen. The `desc` field builds `F` by gluing the legs at singleton indices, the legs at two-element indices being what makes those agree on overlaps; the legs at larger intersections are then automatically matched, so using all finite intersections rather than only pairwise ones is the standard Čech shape and adds no hypothesis. Because the objects of `π(X)` are all points, the statement with fundamental groups follows by restricting to a set of basepoints meeting every component of every intersection (Brown's set `A`); that corollary is not yet derived, as Voyager says.

**Universes and edge cases.** The index set and the space may live in different universes (`ι : Type u`, `X : TopCat.{v}`); harmless. An empty family covers only the empty space, and then both sides are the empty groupoid.

**Not vacuous.** Cover `S¹` by two open arcs `U`, `V`, each contractible, with `U ∩ V` two disjoint arcs. Then `π(U)`, `π(V)` are codiscrete groupoids (one morphism between any two objects) and `π(U ∩ V)` is codiscrete on two components; the colimit of this diagram is Brown's pushout `𝓘 ⊔_{{0,1}} 𝓘`, whose vertex group is the free group on one generator, `ℤ`, agreeing with `π₁(S¹) = ℤ` computed from the covering `ℝ → S¹`. This is the two-arc Check Codex links, and it needs the disconnected-intersection form of the theorem.

**Hatcher's theorem and this statement.** Theorem 1B.8 says the homotopy type of a CW complex `K(G, 1)` is determined by `G`; Hatcher deduces it from Proposition 1B.9, which realises every homomorphism `π₁(X, x₀) → π₁(Y, y₀)` by a pointed map, unique up to pointed homotopy. The Lean statement is the uniqueness theorem with its map pinned down: for any isomorphism `φ` of fundamental groups there is a homotopy equivalence inducing `φ`. It is a little more general than Hatcher in one way and weaker in another: the spaces need only be *of CW type*, and the equivalence is not pointed.

**CW type.** `CWType X` is a property: some classical CW complex (Mathlib's `Topology.CWComplex`, a closed subset of a Hausdorff space built from closed cells with characteristic maps, closure-finite, with the weak topology) is homotopy equivalent to `X`. The complex is not part of the data and the conclusion does not depend on which one. Asphericity and CW type are both homotopy invariant, so this is the correct hypothesis for a homotopy-category statement. `X Y : Type u` puts both spaces in one universe, Lean bookkeeping without content.

**How an unpointed map "induces `φ`".** `X ≃ₕ Y` is a pair of continuous maps with homotopies both ways and no basepoints. `FundamentalGroup.map e.toFun x` is `e_* : π₁(X, x) → π₁(Y, e x)`, the induced homomorphism at the basepoint `e x`, which need not be `y`. `γ : Path (e x) y` is a path from `e x` to `y`, and `fundamentalGroupMulEquivOfPath γ` is Mathlib's change-of-basepoint isomorphism `π₁(Y, e x) ≅ π₁(Y, y)`; unfolding `Iso.conj` and `homCongr`, it sends a loop `a` to `γ⁻¹ · a · γ` in the fundamental groupoid (go back along `γ`, run `a`, return along `γ`), the textbook `β_γ`. So the conclusion reads: there are `e` and `γ` with `β_γ ∘ e_* = φ`. Had `e` been pointed one could take `γ` constant; a path is needed because a homotopy inverse moves basepoints, and prescribing `φ` exactly rather than up to an inner automorphism is the strong, correct form. `≃*` is a group isomorphism, so `φ` ranges over all isomorphisms, and `∃` claims existence only; no canonical choice is asserted.

**Not vacuous.** Take `X = Y` the circle (`AddCircle p`, `p ≠ 0`), of CW type by `finiteCWType_addCircle` and aspherical by `AddCircle.isAspherical`, and `φ` the inversion of `π₁ ≅ ℤ`: the theorem yields a self-homotopy-equivalence of degree `−1`, as reflection is. Or `X` the torus and `Y` Milnor's `classifyingSpace (ℤⁿ)`, which `exists_homotopyEquiv_classifyingSpace` instantiates.

**The two groups.** `PresentedGroup R` is Mathlib's `⟨S | R⟩`: the free group on `S` modulo `Subgroup.normalClosure R`, the smallest normal subgroup containing the relators. `FundamentalGroup X x` is the group of endomorphisms of `x` in Mathlib's fundamental groupoid, i.e. homotopy classes of loops at `x`, and `basepoint R` is the single vertex of the complex, the image of the wedge point.

**The one convention to know.** Mathlib multiplies loops right to left: `p * q` is the loop that first traverses `q`, then `p` (`FundamentalGroup.mul_def`). So the loop that Lean attaches to the class of the word `s₁s₂` runs around the `s₂`-circle and then the `s₁`-circle; read with Hatcher's left-to-right convention it spells `s₂s₁`. Thus `PresentationComplex R` is Hatcher's `X_{⟨S | R^rev⟩}`, every relator reversed, and Mathlib's `π₁` is the opposite of Hatcher's group. The two reversals cancel: reversing words is an anti-automorphism of the free group carrying the normal closure of `R^rev` onto that of `R`, so Hatcher's theorem for `X_{⟨S | R^rev⟩}` is, word for word, this statement for `R`. Only a reader identifying `PresentationComplex R` with Hatcher's `X_{⟨S | R⟩}` must take care: for `⟨a, b | aba⁻¹b⁻²⟩`, whose reversal has a different normal closure, the two complexes differ, though both have fundamental group isomorphic to the presented group.

**What `≃*` asserts, and which map.** A `MulEquiv` is a specific bijective homomorphism, not a bare existence statement. The forward map here is the inverse of `fundamentalGroupHom R` (`MulEquiv.ofBijective … .symm`, so `fundamentalGroupMulEquiv_symm_apply` holds by definition): the class of the counterclockwise loop `t ↦ exp(2πit)` on the `s`-th circle goes to `s`, and the content is that this assignment is a well-defined bijective homomorphism.

**The space.** The wedge of copies of the unit circle indexed by `S`, joined at `1`, with one square per relator, one edge glued along a loop in the class of the relator and the other three edges collapsed to the vertex (`TwoCellAttachment`); the file shows it is a CW complex with cells of dimension at most `2`.

**Concrete instances.** `S = {a}`, `R = {a²}`: a disk glued to a circle by the degree-two map, the projective plane, and `⟨a | a²⟩ = ℤ/2 = π₁(ℝP²)`. `S = {a, b}`, `R = {aba⁻¹b⁻¹}` gives the torus and `ℤ²`; here `R^rev = {b⁻¹a⁻¹ba}` has the same normal closure. `S = R = ∅` gives a point and the trivial group.

**The only hypothesis is "G is a group."** `[Group G]` is found automatically; nothing is assumed about `G`: it may be trivial, infinite, uncountable or non-abelian. The `u` in `Type u` only fixes the size level of `G`, and the space is built in the same level.

**The space.** `universalGSpace G` is the polyhedron of the abstract simplicial complex on the vertex set ℕ × G whose faces are the finite sets with at most one vertex over each index: that is the countable join G ∗ G ∗ ⋯ of Milnor's paper. It is topologised with the weak topology (a set is closed when it meets every closed simplex in a closed set), not Milnor's metric topology, which is a choice of model, not of theorem. `G` acts by relabelling, g·(i,h) = (i, gh), extended affinely over simplices; `classifyingSpace G` is the orbit space with the quotient topology and `classifyingSpaceBasepoint G` the orbit of the vertex (0, 1). So the statement is about the actual orbit space, not a space characterised up to homotopy.

**What `IsEilenbergMacLaneSpaceOne G X x` asserts.** By its definition ([EilenbergMacLane/Basic.lean#L123](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/AlgebraicTopology/EilenbergMacLane/Basic.lean#L123)) it is three things: `X` is path connected (Mathlib's `PathConnectedSpace` includes nonemptiness); for every n ≥ 2 the homotopy group π_n(X, x) has at most one element (`Subsingleton`), and since it is a group that means it is trivial; and there exists a group isomorphism π₁(X, x) ≅ G. The last is a bare existence statement (`Nonempty (… ≃* G)`), so the theorem carries no choice of isomorphism; the chosen one is the separate declaration `classifyingSpaceFundamentalGroupMulEquiv`. Hatcher defines a K(G, 1) by a contractible universal cover instead; for spaces of CW type that is the same condition, and here the universal cover is the join itself, whose homotopy groups all vanish, so no reading of "K(G, 1)" is lost.

**Mathlib's reversed multiplication on π₁** (`p * q` is "q then p") does not matter here: π₁ with either order is isomorphic to the other through inversion, so "π₁ ≅ G exists" is the same claim under both conventions.

**Not vacuous.** For G = ℤ/2 the join of countably many copies of the two-point set is S^∞ (the join of n copies of S⁰ is S^{n−1}), the relabelling by the non-identity element is the antipodal map, and the orbit space is ℝP^∞, the familiar K(ℤ/2, 1). For G = ℤ the orbit space is homotopy equivalent to the circle, and the listed test records that this equivalence induces the identity on π₁ ≅ ℤ.

**What it says.** For a based pair `(X, A, a₀)` and an index type `N` of cardinality `n`, a class `b ∈ π_n(A, a₀)` is the boundary of some class in `π_{n+1}(X, A, a₀)` if and only if its image in `π_n(X, a₀)` is the trivial class: the image of `∂` is the kernel of `i_*`.

**The two sides.** `HomotopyGroup N A a₀` is Mathlib's `π_n(A, a₀)`: maps `I^N → A` sending `∂I^N` to `a₀`, modulo homotopy fixed on `∂I^N`. `Set.range boundary` is the image of the boundary map, restriction to the face `{0} × I^N`; that face is a copy of `I^N`, so the degrees match the classical `∂ : π_{n+1}(X, A) → π_n(A)` with no hidden shift. `HomotopyGroup.map X.pair.map.hom rfl` is `i_*` for the embedding `i : A → X` of the pair; the `rfl` proves that `i` sends `a₀` to the basepoint `i(a₀)` used for `π_n(X)`, true by definition. `⟦GenLoop.const⟧` is the class of the constant map at `i(a₀)`.

**Pointed sets, no products.** The statement uses no group law. For `N` nonempty, `⟦GenLoop.const⟧` is the identity (`HomotopyGroup.mk_const_eq_one` in Tau Ceti's `HomotopyGroup/Map.lean`), so "trivial" is "`= 1`" and the right side is the kernel of a homomorphism. For `N` empty, `I^N` is a point, `π_0` is the set of path components pointed by that of the basepoint, and the statement is exactness of `π_1(X, A) → π_0(A) → π_0(X)` as pointed sets, as Hatcher states it. Mathlib's product on `HomotopyGroup` is `⟦p⟧ * ⟦q⟧ = ⟦transAt i q p⟧`, "`q` then `p`", the reverse of the textbook order; it does not enter here, and reversing a product changes neither the identity nor a kernel.

**Generality.** Hatcher proves exactness for an arbitrary pair, and so does this: no CW, cofibration or connectivity hypothesis is assumed, and none is needed.

**Not vacuous, and not trivial.** With `X = D²`, `A = S¹`, `N = Fin 1`: `π_1(D²) = 0`, so every class of `π_1(S¹) ≅ ℤ` must be a boundary, and the generator is the boundary of the relative cube `(s,t) ↦ (1−s)·e^{2πit} + s·a₀`. With `A = X = S¹`: `i_*` is the identity, so only the trivial class is a boundary, consistent with `π_2(S¹, S¹)` being a single point (`subsingleton_of_surjective`).

**What the declaration is.** `abbrev` makes `SymmetricSpectrum` a transparent name for `Mod SymmetricSequence sphere`, Mathlib's category of modules over a monoid object. Unfolding Mathlib's definitions: an object is a symmetric sequence `X` with a map `S ⊗ X ⟶ X` satisfying the unit law (`η ⊗ X` followed by the action is the left unitor) and the associativity law (`μ ⊗ X` then the action equals associator, `S ⊗ action`, action); a morphism is a map of symmetric sequences commuting with the actions. That is exactly HSS's category of `S`-modules, maps included, and transparency means Mathlib's module-category machinery applies to symmetric spectra verbatim. The first argument names the category acted on: the monoidal category acting on itself by its tensor product.

**The index category.** `FiniteBijection` has objects the natural numbers, standing for `Fin n`, and morphisms the bijections `Fin n ≃ Fin m`, which exist only for `n = m`, where they form `Σ_n`. So a functor out of it is precisely a sequence of pointed simplicial sets `X_n` with a based `Σ_n`-action and nothing else, HSS's symmetric sequence (§2.1). `SSet.S1` is the coequaliser of the two endpoint inclusions `Δ[0] ⇉ Δ[1]`, HSS's `Δ[1]/∂Δ[1]`.

**Conventions that do not change the meaning.** The universe is fixed at `0`, so simplices form sets, as in HSS, and the type of all symmetric spectra lives in `Type 1`, where a category of such objects must live.

**Not vacuous.** The sphere acting on itself by its multiplication is a symmetric spectrum, Mathlib's `Mod.regular`: the sphere spectrum. Its levels are `S^n = (S¹)^{∧n}`, with `S^0 = S⁰` two points, and the action `S^p ∧ S^n → S^{p+n}` is block concatenation (`sphere_mul_app_smashMk`).

What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The standing hypotheses.** The square-bracket hypotheses are found automatically and mean: `PathConnectedSpace X` is "nonempty and any two points are joined by a path" (Mathlib's class has the nonemptiness as a field, so the empty space is excluded); `LocallyPathConnectedSpace X` is "every point has a neighbourhood basis of path-connected neighbourhoods" (`Mathlib/Topology/Connected/LocallyPathConnected.lean`), Hatcher's local path-connectedness. Both are exactly Hatcher's standing assumptions for the whole of §1.3.

**The left side.** Tau Ceti's `SemilocallySimplyConnectedSpace X` unfolds to: every point `x` has a neighbourhood `U` such that every loop at `x` with image in `U` is homotopic, *in `X`*, to the constant loop. Two conventions matter. `Path.Homotopic` is homotopy with endpoints fixed (`Path.Homotopy` is `ContinuousMap.HomotopyRel … {0, 1}`), so this is the triviality of `π₁(U, x) → π₁(X, x)`, not a free null-homotopy. And `U ∈ 𝓝 x` is any neighbourhood, open or not; this agrees with Hatcher's open `U` because loops in the interior of `U` lie in `U`, and the file records the open version as `exists_isOpen_mem_nhds_subset_loops_nullhomotopic`.

**The right side.** It asks for a space `E` (`∃ (E : Type u) (_ : TopologicalSpace E)` is "there is a topological space", in the same universe as `X`, which is harmless) and a map `p : E → X` that is a covering map in Mathlib's sense, every point of `X` having an open neighbourhood `U` with `p⁻¹(U) ≅ U × p⁻¹(x)` over `U` and `p⁻¹(x)` discrete, together with `SimplyConnectedSpace E`: Mathlib defines this as the fundamental groupoid being equivalent to a point, which is the same as nonempty, path-connected and `π₁ = 1` (`simply_connected_iff_unique_homotopic`). So the right side is precisely "`X` has a universal cover" as Hatcher uses the phrase; the statement does not claim uniqueness of `E`, which is a separate matter.

**What `↔` asserts.** Both directions are content. Forward is the existence theorem (built from based paths modulo homotopy); backward is the necessity Hatcher proves in a few lines. Nothing is made trivial by the hypotheses: the circle satisfies all of them, with `ℝ → S¹` as the witness; the Hawaiian earring is path-connected and locally path-connected but not semilocally simply connected, so the theorem says it has no simply connected covering space, as Hatcher states.

Correctly stated; compared with Hatcher, Proposition 2B.1(b) in the case k = n − 1 (the separation statement that follows it) and with the GeometricTopology roadmap's collaring target, which consumes this theorem and lists no tagged Check for it. What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean.

**The spheres.** `E` and `F` are real normed spaces with any norm, not necessarily Euclidean; `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]` is a hypothesis found automatically. `Metric.sphere 0 1` is {x : ‖x‖ = 1}, so the two `↑(Metric.sphere 0 1)` are the unit spheres of `E` and of `F`, as topological subspaces. With n = dim E, the first is an (n − 1)-sphere and, because `hEF` says dim F = n + 1, the second is an n-sphere; a unit sphere for a non-Euclidean norm (the boundary of a cube, say) is homeomorphic to the round one, so no generality is lost or gained. `hEF` is a plain equality of natural numbers; since the right side is at least 1 it also rules out the junk value `finrank = 0` that Mathlib assigns to an infinite-dimensional `F`, so `F` is genuinely (n + 1)-dimensional even though no finiteness instance on `F` appears.

**The embedding.** `h` is a map between the two spheres, `hc` says it is continuous and `hi` injective. The source is compact and the target Hausdorff, so `h` is a topological embedding and `Set.range h` its image, an embedded (n − 1)-sphere; no smoothness, local flatness or tameness is asked, so wild spheres such as Alexander's horned sphere are covered, as in Hatcher.

**What the conclusion asserts.** `(Set.range h)ᶜ` is the complement of the image inside the n-sphere of `F`, with the subspace topology, and `ZerothHomotopy` of it is the set of its path components: points modulo "joined by a path inside the complement" (Mathlib's `Joined`, a path in the subspace). `Nat.card … = 2` says there are exactly two. `Nat.card` returns 0 for an infinite type, so it could never produce 2 by accident: the conclusion really says the set of path components is finite of size two. Path components, not connected components, is the stronger and standard form; the companion `not_isPreconnected_compl_range_sphere` (a listed test) draws the connectedness consequence.

**Not vacuous.** For E = ℝ², F = ℝ³ with Euclidean norms it says every embedded 2-sphere in S³ (tame or horned) has exactly two complementary path components; for E = ℝ, F = ℝ² it is the Jordan curve theorem on S², whose two components are the inside and outside of the curve. The degenerate case dim E = 0 is consistent: the source sphere is empty, `h` is the empty map, and its complement is the two-point sphere S⁰ of a line, which has two path components (2 = 1 + 1, one per point).

What follows is a reading guide for a mathematician who does not read Lean, saying why the [Lean declaration](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/AlgebraicTopology/Sphere/HomotopyGroup.lean#L106) is the classical statement.

**The sphere and the degree.** `E` is a real inner product space (`[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]`), and `b`, an orthonormal basis indexed by `Fin (n + 3)`, is how the statement says `dim E = n + 3`: no separate dimension hypothesis is needed, and the basis is also the datum fixing the sign below. `Metric.sphere 0 1` is `{v : ‖v‖ = 1}`, so it is `S^{n+2}`, and `x` is a point of it (`↑` makes the subset a space). Writing the degree as `n + 2` for a natural number `n` is Lean's way of saying "every degree `≥ 2`", Hatcher's hypothesis for the Hurewicz isomorphism; `π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ` is not claimed here.

**The group.** `π_ (n + 2) X x` is Mathlib's cubical homotopy group: homotopy classes, relative to the boundary, of maps of the cube `I^{n+2}` sending its boundary to `x`. Mathlib builds its product by pulling back path composition in an iterated loop space, where the product is written in the reverse of the textbook order; in degrees `≥ 2` the group is abelian (Mathlib's `commGroup` instance), so the order is immaterial here. `Additive` only renames that product as addition, so that it can be compared with the additive group `ℤ`, and `≃+` is an isomorphism of abelian groups.

**Which isomorphism it is.** A `def` whose type is an isomorphism is a construction, and `homotopyGroupSphereAddEquiv_apply` says which: a class `[g]` goes to the Hurewicz image `g_*[I^{n+2}] ∈ H_{n+2}(S^{n+2}; ℤ)` (cubical homology, compared with singular homology), then reduced homology is identified with unreduced, which is harmless in degree `n + 2 > 0`, and finally `H̃_{n+2}(S^{n+2}; ℤ) ≅ ℤ` is the generator determined by `b` through iterated suspension down to the `0`-sphere `{±b 0}`, where the generator is `[−b 0] − [b 0]`. Reordering or reflecting `b` changes the isomorphism by a sign; its existence and the group it identifies do not depend on `b` or on `x`. The Hurewicz hypothesis that `π_k(S^{n+2}, x)` is trivial for all `k < n + 2`, including path-connectedness (`k = 0`) and simple connectivity (`k = 1`), is discharged inside the definition from the sphere's connectivity, so the only arguments are `b` and `x`.

**A concrete instance.** `E = ℝ³` with its standard basis and `n = 0`: `π₂(S², x) ≃+ ℤ`, with the class of the identity map of `S²`, a generator by Hatcher's Corollary 4.25, going to `±1`, the sign fixed by the orientation of the basis. That `E` lives in the lowest universe (`Type`) is harmless: every finite-dimensional real inner product space is isometric to one there.

name: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem
text: every continuous map from the closed unit ball of ℝⁿ to itself has a fixed point, for every n (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Cor. 2.15).

name: The no-retraction theorem
text: the boundary sphere of the closed unit ball of ℝⁿ is not a retract of the ball: no continuous map Dⁿ → ∂Dⁿ is the identity on ∂Dⁿ (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Cor. 2.15).

name: Menger's theorem for directed graphs, vertex form
text: for non-adjacent vertices s ≠ t of a finite directed multigraph, the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint s–t paths equals the minimum number of vertices whose deletion separates t from s (Schrijver, *Combinatorial Optimization*, §9.1).

name: Menger's theorem for directed graphs, arc form
text: for vertices s ≠ t of a finite directed multigraph, the maximum number of arc-disjoint s–t paths equals the minimum number of arcs whose deletion separates t from s (Schrijver, *Combinatorial Optimization*, §9.1).

name: The isoperimetric inequality in the plane
text: a continuous closed plane curve of length L encloses signed area A with 4π|A| ≤ L², with equality exactly when the curve runs once around a circle at uniform speed in arclength (Osserman, *Bull. AMS* 84, 1978).

name: The relative isoperimetric inequality in a ball
text: in ℝⁿ with n ≥ 2, for every ball B and every set s, min(|s ∩ B|, |B ∖ s|)^{(n−1)/n} ≤ C_n P(s; B) with a constant C_n depending only on n (Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter and Geometric Variational Problems*, Prop. 12.37).

name: Thom's lemma
text: over a real closed field, the set where a polynomial and all its derivatives take prescribed signs is empty, a single point, or an open interval with endpoints in the field or infinite (Basu–Pollack–Roy, *Algorithms in Real Algebraic Geometry*, Ch. 2).

name: The Cohen structure theorem, equal-characteristic case
text: a complete local ring containing a field, with finitely generated maximal ideal, is a quotient of a power series ring in finitely many variables over its residue field (Stacks Project, Tag 032A).

name: The isometry group of the E₈ lattice is its Weyl group
text: the reflections in the 240 roots generate the full group O(E₈) of isometries of the E₈ root lattice, which contains −1 and is the automorphism group of the E₈ root system (Conway–Sloane, *SPLAG*, Ch. 4 §8).

name: Class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields count reduced forms
text: for a fundamental discriminant −n, the class number of ℚ(√−n) is the number of primitive reduced positive definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant −n; in particular ℚ(√−5) has class number two (Cox, *Primes of the Form x² + ny²*, Thm. 7.7).

name: Uniqueness of Wasserstein geodesics
text: on a Polish space with 1 < p < ∞, a unique optimal coupling that a.e. joins points by unique geodesics gives a unique P_p geodesic; in Euclidean P₂ from an absolutely continuous μ it is McCann's displacement interpolation (Villani, *Optimal Transport: Old and New*, Cor. 7.23).

name: Schur's lemma for the Ricci tensor
text: if a metric-compatible torsion-free connection on a connected manifold of dimension n ≠ 0, 2 has Ricci tensor Ric = a·g for a function a, then a is constant (Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds*, Ch. 7).

name: The orders of the orthogonal groups over finite fields
text: for a nondegenerate symmetric form over 𝔽_q with q odd, |O_{2m+1}| = 2q^{m²}∏_{i=1}^{m}(q^{2i} − 1) and |O_{2m+2}| = 2q^{m(m+1)}(q^{m+1} − ε)∏_{i=1}^{m}(q^{2i} − 1), where ε = χ((−1)^{m+1} det) (Grove, *Classical Groups and Geometric Algebra*).

name: Weierstrass division for overconvergent power series
text: in the Monsky–Washnitzer algebra K⟨X₁, …, Xₙ, Y⟩†, division by a series distinguished of degree d in Y gives a unique overconvergent quotient and polynomial remainder of degree below d, extending the restricted-series case announced earlier (Grosse-Klönne, *Rigid analytic spaces with overconvergent structure sheaf*, §1.3).

name: The Dunford–Pettis property
text: a Banach space has it when every weakly compact operator out of it maps weakly convergent sequences to norm-convergent ones, equivalently when fₙ(xₙ) → 0 for all weakly null xₙ and fₙ; ℓ¹ has it (Albiac–Kalton, *Topics in Banach Space Theory*, §5.4).

name: Tamagawa numbers of an elliptic curve
text: at a discrete valuation v, the index c_v = [E(K_v) : E₀(K_v)] of the points with nonsingular reduction on a minimal model, together with the finite positive product ∏_v c_v that enters the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer formula (Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*, VII.6).

name: The Szegő kernel
text: the reproducing kernel k_w(z) = (1 − w̄z)⁻¹ of the Hardy space H² of the unit disk, representing evaluation at w, with ‖k_w‖ = (1 − |w|²)^{−1/2} (Duren, *Theory of Hᵖ Spaces*, Ch. 1).

name: The Baer sum of extensions
text: in an abelian category, the pullback–pushout sum of two short exact sequences 0 → A → E → C → 0, whose class in Ext¹(C, A) is the sum of the two classes (Weibel, *An Introduction to Homological Algebra*, §3.4).

name: The Bates distribution
text: the law of the mean of n independent uniform variables on [0, 1], with its piecewise-polynomial density and distribution function, mean 1/2, variance 1/(12n), and transforms (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan, *Continuous Univariate Distributions* 2, Ch. 26).

Correctly stated: for L/K abelian and v unramified at Q above it, an element whose class is the global Artin symbol of the prime idele class at v is an arithmetic Frobenius at Q, the Frobenius normalisation of the idelic Artin map (Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, VI (5.6); Milne, *Class Field Theory*, V §5); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the lower inequality 2ⁿ/n!·covol(L) ≤ ∏λᵢ·μ(K) of Minkowski's second theorem for a symmetric convex body with 0 interior and any Haar measure (Cassels, *Geometry of Numbers*, VIII Thm. V; Evertse, §2.3 Thm. 2.9); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Thm. 3.2 with Remark 3.3, as a strong deformation retraction of {f ≤ c+ε} onto {f ≤ c−ε} with one λ_p-cell per critical point on the level; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the fundamental-domain conclusion of Poincaré's polygon theorem for a compact side-paired polygon under the vertex-cycle angle condition (Beardon, *The Geometry of Discrete Groups*, Thm. 9.8.4; Katok, *Fuchsian Groups*, Thm. 4.3.2); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: exactness of HH^(m+1) →B H^m(Tot) →S H^(m+2)(Tot) in Connes' SBI sequence for the total cyclic bicomplex of a unital algebra (Loday, *Cyclic Homology*, Thm. 2.2.1; Connes, NCG III §1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the perfect set theorem for Borel subsets of Polish spaces, as a continuous injection of Cantor space into the set (Kechris, *Classical Descriptive Set Theory*, Thm. 13.6); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: vanishing of positive-degree cohomology of a quasi-coherent sheaf on any affine open, with no Noetherian hypothesis (Stacks Project, Tag 01XB; Hartshorne III.3.5 for the Noetherian case); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the F. and M. Riesz uniqueness theorem for functions of bounded characteristic, with the bounded-characteristic hypothesis phrased as frequently bounded circle averages of log⁺|f| (Duren, *Theory of Hᵖ Spaces*, Thm. 2.5); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Nica–Speicher, *Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability*, Thm. 11.16, both directions, for unital subalgebras and a normalised functional; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: ht p + dim A/p = dim A for a finitely generated algebra over a field with irreducible spectrum (Hartshorne I.1.8A(b); Matsumura, *Commutative Algebra*, Thm. 5.6 for domains, nilpotents allowed here); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the classification Iₙ, E₈, I₁ ⊕ E₈ of positive definite unimodular lattices of rank ≤ 9 (Conway–Sloane, *SPLAG*, Ch. 16 Table 16.7; Kneser 1957); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the equivalence E ↦ Spec_X(Sym E^∨) between finite locally free sheaves and geometric vector bundles, with the dual making it covariant (Hartshorne Ex. II.5.18; Stacks Tag 01M1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: a subset of a Polish space is Polish iff Gδ (Kechris, *Classical Descriptive Set Theory*, Thm. 3.11); the forward direction is also Mathlib master's IsGδ.polishSpace; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: M₂(Γ) = E₂(Γ) ⊕ S₂(Γ) for Γ ⊇ Γ(N), with E₂(Γ) the forms whose restriction to Γ(N) lies in the span of the weighted series G₂^W; the identification with the span of E₂^{ψ,φ,t} (Diamond–Shurman Thm. 4.6.2) is not claimed; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Ricci identity ∇²σ(u,v) − ∇²σ(v,u) = R(u,v)σ for a torsion-free tangent connection (Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds*, 2nd ed., Prop. 7.5 / Ch. 7); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Noether normalisation for algebras finite over a Monsky–Washnitzer algebra, with at most as many variables (Grosse-Klönne, *J. reine angew. Math.* 519 (2000), §1.4(2); BGR §6.1.2 for the affinoid analogue); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: G ⊆ I with ⟨LT(I)⟩ = ⟨LT(G)⟩ (Cox–Little–O'Shea, *Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms*, Ch. 2 §5 Def. 5); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Verdier quotient D^b(C)/Perf(C) with Perf(C) the thick subcategory generated by projectives in degree zero (Buchweitz 1986, Def. 1.2.2; Orlov 2004 §1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: N_J(X,Y) = [JX,JY] − [X,Y] − J[JX,Y] − J[X,JY] with no factor 1/4, tensorial (Kobayashi–Nomizu Vol. II, IX §2; Huybrechts, *Complex Geometry*, §2.6); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: X_f = (σ♭)⁻¹ df, i.e. ι_{X_f}σ = df for nondegenerate σ in finite dimensions, junk zero where σ♭ is not invertible (McDuff–Salamon, *Introduction to Symplectic Topology*, §3.1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: ζ(z) = 1/z + Σ_{l≠0}(1/(z−l) + 1/l + z/l²), the standard Weierstrass ζ, with ζ' = −℘ and quasi-periodicity proved beside it (DLMF §23.2(iii); Abramowitz–Stegun Ch. 18); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: α_p(A) as the limit of #{X mod pʳ : XᵀAX = A}/p^{r·n(n−1)/2}, the normalisation of Siegel 1935 / Kitaoka Ch. 5 (Conway–Sloane's convention differs by constant factors); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Cartan's criterion for quasi-compact basis opens and finite covers, a correctly labelled narrower form of Stacks Lemma 20.11.9 (Tag 01EW), which allows arbitrary basis opens and cofinal covering systems; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: an Abelian theorem for Dirichlet series at s = 1 along real σ → 1⁺, under absolute convergence for σ > 1; the hypotheses are stated honestly and are stronger than Hardy–Riesz's Abel theorem (which needs only convergence at 1 and allows sectorial approach); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: |O(E₈)| = 696729600 = 240·126·23040 (Bourbaki, Lie VI §4.10 Plate VII; Conway–Sloane Ch. 4 §8.1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩† is noetherian over a complete ultrametric field (Grosse-Klönne §1.4(1); Fulton, *A note on weakly complete algebras*, 1969); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩† is a UFD (Grosse-Klönne §1.4(3); BGR §5.2.6 for the Tate-algebra analogue); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩† is a Jacobson ring (Grosse-Klönne §1.4(4)); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Gal(Puiseux field / K((X))) ≅ lim_n μₙ(K) as topological groups when K has all roots of unity, the Kummer description of the Galois group of the Puiseux series (Serre, *Local Fields*, IV §2 Ex.; Puiseux's theorem); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: H^•(C₂; 𝔽₂) ≅ 𝔽₂[x] with |x| = 1 (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Thm. 3.19 via RP^∞ = BC₂; Brown, *Cohomology of Groups*, V §3); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: vol(O(n)) = ∏_{j=1}^n 2π^{j/2}/Γ(j/2) for the Haar measure normalised along the fibrations O(j) → S^{j−1} with Euclidean sphere areas (Conway–Sloane, *Low-dimensional lattices IV*, eq. (6)); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: dφ has only the bidegrees (p+2,q−1), (p+1,q), (p,q+1), (p−1,q+2) for φ of type (p,q) on an almost complex manifold (Huybrechts, *Complex Geometry*, §2.6; Kobayashi–Nomizu IX Prop. 2.8); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: a subgroup of GL(V) over a nonarchimedean local field stabilises a lattice iff its closure is compact (Darmon–Diamond–Taylor, *Fermat's Last Theorem*, §2.1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the graph of a one-form α in T*M is Lagrangian iff dα = 0 (Cannas da Silva, *Lectures on Symplectic Geometry*, §3.2; McDuff–Salamon §3.2); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

name: Artin reciprocity for number fields
text: for a finite abelian extension L/K of number fields, the Artin map C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L) ≅ Gal(L/K) sends the class of a uniformizer at an unramified prime v to the Frobenius at v; the idelic law is now in full (Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, VI §5).

name: Minkowski's second theorem
text: for a lattice L in ℝⁿ and a symmetric convex body K with successive minima λ₀ ≤ ⋯ ≤ λₙ₋₁, 2ⁿ/n! · covol(L) ≤ λ₀⋯λₙ₋₁ · vol(K) ≤ 2ⁿ · covol(L), now both inequalities for every symmetric convex body (Cassels, *An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers*, Ch. VIII).

name: Milnor's cell attachment theorem
text: for a Morse function f with compact band f⁻¹[c−δ, c+δ], the sublevel set {f ≤ c+ε} deformation retracts onto {f ≤ c−ε} with one cell of dimension λ_p attached at each critical point p on the level c (Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Thm. 3.2).

name: Poincaré's polygon theorem for compact polygons
text: if the side pairing of a compact hyperbolic polygon P satisfies the angle condition at every vertex cycle, the group it generates is discrete, has P as a fundamental domain, and is presented by the side and cycle relations (Beardon, *The Geometry of Discrete Groups*, §9.8).

name: Connes' SBI exact sequence
text: for a unital algebra, with cyclic cohomology defined by the cyclic bicomplex, the sequence ⋯ → HCⁿ⁻¹ →S HCⁿ⁺¹ →I HHⁿ⁺¹ →B HCⁿ →S HCⁿ⁺² → ⋯ of Hochschild and cyclic cohomology is exact at every term (Loday, *Cyclic Homology*, §2.2).

name: The perfect set theorem for Borel sets
text: an uncountable Borel subset of a Polish space contains a homeomorphic copy of Cantor space, and so has cardinality 𝔠 (Kechris, *Classical Descriptive Set Theory*, Thm. 13.6).

name: Serre's vanishing theorem on affine schemes
text: a quasi-coherent sheaf on an affine open of any scheme has no cohomology in positive degrees, the Noetherian hypothesis of the earlier announcement now removed (Stacks Project, Tag 01XB).

name: The F. and M. Riesz uniqueness theorem
text: a holomorphic function of bounded characteristic on a disc whose radial limits vanish on a set of boundary angles of positive measure is identically zero (Duren, *Theory of Hᵖ Spaces*, Thm. 2.5).

name: Freeness is the vanishing of mixed free cumulants
text: for a normalised linear functional, unital subalgebras are freely independent exactly when every free cumulant with arguments from at least two of them vanishes (Nica–Speicher, *Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability*, Thm. 11.16).

name: The dimension formula for finitely generated algebras
text: for a finitely generated algebra A over a field with irreducible spectrum and a prime p, ht p + dim A/p = dim A; for any finitely generated A, dim_p Spec A = dim A_p + trdeg κ(p) (Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*, I.1.8A).

name: Positive definite unimodular lattices of rank at most nine
text: such a lattice is Iₙ, E₈ or E₈ ⊕ I₁; in particular E₈ is the only even unimodular positive definite lattice of rank eight (Conway–Sloane, *SPLAG*, Ch. 16).

name: Vector bundles are finite locally free sheaves
text: for every scheme X, the functor E ↦ 𝕍(E) = Spec_X(Sym E^∨) is an equivalence from finite locally free sheaves on X to geometric vector bundles over X (Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*, Ex. II.5.18).

name: Alexandrov's theorem and its converse
text: a subset of a Polish space is Polish in the subspace topology exactly when it is Gδ, and likewise for completely metrizable spaces; the Gδ-implies-Polish half landed independently in Mathlib master (Kechris, *Classical Descriptive Set Theory*, Thm. 3.11).

name: The weight-two cusp–Eisenstein decomposition
text: M₂(Γ) = E₂(Γ) ⊕ S₂(Γ) for every congruence subgroup Γ ⊇ Γ(N), with E₂ spanned by the weighted series G₂^W, and likewise in each nebentypus space M₂(N, χ); the weight k ≥ 3 case was announced earlier (Diamond–Shurman, §4.6).

name: The Ricci identity
text: for a connection ∇ on a vector bundle and a torsion-free connection on the tangent bundle, ∇²σ(u,v) − ∇²σ(v,u) = R(u,v)σ, with the correction −∇_{T(u,v)}σ when the tangent connection has torsion T (Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds*, Ch. 7).

name: Noether normalisation for Monsky–Washnitzer algebras
text: a nonzero algebra finite over K⟨X₁, …, Xₙ⟩† is finite over an injectively embedded K⟨Y₁, …, Y_m⟩† with m ≤ n, so the quotient of a dagger algebra by an ideal with maximal radical is finite over K (Grosse-Klönne, *J. reine angew. Math.* 519, §1.4).

name: Gröbner bases
text: G ⊆ I is a Gröbner basis when the leading terms of G and of I span the same ideal; remainders on division by G are unique and vanish exactly on I, which G generates; also being formalised in mathlib4#29203 (Cox–Little–O'Shea, *Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms*, Ch. 2).

name: The singularity category
text: D_sg(C) = Dᵇ(C)/Perf(C), the Verdier quotient of the bounded derived category of an abelian category by the thick subcategory generated by the projectives, with its triangulated structure, together with Iwanaga–Gorenstein rings (Buchweitz, *Maximal Cohen–Macaulay Modules and Tate Cohomology*, §1).

name: The Nijenhuis tensor
text: for a smooth almost complex structure J, the tensor N_J(X, Y) = [JX, JY] − [X, Y] − J[JX, Y] − J[X, JY] on each tangent space, skew-symmetric with N_J(Jv, w) = N_J(v, Jw) = −J N_J(v, w) (Kobayashi–Nomizu, *Foundations of Differential Geometry*, Vol. II, Ch. IX).

name: Hamiltonian vector fields on manifolds
text: for a nondegenerate 2-form σ on a finite-dimensional manifold and a function f, the unique vector field X_f with ι_{X_f}σ = df; it is Cⁿ for Cⁿ⁺¹ f, and f is constant along its integral curves (McDuff–Salamon, *Introduction to Symplectic Topology*, §3.1).

name: The Weierstrass ζ function
text: ζ(z) = 1/z + Σ_{l ≠ 0} (1/(z − l) + 1/l + z/l²) over a lattice Λ, odd with ζ' = −℘, and quasi-periods η : Λ → ℂ, ζ(z + l) = ζ(z) + η(l), η(l) = 2ζ(l/2) (DLMF, §23.2).

name: Siegel's local density
text: α_p(A) = lim_r #{X ∈ Mₙ(ℤ/pʳ) : XᵀAX = A} / p^{r·n(n−1)/2} for a nonsingular symmetric A over ℤ_p; the normalised counts are constant from r = 2v_p(2 det A) + 1 on, at every prime, p = 2 included (Kitaoka, *Arithmetic of Quadratic Forms*, Ch. 5).
With the additional χ(p)=1 condition, the arithmetic Satake roots are p^((k−1)/2)e^(±iθ).

Correctly stated for the elliptic-curve rank requested by LeanBridge: instantiate `Module.finrank` as `Module.finrank ℤ W.Point`, where `W` is an elliptic Weierstrass curve over a number field. This review adds the connection to the [LeanBridge rank blueprint](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.rank) and concrete torsion tests to the existing general review of `finrank`.

The natural-language definition is the integer r in a decomposition E(K) ≅ T ⊕ ℤʳ, with T the finite torsion subgroup. In Lean, an abelian group is automatically a module over ℤ: multiplying a point by an integer means repeated addition, with negatives using the inverse. Thus the coefficient ring `ℤ` is essential. It does not mean that the curve is defined over the integers. The field K is already part of the type of `W.Point`.

Why does this return r? Integer-linear independence says that an integer relation among the selected points forces every coefficient to vanish. A torsion point cannot be an independent generator, because some nonzero integer kills it. More generally, passage to E(K)/T preserves rank: an independent family in E(K) stays independent modulo torsion, since any relation with torsion value can be multiplied by a nonzero integer to become a relation equal to zero; conversely, lifts of independent classes are independent. The quotient is ℤʳ, whose basis has r elements. This is formalized generically by [finrank_quotient_eq_of_le_torsion](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Dimension/Torsion/Basic.lean#L39). Tau Ceti explicitly uses that construction in [PointModTorsion](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/36f24f5d94ccf25e167520cf4c0f1a028c064fb0/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/PointModTorsion/Basic.lean#L25).

The input really is the full elliptic-curve group. Despite the word `Affine` in its namespace, [Point](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/Affine/Point.lean#L477) includes the point at infinity as `zero`, as well as the nonsingular affine solutions. With nonzero discriminant every solution is nonsingular. The rank therefore includes the identity and uses the usual chord-and-tangent group, rather than just a set of coordinate pairs.

The crucial finiteness hypothesis is supplied by [Mordell–Weil and its module instance](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/36f24f5d94ccf25e167520cf4c0f1a028c064fb0/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/FinitelyGenerated.lean#L139). `Module.Finite ℤ W.Point` means finitely generated over ℤ, not that there are finitely many rational points. This rules out the infinite-rank fallback in the general `finrank` definition. Rank zero permits nontrivial finite torsion; it does not assert that the identity is the only point. The definition makes no algorithmic promise about computing generators or ranks.

The blueprint's literal name `CommGroup.freeRank` still exists in the pinned Mathlib: it takes the minimum number of generators after quotienting by torsion, using multiplicative notation. Its additive counterpart is `AddCommGroup.freeRank`. For a finitely generated abelian group the quotient is finite free, so this and the module rank above give the same integer. The review site does not index `CommGroup.freeRank`; `Module.finrank` is the actual indexed definition used in Tau Ceti's elliptic-curve results. I am explaining their mathematical agreement, not claiming a direct named comparison lemma exists.

Checks: four supplementary Lean examples compiled successfully against the site's pinned Mathlib: rank(ℤ/5ℤ)=0; quotienting by the full torsion preserves rank; rank(ℤʳ × ℤ/5ℤ)=r for every natural r; and, under finite generation, rank zero is equivalent to every point being annihilated by some nonzero integer. These isolated examples were not added to Tau Ceti. The [roadmap's named-curve rank check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/2172af4ad0d340223ad59e6a5f698766118142c1/TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves/README.md#L1492) has a proved [positive-rank check for 37.a1](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/36f24f5d94ccf25e167520cf4c0f1a028c064fb0/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/WorkedExamples/Curve37a1.lean#L175); its requested upgrade to exact rank one is missing at this commit. Separately, [y²=x³−x+1 has proved rank one](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/36f24f5d94ccf25e167520cf4c0f1a028c064fb0/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/WorkedExamples/X3SubXAddOne/Rank.lean#L174). Both existing named tests have no transitive `sorry` in the site's extraction; their curve modules were not rebuilt locally. The missing 37.a1 upgrade is an unfinished roadmap calculation, not a failed test or a defect in `Module.finrank`.

Not checked here: the isogeny-invariance theorem mentioned in the knowl, analytic rank, BSD, or the full Mordell–Weil proof. Acceptance concerns this definition and its specialization, not completion of those results.

Correctly stated. The existing reviews already explain the two real branches and minimal-model normalization. The additional LeanBridge distinction is the scope of its links: `ec.q.real_period` is obtained by evaluating this equation-level function on a minimal equation over ℚ and extending coefficients to ℝ. The link from `ec.period` supplies only the real local factor of the global number-field period. It does not construct the product over all infinite places, the complex-place area integral, or the correction for a nonminimal model. Likewise, the link from `ec.q.faltings_height` is a prerequisite only: a one-dimensional real period does not determine the covolume of the complex period lattice. Those mappings must not be read as completed definitions of the global period or Faltings height. The definition itself is the intended real period; accepting it asserts none of those extra constructions.

Correctly defines local potential good reduction. The existential quantifiers say: choose a finite extension L/K and a discrete valuation ring S of L lying over the original local ring R; after changing to a minimal equation over S, the reduction is good. `IsLocalHom` prevents an unrelated place from being substituted, and equality of the two maps R → L ensures that the valuation extension and the field extension describe the same base change. Minimizing after extension matters because an equation minimal over K may cease to be minimal over L. No arbitrary chosen extension affects the truth of this existential statement.

The blueprint knowl is global: it asks for everywhere good reduction over a finite extension of a number field. This declaration is its local ingredient, not that entire global quantification. Over a DVR, the proved integral-j criterion matches the local natural-language criterion; obtaining the global knowl requires applying it at all finite places and the appropriate local-to-global argument. The broad ring parameter is harmless in the intended DVR/fraction-field application, but this review does not assert that arbitrary commutative rings have the same valuation-theoretic interpretation.

Correctly matches the LMFDB quality formula. A rational number in Lean has a reduced numerator and a positive denominator. Correctly defines the nonnegative integral of 1/√D(x) on D(x)>0, where D(x)=4x³+b₂x²+2b₄x+b₆. Completing the square gives (2y+a₁x+a₃)²=D(x), so the integrand is the absolute invariant differential on one real y-branch. The domain picks out exactly those x with two distinct real points. The codomain ℝ≥0∞ permits an honest value +∞ for divergent singular examples. For elliptic equations the finiteness theorem rules this out. This definition is half the full real period; `realPeriod` multiplies by two for the two branches. It is consequently a supporting integral for the LMFDB knowl, not itself the displayed Ω. `IntermediateField.adjoin F ((X² − C f.discr).rootSet E)` means the smallest subfield of the ambient extension E containing F and all square roots of disc(f) that lie in E. If δ² = disc(f), those roots are δ and −δ, and adjoining both is exactly F(δ). Thus the root-set formulation avoids making an arbitrary choice of square root without changing the usual field. For a number-field defining polynomial, take E to be its splitting field or an algebraic closure: the root-difference product supplies δ. The fixed-field comparison then identifies this extension with the field fixed by the even part of the Galois action, as the knowl describes.

The ambient field condition matters. If E contains no square root, this deliberately more general definition returns F; one must not apply it with E equal to a root field that lacks δ and still claim to have constructed the discriminant root field. The docstring explicitly records that case. If the discriminant is already a square, the extension is F; if non-square and a root is present, its degree is two. The characteristic-two exclusion belongs to the alternating-group comparison, not to the adjunction itself. Over number fields it is automatic.
