A `comap` of a subgroup is its inverse image under a homomorphism. Here an F-automorphism of E first restricts to the splitting field of f, then acts on the roots; the definition retains it precisely when that permutation is in the alternating group. Consequently it is the kernel of the sign character. When E is the splitting field, the action is faithful and this is exactly the subgroup denoted G ∩ Aₙ in the knowl. In a larger splitting extension the definition correctly retains the kernel of restriction as well: it is the inverse image of that even subgroup, not an assertion that every ambient automorphism acts faithfully on these roots.

The roots form an intrinsic finite set, so no numbering is chosen. Changing a numbering merely conjugates the permutations and preserves their parity. The subgroup is meaningful even for a polynomial with repeated roots; identifying its fixed field with F(√disc(f)) requires separability and characteristic different from two, and the comparison theorem has those hypotheses. They hold for a number-field minimal polynomial.

The knowl defines the Galois group of a possibly non-normal extension K/F using the automorphisms of its normal closure, rather than Aut(K/F). Tau Ceti implements the needed bridge: for a generator x, `minpoly F x` is its minimal polynomial; its `.Gal` is the automorphism group of its splitting field. The target of `galEquivNormalClosure` is explicitly the F-automorphism group of the normal closure of F(x) inside E. The symbol `≃*` means a group isomorphism.

The construction takes an F-field isomorphism s between those two models and sends an automorphism σ to s ∘ σ ∘ s⁻¹ (`autCongr`). That preserves composition and has the inverse conjugation, so the identification is of group structures, not just a bijection of underlying sets. The hypothesis `[Normal F E]` includes algebraicity and makes E large enough to contain all conjugates of x. Choosing E as an algebraic closure recovers every finite separable extension from the knowl. The choice of splitting-field isomorphism does not claim a distinguished labelling: another choice conjugates the identification. The separate stabilizer comparison records which root field is being recovered, and the stabilizer-index theorem assumes separability where required.

This is the index i(θ) of an integral primitive element, the first quantity defined in the knowl. The input type requires θ to be an algebraic integer and ℚ[θ]=K. Its `adjoin` is ℤ[θ] inside the ring of integers, `toSubmodule` forgets multiplication and remembers its additive lattice, and `cardQuot` counts the cosets of that lattice in O_K. Thus the value is exactly [O_K:ℤ[θ]]. It counts additive cosets, not residue classes modulo an ideal: ℤ[θ] is a subring and ordinarily not an ideal of O_K.

The primitive-element condition is essential. It makes ℤ[θ] a full-rank lattice; the quotient is therefore finite, and the accompanying `index_pos` theorem proves that the result is positive. This avoids the convention that `Nat.card` of an infinite type is zero. Integral translation and negation leave the generated subring, hence the index, unchanged. The rational-field index is one, the Gaussian example has index one, and the Dedekind cubic generator has index two.

The blueprint link is only partial: the final quantity called the *index of the number field* in `nf.zk_index` is the gcd of all i(θ). This declaration takes θ as an argument and does not define that gcd. Its correctness should not be read as completion of that remaining blueprint quantity.

For a prime p, the knowl says that p divides the gcd of the indices i(θ) over all integral primitive elements. Dividing that gcd is equivalent to dividing every i(θ). The Lean predicate states precisely the latter universal condition: `∀ θ : IntegralPrimitiveElement K, p ∣ θ.index`. The index used here is the finite positive additive index [O_K:ℤ[θ]], so no non-generator can contribute an artificial zero from an infinite quotient.

The declaration accepts any natural number p. It is therefore the common-divisor predicate, and the blueprint's *inessential prime* is recovered by adding `p.Prime`. In particular p=1 satisfies this predicate but is not an inessential prime; this is consistent with the broader name and docstring. For number fields the family of integral primitive elements is mathematically nonempty, by the primitive element theorem and clearing denominators; no formal existence theorem for that family is being claimed here. The negative monogenicity result needs p≠1, which is exactly the condition that a common divisor cannot divide an index equal to one.

It includes ℚ, quadratic fields and cyclotomic fields, and rejects Dedekind's classical nonmonogenic cubic. The declaration is extended to any field through its ring of elements integral over ℤ; all the number-field conclusions inspected here carry the number-field hypothesis.

A `NumberFieldOrder K` packages a ℤ-subalgebra of K, a proof that it is finitely generated as a ℤ-module, and a proof that its ℚ-linear span is all of K. A ℤ-subalgebra is a unital subring containing the rational integers. Since it sits in a characteristic-zero field, its additive group is torsion-free; finite generation makes it a free ℤ-module, and the spanning condition makes its rank [K:ℚ]. These are exactly the algebraic conditions for a full lattice in K. No arbitrary topological discreteness assumption is being substituted for full rank.

Finite generation as a module also implies every element is integral over ℤ. The accompanying `le_ringOfIntegers` theorem therefore proves every such order lies in O_K, matching the knowl. The definition does not require the order to be integrally closed or every ideal to be invertible: proper suborders such as ℤ[√5] are meant to be included. The maximal-order constructor supplies O_K as a nonvacuous example. The more elaborate Picard-group restrictions in Layer 11 belong to subsequent definitions, not to the carrier of orders itself.

A nonzero square passes at every real embedding, since field embeddings preserve multiplication and do not kill a nonzero element. If there are no real embeddings, the universal condition is vacuous, including at x=0; this is the literal convention in the knowl and the docstring. In applications to principal fractional ideals the generator is separately required to be nonzero by using Kˣ. Allowing arbitrary fields in the predicate does not claim number-field arithmetic beyond the hypotheses of the later results.

Its kernel need not be trivial over a real field; the kernel consists of narrow classes represented by principal ideals and every such class has square one, because a nonzero square is totally positive. If there are no real embeddings, the function space on the empty index type has one element, so the image is trivial and its F₂-dimension is zero. The link only covers the subspace itself. `integerUnitSignatures` is group-valued, not natural-number-valued; obtaining the *unit signature rank* still requires its dimension after the F₂ interpretation (equivalently log₂ of its cardinality). The LMFDB sign at an exact divisor Q is the eigenvalue by which the normalized involution w_Q acts on a newform with trivial character. Tau Ceti chooses a scalar from a proved existence theorem whose conclusion includes both the eigenvector equation and ε=1 or ε=−1. Thus the word `choose` does not introduce arbitrary numerical data: the underlying newform is nonzero, making the scalar unique. The hypotheses require χ=1 and Q|N with gcd(Q,N/Q)=1, precisely where the classical sign statement applies. At Q=1 the value is 1 and at Q=N it is the Fricke eigenvalue. The functional-equation root number is i^k times the latter, so in weight two it has the opposite sign. No ±1 claim is being made for general complex nebentypus.

The LMFDB involution w_Q is obtained from an Atkin–Lehner matrix, with the normalization making its square the identity. Tau Ceti's arithmetic slash action initially squares to Q^(k−2); multiplying it by (√Q)^(2−k) cancels precisely that scalar. The displayed definition performs this multiplication on the cusp-form operator, so its result acts on genuine holomorphic forms vanishing at every cusp. The exact-divisor hypothesis supplies Q>0 and the Bézout matrix, and changing a permitted matrix changes no operator on Γ₀(N)-invariant forms. The square law and the identity at Q=1 are proved. The LMFDB plus/minus spaces are then the ±1 eigenspaces of this operator with Q=N; this declaration supplies their operator rather than naming those two subspaces itself. Odd weights cause no conflict because S_k(Γ₀(N)) is then zero.

`MvPolynomial PUnit (ULift ℤ)` is simply the polynomial ring over ℤ in one variable: `PUnit` has one element, so there is one indeterminate; `ULift` only adjusts Lean's universe bookkeeping. Thus `Spec` of that ring is A¹ over ℤ. A morphism S→A¹ is equivalent to a global regular function on S. When S=Spec K this is an element of K, precisely the ordinary numerical j-invariant. The domain is the base S, not the elliptic curve's total space: each fibre of the family gets its own j-value.

The implementation follows the local-to-global mathematical construction. `EllipticCurveGeom` includes existence of a Zariski cover on which the curve, with its chosen zero section, is a projective elliptic Weierstrass model. On a chart, `jSection` uses Mathlib's `WeierstrassCurve.j`. In the [pinned Mathlib definition](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/Weierstrass.lean#L385), this is the inverse of the discriminant *as a unit* times c₄³. Hence it is a regular function on the chart, not a rational function whose poles have been ignored. Ellipticity supplies the unit discriminant, so division by zero and singular fibres never enter this construction.

On the overlap of two charts their pointed Weierstrass models are isomorphic. Such an isomorphism is an admissible change of variables; c₄³ and Δ acquire the same twelfth-power scale, leaving their quotient unchanged. Tau Ceti's `WeierstrassCurve.j_eq_of_isPullback` supplies exactly this compatibility, also allowing change of the coefficient ring. `map_pieceJMap` feeds that compatibility into `glueMorphisms`, which glues the local morphisms on the open cover. The sheaf/gluing uniqueness shows that the result is independent of the atlas and local equations. The chart characterization and the comparison for `toEllipticCurveGeom W` verify that the construction returns the original c₄³/Δ, not merely some isomorphism invariant.

This construction works over arbitrary bases, including characteristics 2 and 3: it divides by Δ, not by 2 or 3. It is compatible with pullback to any new base and with pointed isomorphisms. Equal j-values do not assert isomorphism over the original field (twists can have the same j); over a scheme this definition also does not construct a universal elliptic curve on the j-line or prove the coarse-moduli universal property. Those are separate assertions.

Correctly stated. This is an elliptic-curve-specific theorem establishing finite generation, and hence finite rank, of E(K) over a number field. It is the appropriate module-language result to link to the finiteness assertion behind LeanBridge’s [`ec.rank`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.rank), alongside [`ec.mordell_weil_theorem`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.mordell_weil_theorem). The [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/36f24f5d94ccf25e167520cf4c0f1a028c064fb0/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/FinitelyGenerated.lean#L152) states:

```lean
WeierstrassCurve.Affine.moduleFinite_point_of_numberField
  {F : Type*} [Field F] [NumberField F] [DecidableEq F]
  {W : WeierstrassCurve.Affine F} [W.toAffine.IsElliptic] :
  Module.Finite ℤ W.Point
```

Here F is the number field K of the natural-language statement. `W.IsElliptic` asserts a nonzero discriminant, so the Weierstrass equation is nonsingular. `W.Point` is the full elliptic-curve group: it contains O, the point at infinity, as well as the affine solutions. The namespace `Affine` describes its coordinate presentation, not the omission of O. `DecidableEq F` enables branching in coordinate formulas and imposes no mathematical restriction in classical Lean.

What does the conclusion mean? `Module.Finite ℤ W.Point` says there exist finitely many points P₁,…,Pₙ such that every K-rational point is an integer linear combination of them. Integer multiplication is repeated addition in the elliptic-curve group. The ℤ here is the scalar ring of the abelian group; it does not say that the curve is defined over ℤ. Nor does `Finite` here say that E(K) is a finite set. A group isomorphic to ℤ is an important example satisfying the conclusion.

Why does this establish the finite rank in the blueprint? A finitely generated abelian group has a decomposition E(K) ≅ T ⊕ ℤʳ, where T is finite torsion and r is a finite nonnegative integer. Equivalently, tensoring with ℚ gives a vector space generated by the finitely many images Pᵢ⊗1; torsion vanishes in this tensor product, and its dimension is r. Quotienting by T gives a finite free ℤ-module of rank r. Thus the theorem supplies the arithmetic finiteness needed for the rank definition. Finite generation is stronger than finite rank: for example ℚ has rank one as a ℤ-module but is not finitely generated. In particular, the conclusion is substantive arithmetic information about E(K).

The general function `Module.finrank` only extracts a natural-number rank once a module is supplied; by itself it proves no finiteness theorem for elliptic curves. It is therefore not the primary declaration for this finiteness assertion. After the theorem above is available, `Module.finrank ℤ W.Point` expresses the integer r. This distinction corrects the target of the earlier generic-rank review.

The proof is a conversion of the already established [Mordell–Weil theorem `fg_point_of_numberField`](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/36f24f5d94ccf25e167520cf4c0f1a028c064fb0/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/FinitelyGenerated.lean#L145) through `Module.Finite.iff_addGroup_fg`. The latter equates finite generation of an additive group with finite generation of its associated ℤ-module. Declaring this proof as an `instance` lets Lean reuse it automatically; it introduces no additional hypothesis or axiom. The underlying theorem handles a general Weierstrass model by an admissible change of variables, invokes the number-field descent theorem, and transports finite generation back through the group isomorphism. The required class-group and unit-group finiteness hypotheses are discharged for the factor fields in the same file.

The [roadmap’s Mordell–Weil milestone](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/2172af4ad0d340223ad59e6a5f698766118142c1/TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves/README.md#L1151) has no separately tagged Check for this instance. Existing named curve checks supply concrete calibrations:

For a finite abelian extension L/K of number fields unramified outside a finite set S of finite places, any group homomorphism from the fractional ideals prime to S to Gal(L/K) whose value at each prime v outside S represents the global Artin symbol of the prime idele class at v is the ideal-theoretic Artin map. Correct because the group of fractional ideals prime to S is freely generated by the primes outside S, so a homomorphism on it is determined by its values on those primes, and the Frobenius normalisation identifies each such value with the Frobenius at v; this is the uniqueness half of the comparison of the idelic and ideal-theoretic reciprocity maps (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, VI §7). Red-team checks: the hypothesis on φ is satisfiable (by the ideal-theoretic Artin map itself, via the previous result) and is what forces the conclusion; only the standard axioms.

States that the prime idele class at v is the class of the idele concentrated at v whose v-component is some uniformizer π of K_v (an element with ord_v(π) = 1). This is the defining property of the construction and is all a user needs, since the particular uniformizer chosen is deliberately hidden. True by construction. Red-team checks: the uniformizer predicate agrees with ord_v(π) = 1, the usual meaning.

For a finite abelian extension L/K of number fields unramified outside a finite set S of finite places, and a finite place v outside S, the global Artin symbol of the prime idele class at v equals the class of the ideal-theoretic Artin map evaluated at the prime ideal v; that is, the idelic and the ideal-theoretic Artin symbols agree at primes outside S (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, VI §7; Milne, Class Field Theory, V §3 and §5). Correct because both sides are the Frobenius at v: the idelic side by the Frobenius normalisation above, the ideal side by the defining property of the ideal-theoretic Artin map. Red-team checks: the prime v is passed as an element I of the group of ideals prime to S together with a proof that I is v, so the statement really is about the prime v (the extra hypothesis v ∉ S is implied by this and costs nothing); only the standard axioms.

For a finite abelian extension L/K of number fields, a finite place v of K and a prime Q of L above v at which L/K is unramified, every automorphism σ whose class is the global Artin symbol of the prime idele class at v is an arithmetic Frobenius at Q (σ(x) ≡ x^{N v} mod Q for all integers x of L); in other words the idelic Artin map sends the class of the uniformizer idele at v to the Frobenius at v. This is the Frobenius normalisation of Artin reciprocity in idelic form (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, VI §5; Milne, Class Field Theory, V §5, Theorem 5.3). Proof idea: a Frobenius τ at Q exists, the previous result identifies the Artin symbol with the class of τ, and for an abelian Galois group passing to the abelianization loses nothing, so σ = τ. Conventions: 'the prime idele class' is built from one fixed uniformizer; the same conclusion for any other uniformizer follows from the file's general formula (Artin symbol of x = Frobenius^{ord_v(x)}), and the isomorphism C_K/N(C_L) ≅ Gal(L/K) itself is the separate declaration globalArtinEquiv. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses (a σ satisfying the hypothesis always exists, compiled); commutativity and unramifiedness are both used; specialised to ℚ(ζ₅)/ℚ at the prime 2, where it gives σ(ζ) = ζ², arithmetic Frobenius, as expected; only the standard axioms.

For a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields, a finite place v of K, a prime Q of L above v at which L/K is unramified, and an arithmetic Frobenius σ at Q (σ(x) ≡ x^{N v} mod Q for every integer x of L), the global Artin symbol of the class of the idele concentrated at v with component x ∈ K_v^× is σ raised to the power ord_v(x), in the abelianized Galois group. This is the standard computation of the idelic norm residue symbol at an unramified place (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, VI §5): the global symbol restricted to K_v^× is the local symbol, and for an unramified local extension the local symbol sends x to Frobenius^{ord_v(x)}; the proof is exactly that composition of the library's local-global compatibility and its unramified local computation. Red-team checks: unramifiedness is genuinely needed (when Q is ramified a Frobenius is only determined up to inertia, so the formula fails for some choices); the normalisation is arithmetic, not geometric, matching Neukirch; checked downstream in ℚ(ζ₅)/ℚ, where the symbol at 2 sends ζ to ζ²; only the standard axioms.

With L/K a finite Galois extension of number fields, v a finite place unramified at a prime Q of L above it, and σ an arithmetic Frobenius at Q, the global Artin symbol of the prime idele class at v is the class of σ in the abelianized Galois group. This is the uniformizer case (ord_v = 1) of the preceding formula, i.e. the classical fact that the Artin map sends the prime idele at an unramified place to Frobenius (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, VI §5). Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (a Frobenius always exists at a prime of a Galois extension of number fields); a one-line consequence of the general formula; only the standard axioms.

Defines, for a finite place v of a number field K, the prime idele class: the class in the idele class group C_K (ideles modulo the principal ideles K^×) of the idele whose v-component is a uniformizer of the completion K_v and whose components at all other places, finite and infinite, are 1. This is the standard prime idele of class field theory, the idelic counterpart of the prime ideal v (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. VI). Convention: the uniformizer is one fixed but unspecified choice, so the class itself depends on that choice (for K = ℚ, v = 3, the uniformizers 3 and 6 give different classes); only its Artin symbol at an unramified place is choice-free, which the file proves. Red-team checks: 'uniformizer' means normalized valuation 1, and the normalized valuation on K_v is the inverse of the v-adic valuation, i.e. ord_v; the class is genuinely nontrivial, since at a prime of norm 2 in ℚ its Artin symbol in ℚ(ζ₅) has order 4, so it is not 1 (compiled).

Correctly stated. In words: let f be a Morse function on a Hausdorff, boundaryless, finite-dimensional smooth manifold whose band f^-1[c-δ, c+δ] is compact for some δ > 0; then for some 0 < ε ≤ δ there are charts with pairwise disjoint domains, one centred at each critical point p on the level f = c, in which f = c - y_1^2 - ... - y_λ^2 + y_(λ+1)^2 + ... + y_n^2 with λ the Morse index of f at p, and the sublevel {f ≤ c+ε} strong deformation retracts (a retraction, plus a homotopy to the identity that fixes the retract pointwise) onto {f ≤ c-ε} together with, for each such p, the closed disc {|y|^2 ≤ ε, y_j = 0 beyond the first λ coordinates} read through its chart. This is Milnor, Morse Theory, Theorem 3.2 with Remark 3.3 (several critical points on one level): each disc is a λ_p-cell whose boundary sphere lies on the level f = c-ε and whose interior lies above it, so the retract is {f ≤ c-ε} with one λ_p-cell attached at each p, and a strong deformation retraction gives Milnor's homotopy equivalence. The proof follows Milnor: lower f inside small ellipsoids of the charts to a function F with the same sublevel at c+ε but no critical points in its band, deform {F ≤ c+ε} onto {F ≤ c-ε} by the no-critical-value theorem (Milnor 3.1), then retract that set onto {f ≤ c-ε} plus the cells by shrinking the positive coordinates. Two conventions to know: it produces one ε for each δ, where Milnor says for all sufficiently small ε (the same charts in fact work for every smaller ε), and it assumes f is Morse on all of the manifold rather than only at the level c; both are recorded as generality notes, neither makes the statement wrong. Red-team checks: specialised to the height function on the round n-sphere at its maximum, where it yields the north pole with index n and a full n-cell; proved separately that each cell meets {f ≤ c-ε} exactly in its boundary sphere, so the cells are genuinely attached; hypotheses satisfiable and each one needed; no Mathlib counterpart. (With no critical point on the level, the statement is Milnor 3.1, as it should be.)

Correctly stated. In words: let f be a smooth function on a Hausdorff, boundaryless, finite-dimensional manifold, and let finitely many smooth charts with pairwise disjoint domains each contain the closed ball of radius sqrt(2ε) about the origin in their image and put f in the normal form c - (squares of the first k coordinates) + (squares of the others); if the band f^-1[c-ε, c+ε] is compact and every critical point in it lies in a chart domain, then {f ≤ c+ε} strong deformation retracts onto {f ≤ c-ε} together with the discs {|y|^2 ≤ ε, y_j = 0 beyond the first k coordinates} of the charts. This is the chart-level form of Milnor, Morse Theory, Theorem 3.2 and Remark 3.3, with the Morse-lemma charts given as hypotheses instead of constructed. Proof as in Milnor: the modified function F = f - μ(|u|^2 + 2|v|^2), with μ a smooth nonincreasing cutoff equal to 2ε up to ε and vanishing beyond 2ε, has the same sublevel at c+ε and no critical point in its own band (at a critical point in a chart the positive coordinates v vanish, and there F < c-ε), so the no-critical-value theorem deforms {F ≤ c+ε} onto {F ≤ c-ε}, which retracts onto {f ≤ c-ε} plus the cells by shrinking the positive coordinates; the two retractions compose. Convention: if k exceeds the dimension n, every coordinate counts as negative and the disc is the full n-ball, so the cell has dimension min(k, n). Red-team checks: every hypothesis load-bearing; hypotheses satisfiable (the Morse version applies it, specialised to the sphere's height function); each disc is a cell meeting {f ≤ c-ε} exactly in its boundary sphere (proved); no Mathlib counterpart.

Says: let X be a Polish space (separable and completely metrizable) whose measurable sets are exactly its Borel sets, and let s be an uncountable Borel subset of X; then there is a continuous one-to-one map from Cantor space {0,1}^N into X whose image lies inside s. Because Cantor space is compact and X is Hausdorff, such a map is automatically a homeomorphism onto its image, so this is exactly the perfect set theorem for Borel sets of Alexandrov and Hausdorff as stated in Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Theorem 13.6 (an uncountable Borel set contains a homeomorphic copy of Cantor space), in the same form Mathlib uses for closed sets. Why it holds: by Kechris Theorem 13.1 (in Mathlib) every Borel set is closed, indeed clopen, for some finer Polish topology with the same Borel sets; the perfect set theorem for closed sets in that finer topology gives the map, and a map continuous into a finer topology is continuous into the original one. Convention: 'Borel' really means Borel here, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra itself, not merely for some sigma-algebra containing the open sets (for which the claim fails, e.g. for a Bernstein set when every set is declared measurable). Red-team checks at 84465ed195: derived the homeomorphic-embedding (closed embedding) form from the conclusion in one line; hypotheses satisfiable (all of R, and the irrationals in [0,1]); uncountability is needed (the empty set) and separability is needed (an uncountable discrete space admits no such map though every set is Borel); not stated in pinned Mathlib 2cabef97 for Borel or analytic sets (grep, loogle, leansearch, leanfinder, exact?); Astra's blind pass found no correctness problem.

Says: an uncountable Borel subset s of a Polish space has exactly continuum many points, |s| = 2^aleph_0, the cardinality computed in the same universe as the space so no size convention is hidden; this is the 'in particular' of Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Theorem 13.6 (uncountable Borel sets have the cardinality of the continuum, i.e. Borel sets satisfy the continuum hypothesis, without asserting the continuum hypothesis itself). Why it holds: s has at most continuum many points because a standard Borel space injects measurably into Cantor space, and at least continuum many because, by the perfect set theorem for Borel sets proved just above, s contains a one-to-one image of Cantor space, which has 2^aleph_0 points; independently, Mathlib's Borel isomorphism theorem (an uncountable standard Borel space is Borel-isomorphic to Cantor space) gives the same value. Red-team checks at 84465ed195: hypotheses satisfiable and specialised to all of R (giving |R| = continuum); uncountability is needed (countable sets have at most aleph_0 < continuum points); the value cross-checked by a second, independent proof from the Borel isomorphism theorem; it holds more generally in any standard Borel space, recorded as a generality note, not a correctness issue.

Correctly stated: let U be an affine open of a scheme X, M a quasi-coherent sheaf of modules, and take the basic opens D(f) ⊆ U given by sections f of the structure sheaf over U. For every such basic open Y and every finite nonempty family of such basic opens whose union contains Y, the augmented Čech complex 0 → M(Y) → ∏ M(Y ∩ Vᵢ) → ∏ M(Y ∩ Vᵢ ∩ Vⱼ) → ⋯ of the induced cover of Y is exact. This is the standard acyclicity of covers by standard opens that feeds Cartan's criterion in the Stacks Project's proof of Tag 01XB; algebraically it is the exactness of the Čech complex M_g → ∏ M_{g fᵢ} → ⋯ of a module localised at elements generating the unit ideal. Proof: induction on the number of opens, reducing to two basic opens D(c), D(d), where powers c^m, d^n generate the unit ideal. Red-team checks: the Čech-acyclicity predicate unfolds (by definition) to exactly this exactness statement, with Mathlib's Čech complex; hypotheses satisfiable; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated. It says: for any scheme X, any affine open subset U of X and any quasi-coherent sheaf of modules M on X, the cohomology groups Hⁿ(U, M) vanish in every degree n ≥ 1, with no Noetherian, finiteness or separatedness hypothesis. This is exactly the Stacks Project, Lemma 30.2.2 (Tag 01XB); Hartshorne's Theorem III.3.5 is the special case of a Noetherian affine scheme. The groups are genuine sheaf cohomology: Hⁿ(U, M) is the Ext group from the free abelian sheaf on U to M in the category of sheaves of abelian groups on X, i.e. the derived functors of sections over U applied to M as an abelian sheaf, which by Hartshorne III.2.6 agree with those computed among sheaves of modules; and quasi-coherence is the standard notion (locally a cokernel of a map between free modules), which on an affine scheme is equivalent to coming from a module. The proof follows Stacks: Cartan's criterion applied to the basic opens D(f) inside U (quasi-compact, closed under intersection, a basis of U), plus exactness of the Čech complex of every finite cover of a basic open by basic opens, proved by induction on the number of opens from the two-open case, where suitable powers c^m, d^n generate the unit ideal and so split every section over D(c) ∩ D(d) as a difference of sections over D(c) and D(d). Degree 0, where the group is the module of sections, is correctly excluded. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: hypotheses are satisfiable (the sheaf associated with any module over any ring, on Spec of that ring); specialised through the open-immersion comparison to the vanishing of Hⁿ⁺¹ of the restricted sheaf on the scheme U itself; only the three standard axioms; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (leansearch, leanfinder, loogle, grep). One MINOR generality note recorded separately: quasi-coherence on U alone would suffice.

Correctly stated: for an affine scheme X and a quasi-coherent sheaf of modules M on X, the sheaf cohomology Hⁿ(X, M) (the Ext groups from the constant sheaf ℤ to M among abelian sheaves, i.e. the derived functors of global sections) vanishes for every n ≥ 1. This is Serre's vanishing theorem as in the Stacks Project, Tag 01XB, taken with U = X, and Hartshorne III.3.5 without the Noetherian hypothesis. It is deduced from the affine-open version in the same file applied to the whole of X, transported along the identification of the cohomology of the open set X with the cohomology of the scheme X. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (Spec of any ring with the sheaf of any module); degree 0 not affected; it also works verbatim as an automatically found instance (probe).

Correctly stated: if f : X → S is an affine morphism and S is an affine scheme, then X is itself affine (an affine morphism to an affine scheme has affine source, Mathlib's isAffine_of_isAffineHom), so every quasi-coherent sheaf of modules on X has Hⁿ(X, M) = 0 for n ≥ 1 by Serre's vanishing theorem; the docstring's example, a scheme finite over a field, is such an X. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed for X to be affine; used by two consumers (cohomology of closed subschemes over a field and the ideal-sheaf Euler characteristic); only the three standard axioms.

Correctly stated: for any commutative ring R (no Noetherian hypothesis, which an earlier version carried) and any quasi-coherent sheaf of modules N on Spec R, the sheaf cohomology Hⁿ(Spec R, N) is zero for every n ≥ 1 — Serre's vanishing theorem on the spectrum of a ring (Stacks Project, Tag 01XB; Hartshorne III.3.5 in the Noetherian case). It is the affine-scheme version of the same file applied to Spec R; being an instance only lets Lean find the vanishing automatically and asserts nothing more. Red-team checks at 84465ed195: the instance is found for degree n + 1 and for numerals; witness: the sheaf associated with an arbitrary module over an arbitrary ring.

Correctly stated: if f is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed disc of radius |r| about c, with r nonzero, then the mean of log|f| over the circle of radius |r| about c is at least k log|r| + log|t|, where k is the order of vanishing of f at c and t is its first nonzero Taylor coefficient there (t = lim f(z)/(z-c)^k). This is Jensen's formula (e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, Ch. 15; in Mathlib as the meromorphic Jensen formula) with the terms log(|r|/|a-c|) of the zeros a other than c dropped, each nonnegative because a lies in the closed disc. Conventions: the logarithm used is even, so log r means log|r| when r is negative, matching the circle of radius |r|; if f vanishes identically, the order and coefficient are recorded as 0 and both sides are 0 (log 0 = 0), the degenerate case where the classical statement reads minus infinity on both sides. With k = 0 it is the sub-mean-value inequality log|f(c)| <= circle mean of log|f|. Red-team checks: specialised to f(c) nonzero, recovering log|f(c)| <= the circle mean; r nonzero is needed (for f = 2z at r = 0 the claim would be log 2 <= 0); Mathlib has only the equality case f(c) nonzero, not this inequality (loogle, leansearch).

Correctly stated: a bounded holomorphic function on the open disc of radius R about c whose radial limit equals a at every angle of a set of positive (outer) measure is the constant a on the whole disc; this is the F. and M. Riesz uniqueness theorem for bounded analytic functions (Duren, Theory of Hp Spaces, Ch. 2). It follows from the Nevanlinna-class theorem applied to f - a, since log+|f - a| <= log+(M + |a|) on every circle inside the disc; an empty disc (R <= 0) is handled trivially. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (f constant a); all four hypotheses are needed (lean_minimal_hypotheses); specialised on the unit disc with bound 1 and angles in [0,1]. Boundedness could be weakened to bounded characteristic (recorded separately as a generality note); that does not affect correctness.

Correctly stated: if f is holomorphic on the open disc of radius R about c, the circle means (1/2pi) of the integral of log+|f(c + r e^{i theta})| over a period are at most C for radii r accumulating at R from below, and f(c + r e^{i theta}) tends to 0 as r increases to R for every angle theta in a set of positive (outer) Lebesgue measure, then f vanishes on the whole disc. This is the F. and M. Riesz uniqueness theorem for the Nevanlinna class (F. and M. Riesz 1916; Duren, Theory of Hp Spaces, Ch. 2, Thm. 2.2: a nonzero function of bounded characteristic has log|f| integrable on the boundary, so its radial limits vanish only on a null set). The hypothesis is exactly bounded characteristic, neither weaker nor stronger: log+|f| is subharmonic, so its circle means increase with r and a bound along radii tending to R bounds them for every r < R with the same constant, while conversely the supremum of the means is an admissible C. Angles are real numbers; since the set of angles with radial limit 0 is 2pi-periodic, a positive-measure set of reals is the same as a positive-measure set of boundary points. Proof idea: if f is not identically 0, Jensen bounds the means of log|f| from below near the boundary, so the means of log+(1/|f|) stay bounded along radii tending to R, while on the given angles (minus the countably many zeros on those circles) log+(1/|f|) tends to infinity; Fatou's lemma gives the contradiction. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (f = 0), so the statement is not vacuous; all four hypotheses are needed (lean_minimal_hypotheses; without the growth bound the Lusin-Privalov function is nonzero with radial limit 0 almost everywhere); the textbook form on the unit disc with a bound for every radius in (0,1) and radial limits along r e^{i theta} follows in three lines; no junk value enters, since the integrands are continuous on every circle inside the disc; Astra (blind pass and refutation pass) found no encoding problem.

Correctly stated. In words: if the unital subalgebras (B_i) are freely independent for a linear functional φ with φ(1) = 1, then the free cumulant of any finite word — letters indexed by a finite set of ordered positions, each letter lying in the subalgebra of its label — vanishes as soon as two of the labels differ. This is the 'freeness implies vanishing of mixed cumulants' half of Nica–Speicher, Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability, Theorem 11.16, stated for an arbitrary finite set of ordered positions so that it applies to every subword; the usual κ_n(a₁,…,aₙ) is the case of positions 1,…,n. Proof idea: induction on the length; if two neighbouring letters share a label, group them into one letter and use the formula for free cumulants with products as arguments (Nica–Speicher Thm 11.12), so the shorter mixed cumulant, which vanishes by induction, equals this one; otherwise centre every letter (cumulants of order ≥ 2 do not change when scalars are added, Prop. 11.15), the centred alternating moment vanishes by freeness, and every other non-crossing partition has a centred singleton block or a shorter mixed block. Red-team checks at 84465ed195: φ(1) = 1 is necessary (φ = 2·identity on ℚ: the scalar family is free but κ₂(1,1) = −2); hypotheses jointly satisfiable by a non-trivial family (evaluation at 0 on ℚ[X], two copies of the whole algebra, where it gives the vanishing of a mixed κ₂ of arbitrary polynomials); every hypothesis is used; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated. In words: let φ be a linear functional on an algebra A over a commutative ring with φ(1) = 1, and (B_i) a family of unital subalgebras; then the family is freely independent (φ(a₁⋯aₙ) = 0 whenever n ≥ 1, each a_j is centred, φ(a_j) = 0, lies in some B_{i_j}, and neighbouring labels differ, i_j ≠ i_{j+1}) if and only if every mixed free cumulant vanishes, i.e. κ_n(a₁,…,aₙ) = 0 whenever a_k ∈ B_{ℓ(k)} and the labels ℓ(1),…,ℓ(n) are not all equal. This is exactly Nica–Speicher, Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability, Theorem 11.16 (there over ℂ; here over any commutative ring and any index set), with Nica–Speicher's definition of freeness and their notion of 'mixed'. The free cumulants are the genuine ones: Möbius inversion of the block moments over the lattice of non-crossing partitions (not all partitions, which would give classical cumulants), and they satisfy the multiplicative moment–cumulant formula φ(a₁⋯aₙ) = Σ_{π non-crossing} Π_{blocks} κ. Why it holds: the moment of a centred alternating word is that sum, and every non-crossing partition has a one-point block (a centred mean, zero) or a block with two neighbouring letters (a mixed cumulant), which gives 'cumulants vanish ⇒ free'; conversely, by induction on length, neighbouring letters with equal labels are merged using the formula for cumulants with products as arguments (Nica–Speicher Thm 11.12), and otherwise the letters are centred, which leaves cumulants of order ≥ 2 unchanged because φ(1) = 1 (Prop. 11.15), and the centred alternating moment vanishes by freeness. Words of length 0 or 1 are never mixed, so the condition says nothing there; for a single subalgebra both sides hold trivially. Red-team checks at 84465ed195: the normalisation φ(1) = 1 is necessary for 'free ⇒ cumulants vanish' (φ = 2·identity on ℚ: the scalar family is free, but the mixed κ₂(1,1) = 2 − 4 ≠ 0); the hypotheses are satisfiable by a non-trivial family (evaluation at 0 on ℚ[X], two copies of the whole algebra); at n = 2 with the second-cumulant formula it recovers φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for free a, b; the non-crossing lattice on 4 points has 14 elements (Catalan, not the Bell number 15); no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; standard axioms only; an independent blind pass by GPT-6 Astra found no correctness defect.

Correctly stated. In words: for any linear functional φ on an algebra over a commutative ring (no normalisation φ(1) = 1 needed), if every mixed free cumulant vanishes — κ_n(a₁,…,aₙ) = 0 whenever a_k lies in the subalgebra B_{ℓ(k)} and the labels are not all equal — then the subalgebras (B_i) are freely independent. This is the 'vanishing of mixed cumulants implies freeness' half of Nica–Speicher, Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability, Theorem 11.16. Why it holds: by the moment–cumulant formula, the moment φ(a₁⋯aₙ) of a centred alternating word is a sum over non-crossing partitions of products of cumulants along the blocks; every non-crossing partition has a block that is a single point, whose cumulant is the mean φ(a_j) = 0, or a block containing two neighbouring positions, whose labels differ because the word alternates, so that block's cumulant is mixed and vanishes. Normalisation is genuinely not used in this direction, as the docstring says. Red-team checks at 84465ed195: the hypothesis is load-bearing (without it every family would be free); freeness here is Nica–Speicher's definition (centred letters, neighbouring labels distinct, non-neighbouring labels may repeat); no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated, in slightly more generality than the textbook. Let A be a finitely generated algebra over a field k whose prime spectrum is irreducible, meaning its nilradical is prime (for example, any domain), and let p be a prime ideal. Then ht p + dim A/p = dim A. Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Thm I.1.8A(b), states this for finitely generated k-domains. Allowing nilpotents keeps it true, because quotienting by the nilradical changes neither the dimension nor any prime's height. Proof for domains: by induction on dim A. A nonzero p contains a height-one prime P. Over a Noether normalization, P contracts to a principal height-one prime of the polynomial ring, so dim A/P = dim A − 1. Conventions: heights lie in ℕ ∪ {∞} and dimensions in {−∞} ∪ ℕ ∪ {∞}. Here every value is finite, and the ring is nonzero because an irreducible space is nonempty, so the zero-ring value −∞ never occurs. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: the domain case follows by instantiation (domains have irreducible spectrum). Specialised to k[X,Y], where maximal ideals get height 2. Irreducibility is genuinely needed: in k[x,y,z]/(xz,yz) (a plane union a line), a closed point of the line off the plane has ht p + dim A/p = 1, not 2. Only the standard axioms are used. No Mathlib duplicate found (exact?, loogle, leansearch, grep).

Correctly stated: let R be a finitely generated algebra over a field and S an integral domain that contains R and is a finitely generated R-module. Then every prime P of S has the same height as its contraction P ∩ R. This holds because both rings are finitely generated domains of the same dimension satisfying the dimension formula ht + dim of quotient = dim, and S/P is integral over R/(P ∩ R). The proof goes through a Noether normalization of R, a polynomial ring, which is normal, so going down holds. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: each hypothesis is needed. If S is not a domain it fails: in k[x] → k[x] × k, the minimal prime k[x] × 0 has height 0 but contracts to (x), of height 1. If R → S is not injective it fails: k[x] → k sends the zero ideal to (x). If S is not integral over R it fails: k[x] ⊂ k[x,y], where (xy − 1) has height 1 but contracts to 0. (Module-finiteness could be weakened to integrality; that is recorded separately as a generality note.) No Mathlib duplicate found.

Correctly stated: if A → B is a map of k-algebras and B is finitely generated over k, then every maximal ideal of B pulls back to a maximal ideal of A, with no condition on A. Proof: by Zariski's lemma, B/m is a finite field extension of k. A/(m ∩ A) embeds in it, and a domain that is finite-dimensional over a field is a field. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: no Mathlib duplicate (Mathlib has the integral-extension version Ideal.IsMaximal.under and the polynomial-ring Jacobson version only; exact? fails).

Correctly stated: for a prime p of a finitely generated k-algebra A, dim A/p equals the transcendence degree over k of the residue field κ(p), which is the fraction field of the domain A/p (Stacks, tag 00P0, applied to A/p). The transcendence degree is finite here, so reading it as a natural number is exact. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: κ(p) carries the k-algebra structure coming from A (the scalar tower k → A/p → κ(p) is found automatically).

Correctly stated: every maximal ideal of a polynomial ring over a field in finitely many variables has height equal to the number of variables. Stacks, tag 00P0, says that the local ring at every maximal ideal has dimension r; over an algebraically closed field these are the ideals (X_1 − a_1, ..., X_n − a_n). Proof by induction on the variables: a maximal ideal of R[X], for R a Jacobson ring, contracts to a maximal ideal of R and has height one more. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: the simp attribute fires (the height of a maximal ideal of k[X,Y,Z] simplifies to 3); no variables gives height 0; no Mathlib duplicate found (leansearch, loogle, grep; Mathlib has only the one-step R[X] lemma it uses).

Correctly stated: a nonzero finitely generated algebra over a field has finite Krull dimension, that is, its dimension is a natural number (neither infinite nor the value minus infinity that the zero ring gets by convention). By Noether normalization it is integral over a polynomial ring in s variables, so its dimension is exactly s. The nonzero hypothesis is genuinely needed, since the zero ring's dimension is minus infinity. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: no Mathlib duplicate found (exact?, instance search, leanfinder, grep of the pinned Mathlib).

Correctly stated: in a finitely generated k-algebra with irreducible spectrum, every maximal ideal has height equal to dim A. Geometrically, all closed points of an irreducible affine variety have local dimension dim X (Stacks, tag 00P0). It is immediate from the dimension formula, since A/m is a field of dimension 0. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: specialised to k[X,Y] (height 2). The finite-type hypothesis is what makes it true: in k[x]_(x)[y], which has dimension 2, the maximal ideal (xy − 1) has height 1.

Correctly stated: if a k-algebra A contains a copy of the polynomial ring k[X_i : i in a finite set I] (an injective k-algebra map) and A is integral over it, then dim A equals the number of variables |I|. This is the dimension count behind Noether normalization (Stacks, Lemma 10.115.4, tag 00OY): an injective integral extension has the same Krull dimension (lying over, going up, incomparability), and k[X_1,...,X_n] has dimension n. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: each hypothesis is needed (k[X] inside k[X,Y] is injective but not integral, dimensions 1 vs 2; a non-injective map can land in a smaller quotient); finiteness of I is assumed, so the count is never a junk value; no Mathlib duplicate found (exact?, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle, grep).

Correctly stated: if A → B is an injective map of finitely generated k-algebras, B is a domain and B is algebraic over A, then dim A = dim B, because both equal their common transcendence degree over k. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: injectivity is needed: k[x] → k sending x to 0 makes k algebraic over k[x], but the dimensions are 1 and 0.

Correctly stated: a finitely generated k-algebra that is an integral domain has Krull dimension equal to its transcendence degree over k (Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Thm I.1.8A(a); Stacks, Lemma 10.116.1, tag 00P0). The transcendence degree is a finite cardinal here, so reading it as a natural number loses nothing: no junk value. Proof: the variables of a Noether normalization form a transcendence basis, since A is integral (hence algebraic) over them. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: specialised at k[X,Y,Z], giving 3; no Mathlib duplicate found (loogle for ringKrullDim with trdeg, leansearch, grep).

Correctly stated: a finitely generated k-domain A has Krull dimension equal to the transcendence degree over k of its fraction field. This is the literal form of Hartshorne I.1.8A(a) and Stacks, tag 00P0. It reduces to the previous result because the fraction field is algebraic over A, so A and its fraction field have the same transcendence degree, which is finite. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: the fraction field enters only through the universal property, so any model of it works.

Correctly stated: for a finitely generated k-domain A and a nonzero element f, the localization A[1/f] has the same Krull dimension as A. Geometrically, a nonempty basic open subset of an irreducible affine variety has the full dimension. A[1/f] is again a finitely generated domain with the same fraction field, so both dimensions equal the transcendence degree. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: f ≠ 0 is needed (f = 0 gives the zero ring); the finite-type hypothesis is needed (a DVR localized at its uniformizer drops from dimension 1 to 0).

Correctly stated: extending the base field does not change the Krull dimension of a finitely generated algebra, dim(K ⊗_k A) = dim A for any field extension K/k. Stacks, Lemma 10.116.6 (tag 00P4), is the pointwise version. It is the case dim K = 0 of the Noetherian tensor-product formula. The zero ring is included, with both sides minus infinity. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: closes by simp from the general formula; 5 consumers.

Correctly stated: for a Noetherian k-algebra K and a finitely generated k-algebra A over a field k, dim(K ⊗_k A) = dim K + dim A. Proof idea: a Noether normalization k[X_1,...,X_s] → A is injective and finite. Tensoring with K keeps it finite, and keeps it injective because every module over a field is flat. So K ⊗ A is integral over K[X_1,...,X_s], whose dimension is dim K + s since K is Noetherian. Convention: if A or K is the zero ring, both sides are minus infinity (the tensor product is zero, and minus infinity plus anything is minus infinity), which is right. Noetherianity of K cannot simply be dropped: for non-Noetherian K, dim K[X] can exceed dim K + 1. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: specialised at A = k[X,Y], giving dim K + 2; the simp attribute fires; no Mathlib duplicate found (loogle for the tensor-product shape, leanfinder, grep).

Correctly stated: for any finitely generated algebra A over a field (no irreducibility needed) and any point p of Spec A, the local dimension of Spec A at p equals ht p + dim A/p. Here local dimension means the smallest dimension of an open neighbourhood, Stacks' dim_x X. Reason: near p only the irreducible components V(q) through p matter, each has dimension dim A/q = ht(p/q) + dim A/p by the dimension formula, and the largest ht(p/q) is ht p. This is equivalent to Stacks, Lemma 10.116.3 (tag 00P1). Red-team audit at 84465ed195: checked on the reducible example k[x,y,z]/(xz,yz): at a closed point of the line off the plane both sides are 1.

Correctly stated, and exactly Stacks, Lemma 10.116.3 (tag 00P1): for X = Spec A with A finitely generated over a field k and a point p, dim_p X = dim A_p + trdeg_k κ(p). The local dimension is the infimum over open neighbourhoods of their Krull dimension, matching Stacks' dim_x X. A_p is the local ring (stalk) at p and κ(p) its residue field. The trdeg is finite, since κ(p) is finitely generated as a field over k, so no junk value arises. It follows from the previous theorem since dim A_p = ht p and dim A/p = trdeg_k κ(p). Red-team audit at 84465ed195: the generic point of the affine line gives 0 + 1 = 1; only the standard axioms are used.

Correctly stated: in Spec A, for A finitely generated over a field, if Z is an irreducible closed subset and U an open set meeting Z, then Z ∩ U has the same dimension as Z. This is the affine case of Hartshorne I, Prop. 1.10 (an open subset of an irreducible variety has its dimension). Proof: Z = Spec(A/p), and Z ∩ U contains a nonempty basic open Spec((A/p)[1/g]), whose dimension equals that of A/p. Red-team audit at 84465ed195: every hypothesis is needed. Without closedness, Z = {generic point, one closed point} of the affine line is irreducible of dimension 1 but meets the complement of that closed point in a single point. Without irreducibility, take a line union a point. Without openness, take U a closed point. If Z ∩ U is empty, its dimension is minus infinity.

Correctly stated: if the curvature of a smooth connection ∇ vanishes at the point x and ∇ᵀ is a torsion-free connection on the tangent bundle, then the second covariant derivative of a smooth section σ is symmetric at x, ∇²σ(u,v) = ∇²σ(v,u) for all tangent vectors u, v there. This is the standard consequence of the Ricci identity (Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 7): the difference ∇²σ(u,v) − ∇²σ(v,u) equals R(u,v)σ(x), which is zero. Note the hypothesis is only flatness at the single point x, so the statement is stronger than the docstring's 'flat connection'. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (simp_all, grind, exact?); the curvature and torsion hypotheses are needed; the smoothness hypothesis on σ is in fact removable (recorded as a generality finding, not a correctness problem).

Correctly stated: the Ricci identity with torsion. For a smooth connection ∇ on a finite-rank real vector bundle over a finite-dimensional Hausdorff smooth manifold, any connection ∇ᵀ on the tangent bundle, a smooth section σ and tangent vectors u, v at a point x, it says ∇²σ(u,v) − ∇²σ(v,u) = R(u,v)σ(x) − ∇_{T(u,v)}σ, where ∇²σ(u,v) = ∇_u(∇_Y σ) − ∇_{∇ᵀ_u Y}σ for any smooth vector field Y with Y(x) = v, R(X,Y) = ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_Y∇_X − ∇_[X,Y] (Lee's sign convention, with the standard bracket [X,Y] = DY·X − DX·Y) and T(X,Y) = ∇ᵀ_X Y − ∇ᵀ_Y X − [X,Y] is the torsion of ∇ᵀ. This is the commutation rule for second covariant derivatives (Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 7, in the torsion-free case; the −∇_{T(u,v)}σ term is the standard correction when ∇ᵀ has torsion). Why it holds: extend u and v to smooth fields X and Y; the difference is ∇_X∇_Yσ − ∇_Y∇_Xσ − ∇_{∇ᵀ_X Y − ∇ᵀ_Y X}σ, and ∇ᵀ_X Y − ∇ᵀ_Y X = [X,Y] + T(X,Y). Conventions: ∇ᵀ needs no smoothness (it is only evaluated on smooth fields, never differentiated); σ must be smooth because the library defines the second covariant derivative of a non-smooth section to be 0, where the right side need not vanish. Red-team checks: read the definitions of the second covariant derivative, the curvature tensor, Mathlib's torsion and Lie bracket and checked their signs and argument order against Lee; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (simp_all, grind, exact?); the conclusion is not closable by simp/grind/exact? (not tautological); the smoothness hypothesis is needed; specialised to the tangent bundle and instantiated at the Levi-Civita connection of a smooth Riemannian metric (compiles); no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib (which has no curvature) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: the Ricci identity ∇²σ(u,v) − ∇²σ(v,u) = R(u,v)σ(x) for a smooth connection ∇ on a finite-rank real vector bundle, a torsion-free connection ∇ᵀ on the tangent bundle (one with ∇ᵀ_X Y − ∇ᵀ_Y X = [X,Y], e.g. a Levi-Civita connection), a smooth section σ and tangent vectors u, v at x. Here ∇²σ(u,v) = ∇_u∇_Yσ − ∇_{∇ᵀ_u Y}σ for any smooth field Y with Y(x) = v is the genuine second covariant derivative, and R(X,Y) = ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_Y∇_X − ∇_[X,Y] is the curvature with Lee's sign, so this is exactly Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 7 (Ricci identities), stated for a general vector bundle. It follows from the version with torsion in the same file, since the torsion tensor of a torsion-free connection is zero. The statement is pointwise in the tangent vectors u, v (no regularity is asked of vector fields); σ must be smooth because the second covariant derivative of a non-smooth section is defined to be 0, which would make the identity false there, so the hypothesis excludes only the junk case. Red-team checks: definitions and sign conventions of ∇², curvature, torsion and bracket read in their own files and Mathlib; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; both hypotheses needed; instantiated at the smooth, torsion-free Levi-Civita connection of a smooth Riemannian metric with σ any smooth vector field (compiles), which gives the classical vector-field identity.

The category of geometric vector bundles over X: linear schemes over X whose degree-one part is finite locally free, with all morphisms of linear schemes between them, i.e. morphisms of schemes over X whose pullback on functions preserves the gradings. These are exactly the linear morphisms of vector bundles (given locally by matrices of regular functions), since a grading-preserving map of symmetric algebras is determined by a linear map in degree one; they are the morphisms of vector bundles in Stacks Tag 01M1, Definition 27.6.2. Red-team audit at 956e316250: checked in Lean that morphisms between total spaces V(E) -> V(F) in this category correspond bijectively to O_X-linear maps E -> F, and that every object is isomorphic to a total space.

Defines when a linear scheme over X (an affine scheme over X whose sheaf of functions is graded and generated freely by its degree-one part, so that it is Spec of a symmetric algebra) is a geometric vector bundle: when that degree-one part is a finite locally free sheaf. This is the Stacks Project's definition of a vector bundle (Tag 01M1, Definition 27.6.2: an affine morphism with pushed-forward functions graded as a direct sum of E_n, with E_0 the structure sheaf and Sym^n E_1 isomorphic to E_n), with E_1 required to be finite locally free. It agrees with Hartshorne's definition by charts (Ex. II.5.18): locally E_1 is free, so the bundle is affine space over the open set, and two grading-preserving trivialisations differ by a grading-preserving, that is linear, change of fibre coordinates, which is exactly Hartshorne's linear transition condition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: compared clause by clause with Stacks 27.6.2 (being freely generated in degree one is equivalent to the canonical maps Sym^n E_1 -> E_n being isomorphisms); witness: the total space of the structure sheaf satisfies it; non-witness: Spec Sym F for a quasi-coherent F that is not finite locally free does not (via isGeometricVectorBundle_linearSpec_obj_iff).

Unfolds the definition: a linear scheme over X is a geometric vector bundle exactly when the degree-one part of its grading is a finite locally free sheaf. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: name and docstring match the statement; no hypotheses.

For a quasi-coherent sheaf F on X, the linear scheme Spec_X(Sym F) is a geometric vector bundle exactly when F is finite locally free. It holds because the degree-one part of Sym F is F itself (Sym^1 F = F) and finite local freeness is invariant under isomorphism. Red-team audit at 956e316250: no hypotheses; used as the non-witness test for the definition.

The contravariant equivalence between finite locally free sheaves on X and geometric vector bundles over X, sending E to Spec_X(Sym E), with inverse taking the degree-one part of the grading. This is Stacks Lemma 27.6.3 (vector bundles over S are anti-equivalent to quasi-coherent sheaves, via V(E) = Spec Sym E and the degree-one part; the same convention as EGA II 1.7.8) restricted on both sides to the finite locally free case. It is obtained by restricting the anti-equivalence between quasi-coherent sheaves and linear schemes, since a linear scheme lies in the subcategory exactly when its degree-one part is finite locally free. Red-team audit at 956e316250: compared with Stacks 27.6.2-27.6.3; checked in Lean that the unit gives back E and that the functor is literally Spec Sym on objects; the equivalence uses no sorry.

The counit of the contravariant equivalence at a geometric vector bundle V is the canonical isomorphism Spec_X(Sym A_1) = V, where A_1 is the degree-one part of the grading of V. It follows from the same statement for all linear schemes. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.
On morphisms, the contravariant equivalence acts as Spec Sym of the given map of sheaves. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The geometric vector bundle attached to E by the contravariant equivalence has underlying linear scheme Spec_X(Sym E). It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

On morphisms, the inverse of the contravariant equivalence takes the degree-one part of the grading-preserving algebra map. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The inverse of the contravariant equivalence sends a geometric vector bundle to the degree-one part of its grading, viewed as a finite locally free sheaf. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The unit of the contravariant equivalence at E is the canonical identification Sym^1 E = E of the degree-one part of Sym E with E. It follows from the same statement for all quasi-coherent sheaves (the unit of the anti-equivalence between quasi-coherent sheaves and linear schemes). Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The covariant total-space functor sending a finite locally free sheaf E to the geometric vector bundle V(E) = Spec_X(Sym E^dual), where E^dual = Hom(E, O_X); a morphism E -> F acts through the dual map F^dual -> E^dual, so the functor is covariant. This is the total space whose sheaf of sections is E (in Stacks/EGA notation it is V(E^dual)). Red-team audit at 956e316250: checked in Lean that the T-points of its underlying scheme, for any scheme T over X, are the global sections of the pullback of E (not of its dual), via totalSpaceHomEquiv and the identity comparison totalSpaceForgetIso.

For every scheme X, the total-space functor E -> V(E) = Spec_X(Sym E^dual) is an equivalence of categories from finite locally free O_X-modules (any, possibly varying, finite rank, with all O_X-linear maps) to geometric vector bundles over X (with linear morphisms over X, i.e. those preserving the gradings); the inverse sends a bundle to the dual of the degree-one part of its grading. This is the covariant form of Stacks Lemma 27.6.3 and EGA II 1.7, and it strengthens Hartshorne Ex. II.5.18, which gives a bijection on isomorphism classes for a fixed rank n: here it is a full equivalence of categories and no rank is fixed. The proof composes the duality anti-equivalence E -> E^dual of finite locally free sheaves (E is canonically its double dual) with the anti-equivalence E -> Spec_X(Sym E), which comes from relative Spec (affine schemes over X versus quasi-coherent algebras) and the symmetric algebra (quasi-coherent sheaves versus graded algebras freely generated in degree one). Convention: geometric vector bundles are defined in the graded form of Stacks Tag 01M1, Definition 27.6.2, not by charts; the two are equivalent because grading-preserving trivialisations differ by linear coordinate changes. Red-team audit at 956e316250: it is a genuine equivalence (natural unit and counit isomorphisms), covariant, with functor Spec(Sym E^dual) as announced; checked in Lean that it gives Hom(V(E), V(F)) = Hom(E, F), that every geometric vector bundle is isomorphic to some V(E), and that the T-points of V(E) are the sections of E; no sorry in its axioms.

The counit of the equivalence at a geometric vector bundle V with degree-one part A_1 is Spec Sym of the double-dual isomorphism of A_1 followed by the canonical isomorphism Spec_X(Sym A_1) = V. It follows by unfolding the composite of the two equivalences. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The functor of the equivalence between finite locally free sheaves and geometric vector bundles is the total-space functor. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.
The inverse of the equivalence takes the degree-one part of the grading and then dualises. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The unit of the equivalence at E is the canonical isomorphism of E with its double dual followed by the dual of the identification Sym^1(E^dual) = E^dual. It follows by unfolding the composite of the two equivalences. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

Forgetting the grading, the geometric total space of E is the affine scheme Spec_X(Sym E^dual) over X built in the total-space file, naturally in E; the comparison is the identity. Red-team audit at 956e316250: checked in Lean that the two functors are definitionally equal (the isomorphism can be taken to be the identity).
Each component of the comparison between the two total-space functors is the identity. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.
Each component of the inverse comparison between the two total-space functors is the identity. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

The total-space functor from finite locally free sheaves to geometric vector bundles is an equivalence of categories, in particular fully faithful and essentially surjective, as a direct consequence of totalSpaceEquiv. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring; it is obtained directly from the equivalence.
A morphism E -> F acts on total spaces as Spec Sym of its dual map F^dual -> E^dual. It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.
The linear scheme underlying the total space of E is Spec_X(Sym E^dual). It holds by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement matches its docstring.

Says: in a positive definite unimodular lattice of rank between 2 and 9, every vector r with r·r = 2 is orthogonal to some nonzero s with s·s ≤ 2. Proof: the vectors pairing evenly with r form a sublattice N of index 2 (determinant 4) in which r splits off orthogonally; its complement has rank n − 1 ≤ 8 and determinant 2, and Hermite's inequality bounds the complement's minimum by 2. Correct as stated; the lower rank bound is in fact implied by the existence of r (a red-team generality note, not a correctness issue). Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (E₈ with a root r).

Says: a positive definite unimodular lattice of rank n with 2 ≤ n ≤ 9 contains a vector with x·x = 2. Proof: the vectors of even norm form a sublattice of index at most 2, hence of determinant at most 4; Hermite's inequality in rank ≤ 9 puts its minimum below 4, and that minimum is even and positive, so it is 2. Rank 1 is rightly excluded (ℤ has only square norms). Red-team checks: specialised at E₈ (its roots); both rank bounds load-bearing for the proof (lean_minimal_hypotheses).

Says: a nonzero positive definite unimodular lattice of rank n ≤ 5 has a vector of norm 1, i.e. minimum 1. Proof: Hermite's inequality min^n ≤ (4/3)^(n(n−1)/2) · det with det = 1 gives min^n < 2^n for 1 ≤ n ≤ 5 (at n = 5, (4/3)^10 ≈ 17.8 < 32), so min < 2, while min ≥ 1 by positivity and integrality. Red-team checks: specialised to I₃ (minimum 1); nontriviality needed (the zero lattice has minimum 0 by convention); fails at rank 8 (E₈ has minimum 2).

Says: a nonzero even positive definite unimodular lattice of rank at most 8 has minimum 2: evenness gives minimum ≥ 2 and Hermite's inequality gives ≤ 2. Such a lattice is in fact E₈ (even unimodular positive definite lattices have rank divisible by 8; Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. V), whose minimum is 2. Red-team checks: consistent with the library's E₈ minimum; nontriviality needed.

Says: a nonzero positive definite unimodular lattice of rank at most 8 without vectors of norm 1 has minimum exactly 2: Hermite gives minimum ≤ 2, positivity gives ≥ 1, and 1 is excluded by hypothesis. Red-team checks: specialised at E₈, giving minimum 2, in agreement with the library's independent computation of E₈'s minimum; each hypothesis needed (zero lattice, I₈).

Says: a positive definite unimodular lattice of rank at most 8 has minimum at most 2; for the zero lattice the minimum is 0 by convention. Proof: Hermite's inequality with det = 1 gives min^n ≤ (4/3)^(n(n−1)/2) < 3^n for 1 ≤ n ≤ 8 (at n = 8, ≈ 3155 < 6561), so min < 3. Red-team checks: E₈ satisfies the hypotheses with minimum exactly 2, so the bound is attained; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Says: every positive definite unimodular lattice L of rank n ≤ 9 is isometric to Iₙ (ℤⁿ with the dot product), or to E₈, or to I₁ ⊕ E₈; since an isometry preserves rank, the second case can only occur for n = 8 and the third only for n = 9, so the statement is exactly the classical list (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG, Ch. 16, Table 16.7; Kneser 1957; Chenevier, Unimodular hunting, Table 1.1), and the zero lattice is the case n = 0 of Iₙ. Here a lattice is a full-rank subgroup of a rational vector space with an integer-valued symmetric form, the norm of x is x·x, unimodular means the lattice equals its dual (so the Gram determinant is 1 in the positive definite case), and the minimum is the least norm of a nonzero vector (0 for the zero lattice). The objects are the genuine ones: Iₙ has the identity Gram matrix, E₈ has Mathlib's E₈ Cartan matrix as Gram matrix (even, determinant 1, positive definite, all proved in the library), and an isometry is a form-preserving linear bijection carrying one lattice onto the other. Proof idea: split L as I_k ⊕ L₀ with L₀ free of norm-1 vectors; Hermite's inequality gives L₀ two orthogonal roots r, s, and the Kneser 2-neighbour along r + s is again I_m ⊕ M₀ with M₀ of rank ≤ 5, hence M₀ = 0, so the neighbour is Iₙ, which forces 4 | rank L₀ and then L₀ = E₈ (or 0). Red-team checks at 84465ed195: hypotheses satisfiable (E₈, Iₙ); specialised at E₈; the E₈ and I₁ ⊕ E₈ disjuncts proved to force rank 8 and 9; rank hypothesis load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); only the standard axioms (lean_verify); an independent blind pass by GPT-6 Astra found no correctness defect.

Says: every even (all norms x·x even) positive definite unimodular lattice of rank 8 is isometric to E₈; with the library's proof that E₈ itself is even, unimodular and positive definite of rank 8, this is the uniqueness of E₈ — the 'in particular' of the classification (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG, Ch. 16; Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. V). Proof: an even lattice has no vectors of norm 1, so the file's characterisation of E₈ as the only nonzero such lattice of rank ≤ 9 applies. Red-team checks: specialised to D₈⁺ (the library's even unimodular checkerboard lattice), giving an isometry from E₈; E₈ is defined by its Cartan matrix, a genuine construction.

Says: a nonzero positive definite unimodular lattice of rank at most 9 with no vector of norm 1 is isometric to E₈ (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG, Ch. 16: E₈ is the first unimodular lattice without norm-1 vectors). Proof: the rank is at least 6; two orthogonal roots give a Kneser 2-neighbour whose norm-1 part has rank ≥ 2 and whose complement, of rank ≤ 7 and free of norm-1 vectors, vanishes, so the neighbour is Iₙ with 4 | n, hence n = 8, and a 2-neighbour of I₈ without norm-1 vectors is E₈. Red-team checks: specialised to E₈ itself (which has no norm-1 vectors); nontriviality is needed (the zero lattice satisfies the other hypotheses).

Says: a positive definite unimodular lattice of rank n ≤ 5 is isometric to Iₙ, ℤⁿ with the dot product (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG, Ch. 16). Proof: split off the sublattice spanned by the norm-1 vectors, L ≅ I_k ⊕ L₀, with L₀ unimodular and free of norm-1 vectors; a nonzero such L₀ has rank ≥ 6 by Hermite's inequality, so L₀ = 0. The rank-0 case is I₀. Red-team checks: isometry is a genuine form-preserving bijection of lattices; rank bound load-bearing in the stated form (E₈ in rank 8).

Says: a nonzero positive definite unimodular lattice without vectors of norm 1 has rank at least 6, because in rank ≤ 5 the minimum is 1. True but not sharp: the sharp bound is 8 (E₈), which the file obtains later from its rank-seven vanishing theorem; the weaker bound is the stepping stone. Red-team checks: specialised at E₈ (no norm-1 vectors, rank 8); nontriviality needed (zero lattice).

Says: a positive definite unimodular lattice of rank at most 7 with no vector of norm 1 is the zero lattice. This is sharp (E₈ in rank 8) and standard (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG, Ch. 16, Table 16.7). Proof: a nonzero such lattice has rank ≥ 6, contains orthogonal roots r, s, and its 2-neighbour along r + s is I_k ⊕ M₀ with k ≥ 2 and M₀ of rank ≤ 5 free of norm-1 vectors, so M₀ = 0 and the neighbour is Iₙ; that forces 4 | n, impossible for n = 6, 7. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfied by the zero lattice I₀ (no contradiction derivable); rank bound cannot be raised to 8 (E₈).

Correctly stated: if X is completely metrizable (its topology comes from some complete metric) and S is a Gδ subset of X (a countable intersection of open sets), then S with the subspace topology is again completely metrizable. This is the second half of Alexandrov's theorem as stated in Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Thm. 3.11. The proof writes S as the intersection of open sets U_n and maps S into X × [0,∞)^ℕ by x ↦ (x, (1/d(x, X∖U_n))_n); these coordinates blow up at the boundary of each U_n, so the image is closed and homeomorphic to S, and a closed subspace of a completely metrizable space is completely metrizable (Bernshteyn's argument, as in Tserunyan's notes). Note that the complete metric on S is a new one, not the restriction of X's metric (the irrationals are not complete for the usual metric). Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (X = ℝ); the Gδ hypothesis is needed (ℚ in ℝ is not completely metrizable, derived in Lean via the converse); standard axioms only; not in the pinned Mathlib (Mathlib master now has it under the same name).

Correctly stated: a Gδ subset of a Polish space (separable and completely metrizable), with the subspace topology, is Polish, as in Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Thm. 3.11. It follows from the completely metrizable version together with the fact that every subspace of a separable metrizable space is separable. Red-team checks: specialised in Lean to show that the irrationals and the open interval (0,1) are Polish subspaces of ℝ; the Gδ hypothesis is needed (ℚ in ℝ is not Polish); not in the pinned Mathlib (Mathlib master now has it under the same name).

Correctly stated: in a completely metrizable space X, a subset is Gδ (a countable intersection of open sets) exactly when it is completely metrizable in the subspace topology, which is Alexandrov's theorem with its converse (Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Thm. 3.11). It combines the two directions in this file: Gδ implies completely metrizable by the closed-embedding argument, and the converse holds because a metrizable space is perfectly normal and Hausdorff. Red-team checks: both directions are present, with no hypothesis beyond complete metrizability of X; standard axioms only; not in Mathlib (pinned or master).

Correctly stated: a subset S of a Polish space X is Polish in the subspace topology exactly when S is a Gδ subset of X (a countable intersection of open sets). This is Alexandrov's theorem with its converse as in Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Thm. 3.11 (Tserunyan's notes, Thm. 1.11). Gδ implies Polish because S embeds as a closed subset of X × [0,∞)^ℕ via x ↦ (x, (1/d(x, X∖U_n))_n), and subspaces of separable metrizable spaces are separable; Polish implies Gδ because a complete metric on S makes S = closure(S) ∩ ⋂ U_n with U_n the open sets on which S has small d-oscillation, and closed sets of a metrizable space are Gδ. The empty set is covered, being both Gδ and Polish. Red-team checks: full-statement test passed (both directions, for Polish and for completely metrizable spaces, with no extra hypothesis); specialised in Lean to prove that the irrationals are a Polish subspace of ℝ and that ℚ is not (it is not Gδ, by Baire); standard axioms only; the equivalence is not in Mathlib (pinned or master), only its forward half is in Mathlib master.

Correctly stated: if X is a perfectly normal Hausdorff space (every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets; every metrizable space is one) and S ⊆ X is completely metrizable in the subspace topology, then S is a Gδ subset of X. Kechris, Classical Descriptive Set Theory, Thm. 3.11 states this for metrizable X; the statement here is more general and contains that case. Proof idea: fix a complete metric d on S and let U_n be the union of the open sets of X whose points in S are pairwise less than 1/(n+1) apart in d; each U_n is open and contains S, and S equals closure(S) ∩ ⋂ U_n, because at a point x on the right the traces on S of the neighbourhoods of x form a d-Cauchy filter, whose limit in S must be x since X is Hausdorff; closure(S) is Gδ by perfect normality. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (X = ℝ); the separation hypothesis cannot be dropped (a two-point indiscrete space is perfectly normal and its one-point subsets are completely metrizable but not Gδ, checked in Lean), and perfect normality cannot simply be dropped (the point at infinity of the one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete set is not Gδ), though the proof only uses that the closure of S is Gδ; used in Lean to show ℚ is not a Polish subspace of ℝ; Hausdorff could be stated as T0, but Lean derives Hausdorff from T0 plus perfect normality automatically, so nothing is lost.

Correctly stated, in full. Let K be a complete non-archimedean valued field (the trivial absolute value is allowed) and W_n = K<X_1,...,X_n>† the Monsky-Washnitzer algebra: power series whose coefficients satisfy |a_ν| ρ^|ν| → 0 for some radius ρ > 1. The theorem says: if a nonzero commutative K-algebra A is a finitely generated module over W_n through some K-algebra map W_n → A, then for some m ≤ n there is an injective K-algebra map W_m → A over which A is again a finitely generated module. This is Grosse-Klönne's Noether normalisation (J. reine angew. Math. 519 (2000), §1.4(2): every dagger algebra admits a finite injection from some W_d), here proved for every algebra finite over W_n (a dagger algebra W_n/I ≠ 0 is the case of a surjective map) and with the extra bound m ≤ n. Proof idea: induct on n; if the map is injective, stop; otherwise a triangular change of variables X_i ↦ X_i + Y^(α_i) makes a nonzero kernel element distinguished in the last variable Y, and Weierstrass division by it (Grosse-Klönne §1.3(iii)) shows A is already finite over W_(n-1). For n = 0, W_0 = K and K → A is injective because A ≠ 0; the zero algebra has to be excluded since nothing nonzero injects into it.
