Red-team checks (at 956e316250): W checked against Grosse-Klönne §1.2 (a strict radius ρ > 1, constant in all variables, so neither the Tate algebra ρ = 1 nor polynomials); the hypotheses are satisfiable (instantiated at A = W_2 with the identity and at an arbitrary surjective presentation W_3 → A) and give no contradiction under simp_all/omega/aesop/grind; with zero variables it forces m = 0; finiteness is Mathlib's standard notion (A finitely generated as a module through the given map); axioms are only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; Mathlib's own Noether normalisation covers only polynomial rings, and no other Tau Ceti declaration states this.

Correctly stated: if a commutative ring L that is a field is a finitely generated module over a Monsky-Washnitzer algebra W_n (n finite) through some K-algebra map, then L is finite-dimensional over K. This is the residue-field part of Grosse-Klönne §1.4(3), the overconvergent analogue of BGR §6.1.2, Corollary 3 for affinoid algebras. Proof idea: Noether normalisation makes L finite over an injectively embedded W_m; a subring over which a field is integral is itself a field, and W_m is not a field for m ≥ 1 (the variable X_1 is a nonzero non-unit), so m = 0, W_0 = K, and L is finite over K. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed (W_1 is finite over itself but is not finite-dimensional, and the field K(t) is not finite over W_0 = K); the field hypothesis already makes L nonzero, so no separate nonzero assumption is required; instantiated at a field finite over W_0.

Correctly stated: if A is finite over a Monsky-Washnitzer algebra W_n (n finite) and m is a maximal ideal of A, then the residue field A/m is finite-dimensional over K, as in Grosse-Klönne §1.4(3) for maximal ideals (BGR §6.1.2, Corollary 3 in the affinoid case). It follows from the previous result, since A/m is a field and is still finite over W_n. Red-team checks: instantiated at A = W_2 with the identity; maximality is needed (the zero ideal of W_1 has an infinite-dimensional quotient).

Correctly stated: if A is finite over a Monsky-Washnitzer algebra W_n (n finite) and q is an ideal of A whose radical is a maximal ideal, then A/q is finite-dimensional over K. This is exactly Grosse-Klönne §1.4(3) ('if the nilradical of the ideal q is a maximal ideal, then k → A/q is finite'), stated for every algebra finite over W_n, which includes every dagger algebra. Proof idea: A is noetherian, being finite over the noetherian ring W_n, so a power of rad q lies in q; A/q then has a finite filtration by powers of rad q whose layers are finite-dimensional over the residue field A/rad q, which is finite over K by the maximal-ideal case. Red-team checks: instantiated at A = W_2 with the identity and at the powers m^k (k ≥ 1) of a maximal ideal of an arbitrary dagger algebra; the radical hypothesis is needed (q = 0 in W_1). The docstring omits the hypothesis that A is finite over W_n; that is recorded as a documentation finding, the Lean statement carries it.

G is a Gröbner basis of the ideal I when G ⊆ I and the ideal generated by the leading terms of the elements of G equals the ideal generated by the leading terms of all elements of I. This is the standard definition (Cox–Little–O'Shea, Ch. 2 §5 Def. 5, over a field; Adams–Loustaunau, An Introduction to Gröbner Bases, Def. 4.1.13, over a ring), and it rightly uses leading terms (coefficient included) rather than leading monomials, which is what matters over rings: over ℤ, {2x} is not a Gröbner basis of ⟨x⟩ although its leading monomial is x. G may be infinite or contain 0 (the leading term of 0 is 0 and contributes nothing); the zero ideal has the empty Gröbner basis, matching Cox–Little–O'Shea's convention. Red-team checks: witness {x, y} for ⟨x, y⟩ under lex over ℚ proved; non-witness {2x} for ⟨x⟩ over ℤ refuted; ∅ is a Gröbner basis of the zero ideal and not of the unit ideal; agrees verbatim with Mathlib PR 29203; no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Remainders on division by a Gröbner basis are unique (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §6 Prop. 1), over any commutative ring and with no condition on leading coefficients; the case f1 = f2 of the previous result. Specialised: every remainder of 1 modulo x0 over ℚ is 1.

For a Gröbner basis whose nonzero members have unit leading coefficients, every polynomial has exactly one remainder (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §6 Prop. 1): existence by the division algorithm, uniqueness by the uniqueness of remainders modulo a Gröbner basis. The unit hypothesis is needed for existence (x modulo {2x} over ℤ has no remainder).

If G is a Gröbner basis of I, the leading monomial of every nonzero element of I is divisible by the leading monomial of a nonzero element of G (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §5): the leading term lies in the ideal generated by the leading terms of G, and that ideal's monomials are all divisible by such leading monomials. Holds over any commutative semiring, with no condition on leading coefficients.

A Gröbner basis of I whose nonzero members have unit leading coefficients generates I (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §5 Cor. 6): every element of I has remainder 0, hence lies in the ideal generated by G, and G ⊆ I gives the reverse inclusion. Correct as stated; over a field the hypothesis is automatic, and over a general ring it can be dropped (recorded separately as a generality improvement).

For a Gröbner basis of I whose nonzero members have unit leading coefficients, 0 is a remainder of f iff f lies in I (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §6 Cor. 2): one direction is the membership test, the other uses existence of a remainder, which must then be 0. Correct as stated; the unit hypothesis can in fact be dropped (recorded separately as a generality improvement).
A subset of I whose leading terms generate the ideal of leading terms of I is a Gröbner basis of I; this is the definition, packaged as a constructor.

Enlarging a Gröbner basis of I by further elements of I keeps it a Gröbner basis: the ideal generated by the leading terms can only grow, and it is bounded by the ideal of leading terms of I. All three hypotheses are needed.

A remainder of f on division by a Gröbner basis of I is zero iff f lies in I — the ideal membership test (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §6 Cor. 2) — over any commutative ring with no condition on leading coefficients; it is the case f2 = 0 of the remainder comparison. Specialised: 1 ∉ ⟨x0⟩ over ℚ, read off from the remainder 1.
The leading terms of a Gröbner basis of I generate the same ideal as the leading terms of all of I; part of the definition.

For a Gröbner basis G of I and remainders r1, r2 of f1, f2 on division by G, f1 − f2 lies in I exactly when r1 = r2 (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §6 Prop. 1 and Cor. 2). Proof idea: f1 − f2 − (r1 − r2) lies in I; if r1 − r2 were a nonzero element of I its leading monomial would be divisible by that of a nonzero element of G, yet it is a monomial of r1 or r2, which no such leading monomial divides. It needs no condition on leading coefficients and holds over every commutative ring. Red-team checks: specialised over ℚ with G = {x0}: the remainders of x0·x1 + 1 and of 1 agree; hypotheses jointly satisfiable (witnesses compiled).
A Gröbner basis of I is contained in I; part of the definition.

Defines when r is a remainder of f on division by a set B of polynomials for a fixed monomial order: f = Σ g_b·b + r with finitely many nonzero quotients g_b, each satisfying deg b + deg g_b ≤ deg f (the zero polynomial having degree −∞), and no monomial of r divisible by the leading monomial of a nonzero b in B. This is the output specification of the multivariate division algorithm (Cox–Little–O'Shea, Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms, Ch. 2 §3 Thm. 3), in the form used over rings by Adams–Loustaunau (standard representations with lp(h_i)·lp(g_i) ≤ lp(f)), and it agrees verbatim with the definition in Mathlib PR 29203. Excluding b = 0 matters: the zero polynomial's leading monomial is the constant monomial by convention and would otherwise forbid every remainder except 0. Divisibility is the componentwise order on exponent vectors, not the monomial order. Red-team checks: value tests over ℚ (1 is the unique remainder of 1 and of x0·x1 + 1 modulo x0) and over ℤ (x has no remainder modulo 2x, so existence genuinely needs unit leading coefficients); the remainders of 0 are exactly 0.
A remainder r of f comes with a representation f = Σ g_b·b + r in which deg b + deg g_b ≤ deg f for each divisor b; this is the first half of the definition.
No monomial of a remainder is divisible by the leading monomial of a nonzero divisor; this is the second half of the definition.
A polynomial and any of its remainders on division by B differ by an element of the ideal generated by B, directly from f = Σ g_b·b + r.

If a nonzero f has remainder 0 on division by B, the leading monomial of f is divisible by the leading monomial of some nonzero b in B: the leading monomial of f occurs in some product g_b·b, whose degree is at most deg b + deg g_b ≤ deg f, which forces deg f = deg b + deg g_b.

Every monomial occurring in an element of the ideal generated by the leading terms of G is divisible by the leading monomial of a nonzero element of G: that ideal lies inside the monomial ideal generated by those leading monomials, and membership in a monomial ideal is decided monomial by monomial (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §4, Lemmas 2–3); valid over any commutative semiring.

If every nonzero element of B has a unit leading coefficient, every polynomial has a remainder on division by B: the multivariate division algorithm (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §3 Thm. 3), obtained from Mathlib's division by a set applied to the nonzero elements of B. The unit hypothesis is necessary: over ℤ, x has no remainder on division by {2x} (checked in Lean).
Restates the definition: G is a Gröbner basis of I iff G ⊆ I and the leading terms of G and of I generate the same ideal; true by definition.

For G ⊆ I whose nonzero members have unit leading coefficients, G is a Gröbner basis of I iff the leading monomial of every nonzero element of I is divisible by the leading monomial of a nonzero element of G — the usual field characterisation (Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §5, using that the ideal of leading terms is then a monomial ideal). The unit hypothesis is needed: over ℤ, {2x} ⊆ ⟨x⟩ satisfies the divisibility condition but is not a Gröbner basis (both checked in Lean).

For G whose nonzero members have unit leading coefficients, G is a Gröbner basis of I iff G ⊆ I and every element of I has remainder 0 on division by G (Adams–Loustaunau Thm. 4.1.12; Cox–Little–O'Shea Ch. 2 §6). Forward by the membership test; backward because remainder 0 makes every leading monomial of I divisible by one from G. Correct as stated; the unit hypothesis can in fact be dropped (recorded separately as a generality improvement).
Removing the zero polynomial from G does not change whether G is a Gröbner basis of I, since the leading term of 0 is 0 and 0 lies in every ideal.
Every ideal is a Gröbner basis of itself (the definition allows infinite sets); immediate from the definition.

Restates the definition of a remainder (the representation f = Σ g_b·b + r with deg b + deg g_b ≤ deg f, and no monomial of r divisible by the leading monomial of a nonzero divisor) as an equivalence; it holds by definition.
The only remainder of the zero polynomial is 0: each product g_b·b must have degree at most that of 0, i.e. vanish, so 0 = 0 + r. Holds over any commutative semiring.

For nonzero polynomials p, q, f, the inequality deg p + deg q ≤ deg f, with degrees taken in the order extended by −∞ for the zero polynomial, is the same as the inequality between the ordinary degrees, since nonzero polynomials have finite degree. Each nonzero hypothesis is needed (with f = 0 the left side fails while the right side holds for constants p, q).

ζ is holomorphic on ℂ with the lattice removed, an immediate consequence of ζ′ = −℘ there; this is the standard fact that ζ is meromorphic with simple poles exactly at the lattice points (DLMF §23.2). Red-team checks: the excluded set is exactly the set of poles.

At every z off the lattice, ζ is complex differentiable with derivative −℘(z), as in DLMF §23.2 (ζ′ = −℘). Proof: differentiate the locally uniformly convergent series term by term (Weierstrass's theorem on locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions). The derivative of 1/(z−l) + 1/l + z/l² is −(1/(z−l)² − 1/l²), minus the corresponding term of the ℘ series. The hypothesis z ∉ Λ is necessary, since ζ has a pole at each lattice point. Red-team checks: sign checked against DLMF; the hypothesis is satisfiable (ω₁/2 ∉ Λ) and needed; ℘ is Mathlib's Weierstrass function.

The partial sums of Σ_{l∈Λ} (1/(z−l) + 1/l + z/l²) converge to ζ uniformly on a neighbourhood of every point of ℂ. This is the Weierstrass M-test applied with the O(|l|⁻³) bound, using that Σ|l|⁻³ converges over a rank-two lattice: the standard argument (DLMF §23.2; Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, Ch. 7). Near a lattice point only finitely many terms have a pole, and the finite partial sums absorb them, so the statement is meaningful on all of ℂ. Red-team checks: the limit is the defined ζ itself, not some other sum; the bound and the summability argument are those of Mathlib's proof for ℘.

For every complex z, the lattice series Σ_{l∈Λ} (1/(z−l) + 1/l + z/l²) (whose l = 0 term is 1/z) converges unconditionally to ζ(z). It is the pointwise case of the locally uniform convergence, and it shows that the infinite sum in the definition is a genuine limit, not a junk value. Red-team checks: holds for every z, lattice points included, where the series still converges with the pole term read as 0.

Defines the quasi-period map η : Λ → ℂ by η(l) = ζ(ω₁/2 + l) − ζ(ω₁/2), packaged as an additive homomorphism. Because ζ(z + l) − ζ(z) is constant on ℂ ∖ Λ (its derivative ℘(z) − ℘(z + l) vanishes and ℂ ∖ Λ is connected), this is the standard quasi-period of DLMF §23.2. In DLMF's normalisation, with lattice 2ω₁ℤ + 2ω₃ℤ, it takes the value 2η_j at 2ω_j. The base point ω₁/2 is not a lattice point, so no value at a pole enters. Red-team checks: independence of the base point and additivity are proved; matches DLMF's ζ(z + 2ω_j) = ζ(z) + 2η_j.

If l = mω₁ + nω₂ with integers m and n, then η(l) = m η(ω₁) + n η(ω₂): since η is additive, the quasi-periods of the two generators determine all of them (in DLMF §23.2's normalisation, η at 2mω₁ + 2nω₃ is 2mη₁ + 2nη₃). Red-team checks: no hypothesis beyond the representation of l; specialised at l = ω₁ (m = 1, n = 0).

For a lattice vector l with l/2 not in the lattice, η(l) = 2ζ(l/2). In DLMF's normalisation (lattice 2ω₁ℤ + 2ω₃ℤ) this is η_j = ζ(ω_j), DLMF §23.2. Proof: apply quasi-periodicity at z = −l/2, which is off the lattice, and use oddness: ζ(l/2) = ζ(−l/2) + η(l) = −ζ(l/2) + η(l). The hypothesis excludes exactly the cases where l/2 is a pole of ζ, so no value at a pole is used. With Lean's value at poles (ζ(m) = η(m) for m in Λ) the identity holds there too, so the hypothesis is a minor generality point. Red-team checks: specialised at l = ω₁ and l = ω₂, as used downstream; the hypothesis is satisfiable.

Defines the Weierstrass zeta function of the lattice Λ = ℤω₁ + ℤω₂ as ζ(z) = 1/z + Σ_{l∈Λ, l≠0} (1/(z−l) + 1/l + z/l²), exactly the series of DLMF §23.2 and Abramowitz–Stegun Ch. 18 (the sum runs over all of Λ, and its l = 0 term is 1/z because 1/0 is read as 0). The series is genuinely summed: its terms equal z²/(l²(z−l)) = O(|l|⁻³), and convergence is proved for every z (hasSum_weierstrassZeta), so the infinite sum is never the default value 0 that a divergent sum would get. At a lattice point l₀, where ζ has a pole, the formula gives the series with the undefined term read as 0; this works out to the constant term of the Laurent expansion at l₀, which equals the quasi-period η(l₀) (in particular ζ(0) = 0), and each theorem about the meromorphic function either assumes z ∉ Λ or also holds at this value. Red-team audit at 956e316250: compared term by term with DLMF; convergence proved, not assumed; the value at lattice points computed in Lean (ζ(l) = η(l)); no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib (which has only ℘ and ℘′) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Quasi-periodicity: for z off the lattice and l in the lattice, ζ(z + l) = ζ(z) + η(l), which is DLMF §23.2's ζ(z + 2ω_j) = ζ(z) + 2η_j. Proof: ζ(z + l) − ζ(z) has derivative ℘(z) − ℘(z + l) = 0 on the connected open set ℂ ∖ Λ, so it is constant, and by definition the constant is η(l). Red-team checks: the hypothesis is satisfiable and the statement is not vacuous; a Lean probe shows the identity also holds at lattice points, so the hypothesis is recorded as a minor generality point, not a correctness issue.

For |s| < r and |l| ≥ 2r, the term 1/(s−l) + 1/l + s/l² of the zeta series, which equals s²/(l²(s−l)), has absolute value at most 2r²|l|⁻³, because |s|² < r² and |s−l| ≥ |l|/2. This estimate makes the series converge absolutely and locally uniformly; it is the analogue of Mathlib's bound for ℘. Red-team checks: the algebraic identity and the constant re-derived by hand; hypotheses satisfiable; the assumption r > 0 already follows from |s| < r (recorded as a minor generality point, not a correctness issue).

ζ is odd: ζ(−z) = −ζ(z) for every z (DLMF §23.2). Proof: substitute l ↦ −l in the lattice series, using −Λ = Λ; each term goes to minus a term. The substitution works on the series itself, so the identity holds at lattice points too. Red-team checks: no hypothesis to drop; consistent with the value ζ(l) = η(l) at lattice points, since the additive map η is odd.

For z off the lattice and l in the lattice, ζ(z − l) = ζ(z) − η(l): this is quasi-periodicity applied at z − l, which is also off the lattice. Red-team checks: as for the addition form; the hypothesis can likewise be removed (recorded as minor generality).

At the pole z = 0, the defining series takes the value 0: its l = 0 term is read as 0, and the remaining terms cancel in pairs l, −l. This 0 is also the constant term of the Laurent expansion of ζ at 0, because ζ(z) − 1/z is odd and holomorphic near 0. So the lemma records the convention at the pole, like Mathlib's ℘(0) = 0, and downstream files use it as exactly that. Red-team checks: computed directly from the series in Lean; the docstring's wording is recorded as a nit.

Says that every continuous self-map of a closed ball of radius r at least 0, about any centre, in a finite-dimensional real normed space (any norm) has a fixed point. A closed ball of nonnegative radius is nonempty, compact and convex, so this is the compact-convex form of Brouwer's theorem; the radius condition is exactly what makes the ball nonempty (for negative radius the ball is empty and the claim fails), and radius 0 gives a single point. Finite dimension cannot be dropped: in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space the closed unit ball has fixed-point-free continuous self-maps (Kakutani). Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to the Euclidean closed unit ball of the plane; compiled the counterexample at negative radius; every hypothesis used.

Says that every continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex subset C of a finite-dimensional real normed space (any norm) has a fixed point. This is the standard general form of Brouwer's theorem, as in fixed-point texts such as Granas and Dugundji's Fixed Point Theory; C may have empty interior, for instance a segment in the plane. Why it holds: C has a point in its relative interior and is then homeomorphic to the closed unit ball of the linear subspace parallel to its affine hull, which is homeomorphic to the Euclidean ball of the same dimension, and having the fixed-point property is preserved by homeomorphisms; the ball case is Brouwer's theorem for the disk proved just above. Finite dimension is the Brouwer setting; dropping it is Schauder's theorem, and a later theorem in this file covers sets inside a finite-dimensional subspace of any normed space. Red-team audit at 956e316250: each hypothesis is necessary, with compiled counterexamples (the empty set; the translation x to x+1 of the real line, convex but not compact; the swap of the two-point set {0, 1}, compact but not convex); applied to a segment with empty interior in the plane; satisfiable hypotheses, so nothing is vacuous; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Says that if C is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed space and f is a function on the whole space that is continuous on C and maps C into C, then f has a fixed point lying in C. It is Brouwer's theorem for compact convex sets phrased for a function on the ambient space rather than a self-map of C, and follows by restricting f to C; its one-dimensional case is the familiar fact that a continuous map of [0, 1] into itself has a fixed point. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to [0, 1] in the real line; every hypothesis is used (removing any one breaks the proof) and each is necessary by the counterexamples recorded for the self-map version; satisfiable hypotheses.

Says that in an arbitrary real normed space, possibly infinite-dimensional, every continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex set that lies inside some finite-dimensional linear subspace has a fixed point. Viewing the set inside that subspace, where it has the same topology and is still compact and convex, reduces this to the finite-dimensional compact-convex Brouwer theorem. It is a modest step from Brouwer's theorem toward Schauder's theorem, which drops the finite-dimensional-subspace condition but needs a different proof. Red-team audit at 956e316250: applied in the infinite-dimensional space of square-summable sequences; every hypothesis is used and the compactness, convexity and nonemptiness conditions are necessary by the counterexamples recorded for the finite-dimensional version; satisfiable hypotheses.

Says that every continuous map from the closed unit ball of n-dimensional Euclidean space to itself has a fixed point, for every n. This is Brouwer's fixed-point theorem exactly as in Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Corollary 2.15; the ball is the genuine Euclidean closed unit ball with the subspace topology (not a cube for the maximum norm), and for n = 0 it is a single point, where the claim is trivial. The proof is the standard one: if f had no fixed point, sending each x to the point where the ray from f(x) through x meets the boundary sphere would be a continuous retraction of the ball onto its boundary, contradicting the no-retraction theorem. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to continuous self-maps of the Euclidean closed unit ball of R^n written directly, and of the plane; there are no hypotheses to contradict; only the three standard axioms; pinned Mathlib has only the one-dimensional case for intervals, and no other Tau Ceti file states Brouwer's theorem.

Says that, for every n including 0, the boundary sphere of the closed unit ball of n-dimensional Euclidean space (Euclidean norm, subspace topology) is not a retract of the ball: there are no continuous maps i from the sphere to the ball and r from the ball to the sphere with r after i equal to the identity of the sphere. This is Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Corollary 2.15, in a slightly stronger form, since i may be any continuous map rather than only the inclusion; the usual form (no continuous map from the ball onto its boundary fixing every boundary point) follows in one step. Why it holds: for n at least 1, reduced singular homology in degree n-1 would make the identity of the infinite cyclic group of the (n-1)-sphere factor through the reduced homology of the ball, which is zero because the ball is contractible. For n = 0 the ball is a single point and its boundary is empty, so no map from the ball to the boundary exists and the statement is trivially, but correctly, true. Red-team audit at 956e316250: derived both the boundary-inclusion form and the concrete form for maps from the Euclidean closed ball to the sphere fixing the sphere; checked the boundary is nonempty for n = 1, so the statement is not vacuous there, and empty for n = 0; only the three standard axioms; pinned Mathlib has no no-retraction or Brouwer theorem and no other Tau Ceti file states one.

Defines, for a smooth almost complex structure J on a finite-dimensional real manifold (boundary and corners allowed) and a point x, the Nijenhuis tensor of J at x as a bilinear map on the tangent space at x: on two tangent vectors it takes the value [JX, JY] − [X, Y] − J[JX, Y] − J[X, JY] at x, where X and Y are any vector fields differentiable at x with those values and the bracket is the usual Lie bracket of vector fields ([X, Y]f = X(Yf) − Y(Xf)). This is the standard Nijenhuis tensor with the sign used by Kobayashi–Nomizu (Foundations of Differential Geometry II, Ch. IX §2, who put an extra overall factor 2 in front); other sources use the opposite overall sign (e.g. W. Zhang's Warwick complex-geometry notes, §2.3) or divide by 4, which changes neither its vanishing nor any of its identities. It is a genuine tensor: the four-term expression is additive and linear over differentiable functions in each slot (proved in the file), so by the standard tensoriality criterion its value at x depends only on X(x) and Y(x); the construction picks particular extensions of the tangent vectors, but the evaluation theorem shows that every differentiable extension gives the same value, so no arbitrary choice affects the result. Red-team checks at 956e316250: the value is pinned for all differentiable fields (choice-independence probe compiles); the standard structures on ℝ² and on ℂⁿ = ℝⁿ × ℝⁿ have zero tensor; skew-symmetry and N(Jv, w) = N(v, Jw) = −J N(v, w) are proved; no Nijenhuis tensor exists in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Skew-symmetry, N_J(v, w) = −N_J(w, v), a standard property of the Nijenhuis tensor (e.g. T. Zheng, An almost complex Chern–Ricci flow, Lemma 2.2); it follows from antisymmetry of the Lie bracket, which reverses the sign of the first two terms and exchanges the last two.

Says that the Nijenhuis tensor at x, evaluated on the values at x of two vector fields X and Y that are differentiable at x, equals [JX, JY] − [X, Y] − J[JX, Y] − J[X, JY] at x: the textbook formula for the Nijenhuis tensor (Kobayashi–Nomizu II, Ch. IX §2, up to their overall factor 2). It holds because the four-term expression is linear over functions in each argument, hence depends only on the values of the fields at x. Red-team checks: both differentiability hypotheses are needed (without them the brackets are not defined and take meaningless values); specialised to constant fields and a constant J on a vector space, it gives the zero tensor.
N_J(Jv, Jw) = −N_J(v, w), obtained by applying the two one-sided identities and J² = −1; standard (T. Zheng, An almost complex Chern–Ricci flow, Lemma 2.2).

N_J(Jv, w) = −J N_J(v, w): substituting JX for X and using J² = −1 turns the four-term expression into −J applied to the original one. This is the standard identity (e.g. T. Zheng, An almost complex Chern–Ricci flow, Lemma 2.2), the real form of the statement that N_J pairs two (0,1)-vectors to a (1,0)-vector.

N_J(v, Jw) = −J N_J(v, w), the second-slot version of the previous identity, obtained from it by skew-symmetry; the same standard identity (T. Zheng, Lemma 2.2). Together with the first-slot version it gives N_J(Jv, w) = N_J(v, Jw).

A constant almost complex structure on a finite-dimensional real vector space (for example the standard complex structure of ℂⁿ viewed as ℝ²ⁿ) has zero Nijenhuis tensor at every point: constant vector fields stay constant under a constant J, all Lie brackets of constant fields vanish, and by tensoriality it suffices to test on constant fields. This is the basic example confirming that the flat integrable model has N = 0. Red-team checks: specialised to the standard structure (v, w) ↦ (−w, v) on ℝ² and on ℝⁿ × ℝⁿ.

Says the Nijenhuis tensor vanishes at every point exactly when [JX, JY] = [X, Y] + J[JX, Y] + J[X, JY] holds at x for every point x and all vector fields X, Y differentiable at x: the usual integrability condition written with brackets. It follows from the evaluation formula together with the fact that every tangent vector is the value of some differentiable vector field. Red-team checks: both directions proved, no hypotheses beyond the setting.

The almost complex structure −J has the same Nijenhuis tensor as J at every point: in each of the four bracket terms J occurs an even number of times, so the signs cancel by linearity of the bracket. Standard.
N_J(v, v) = 0 for every tangent vector v, immediate from skew-symmetry over the reals.

Correctly stated: weak duality for arc-disjoint walks between vertex sets. In a directed multigraph (parallel arcs counted separately), if finitely many walks each run from a vertex of A to a vertex of B and no two traverse a common arc, and F is a finite set of arcs whose deletion leaves no vertex of B reachable from any vertex of A, then the number of walks is at most the number of arcs in F. This is the easy inequality of Menger's theorem (Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, Section 9.1): every walk must use an arc of F, or it would survive the deletion, and different walks use different arcs, so choosing one such arc per walk is injective. Allowing walks rather than paths makes it slightly more general than the textbook form. Red-team checks: hypotheses are consistent (satisfied in a compiled two-parallel-arc example) and each is needed; no Mathlib counterpart (pinned Mathlib has edge connectivity only for simple undirected graphs and no Menger theorem); the finiteness of A and B is in fact unnecessary (recorded separately as a generality point), which does not affect correctness.

Correctly stated: the two-vertex case of weak duality. A finite family of walks from s to t, no two traversing a common arc, has at most as many members as any finite set of arcs whose deletion leaves t unreachable from s, because each walk must use an arc of the set and different walks use different arcs (Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, Section 9.1, the easy half of Menger's theorem). Red-team checks: it is the set-to-set version at A = {s}, B = {t}; used in a compiled specialisation showing that two parallel arcs from s to t force every Menger witness to have size 2; hypotheses consistent and both (arc-disjointness and separation) needed.

Correctly stated: Menger's theorem in its arc form for finite directed multigraphs. For distinct vertices s and t it gives a number k, a family of k directed paths from s to t (no vertex repeated) of which no two share an arc, and a set of exactly k arcs whose deletion leaves t unreachable from s; together with the weak-duality lemma beside it, this is the statement that the maximum number of arc-disjoint s-t paths equals the minimum number of arcs separating t from s (Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, Corollary 9.1b in Section 9.1; Ford and Fulkerson 1956). The proof takes an integer maximum flow with capacity one on every arc and a cut of the same value (max-flow/min-cut): the arcs leaving the cut separate t from s and their number is the flow value, and a path decomposition of the flow yields that many arc-disjoint paths. Conventions: arcs are identified individually, so parallel arcs are distinct and can carry different paths; s different from t is necessary, since nothing separates a vertex from itself; when t is unreachable the witness is k = 0 with the empty separator. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; s different from t and both finiteness assumptions are needed; compiled specialisations to two parallel arcs from s to t (every witness has k = 2) and to the graph with no arcs (k = 0, empty separator); no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib, which has neither Menger's theorem nor max-flow/min-cut.

Correctly stated: Menger's theorem in its arc form between vertex sets. For disjoint vertex sets A and B of a finite directed multigraph it gives k directed paths, each from a vertex of A to a vertex of B with no other vertex in A or B, of which no two share an arc (endpoints may be shared), together with a set of k arcs whose deletion leaves no vertex of B reachable from any vertex of A; with weak duality this is max = min, the arc version of the A-B Menger theorem (Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, Section 9.1, where it follows by adding a super-source and super-sink). The proof runs max-flow/min-cut between the two vertex sets with unit capacities, decomposes the flow into paths, and trims each path to an A-B path, which only drops arcs. Disjointness of A and B is necessary, since a common vertex cannot be separated from itself. Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent (compiled application with A = {s}, B = {t} in a two-parallel-arc example) and needed; no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib.

Correctly stated: the predicate form of the set-to-set arc Menger theorem. For disjoint vertex sets A and B of a finite directed multigraph and any k, after deleting any fewer than k arcs some vertex of B stays reachable from some vertex of A exactly when there are k paths from A to B, each with no interior vertex in A or B, of which no two share an arc (Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, Section 9.1). One direction is weak duality, the other keeps k of the paths from the witness form. Empty A or B and k = 0 behave as expected. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; the disjointness hypothesis turns out to be unnecessary (recorded as a generality point: with a common vertex both sides hold via trivial paths), which does not affect correctness.

Correctly stated: the predicate form of arc Menger. For distinct vertices s and t of a finite directed multigraph and any number k, the vertex t stays reachable from s after deleting any fewer than k arcs exactly when there are k directed s-t paths of which no two share an arc; this is the local k-arc-connectivity form of Menger's theorem (Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, Section 9.1). One direction is weak duality; for the other, the witness form supplies a separator, which must have at least k arcs, and as many arc-disjoint paths, of which k are kept. For k = 0 both sides hold trivially. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; the hypothesis that s and t differ turns out to be unnecessary (recorded as a generality point: at s = t both sides hold), which does not affect correctness.

Correctly stated: an integer matrix has determinant a unit in the p-adic integers exactly when p does not divide its integer determinant, because an integer is a p-adic unit iff p does not divide it; this lets the good-prime results apply to integral lattices at every p ∤ 2 det A.

Correctly stated. It defines Siegel's local density α_p(A) of a symmetric n×n matrix A over the p-adic integers as the limit, as r grows, of the number of n×n matrices X modulo p^r with XᵀAX ≡ A (mod p^r), divided by p^{r·n(n−1)/2}; the exponent n(n−1)/2 is n² unknowns minus n(n+1)/2 equations, the dimension of the orthogonal group, exactly as in Siegel (1935). The limit is a genuine one, not a junk value: for nonsingular symmetric A the file proves the normalised counts are constant from r = 2v_p(2 det A) + 1 on, at every prime including p = 2, by a Newton lifting of solutions plus a count of the kernel of the linearised map Z ↦ AZ + (AZ)ᵀ. Convention to know: this is Siegel's un-halved density α_p(A,A), so it tends to 2 at primes not dividing 2·det A; other standard sources (e.g. Cho's positive-rank convention, Katsurada-school papers) put a factor 1/2 in front, and some use a congruence modulo half-integral matrices at p = 2, so their values are half of these. For singular or non-symmetric A the value is unspecified, as the docstring says. Red-team audit at 956e316250: convergence proved for every nonsingular symmetric A; values computed in Lean: α_3((1)) = 2, α_2((1)) = 4 (four square roots of 1 mod 8), the empty form gives 1, and x²+y² at p = 3 gives 8/3 = |O(x²+y², 𝔽₃)|/3 with |O| = 8 checked by brute force.

Correctly stated: the number of n×n matrices X over ℤ/p^r with XᵀĀX = Ā, where Ā is A reduced modulo p^r — the solution count inside Siegel's definition of the local density. Red-team audit at 956e316250: brute-force values agree with the definition (2 solutions of x² = 1 mod 4 and 4 mod 8; 24 = |SL₂(𝔽₃)| for the antisymmetric form [[0,1],[−1,0]]; 8 for x²+y² mod 3), and level 0 gives 1.

Correctly stated: the defining equation of the count (the number of solutions of XᵀAX = A modulo p^r), given as a lemma because importing files do not see the definition's body; it holds by definition.

Correctly stated: the canonical case e = v_p(2 det A) of the previous result — for symmetric A with nonzero determinant the normalised count equals α_p(A) at every level r > 2·v_p(2 det A), the threshold announced for the definition, valid at p = 2 as well.

Correctly stated: if A is symmetric and 2·det A divides p^e, the normalised count at any level r > 2e already equals α_p(A), because the stabilisation step makes the normalised counts constant from level 2e+1 on, so the limit is that constant. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised at p = 2, A = (1), e = 1, r = 3 to compute α_2((1)) = 4.
Correctly stated: under the same hypotheses the normalised count takes the same value at every level r ≥ 1, the level-1 count divided by p^{n(n−1)/2}.

Correctly stated: the level-1 count equals the number of matrices over the field 𝔽_p preserving the reduction of A modulo p (ℤ/p¹ identified with 𝔽_p); when that reduction is symmetric and nondegenerate this is the order of its orthogonal group. It holds for every A.
Correctly stated: the count is at least 1 for every A and every level r (r = 0 included), because the identity matrix is always a solution.
Correctly stated: under the same hypotheses (p odd, det A a unit, A symmetric) the count at level r+1 is p^{r·n(n−1)/2} times the count at level 1, by iterating the one-step growth.

Correctly stated: if A is symmetric and 2·det A divides p^e, then for every level r > 2e the count at level r+1 is p^{n(n−1)/2} times the count at level r. Idea: for r > e every solution is invertible, so the solutions form a group and the count factors as (images modulo p^{r−e}) × (solutions ≡ 1); a Newton step shows the images at levels r and r+1 coincide, and the solutions ≡ 1 correspond to the kernel of Z ↦ AZ + (AZ)ᵀ, which grows by p^{n² − n(n+1)/2}. This is the stabilisation of the local-density counts (Kitaoka, Ch. 5), with a threshold read off the determinant. Red-team audit at 956e316250: every hypothesis is needed — symmetry (the antisymmetric form with determinant 1 has SL₂ as solutions, growing by p³ per level), the divisibility (it forces det A ≠ 0), and r > 2e (at p = 2, A = (1), e = 1 the step from level 2 to 3 goes from 2 to 4 solutions).

Correctly stated: at an odd prime p with det A a p-adic unit (that is, p ∤ 2 det A) the count grows by exactly p^{n(n−1)/2} at every level r ≥ 1 — the stabilisation step with e = 0. Red-team audit at 956e316250: p ≠ 2 is needed (at p = 2, A = (1) the counts at levels 1 and 2 are 1 and 2) and so is r ≥ 1.

Correctly stated: replacing A by PᵀAP with P invertible over the p-adic integers does not change the count at any level, since X ↦ P⁻¹XP is a bijection between the two solution sets modulo p^r. Red-team audit at 956e316250: invertibility of P is needed (P = p·I turns A into p²A, which changes the count); symmetry of A is not needed and not assumed.

Correctly stated: at a prime p ∤ 2 det A, α_p(A) equals the level-1 count divided by p^{n(n−1)/2}, the order of the orthogonal group of A mod p normalised by p to the dimension of the orthogonal group. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to the empty form (value 1) and used to identify α_3((1)) = 2.
Correctly stated: for symmetric A with nonzero determinant α_p(A) > 0, since it equals a normalised count at a large level and every count is at least 1.

Correctly stated: the local density is a basis-independent invariant, α_p(PᵀAP) = α_p(A) for P invertible over the p-adic integers, because the counts agree at every level; it holds for every A, as stated.

Correctly stated: the hyperbolic plane (Gram matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]) at p = 3 has local density 4/3 — its orthogonal group over 𝔽₃ is the split dihedral group of order 2(3 − 1) = 4, divided by 3¹. As the docstring says, the sign uses the signed determinant (−1)·(−1) = 1, a square, not det = −1, a non-square modulo 3.

Correctly stated: at an odd prime p not dividing det A, for n = 2m+1 the normalised counts converge to 2∏_{i=1}^{m}(1 − p^{−2i}), i.e. α_p(A) = |O_{2m+1}(𝔽_p)|/p^{m(2m+1)} with |O_{2m+1}(q)| = 2q^{m²}∏(q^{2i} − 1), the standard value at a good prime (Siegel; Conway–Sloane's standard factor std_p is its inverse). Red-team audit at 956e316250: m = 0 gives α_p((u)) = 2, the two square roots of a unit; every hypothesis is needed.

Correctly stated: at an odd prime p not dividing det A, for n = 2m+2 the normalised counts converge to 2(1 − ε p^{−(m+1)})∏_{i=1}^{m}(1 − p^{−2i}), where ε is the Legendre symbol of (−1)^{m+1} det A modulo p (+1 exactly when the reduced form is split), from |O^ε_{2m+2}(q)| = 2q^{m(m+1)}(q^{m+1} − ε)∏(q^{2i} − 1). Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to x²+y² at p = 3 (ε = −1, value 8/3, matching the brute-force count |O| = 8 divided by 3) and to the hyperbolic plane (ε = +1, value 4/3).

Correctly stated: for symmetric A with nonzero determinant the normalised counts converge to α_p(A) (they are eventually constant), so the local density is a genuine limit. Red-team audit at 956e316250: both hypotheses are needed for convergence (for A = 0 the normalised counts grow without bound; for the antisymmetric [[0,1],[−1,0]] they grow like p^{2r}).

Correctly stated: at a prime p ∤ 2 det A the normalised counts converge to the number of matrices over 𝔽_p preserving the reduction of A, divided by p^{n(n−1)/2}, i.e. to |O(A mod p)|/p^{n(n−1)/2}, the classical value of the local density at a good prime.

For a closed plane curve traversed at constant speed on [a, b] (a < b), L² = 4π|A| exactly when the curve is constant or runs once around a circle at constant speed, γ(t) = c + w·e^{±2πit/(b − a)}, in either orientation: the equality case of the isoperimetric inequality for arclength-type parametrizations (Hurwitz 1902). It is the area–energy equality case with (b − a)∫|γ′|² = L². Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent; the reduction to the area–energy equality uses only that constant speed gives energy L²/(b − a).

For a closed plane curve traversed at constant speed on [a, b] (a ≤ b), 4π|A| ≤ L², where L is its length (total variation) and A = ½∫(x y′ − y x′) its signed area: the isoperimetric inequality for constant-speed, in particular arclength, parametrizations (Hurwitz 1902). At constant speed (b − a)∫|γ′|² = L², so this is the area–energy inequality rewritten; on a degenerate interval both sides are 0. Red-team checks: constant speed makes the curve Lipschitz, hence absolutely continuous with bounded velocity, so the length is finite and genuine and every hypothesis of the area–energy inequality holds.

Equality case of the isoperimetric inequality: for a continuous closed curve of finite length L on [a, b], L² = 4π|A| holds exactly when γ(t) = c + w·e^{±2πi s(t)/L}, where s(t) is the length of the curve from a to t, i.e. the curve runs once around a circle uniformly in arclength, in either orientation, or is constant (w = 0, L = 0). This is the classical rigidity statement (Hurwitz 1902; Osserman 1978); the time parametrization may pause or be singular, only the position along the arc is constrained. Finite length is a necessary hypothesis: a non-rectifiable curve has both sides equal to the conventional 0 and would otherwise count as an equality case. Red-team checks: checked in Lean that the unit circle on [0, 2π] (s(t) = t, L = 2π, c = 0, w = 1) satisfies both sides, and that without finite length every non-rectifiable curve satisfies the left side.

The isoperimetric inequality for closed plane curves: if γ is continuous on [a, b] with γ(a) = γ(b), then 4π|A| ≤ L², where L is the length of the curve (its total variation, the supremum of the lengths of inscribed polygons) and A its geometric signed area, the line integral of ½(x dy − y dx) taken along the arclength reparametrization. That is the algebraic area, counting each region with its winding number, as in Osserman (Bull. AMS 84, 1978, §1); for a Jordan curve it is ± the enclosed area. No differentiability of the given parametrization is assumed, and the area is genuine for every continuous curve of finite length (a circle run through a Cantor-type time change still has area π). Proof: pass to the unit-speed arclength reparametrization on [0, L] and apply Hurwitz's Fourier area–energy inequality there. Convention: for a curve of infinite length the library sets both L and A to 0, so the statement reads 0 ≤ 0; the classical statement (L = ∞) says nothing there either, so no content is lost, as the docstring says. Red-team checks: specialised in Lean to the unit circle on [0, 2π] (length 2π, area π, equality); constant curves give 0 = 0; both hypotheses are needed.

The area–energy inequality: for an absolutely continuous closed plane curve on [a, b] (a < b) with square-integrable velocity γ′, 4π|A| ≤ (b − a)∫|γ′|², where A = ½∫(x y′ − y x′) is the signed area. This is the inequality at the heart of Hurwitz's Fourier proof of the isoperimetric inequality (Hurwitz 1901, 1902): in Fourier terms the right side is 4π² Σ n²|c_n|² and 4π|A| = 4π²|Σ n|c_n|²|, and n² ≥ ±n for integers. For a curve parametrized proportionally to arclength the right side is L², which gives the isoperimetric inequality. Red-team checks: specialised in Lean to the unit circle on [0, 2π] (4π·π = 2π·2π, equality); the hypotheses are met by the circle, so not contradictory; every hypothesis is used, and square-integrability is genuinely needed, since a divergent energy integral would be read as 0 (e.g. γ(t) = e^{2πi√t} on [0, 1], area π).

Says that for a closed plane curve γ = x + iy on [a, b], absolutely continuous with square-integrable velocity, the signed area ½∫(x y′ − y x′) equals π Σ_{n∈ℤ} n |c_n|², the series converging, where c_n are the Fourier coefficients of γ on [a, b]. This is Hurwitz's classical Fourier formula for the area (Hurwitz, Ann. ENS 1902; cf. Osserman, Bull. AMS 1978); it is independent of the length of the parameter interval, as it should be. Why it holds: x y′ − y x′ is the imaginary part of conj(γ)·γ′, closedness makes the velocity's coefficients 2πin/(b − a) times those of γ, and Parseval's identity turns the integral into the sum (the proof applies Parseval to γ, γ′ and γ′ − (2πi/(b − a))γ and polarises). Red-team checks: hand-checked on the unit circle (only c₁ = 1, area π, the library's value for the circle); the hypotheses are all met by the circle, so they are consistent; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Equality in the area–energy inequality: (b − a)∫|γ′|² = 4π|A| exactly when γ is constant or runs once around a circle at constant angular speed in either orientation, γ(t) = c + w·e^{±2πit/(b − a)} (Hurwitz 1902). It follows from the two oriented cases since |A| is A or −A. Red-team checks: checked in Lean that the unit circle on [0, 2π] (c = 0, w = 1) satisfies the right side and the equality; hypotheses consistent.

Equality (b − a)∫|γ′|² = 4π|A| holds exactly when, for some centre c and sign s = ±1, γ′(t) = (2πis/(b − a))(γ(t) − c) for almost every t: uniform rotation about c in one of the two orientations, constant curves included. It combines the two oriented velocity characterizations. Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent; matches the explicit circle form of the equality case.

Equality case in positive orientation: under the same hypotheses, (b − a)∫|γ′|² = 4πA exactly when γ(t) = c + w·e^{2πit/(b − a)} on [a, b] for some complex c, w, i.e. γ is constant (w = 0) or runs once counterclockwise around a circle at constant angular speed. This is the classical equality analysis of Hurwitz's proof: equality forces all Fourier coefficients except c₀ and c₁ to vanish, and a continuous function is determined by its coefficients. Red-team checks: the sign convention is right (the counterclockwise unit circle has area +π); the unit circle on [0, 2π] satisfies both sides in Lean.

For orientation s = ±1, equality (b − a)∫|γ′|² = s·4πA holds exactly when, for some centre c, the velocity satisfies γ′(t) = (2πis/(b − a))(γ(t) − c) for almost every t, i.e. γ rotates uniformly about c (constant curves, γ ≡ c, included). It is the explicit circle form of the equality case rewritten through the uniqueness theorem for this linear differential equation for absolutely continuous functions. Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent; the circle c + w e^{2πist/(b − a)} satisfies exactly this velocity equation.

Equality case in negative orientation: (b − a)∫|γ′|² = −4πA exactly when γ(t) = c + w·e^{−2πit/(b − a)} on [a, b], i.e. γ is constant or runs once clockwise around a circle at constant angular speed; equality now forces all coefficients except c₀ and c₋₁ to vanish (Hurwitz 1902). Red-team checks: mirror image of the positive case with the sign of the area and the frequency reversed, as it should be.

Says: in a real inner product space of finite dimension n ≥ 2 with a Haar measure μ (for instance ℝⁿ with Lebesgue measure), for every ball B = B(c, r) contained in an open set Ω and every set s that is measurable inside B, min(μ(s ∩ B), μ(B ∖ s))^((n−1)/n) ≤ 2^(n+1) ω^(−1/n) P(s; Ω), where ω = μ(B(0, 1)) and P(s; Ω) is De Giorgi's perimeter of s in Ω (the total variation of the indicator of s, the supremum of ∫_s div φ over smooth compactly supported vector fields in Ω with |φ| ≤ 1, valued in [0, ∞], so an infinite perimeter makes the bound trivially true instead of collapsing to 0). This is the relative isoperimetric inequality as stated in Maggi, Sets of Finite Perimeter, Prop. 12.37, and Evans–Gariepy §5.6.2: taking Ω = B gives the textbook form with P(s; B), the constant is explicit and is fixed before the centre, the radius and the set are chosen, and the exponent (n−1)/n is the scale-invariant one (both sides scale like r^(n−1) under dilation, and both scale the same way if μ is rescaled). Why it holds: the indicator of s differs from its average over B by at least 1/2 either on s ∩ B or on B ∖ s; on that piece A the localized Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality for functions of bounded variation on the convex set B bounds the integral of the deviation by a constant times μ(A)^(1/n) times the variation of the indicator in B, and dividing by μ(A)^(1/n) gives the claim, with the Poincaré constant on a ball computed as 2^n ω^(−1/n). Conventions: n ≥ 2 is genuinely needed (for n = 1 the exponent is 0 and s = ∅ would give 1 ≤ 0), measurability of s in B is the standard standing assumption (Maggi works with Lebesgue-measurable sets), the perimeter in a larger Ω is at least the perimeter in B, and a radius r ≤ 0 gives an empty ball where the left side is 0. Red-team checks: hypotheses jointly satisfiable (ℝ², half-plane, unit ball), so nothing is vacuous; every hypothesis load-bearing; specialised to Euclidean ℝⁿ with Lebesgue measure and Ω = B as ∃ C < ∞, ∀ c r s, min(…)^((n−1)/n) ≤ C·P(s; B); the n = 1 counterexample compiles; zero perimeter in B forces s to be a.e. empty or a.e. full in B; perimeter is [0, ∞]-valued with divergence the trace of the derivative; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; standard axioms only.

When the residue field is formally etale over k (formally smooth and formally unramified, e.g. separable algebraic over a field k), every k-algebra section of reduction equals the chosen coefficient field, so the coefficient field containing the image of k is unique. This is the uniqueness half of the standard statement (Matsumura, Section 28; EGA 0_IV 19.6): two such sections agree modulo every power of m by formal unramifiedness, and they then agree because R is separated (the intersection of the powers of m is zero). Unramifiedness cannot be dropped: in Q(t)[[T]] over Q both t -> t and t -> t + T give sections. Red-team checks: hypothesis load-bearing; specialised to a separable residue field over a field k to show any two k-algebra sections coincide.

Cohen's theorem on coefficient fields: a local ring R that is complete and separated for the topology of powers of its maximal ideal and contains a field (is an algebra over some field k) has a coefficient field, i.e. the reduction map from R onto its residue field has a ring-homomorphism section. This is Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, Theorem 28.3, and the coefficient-field part of the Cohen structure theorem (Stacks Tag 032A); 'contains a field' is exactly the equal-characteristic hypothesis and is not strengthened (no characteristic-zero, perfectness, Noetherian or residue-field-algebra assumption), and completeness includes separatedness. Proof idea: R contains a perfect prime field (Q in characteristic 0, F_p in characteristic p); every field extension of a perfect field is formally smooth (EGA 0_IV 19.6.1, proved in Tau Ceti without finiteness hypotheses), so the identity of the residue field lifts through the complete ring R. This covers the hard case of imperfect residue fields in characteristic p, and the theorem rightly asserts only a ring homomorphism, since a section linear over the given k need not exist (the module's F_p(s)[[T]] example). Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; specialised to every complete local ring of prime characteristic p with no condition on its residue field, to every complete local Q-algebra, to F_p(t)[[X]] (imperfect residue field) and to the completion of any Noetherian local ring containing a field; no Mathlib counterpart; sorry-free.

Cohen structure theorem, equal characteristic: if R is a complete separated local ring containing a field and x_1, ..., x_n is any finite family generating its maximal ideal, then R has a coefficient field s and there is a surjective ring homomorphism from the power series ring K[[X_1, ..., X_n]] over the residue field K onto R that agrees with s on constants and sends X_i to x_i, so R is a quotient of K[[X_1, ..., X_n]]. This is Stacks Tag 032A (Cohen 1946) in the equal-characteristic case, with 'Noetherian' replaced by 'maximal ideal finitely generated', which is equivalent for a complete local ring, so nothing is lost. Proof: take a coefficient field from Cohen's theorem; power series in elements of the maximal ideal converge in the complete ring R, which defines the map, and it is onto by successive approximation modulo powers of the maximal ideal, since its image meets every residue class and contains generators of the maximal ideal. With no variables the maximal ideal is zero and R is its residue field. Red-team checks: every hypothesis load-bearing; no contradiction from the hypotheses; specialised to K[[X]] with X -> X and to the Noetherian 'some n' form of Stacks; sorry-free. (The same proof works for any given coefficient field; recorded as a generality suggestion, not a correctness issue.)

The Cohen structure theorem with the fewest variables: if R is a complete separated local ring containing a field whose maximal ideal is finitely generated, then R is a quotient of the power series ring over its residue field in d variables, d the minimal number of generators of the maximal ideal (its embedding dimension), by a surjection that is a coefficient field on constants and sends the variables to generators of the maximal ideal. It follows from the previous theorem by choosing a generating family of minimal size; finite generation is needed, since otherwise the minimal number of generators is not defined. Red-team checks: hypothesis load-bearing; specialised to the Noetherian form of Stacks Tag 032A (some K[[X_1, ..., X_n]] maps onto R).

Defines a coefficient field: for a local ring R that is complete and separated for the topology of powers of its maximal ideal m and is an algebra over a base ring k, with residue field formally smooth over k (for instance separable over a field k), it is a chosen k-algebra homomorphism from the residue field back into R whose composite with reduction R -> R/m is the identity, so its image is a subfield of R containing the image of k that reduction maps isomorphically onto the residue field. This is the standard notion of a coefficient field (Cohen 1946; Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, Section 28; Stacks Tag 032A). It exists because formal smoothness lets the identity of the residue field be lifted step by step through R/m^n, and completeness assembles the lifts (Hensel's lemma in the form of the infinitesimal lifting property). The choice is arbitrary when several sections exist; it is canonical exactly when the residue field is also formally unramified, as the uniqueness lemma below records. Red-team checks: defining section property and uniqueness under etaleness both proved; witness at k[[X]] for any field k; no coefficient-field definition in Mathlib (searched five ways) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti; sorry-free.

Reducing the chosen coefficient-field map modulo the maximal ideal gives back the original residue class: the map is a section of reduction, which is the defining property of a coefficient field and exactly the lifting property used to construct it. Red-team checks: hypothesis load-bearing; the simplification rule fires and is not redundant.

Thom's lemma: over any real closed ordered field, prescribe a sign (negative, zero or positive) for every derivative of a polynomial p, of every order and including p itself; then the set of points where all these signs hold is either empty, a single point, or an open interval whose endpoints are points of the field or minus/plus infinity (so in particular it is connected). This is exactly the Basic Thom's Lemma of Basu-Pollack-Roy, Algorithms in Real Algebraic Geometry (2nd ed.), Proposition 2.27, which prescribes signs on P, P', ..., P^(d) with d = deg P and uses their interval notation (a, b), (a, +infinity), etc.; prescribing signs for all orders is equivalent, because derivatives above the degree vanish, so a nonzero sign prescribed there just gives the empty set. Why it holds: the roots of the nonzero derivatives form a finite set Z; if the condition holds at two distinct points then, by polynomial Rolle, no nonzero derivative vanishes between them, so no point of Z satisfies the condition, and since every derivative keeps a constant sign on an interval free of its roots (intermediate value property of real closed fields), the realizing set is the whole interval between the nearest points of Z on either side of a realizing point. Conventions: 'empty or one point' is stated as a single case; the zero polynomial realizes only the all-zero prescription, on the whole line, which counts as the interval from minus to plus infinity. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (the real numbers); the book's finite form on P, ..., P^(d) derived from it in Lean; specialised to X^2 - 1 with signs (+,+,+), realized exactly on (1, infinity), to the zero polynomial (whole line, or empty for a nonzero prescription) and to X with signs (0,+,0,...), realized exactly at 0; real closedness cannot be dropped: over the rationals the condition (+,+,+) for X^2 - 2 cuts out the rationals beyond the square root of 2, which Lean confirms is neither a point nor an interval with rational or infinite endpoints; only standard axioms; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Thom's lemma for the finite Thom encoding: over any real closed ordered field, prescribe signs only for the derivatives of p of orders 1 up to the degree of p (p itself is not included); the set of points realizing them is empty, a single point, or an open interval with endpoints in the field or infinite. This is Basu-Pollack-Roy, Algorithms in Real Algebraic Geometry (2nd ed.), Proposition 2.27 applied to the derivative p': the prescribed derivatives of p are exactly p' and its derivatives up to the degree of p', and the proof is precisely that reduction, the encoding condition being the full derivative-sign condition of p' with zero signs above its degree. These are the sign vectors used to encode and order real roots (Thom encodings, BPR Proposition 2.28 and Definition 2.29); for a constant p there are no coordinates and the realizing set is the whole line, i.e. the interval from minus to plus infinity. Red-team checks: reduction to the full lemma checked line by line; specialised to p = X, whose encoding is the constant word (+) with the whole line as its fibre (not cut at the root 0 of p, as expected since order 0 is excluded); hypotheses satisfiable; only standard axioms; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Says: let F be a finite field with q elements, q odd, and A an invertible symmetric matrix of size 2m+1 over F; then the number of matrices X with XᵀAX = A (the orthogonal group of the quadratic form xᵀAx; such X are automatically invertible because det A ≠ 0) is exactly 2q^{m²}(q²−1)(q⁴−1)⋯(q^{2m}−1). This is the classical order of the odd-dimensional orthogonal group O_{2m+1}(q) (Dickson, Linear Groups, 1901; Grove, Classical Groups and Geometric Algebra; Wilson, The Finite Simple Groups, ch. 3); in odd dimension it is the same for every nondegenerate form. Why it holds: diagonalise A and split off a 1×1 block c; by Witt's theorem the group acts transitively on the vectors x with xᵀAx = c, with stabiliser the orthogonal group of the complementary form, so |O(A)| = N(c)·|O(A')| where N(c) = q^{2m} ± q^m is the number of points on that quadric, and induction on the dimension, alternating with the even case, gives the product. The case m = 0 gives the two matrices ±1. Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent (instantiated over 𝔽_3 and 𝔽_5); each needed — over 𝔽_2 (characteristic 2) the 1×1 form (1) has 1 isometry, not 2, and the zero 1×1 matrix over 𝔽_3 has 3; brute-force enumeration gives 2 for size 1 and 48 for size 3 over 𝔽_3 and 2 for A = (2) over 𝔽_5, all equal to the formula, and the theorem specialised at 𝔽_3 returns 2 and 48; no counterpart in pinned Mathlib (searched by name, type shape and natural language).

Says: let F be a finite field with q elements, q odd, and A an invertible symmetric matrix of size 2m+2 over F; then the number of matrices X with XᵀAX = A is 2q^{m(m+1)}(q^{m+1} − ε)(q²−1)(q⁴−1)⋯(q^{2m}−1), where ε = χ((−1)^{m+1} det A) is +1 or −1 according as (−1)^{m+1} det A is a square in F or not (χ the quadratic character). Writing n = m+1 this is the standard order |O^ε_{2n}(q)| = 2q^{n(n−1)}(q^n − ε)∏_{i=1}^{n−1}(q^{2i}−1) of the even-dimensional orthogonal groups (Dickson; Grove, Classical Groups and Geometric Algebra; Wilson, The Finite Simple Groups, ch. 3), with the standard type criterion: the form is split (Witt index n, ε = +1) exactly when its discriminant (−1)^n det A is a square — a sum of n hyperbolic planes has det (−1)^n, so ε = +1, while x² + y² over 𝔽_3 is anisotropic, ε = χ(−1) = −1. Why it holds: the same block-splitting induction as in odd rank, splitting a size-(2m+2) form into a size-(2m+1) form plus a 1×1 block c and using that the quadric xᵀAx = c (c ≠ 0) in dimension 2m+2 has q^{2m+1} − εq^m points. Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent; symmetry, det A ≠ 0 and odd characteristic each needed (a non-symmetric 2×2 matrix of determinant 1 over 𝔽_3 has 6 solutions, not the formula's 8); brute-force enumeration of all 2×2 matrices gives, over 𝔽_3, 8 for A = I (ε = −1) and 4 for diag(1,−1) and for the hyperbolic plane (ε = +1), and over 𝔽_5, 8 for A = I (−1 is a square, ε = +1) and 12 for diag(1,2) (ε = χ(−2) = −1), all equal to the formula; the theorem specialised at 𝔽_3 (A = I, diag(1,−1)) and 𝔽_5 (diag(1,2)) returns 8, 4 and 12; no counterpart in pinned Mathlib.

Says that O(E₈) has exactly 696729600 = 2¹⁴·3⁵·5²·7 elements, the order of W(E₈) listed in Bourbaki, Lie VI Plate VII and Conway–Sloane Ch. 4 §8.1. It is transported along the isomorphism with the automorphism group of the E₈ root datum, whose order is computed as 240·126·23040 (roots of E₈, of E₇, and the order of W(D₆)) by an orbit–stabiliser chain. Convention: the count is a cardinality that would be 0 for an infinite group; the value is nonzero, so it also certifies finiteness. Red-team checks: finiteness deduced from it (compiled); the two factorisations of 696729600 checked by norm_num.

Says that W(E₈), the subgroup generated by the 240 root reflections, has 696729600 elements, matching Bourbaki, Lie VI Plate VII. It follows from W(E₈) = O(E₈) and the order of O(E₈). Red-team checks: standard axioms only; the value is nonzero, so it is not a junk cardinality of an infinite group.

Says that for any two of the 240 roots of E₈ some isometry of the lattice carries the first to the second: O(E₈) acts transitively on the roots. This is standard: the Weyl group of an irreducible simply laced root system is transitive on its roots (Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory §10.4; Conway–Sloane Ch. 4 §8.1); it is transported here from the transitivity of the automorphism group of the E₈ root datum. Red-team checks: combined with the library's proof that the 240 enumerated roots are all the norm-2 vectors, it gives transitivity on every pair of norm-2 lattice vectors (compiled).

Says that the isometry x ↦ −x of the E₈ lattice is a product of root reflections, i.e. −1 lies in the Weyl group W(E₈). This is the classical fact that the longest element of W(E₈) acts as −1 (Bourbaki, Lie VI Plate VII; Conway–Sloane Ch. 4 §8.1); here it follows at once from W(E₈) = O(E₈), since −1 is an isometry of every lattice. Red-team checks: −1 is not the identity on E₈ (compiled), so the statement is not about the trivial element.

Defines a group isomorphism from the isometry group O(E₈) of the E₈ lattice (all ℤ-linear automorphisms of the lattice preserving its inner product) onto the automorphism group of the E₈ root datum (the ℤ-linear automorphisms of the weight lattice ℤ⁸ permuting the 240 roots, with the matching action on coroots). The lattice is identified with the weight lattice by sending a vector to its eight inner products with the simple roots; this is a bijection because the E₈ Cartan matrix has determinant 1 (E₈ is unimodular, so lattice, root lattice and weight lattice coincide), and an isometry is transported along it. That O(E₈) is the automorphism group of the E₈ root system is classical (Bourbaki, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras VI §4.10; Conway–Sloane, SPLAG Ch. 4 §8.1). Injectivity is immediate; surjectivity holds because every automorphism of the E₈ root system is a product of reflections, each of which is the image of a lattice reflection. Red-team checks: specialised at −1, where it sends each root to the index of the negated root (compiled); its two characterising lemmas (root indices, reflections) compile and are not redundant simp rules; standard axioms only.

Says that the isomorphism sends the lattice reflection x ↦ x − ⟨x,α⟩α in the i-th root α to the reflection of the root datum in its i-th root. This is the expected compatibility: under the identification of the lattice with the weight lattice, pairing with the lattice root α becomes pairing with the corresponding coroot (E₈ is simply laced, so roots and coroots agree after identification). Red-team checks: simp cannot prove it without this lemma (a genuine simp rule); it is exactly the input the main theorem needs to match the two Weyl groups.

Says that the root-datum automorphism attached to a lattice isometry g permutes the 240 root indices exactly as g permutes the 240 lattice roots: the root with index σ(i) is g applied to the root with index i. Since an automorphism of a root system is determined by what it does to the roots (the roots span), this pins the isomorphism down, as the docstring says. Red-team checks: specialised at g = −1 it gives the negated root (compiled); simp cannot prove it without this lemma, so it is a genuine simp rule.

Says that the subgroup of O(E₈) generated by the reflections s_α(x) = x − ⟨x,α⟩α in the roots α of the E₈ lattice (the vectors with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2; the library proves there are exactly 240) is the whole isometry group O(E₈), meaning every ℤ-linear automorphism of the lattice preserving the inner product, with no extra condition such as determinant 1. The E₈ lattice here is ℤ⁸ with Gram matrix the Bourbaki-numbered E₈ Cartan matrix: even, unimodular, positive definite of rank 8, and shown elsewhere in the library to be isometric to the coordinate model D₈⁺. This is the classical theorem O(E₈) = W(E₈) (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG Ch. 4 §8.1; Bourbaki, Lie VI §4.10 and Plate VII). Proof idea: O(E₈) is isomorphic to the automorphism group of the E₈ root system, which equals the Weyl group because the E₈ Dynkin diagram has no nontrivial symmetry, and the isomorphism matches lattice reflections with root-system reflections. Red-team checks: the textbook form (every form-preserving ℤ-automorphism of the lattice is a product of root reflections) follows in one line (compiled); the statement is not automatic, since for the rank-one lattice ℤ, which has no norm-2 vectors, the same Weyl group is not the whole isometry group (compiled); −1 ≠ 1 on E₈; standard axioms only; the whole file elaborates in about 2 s.

Says: on a finite-dimensional real inner product space, if mu (finite second moment) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue (Haar) measure, then any two geodesic segments of P_2 from mu to nu agree at every time in [0,1]. This is the classical uniqueness of Wasserstein geodesics out of an absolutely continuous law (McCann 1997; Villani, Optimal Transport: Old and New, Ch. 7): Brenier's theorem gives an optimal map T, and by the previous result both geodesics equal the displacement interpolation t -> ((1-t)id + tT) pushed forward from mu. Red-team checks at 956e316250: all explicit hypotheses load-bearing; absolute continuity is needed (the module docstring's two-point example has several geodesics); no Mathlib counterpart.

Says: on a complete separable metric space X, with an exponent p strictly between 1 and infinity, let mu and nu be probability laws with finite p-th moment; if they have exactly one optimal coupling pi for the cost d(x,y)^p, and pi-almost every pair of points (x,y) is joined by at most one constant-speed shortest path of X, then any two geodesic segments from mu to nu in the Wasserstein space P_p(X) coincide at every time in [0,1]. This is the uniqueness of displacement interpolation (Villani, Optimal Transport: Old and New, Ch. 7; Ambrosio-Gigli-Savaré, Gradient Flows, §7.2), with the same two hypotheses and the same conclusion; 'geodesic segment' means W_p(gamma_s, gamma_t) = |s - t| W_p(mu, nu) for s, t in [0,1], the standard constant-speed minimising notion, and uniqueness is assumed of the coupling and of the base geodesics only, never of the Wasserstein geodesic itself. Why it holds: by Lisini's superposition principle each Wasserstein geodesic is the curve of time-marginals of a probability measure on geodesic paths of X whose endpoint law is an optimal coupling, hence pi; when pi-almost every pair has a unique geodesic, such a measure on paths is determined by pi, so the two curves have the same law at each time. The restriction p > 1 is necessary (for p = 1 both (1-t)delta_0 + t delta_1 and delta_t are W_1 geodesics on the real line although coupling and base geodesics are unique), and p = infinity is excluded. Red-team checks at 956e316250: every explicit hypothesis load-bearing; hypotheses satisfiable, shown by compiling the specialisations delta_0 to delta_1 in P_2(R) and mu = nu = delta_x on an arbitrary Polish space; no contradiction derivable; Mathlib has no Wasserstein spaces, and the Tau Ceti analogue on the real line (Quantile/Geodesic.lean) is a different, one-dimensional statement; the announced Euclidean P_2 / McCann corollary is in the same file.

Says: in a strictly convex separable Banach space E, for 1 < p < infinity, if mu and nu have a unique optimal coupling pi for the cost |x - y|^p, then a curve is a geodesic segment of P_p(E) from mu to nu exactly when, at each time t in [0,1], it is the law of (1-t)x + ty with (x,y) distributed by pi (the linear, or displacement, interpolation of pi). This is the unique-coupling case of the characterisation of Wasserstein geodesics in Ambrosio-Gigli-Savaré §7.2. Why: in a strictly convex space the only constant-speed shortest path between two points is the straight segment, so the uniqueness theorem of this file applies and every geodesic agrees with the interpolation of pi, which is itself a geodesic since pi is optimal. Red-team checks at 956e316250: specialised in Lean to delta_0 to delta_1 in P_2(R), where it yields exactly the geodesic t -> delta_t (compiled); all explicit hypotheses load-bearing; strict convexity is needed for the forward direction (for a non-strictly-convex norm straight segments are not the only geodesics). A more general form without uniqueness of pi is recorded as a MINOR generality finding; the statement as given is correct.

Says: on a finite-dimensional real inner product space, if mu (finite second moment) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue (Haar) measure and T is an optimal transport map from mu to nu for the quadratic cost (a Brenier map), then a curve is a geodesic segment of P_2 from mu to nu exactly when, at each time t in [0,1], it is the image of mu under x -> (1-t)x + tT(x). This is McCann's displacement interpolation (McCann, Adv. Math. 1997; Villani, Optimal Transport: Old and New, Ch. 7), here shown to be the only geodesic. Why: by Brenier's theorem the coupling concentrated on the graph of T is the unique optimal coupling when mu is absolutely continuous, so the previous characterisation applies, and the law of (1-t)x + ty under the graph coupling is the image of mu under (1-t)id + tT; the cost |x - y|^2/2 used for T has the same optimal plans as the Wasserstein cost |x - y|^2. Red-team checks at 956e316250: both explicit hypotheses load-bearing; absolute continuity is genuinely needed (without it optimal couplings can be non-unique, as in the module docstring's two-point example in the plane); no contradiction from the hypotheses, since Brenier maps of absolutely continuous laws exist (used by the next declaration).

Defines a bounded linear operator T between real or complex (semi)normed spaces to be Dunford–Pettis (completely continuous) when, for every sequence x_n converging weakly to a, the images T x_n converge in norm to T a. This is word for word the definition of a completely continuous operator in Albiac–Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory, §5.4; 'weakly' here is the weak topology induced by all continuous linear functionals. Red-team checks: witness tests pass (compact operators and every operator out of ℓ¹ satisfy it, both proved in the file); non-witness test passes (the identity of ℓ² fails it — compiled, via the file's compact-set characterisation and Riesz's theorem); no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti (the existing 'completely continuous' name in Tau Ceti is Serre's unrelated notion, as the module docstring says).
The sum of two Dunford–Pettis operators is Dunford–Pettis, because norm limits add. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed in general; matches the standard ideal property.

If T is Dunford–Pettis and S is any bounded operator out of the codomain of T, then S∘T is Dunford–Pettis, because S is norm continuous. This is the left-ideal property. Red-team checks: no hypothesis on S beyond boundedness, as in the source.

If T is Dunford–Pettis and S is any bounded operator into the domain of T, then T∘S is Dunford–Pettis: S is weak-to-weak continuous, so it carries weakly convergent sequences to weakly convergent ones, which T then makes norm convergent. This is the right-ideal property in Albiac–Kalton §5.4. Red-team checks: no hypothesis on S beyond boundedness, as in the source.
The negative of a Dunford–Pettis operator is Dunford–Pettis. Red-team checks: immediate from the definition; correctly stated.

A scalar multiple of a Dunford–Pettis operator is Dunford–Pettis, because multiplying by a fixed scalar preserves norm convergence. Red-team checks: holds for every scalar of the field, zero included; matches the standard ideal property.
The difference of two Dunford–Pettis operators is Dunford–Pettis, as the sum with a negative. Red-team checks: correctly stated; follows from the sum and negation lemmas.

If a normed space E satisfies the sequence condition f_n(x_n) → 0 whenever x_n is weakly null in E and f_n is weakly null in the dual (weak topology of the dual, not weak-star), then every weakly compact operator out of E, into any normed space, is Dunford–Pettis. This is the 'if' half of the sequential characterisation in Albiac–Kalton §5.4. The proof takes norming functionals g_n of T x_n, uses Gantmacher's theorem (the adjoint of T is weakly compact) and Šmulian's theorem to make g_n∘T converge weakly along a subsequence, and applies the condition to the weakly null differences. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed (without weak compactness the identity of c₀ fails; without the condition the identity of ℓ² fails, compiled); the topology on the dual is the weak one, as in the source.

Restates the definition of a Dunford–Pettis operator (weakly convergent sequences go to norm-convergent sequences, with the limit going to the image of the limit) as an equivalence, so that other files can unfold it. It is true by definition. Red-team checks: the two sides are definitionally the same statement; this is the only way an importing file can unfold the definition, since its body is not exported.

Between real or complex normed spaces, an operator is Dunford–Pettis exactly when it maps every weakly compact set onto a norm-compact set. This is the standard characterisation of completely continuous operators (e.g. Albiac–Kalton §5.4). Forward: by Šmulian's theorem a weakly compact set is weakly sequentially compact, so every sequence in the image has a norm-convergent subsequence. Backward: a weakly convergent sequence together with its limit is weakly compact, and on a norm-compact set the weak and norm topologies agree. Red-team checks: used it to show the identity of ℓ² is not Dunford–Pettis (weakly compact unit ball, not norm compact), as expected; axioms are only the standard three.

An operator is Dunford–Pettis exactly when it sends weakly null sequences to norm-null sequences. This is the standard reduction by linearity: apply the null-sequence condition to x_n − a. Red-team checks: both directions are genuine (the limit 0 is a special case, and translation by a preserves weak and norm convergence); no extra hypotheses.
The zero operator is Dunford–Pettis: its images form a constant sequence. Red-team checks: holds trivially, as stated.

Every compact operator between real or complex normed spaces is Dunford–Pettis, a standard fact (Albiac–Kalton §5.4). The proof uses the compact-set characterisation: a weakly compact set K is bounded, so T(K) lies in a norm-compact set; T(K) is weakly compact, hence weakly and so norm closed, hence norm compact. Red-team checks: no hypotheses beyond compactness; consistent with the strict inclusion (the identity of ℓ¹ is Dunford–Pettis but not compact).

Defines the Dunford–Pettis property of a real or complex normed space E: every weakly compact operator from E into a Banach space (here, Banach spaces of the same universe as E) is Dunford–Pettis, i.e. completely continuous.
