This is the definition in Albiac–Kalton §5.4, where 'weakly compact operator' means the image of the unit ball is relatively weakly compact — exactly the meaning of the Tau Ceti predicate used. The universe restriction loses nothing: the file proves the sequence criterion, and from it that the conclusion holds for targets in every universe and even for incomplete targets. Red-team checks: witness ℓ¹(ι) has it (proved in the file, for arbitrary index set); non-witness ℓ² does not — compiled proof that no infinite-dimensional reflexive Banach space, ℓ² in particular, has it, since its identity is weakly compact but not completely continuous; the dual sequences in the criterion are weakly null for the weak topology of the dual (checked definitionally), not weak-star, so this is not the stronger DP* property; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

If E has the Dunford–Pettis property then every weakly compact operator from E into any normed space, of any universe and not necessarily complete, is Dunford–Pettis. It combines the forward half of the sequence criterion with its converse, so it upgrades the definition (which tests only Banach targets in E's universe) to the full textbook quantification over all Banach spaces. Red-team checks: no extra hypotheses; this is what makes the definition equivalent to Albiac–Kalton's.

Forward half of the sequence criterion: if E has the Dunford–Pettis property, x_n is weakly null in E and f_n is weakly null in the dual of E (weak topology of the dual), then f_n(x_n) → 0. This is the 'only if' half of the sequential characterisation in Albiac–Kalton §5.4. The proof follows the book: the map y ↦ (f_n(y))_n is a weakly compact operator into c₀ (here valued in the completion of E, to stay in E's universe), so by the property it sends x_n to a norm-null sequence, whose n-th coordinate dominates |f_n(x_n)|. Red-team checks: each hypothesis is needed (scaling counterexamples in the scalar field for each weak-nullness assumption; ℓ² for the property); the trivial space is handled separately and correctly.

A real or complex normed space E has the Dunford–Pettis property exactly when f_n(x_n) → 0 for every weakly null sequence x_n in E and every weakly null sequence f_n in the dual of E. This is the sequential characterisation in Albiac–Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory, §5.4, with 'weakly null in the dual' meaning the weak topology of the dual (tested against the bidual), as in the book — confirmed definitionally in Lean. Both directions are proved (one via the operator into c₀, the other via Gantmacher's and Šmulian's theorems). Red-team checks: specialised to ℓ² (where the criterion must fail) and to ℓ¹ (where it must hold), consistently; only the standard axioms.

ℓ¹(ι), for any index set ι, has the Dunford–Pettis property, the basic example in Albiac–Kalton §5.4: since every bounded operator out of ℓ¹ is completely continuous (Schur's theorem), in particular every weakly compact one is. Red-team checks: the space is the genuine ℓ¹ of scalar families; holds also for an empty or finite index set (trivially), as it should; no hidden hypotheses.

Every bounded operator out of ℓ¹(ι), for any index set ι, is Dunford–Pettis. This is immediate from Schur's theorem (weakly convergent sequences in ℓ¹ converge in norm), which is the standard reason (Albiac–Kalton §2.3 and §5.4). Red-team checks: ℓ¹ is the genuine space of absolutely summable scalar families; the proof only composes Schur's theorem with continuity of the operator.

Defines, for a Weierstrass curve E over a field F with a discrete valuation v, the number [E(F) : E₀(F)]: the index, in the group of F-points, of the subgroup of points whose reduction modulo v is a nonsingular point of the reduced curve, the reduction being taken on a chosen minimal Weierstrass equation for E (integral, with discriminant of least valuation). When F is the completion K_v of a global field, or more generally any Henselian discretely valued field, this is exactly the local Tamagawa number c_v = [E(K_v) : E₀(K_v)] of Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, VII.6 and C.16; the companion file on the global product applies it to the completion. Minimality matters because E₀ depends on the equation, and the file proves that every minimal equation (and every change of coordinates) gives the same value, so the choice the definition makes is harmless. Conventions: like any group index the value would be 0 if the index were infinite, but positivity is proved over Henselian discrete valuation rings with perfect residue field (Kodaira–Néron finiteness), so this never happens in the local setting; over a non-complete field such as Q itself it is the index over that field, not c_v (for the curve 121d1 at 11 it gives 1, because E(Q) is trivial, while c_11 = 2), so for a global field one applies it to the completion; the red team asked for the docstring to say so. Red-team checks: compared with Silverman's definition clause by clause (minimal model, nonsingular-reduction subgroup, index); value tests derived from the file's results: c_v = 1 at good reduction (even when only another model has good reduction), c_v = ord_v(Δ_min) at split multiplicative reduction, c_v ≤ 4 otherwise; independence of the minimal model checked; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

The unfolding equation: the Tamagawa number is the index of the nonsingular-reduction subgroup on the particular minimal equation the definition chooses. It holds by definition and is how other files see the definition. Red-team checks: holds by definition; no duplicate.

For an elliptic curve given by an equation that is already minimal, the Tamagawa number is the index [E(F) : E₀(F)] computed on that equation itself; it is the previous statement with the identity change of coordinates. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; it is the interface the file's own proofs use.

If W is any minimal Weierstrass equation obtained from the elliptic curve E by a change of coordinates over F, the Tamagawa number of E equals the index [W(F) : W₀(F)] computed on W. This is the standard fact that c_v does not depend on which minimal equation is used: two minimal equations of an elliptic curve differ by a change of coordinates with u a unit and r, s, t integral (Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, VII.1.3(b)), and an integral change of coordinates carries points with nonsingular reduction to points with nonsingular reduction, so it preserves the index; the proof is exactly this. Ellipticity is assumed, as it must be: for a singular cubic every integral equation is minimal and they need not be related integrally. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; both explicit hypotheses are needed; used to show that two arbitrary minimal equations of E give the same index.

If E is a minimal equation with good reduction at v (its discriminant is a v-adic unit), the Tamagawa number is 1. This is the standard value: with good reduction the reduced curve is nonsingular, so every point has nonsingular reduction and E₀(F) = E(F) (Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, VII.2 and VII.6); the proof is exactly this. Together with invariance under coordinate changes it gives c_v = 1 whenever some equation of the curve has good reduction. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypothesis (automated provers find none); specialised, via coordinate invariance, to a curve whose given equation is not the good one.

Over a Henselian discrete valuation ring with finite residue field (e.g. the integers of a nonarchimedean local field): if Tate's algorithm, run on the integral equation of E with a uniformiser, stops at Kodaira symbol s, then the Tamagawa number equals the local index c that Tate's algorithm reports for s (Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, IV.9, Table 4.1). This is how Tamagawa numbers are computed in practice, as in Cremona's tables. The proof combines the formula on a minimal equation with the library's theorem that Tate's local index equals the point-group index. The minimality hypothesis is more than needed, since the algorithm only stops on minimal equations (recorded as a minor generality point); this does not affect correctness. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; both explicit hypotheses are needed; the stopping hypothesis is satisfiable, because Tate's algorithm stops on every minimal elliptic equation over such rings.

Over a field whose valuation ring is a Henselian discrete valuation ring with perfect residue field (for instance the completion of a number field at a finite place), the Tamagawa number of an elliptic curve is positive; that is, the points with nonsingular reduction have finite index. This is the theorem of Kodaira and Néron (Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, VII.6.1): E(F)/E₀(F) is finite, of order at most 4 unless the reduction is split multiplicative, where it is ord_v(Δ). The proof uses the library's finiteness result, obtained by running Tate's algorithm, which stops on a minimal equation under these hypotheses. Positivity is what rules out the index-0 convention, so the product of local Tamagawa numbers is a genuine positive integer. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; they are the standard ones and are met by completions (the global product file uses it there); only the standard axioms are used.

The Tamagawa number of an elliptic curve is unchanged by any change of Weierstrass coordinates over F, so it depends only on the curve up to isomorphism over F, as the local Tamagawa number should (it is an invariant of the curve, not of the equation; Silverman VII.6). The proof puts both equations' minimal models in one orbit and applies independence of the minimal equation. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; used by the global product file to show the product is an isomorphism invariant; ellipticity is needed for uniqueness of minimal models.

Defines, for a point w of the open unit disk, the map sending a Hardy-space function f to the value F_f(w) = Σ_{n≥0} f̂(n) wⁿ of its holomorphic extension, as a bounded linear functional on H² with norm at most (1 − |w|²)^(−1/2). This is the standard point-evaluation functional of H² (Duren, Theory of Hᵖ Spaces; Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis): linearity holds term by term in the absolutely convergent Taylor series, and the bound is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the coefficient sequence against (w̄ⁿ), whose squared length is 1/(1 − |w|²). Points range only over the open disk, so no value is assigned at boundary or exterior points. Red-team audit at 956e316250: agrees by definition with the disk function; coincides with the generic point evaluation of Mathlib's reproducing-kernel-Hilbert-space framework once the Hardy space is registered there (compiled); its norm is later shown to equal the bound exactly.

Says that the bounded evaluation functional at w, applied to a Hardy function f, is the value at w of the holomorphic extension of f; this is true by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: holds by unfolding the definition; fires as a simplification rule.

For w and z in the open disk, the holomorphic extension of the normalised kernel at z is √(1 − |w|²)/(1 − w̄z), the standard formula; it follows by linearity from the formula for k_w. Red-team audit at 956e316250: a restriction on z is necessary (the series diverges at w = 1/2, z = 3); the formula also holds whenever |w̄z| < 1 (compiled); consistent at z = 0.

For w and z in the open unit disk, the holomorphic extension of the Szegő kernel k_w takes the value 1/(1 − w̄z) at z, the textbook formula with the conjugate on w (Duren, Theory of Hᵖ Spaces; Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis). It is the sum of the geometric series Σ (w̄z)ⁿ, which converges because |w̄z| < 1. Red-team audit at 956e316250: some restriction on z is necessary (at w = 1/2, z = 3 the series diverges and the formula fails); |z| < 1 is the natural domain of the disk function, and the formula in fact holds whenever |w̄z| < 1 (compiled); the hypotheses are consistent (z = 0).

A Hardy vector equals the Szegő kernel k_w exactly when pairing with it reproduces evaluation at w for every Hardy function; this is the uniqueness half of the Riesz representation theorem, since a vector of a Hilbert space is determined by its inner products. Red-team audit at 956e316250: both directions proved as stated; used to show k_0 = 1 and to match Mathlib's generic kernel function (compiled).

The n-th Taylor (nonnegative Fourier) coefficient of the Szegő kernel k_w is w̄ⁿ, i.e. k_w = Σ w̄ⁿ zⁿ, the standard expansion (Duren; Conway). It follows from the reproducing property applied to the monomial zⁿ and conjugating. Red-team audit at 956e316250: at n = 1, w = i/2 the coefficient is −i/2 and not i/2 (compiled), confirming that the conjugate sits on w.

Pairing the normalised kernel at w with a Hardy function f gives √(1 − |w|²)·f(w). This follows from the reproducing property, since the scalar √(1 − |w|²) is real and therefore unchanged by the conjugation in the first slot. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the real factor is handled correctly; fires as a simplification rule.

The reproducing property: for w in the open disk and every Hardy function f, the inner product of the Szegő kernel k_w with f is F_f(w), the value at w of the holomorphic extension of f. With the inner product conjugate-linear in its first argument, as here, this is exactly the textbook identity f(w) = ⟨f, k_w⟩ of Duren and Conway written in the analyst's convention; it is the defining property of the Riesz representative of evaluation. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the reversed order ⟨f, k_w⟩ = f(w) is false for f(z) = z and w = i/2 (compiled), so the stated order is the correct one; checked at f = 1 (giving k_0 = 1) and at f = k_w.

The evaluation functional at a point w of the open disk has norm exactly (1 − |w|²)^(−1/2) on H², the sharp form of the bound |f(w)| ≤ ‖f‖ (1 − |w|²)^(−1/2) (Duren; Conway). It holds because the Riesz correspondence is an isometry, so the functional has the norm of its representing vector k_w. Red-team audit at 956e316250: matches the bound used to build the functional, with equality attained at f = k_w.

The normalised Szegő kernel has norm 1, because √(1 − |w|²)·(1 − |w|²)^(−1/2) = 1 when |w| < 1. Red-team audit at 956e316250: positivity of 1 − |w|² comes from w lying in the open disk, so no division by zero is hidden.

‖k_w‖ = (1 − |w|²)^(−1/2), the square root of the squared-norm identity; this is the norm of the Szegő kernel for normalised arc length (Duren; Conway). Red-team audit at 956e316250: consistent with ‖k_0‖ = 1 and ‖k_{1/2}‖² = 4/3.

‖k_w‖² = 1/(1 − |w|²) for w in the open disk, the standard value ⟨k_w, k_w⟩ = k_w(w) = 1/(1 − |w|²) (Duren; Conway) for the circle with normalised measure dθ/2π. It follows from the reproducing property applied to k_w itself and the closed form at z = w. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised at w = 1/2 to give 4/3 (compiled); the normalisation is confirmed by the constant function 1 having norm 1.

Defines the normalised Szegő kernel √(1 − |w|²)·k_w, which is k_w divided by its norm with a positive real scaling factor; this is the standard unit-norm kernel used, for example, in Berezin transforms and Carleson-measure tests. Red-team audit at 956e316250: equal to the general normalisation k_w/‖k_w‖ of Mathlib (compiled); shown to have norm 1 and to pair as √(1 − |w|²) times evaluation; the factor is a positive real number, so no conjugation subtlety arises.
Unfolding equation: the normalised kernel is √(1 − |w|²) times the Szegő kernel, true by definition. Red-team audit at 956e316250: holds by reflexivity.

Defines the Szegő kernel k_w of the Hardy space H² of the unit disk, for w in the open disk, as the unique vector representing evaluation at w (Riesz representation theorem). H² is modelled as the boundary space: square-integrable functions on the circle with normalised arc length dθ/2π whose negative Fourier coefficients vanish, which is isometric to the Taylor-coefficient model of power series with Σ|aₙ|² < ∞ (Duren, Theory of Hᵖ Spaces; Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis); in particular the constant function 1 has norm 1. The file proves that this vector is the textbook kernel: its Taylor coefficients are w̄ⁿ, so as a function on the disk k_w(z) = 1/(1 − w̄z) with the conjugate on w; pairing with it reproduces evaluation, written ⟨k_w, f⟩ = f(w) because the inner product here is conjugate-linear in the first slot, the mirror image of the analyst's f(w) = ⟨f, k_w⟩; and ‖k_w‖ = (1 − |w|²)^(−1/2). Red-team audit at 956e316250: k_0 is the constant function 1 (compiled); ⟨k_w, k_w⟩ = k_w(w) = 1/(1 − |w|²) and ‖k_{1/2}‖² = 4/3 (compiled); the reversed slot order and the unconjugated kernel are both refuted at w = i/2 (compiled); |w| < 1 is built into the points, so no junk value is involved; agrees with the generic kernel function of Mathlib's reproducing-kernel framework (compiled); only the standard axioms.

Correctly stated. It says: on a connected smooth Riemannian manifold (the empty manifold is allowed) of dimension n with n not 0 and not 2, if a smooth connection that preserves the metric and has no torsion (that is, the Levi-Civita connection) has Ricci tensor equal at each point p to a(p) times the metric, for some real function a, then a takes the same value at any two points. This is Schur's lemma for the Ricci tensor, i.e. an Einstein metric with a variable factor has constant factor (Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 7; Wikipedia, Schur's lemma (Riemannian geometry)); the textbook form asks for n at least 3, and here n = 1 is also covered and correct, since the Ricci tensor of a curve is zero and so a is identically 0. No regularity of a is assumed: taking the trace of Ric = a g shows that the scalar curvature is n times a, so a is automatically smooth. The proof is the classical one: since the metric is parallel, the covariant derivative of Ric = a g is da tensor g; contracting the second Bianchi identity twice (2 div Ric = d Scal) then gives 2 da = n da, so (n - 2) da = 0 and da vanishes when n is not 2, and a function with zero differential on a connected manifold is constant. Dimension 2 really must be excluded: on a surface Ric = K g with K the Gaussian curvature, which need not be constant. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are met by the Levi-Civita connection of flat Euclidean 3-space with a = 0 (compiled), so the statement is not vacuous; the conclusion is the full statement that a takes equal values at every pair of points; the second Bianchi identity and its contractions are proved in the library, not assumed (only the standard axioms); the hypothesis n not 0 is the only unnecessary one (zero-dimensional connected manifolds are single points; the theorem compiles without it).

Correctly stated. It says: for a smooth metric-compatible torsion-free connection (the Levi-Civita connection) on a smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension n other than 2, if the Ricci tensor equals a(p) times the metric at every point p for a real function a, then the differential da vanishes at every point; no connectedness is needed. This is the local half of Schur's lemma for the Ricci tensor (Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 7): as the metric is parallel, the covariant derivative of Ric = a g is da tensor g, and contracting the second Bianchi identity twice in a local frame gives (n - 2) da = 0. Convention: the library sets the derivative of a non-differentiable function to zero, but that never matters here because a is automatically smooth (it is the scalar curvature divided by n, and in dimension 0 every function is smooth); a strengthened version stating that a is differentiable with zero derivative also compiles. Dimension 1 is included and correct (there Ric = 0, so a = 0), and dimension 2 must be excluded (Gaussian curvature of a surface). Red-team checks: hypotheses met by flat Euclidean space with a = 0 in dimensions 1 and 3 (compiled); only the standard axioms; the hypothesis Ric = a g is only needed near the point, so it could even be weakened.

If X₁,…,Xₙ (n at least 1, indexed by any nonempty finite set) are independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on [0,1], then their average (X₁+…+Xₙ)/n has the Bates law of order n, which is the defining property of the Bates distribution (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26). Proof idea: the sum has the Irwin–Hall law (proved in the Irwin–Hall file from independence), and dividing by n gives the Bates law. Red-team checks: hypotheses are satisfiable (instantiated in Lean with the three coordinates of the product of uniform laws); nonemptiness is needed because of the order-0 convention.

A Bates-distributed value lies in [0,1] almost surely: an Irwin–Hall sum of n uniforms lies in [0,n], and dividing by n puts it in [0,1]. At order 0 the statement is trivially true for the zero measure, as the docstring says. Red-team checks: the order-0 case is disclosed, not hidden.

Defines the Bates distribution of order n: for n at least 1 it is the law of the sum of n independent uniform variables on [0,1] (the Irwin–Hall law, built as the n-fold convolution of the uniform law) pushed forward by x ↦ x/n, that is the law of the sample mean (U₁+…+Uₙ)/n, which is the definition in Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan, Continuous Univariate Distributions vol. 2, ch. 26. The identification with the mean of n independent uniforms is proved, not assumed: the file shows that pushing the product of n uniform laws forward by the averaging map gives exactly this measure, and that the average of any n independent uniform random variables has this law. Order 0 (an average of no variables, which has no meaning) is set to the zero measure and documented as such, and every statement that needs a genuine probability law assumes n at least 1. Red-team checks: density value tests (order 2 at 1/2 gives 2, order 3 at 1/2 gives 9/4, order 1 is the uniform density) and cdf value tests (order 2 at 1/2 gives 1/2, order 3 at 1/3 gives 1/6); the product-average law checked at two coordinates; mean 1/2, variance 1/(12n) and mgf (n(e^{t/n}−1)/t)^n confirmed; no Bates or Irwin–Hall law in Mathlib and no second construction in Tau Ceti.

Unfolding equation: the Bates law of order n is the zero measure when n = 0 and otherwise the Irwin–Hall law of order n (law of a sum of n independent uniforms on [0,1]) pushed forward by x ↦ x/n. It holds by definition. Red-team checks: matches the definition verbatim.

For n at least 1 the Bates law is the image of the Irwin–Hall law (the law of a sum of n independent uniforms on [0,1]) under division by n, i.e. the law of the sample mean; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: the hypothesis n ≥ 1 is needed, since at n = 0 the left side is the zero measure while the right side is the point mass at 0.

At every order the Bates law equals Lebesgue measure weighted by the Bates density. For n at least 1 this is the change-of-variables formula for the image of the Irwin–Hall density under x ↦ x/n (with Jacobian factor n); at n = 0 both sides are zero. This is what makes the named density the genuine density of the law. Red-team checks: the weighted measure at order 2 has total mass 1; density values agree with the textbook formula.

The Bates law of order 1, the 'average' of a single uniform variable, is the uniform distribution on [0,1], as it must be: the order-1 Irwin–Hall law is the uniform law and dividing by 1 changes nothing. Red-team checks: agrees with the order-1 density being the uniform density.

At order 0 the Bates law is the zero measure, the documented convention for the meaningless average of no variables; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: consistent with the module docstring and with every positive-order statement carrying n ≥ 1.

The Bates density as a nonnegative extended real number, the form measure theory uses for densities: it is the nonnegative lift of the real density, and since the real density is never negative nothing is lost. Red-team checks: the file proves the law equals Lebesgue measure weighted by this function.

Defines the real Bates density as f(x) = n·g(nx), where g is the Irwin–Hall density of order n, the change-of-variables formula for the density of S/n. For n at least 2 this is n/(n−1)! Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k C(n,k) max(nx−k,0)^{n−1}, the textbook Bates density (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26; the truncated powers make the usual sum up to ⌊nx⌋ automatic); for n = 1 it is the uniform density, and at n = 0 it is 0. The file proves that the Bates law is Lebesgue measure weighted by this function. Red-team checks: value tests: order 2 at 1/2 gives 2, order 3 at 1/2 gives 9/4, order 2 at 3/2 gives 0, order 1 at 1/2 gives 1.
Unfolding equation: the Bates density at x is n times the Irwin–Hall density at nx; it holds by definition. Red-team checks: matches the definition verbatim.

For n at least 2 the Bates density is the classical formula f(x) = n/(n−1)! Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k C(n,k) max(nx−k,0)^{n−1} (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26, usually written with the sum up to ⌊nx⌋, which is the same because the truncated powers vanish beyond it and at the knot). Red-team checks: the bound n ≥ 2 is needed, since at n = 1 the formula collapses to the constant 0 (a zeroth power of max(·,0) is 1); value tests give 2 at x = 1/2 for n = 2 and 9/4 at x = 1/2 for n = 3.
The real Bates density is never negative, at any order: it is the nonnegative number n times the nonnegative Irwin–Hall density. Red-team checks: holds with no hypotheses, as stated.
The order-1 Bates density is the uniform density on [0,1], as expected since the order-1 Bates law is the uniform law. Red-team checks: value test at x = 1/2 gives 1.

The order-0 Bates density is zero, matching the order-0 zero-measure convention; immediate because the formula carries a factor n. Red-team checks: consistent with the density representation of the order-0 law.
Unfolding equation: the extended Bates density is the nonnegative lift of the real Bates density; it holds by definition. Red-team checks: matches the definition verbatim.

For n at least 1 the distribution function of the Bates law at x equals the Irwin–Hall distribution function at nx, since P(S/n ≤ x) = P(S ≤ nx) for the sum S. Red-team checks: n ≥ 1 is genuinely used (the order-0 law is not the image of the order-0 Irwin–Hall law).

For n at least 1 the Bates distribution function is F(x) = (1/n!) Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k C(n,k) max(nx−k,0)^n, the textbook formula (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26, written there with the sum up to ⌊nx⌋, equivalent because the truncated powers vanish beyond), valid for every real x including the knots. Red-team checks: value tests: order 2 at 1/2 gives 1/2, order 3 at 1/3 gives 1/6.

For n at least 1 and t ≠ 0 the cumulant generating function (the logarithm of the mgf) of the Bates law is n·log((e^{t/n} − 1)/(t/n)), the logarithm of the mgf formula. Red-team checks: correct as stated; both hypotheses turn out unnecessary because of the conventions log 0 = 0 and 0/0 = 0, recorded separately as a minor generality point.

For n at least 1 and t ≠ 0 the characteristic function E[e^{itX}] of the Bates law is ((e^{it/n} − 1)/(it/n))^n: the uniform characteristic function (e^{is} − 1)/(is) at s = t/n raised to the n-th power, by independence (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26). Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed (at t = 0 the formula gives 0 instead of 1, and the order-0 zero measure has characteristic function 0).

A random variable whose law is a Bates law has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure, because the law is Lebesgue measure weighted by the Bates density. At order 0 it holds trivially for the zero law, as the docstring says. Red-team checks: the order-0 case is disclosed in the docstring.

Every exponential moment E[e^{tX}] of a Bates variable is finite, for every real t, because the variable lies in [0,1] almost surely. It holds at every order, trivially for the order-0 zero measure. Red-team checks: follows from the almost-sure bound, as stated.
Every power x^k is integrable against every Bates law, so all moments exist, since the law lives on [0,1]. Red-team checks: holds for every order and every k, as stated.

For n at least 1 the mean of the Bates law is 1/2 (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26): each uniform has mean 1/2, so the sum has mean n/2 and the average 1/2. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is needed, since the order-0 zero measure has integral 0; specialised at n = 3.
Every Bates law has finite total mass: mass 1 for n at least 1 and mass 0 for the order-0 convention. Red-team checks: both cases checked; no clash with another instance on this measure.

For n at least 1 the Bates law has total mass 1, because it is the image of the Irwin–Hall probability law under a measurable map. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is necessary: Lean confirms the order-0 zero measure is not a probability measure.

The central identification: for a nonempty finite index set of size n, pushing the product of n uniform laws on [0,1] forward by the averaging map x ↦ (x₁+…+xₙ)/n gives the Bates law of order n. This is precisely the textbook definition of the Bates distribution as the law of the mean of n independent uniforms (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan, vol. 2, ch. 26). Proof idea: the coordinate sum has the Irwin–Hall law (proved in the Irwin–Hall file from the convolution description), and composing with division by n gives the Bates law. Nonemptiness is needed because the empty average is assigned the zero measure. Red-team checks: specialised in Lean to two coordinates, (x₀+x₁)/2 has the order-2 Bates law; hypotheses are satisfiable.

For n at least 1, multiplying a Bates variable of order n by n gives the Irwin–Hall law: n times the sample mean is the sum. It follows by composing x ↦ x/n with x ↦ nx. Red-team checks: n ≥ 1 is needed, since at n = 0 the left side is the zero measure and the right side the point mass at 0.

The map sending an order n to its Bates law is measurable; this is automatic because the orders form a countable discrete set. Red-team checks: statement is exactly measurability of the family; no stronger claim is made.
The extended Bates density is measurable, being the nonnegative lift of a measurable function. Red-team checks: holds at every order, as stated.
The real Bates density is a measurable function: a constant times the measurable Irwin–Hall density composed with x ↦ nx. Red-team checks: holds at every order, as stated.

For n at least 1 and t ≠ 0 the moment generating function of the Bates law is ((e^{t/n} − 1)/(t/n))^n, i.e. (n(e^{t/n} − 1)/t)^n as in Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26: the uniform mgf at t/n raised to the n-th power, by independence of the n summands. Red-team checks: rewritten in Lean into the textbook form n(e^{t/n}−1)/t; at n = 1 it reduces to the uniform mgf (e^t − 1)/t; both hypotheses are needed (at t = 0 the formula gives 0 instead of 1, and the order-0 zero measure has mgf 0).

The density of a Bates-distributed random variable equals the Bates density almost everywhere, by the weighted-Lebesgue description of the law and uniqueness of densities up to null sets. Red-team checks: no extra hypotheses; consistent with the order-0 convention.

For n at least 1 and a level u strictly between 0 and 1, the u-quantile of the Bates law is the u-quantile of the Irwin–Hall law divided by n, because dividing by the positive constant n is increasing and so carries quantiles to quantiles (P(S/n ≤ x) = P(S ≤ nx) for the sum S). Red-team checks: n ≥ 1 is used; the restriction on u is in fact unnecessary (the identity also holds at u = 1 and, by convention, outside [0,1]), recorded separately as a minor generality point, which does not affect correctness of what is stated.

The Radon–Nikodym derivative of the Bates law with respect to Lebesgue measure is the Bates density almost everywhere, since the law is Lebesgue measure with that density and such a density is unique up to null sets. Red-team checks: holds at every order, as stated.
Converting the extended Bates density back to a real number recovers the real density, because the real density is nonnegative. Red-team checks: no hypotheses needed, as stated.

For n at least 1 the variance of the Bates law is 1/(12n) (Johnson–Kotz–Balakrishnan vol. 2 ch. 26): each uniform has variance 1/12, independence makes the variance of the sum n/12, and dividing by n divides the variance by n². Red-team checks: at n = 3 it gives 1/36; the hypothesis n ≥ 1 turns out unnecessary (both sides are 0 at n = 0 by convention), recorded separately as a minor generality point, which does not affect correctness.

If both 0→A→E₁→C→0 and 0→A→E₂→C→0 are short exact, so is their Baer sum. This is the standard fact that direct sums, pullbacks and pushouts of short exact sequences are again short exact (Weibel §3.4), and the proof is exactly the composite of those three facts. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are consistent (split sequences satisfy them), and both are needed: if the second input is 0→A→0→C→0 with C nonzero, the last map of the Baer sum is zero and so not onto.

Main theorem. If 0→A→E₁→C→0 and 0→A→E₂→C→0 are short exact, the extension class of their Baer sum in Ext¹(C,A) is the sum of their two classes. Here Ext¹ is Mathlib's Ext group, defined through the derived category, with its usual addition. This is the classical statement that the Baer sum realises the group law of Ext¹ (Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, §3.4; Mac Lane, Homology, III.2). Proof idea: the class of the direct sum is block diagonal; pulling back along the diagonal precomposes with the diagonal map; pushing out along the codiagonal composes with the addition map; the result is e₁ + e₂. Both sides lie in the same Ext group, because the Baer sum literally has end objects C and A, so no identification is hidden, and the statement holds in every abelian category that has Ext groups. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are consistent (split sequences satisfy them) and both are needed; only the standard axioms are used; for the Baer sum of an extension with itself it gives twice the class; the construction's sign convention was checked (the antidiagonal (a,−a) becomes zero); no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti at the pinned versions.

The direct sum of two short exact sequences 0→A→E→C→0 and 0→A′→E′→C′→0 has as its class in Ext¹(C⊕C′, A⊕A′) the block-diagonal element. Explicitly, it is: project to C, apply the first class, include into A⊕A′; plus the same through the second summand. This holds because a class out of C⊕C′ is determined by its restrictions to C and C′, and naturality of extension classes along the summand inclusions computes those restrictions. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed (each class appears in the conclusion); the off-diagonal components are zero, as they must be.

Let 0→A→E→C→0 be short exact with class e in Ext¹(C,A), and let f: Y→C be any map. Then the pulled-back extension 0→A→E×_C Y→Y→0 has class f*(e), that is, e precomposed with f, in Ext¹(Y,A). This is the standard contravariant functoriality of the correspondence between extensions and Ext¹ (Weibel §3.4). It follows from the naturality of extension classes, applied to the evident map from the pulled-back sequence to the original one. Red-team checks: at f = identity it returns the original class; it is not in Mathlib at the pinned version (searched by name, type and meaning).

Let 0→A→E→C→0 be short exact with class e in Ext¹(C,A), and let f: A→B be any map. Then the pushed-out extension 0→B→E⊔_A B→C→0 has class f_*(e), that is, e followed by f, in Ext¹(C,B). This is the standard covariant functoriality of the correspondence between extensions and Ext¹ (Weibel §3.4). It follows from the naturality of extension classes, applied to the evident map from the original sequence to the pushed-out one. Red-team checks: at f = identity it returns the original class; it is not in Mathlib at the pinned version (searched).

Defines the Baer sum of two extensions with the same end objects A and C. Given 0→A→E₁→C→0 and 0→A→E₂→C→0, it takes the direct sum E₁⊕E₂, which is an extension of C⊕C by A⊕A. It pulls this back along the diagonal map C→C⊕C, then pushes the result out along the addition map A⊕A→A. This is exactly the classical Baer sum (Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, §3.4; Mac Lane, Homology, III.2). Equivalently, its middle term is the fibre product E₁×_C E₂ modulo the antidiagonal {(a,−a)}. The second extension is passed as its two maps A→E₂→C rather than as a separate sequence, so that both inputs share their end objects literally. The construction makes sense for any two such pairs of maps with zero composite, and a separate lemma shows the result is short exact when both inputs are. Red-team checks: checked in Lean that an antidiagonal element (a,−a) of the fibre product becomes zero in the Baer sum's middle term while a diagonal element (a,a) goes to 2a, which confirms the sign convention; the Baer sum of an extension with itself has twice its class; each step compared with Mathlib's pullback and pushout of short complexes; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Records that the right-hand end of the Baer sum is the common end object C of the two input sequences. This holds by construction: pulling back along the diagonal C→C⊕C makes C the new right end, and the pushout does not change it. Red-team checks: holds definitionally; the automatically generated projection lemma would state the right-hand side in an unfolded, less useful form, so stating it by hand is justified.

Says: two unimodular integral lattices (integral symmetric lattices whose Gram determinant is ±1) lie in the same genus, meaning they have the same real signature (n₊, n₀, n₋) and become isometric over the p-adic integers at every prime p, exactly when their signatures agree and they are both even (every vector has even squared length) or both odd. This is the classical description of the genus of a unimodular lattice by rank, signature and type (Milnor–Husemoller, Symmetric Bilinear Forms, Ch. II; Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. V). Why it holds: the genus fixes signature and parity; conversely a unimodular lattice has determinant (−1)^{n₋}, so at odd primes both localizations are unimodular of equal rank and determinant, hence isometric, and at 2 unimodular forms are classified by rank, parity, determinant square class and the norm of a characteristic vector mod 8, which van der Blij's theorem identifies with n₊ − n₋ mod 8. Equal signatures force equal ranks, unimodularity forces nondegeneracy, and the rank-zero lattice counts as even and lies in one genus with itself. Red-team checks: axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; both unimodularity hypotheses are needed (⟨1⟩ and ⟨3⟩ share signature and parity but not genus); specialised to I₈ vs E₈ (same signature, different parity: proved not in one genus via the theorem), to I₉ and E₈ ⊕ I₁ (proved in one genus via the converse), and to rank 0.
Only exponents divisible by t occur in the q-expansion of E₂^{ψ,φ,t}, a direct consequence of the substitution q ↦ q^t.

Defines the normalized weight-two Eisenstein series with characters E₂^{ψ,φ} for a Dirichlet character ψ mod u, a character φ mod v and a level N divisible by uv: the series G₂^{ψ,φ}(z) = Σ_c ψ(c) Σ_d φ̄(d)(cvz + d)⁻² (rows summed in the order Diamond–Shurman use in weight two) divided by its expected first Fourier coefficient −8π² g(φ̄)/v², g the Gauss sum. Diamond–Shurman §4.5–4.6 write G₂^{ψ,φ} = −4π² g(φ̄)/v² · E₂^{ψ,φ}, so this is their E₂^{ψ,φ} halved, i.e. rescaled to have q-coefficient 1, the same normalization the library uses in weight k ≥ 3 (the scale is the weight-k scale at k = 2). Convention: if φ is imprimitive with vanishing Gauss sum the scale is 0 and the definition returns 0; the docstring names primitivity of φ as the condition for the normalization. Red-team checks: definition compared clause by clause with Diamond–Shurman and Miyake §7.1; witness test at ψ = the even character χ₈ mod 8, φ = the trivial character mod 1 (q-coefficient 1, q³-coefficient σ₁(3) = 2).

Defines E₂^{ψ,φ,t}(z) = E₂^{ψ,φ}(tz) as a weight-two form for Γ₁(N) whenever t u v divides N: the series is formed at its natural level uv and pushed to level N by the degeneracy operator V_t, normalized so that V_t f(z) = f(tz) exactly. This is Diamond–Shurman's E₂^{ψ,φ,t} (§4.6) with the library's normalization. Red-team checks: the factor t^{1−k} in V_t cancels the slash factor; the companion apply lemma confirms f(tz).
E₂^{ψ,φ,t}(z) = E₂^{ψ,φ}(tz), the defining property of the raised series in Diamond–Shurman §4.6 (E₂^{ψ,φ} taken at its natural level uv). Red-team checks: simp attribute fires.
Unfolding equation: E₂^{ψ,φ,t} is V_t applied to E₂^{ψ,φ} at level uv. True by definition (rfl).
E₂^{ψ,φ,t} equals the raised unnormalized series G₂^{ψ,φ,t} times the same scalar (−8π² g(φ̄)/v²)⁻¹, because V_t is linear. Red-team checks: the scalar matches the base definition.

For all t, u, v, N with tuv dividing N, the raised series E₂^{ψ,φ,t}(z) = E₂^{ψ,φ}(tz) lies in M₂(N, ψφ): it transforms under Γ₀(N) by the character d ↦ ψ(d)φ(d) of the lower-right entry, both characters lifted to modulus N. This is the membership half of Diamond–Shurman Thm 4.6.2 in weight two, which assumes ψ and φ primitive, ψφ(−1) = 1 and (ψ, φ) ≠ (1, 1). Here no hypothesis is needed, and that is a genuine generalization, not a weakening: the transformation law comes from multiplicativity of the characters alone, and in the degenerate cases (wrong parity, or a vanishing Gauss sum) the form is 0, while for the trivial pair the underlying series is the library's regularized modular version. The q-expansion half of Thm 4.6.2 (δ_{u=1}(−B_{2,φ}/4) + Σ σ₁^{ψ,φ}(m) q^{tm}) is stated by the companion theorems qExpansion_normalizedCharG2MFRaise_coeff and qExpansion_normalizedCharG2MFRaise_coeff_zero. Proof: V_t carries M₂(uv, ψφ) into M₂(N, ψφ) when tuv | N, and scalars preserve the space. Red-team checks: specialised at ψ = χ₈, φ trivial, t = 3, N = 24, where the form is a nonzero element of M₂(24, χ₈), so the statement is not vacuous; character convention f|γ = χ(d) f checked; standard axioms only.
Under the hypotheses E₂^{ψ,φ,t} is not the zero form, since its coefficient of q^t is 1. Red-team checks: specialised at ψ = χ₈, φ trivial, t = 3, N = 24.
For t = 1 the raised series is E₂^{ψ,φ} at level uv viewed as a form of level N (restriction to the smaller group Γ₁(N)), since V_1 is the identity.

The defining equation of the normalized series: E₂^{ψ,φ} is G₂^{ψ,φ} multiplied by the inverse of −8π² g(φ̄)/v². It holds by definition and is how other files unfold the sealed definition. Red-team checks: proof is rfl; the right side matches the definition verbatim.

E₂^{ψ,φ} lies in M₂(N, ψφ): for every γ in Γ₀(N) with lower-right entry d it satisfies E|₂γ = ψ(d)φ(d)·E, the classical nebentypus condition of Diamond–Shurman §4.3 and §4.6 (the library's space is the joint eigenspace of the diamond operators, shown equivalent to this condition). No hypothesis is needed because the unnormalized series is in this space for every pair of characters and the space is closed under scalars; in the degenerate cases the form is simply 0. Red-team checks: character convention (lower-right entry, f|γ = χ(d) f) checked against Mathlib's Gamma0Map; both characters lifted to level N.

Under the hypotheses E₂^{ψ,φ} is not the zero form, because its q-coefficient is 1. This makes the coefficient and membership statements non-vacuous. Red-team checks: specialised at ψ = the even character χ₈ mod 8, φ = the trivial character mod 1.
The q-expansion of E₂^{ψ,φ,t} is that of E₂^{ψ,φ} with q replaced by q^t, as z ↦ tz dictates.

Under the coefficient-formula hypotheses, the n-th coefficient (n ≥ 1) of E₂^{ψ,φ,t} is σ₁^{ψ,φ}(n/t) when t divides n and 0 otherwise: the series Σ σ₁^{ψ,φ}(m) q^{tm} of Diamond–Shurman Thm 4.6.2 after normalization. Red-team checks: every hypothesis load-bearing; specialised at ψ = χ₈, φ trivial, t = 3, N = 24 (coefficient of q⁹ is 2, of q² is 0).
Under the hypotheses the coefficient of q^t in E₂^{ψ,φ,t} is 1, since it is σ₁^{ψ,φ}(1) = 1.

Under the hypotheses the constant term of E₂^{ψ,φ,t} is that of E₂^{ψ,φ}: −B_{2,φ}/4 if u = 1 and 0 otherwise, because z ↦ tz does not change constant terms; this is Diamond–Shurman Thm 4.6.2's δ(ψ)L(−1,φ), halved by the normalization.

For ψ mod u, a primitive φ mod v, not both trivial, with ψ(−1)φ(−1) = 1, the n-th Fourier coefficient (n ≥ 1) of E₂^{ψ,φ} is the twisted divisor sum σ₁^{ψ,φ}(n) = Σ_{d|n} ψ(n/d) φ(d) d. This is the weight-two q-expansion of Diamond–Shurman Thm 4.6.2 (their coefficients 2σ₁, halved by the normalization); it follows by dividing the unnormalized coefficient −8π² g(φ̄)/v² · σ₁(n), computed row by row, by the nonzero scale. ψ need not be primitive, a mild generalization of Diamond–Shurman, harmless because ψ only enters as the row weight ψ(c). Red-team checks: hypotheses jointly satisfiable and each needed (wrong parity makes the form 0; the trivial pair is the non-modular E₂; an imprimitive φ can have vanishing Gauss sum); specialised at ψ = the even character χ₈ mod 8, φ = the trivial character mod 1: coefficient of q³ is χ₈(3)+3 = 2.

Under the same hypotheses the q-coefficient of E₂^{ψ,φ} is 1, which is the point of the normalization: it is the case n = 1 of the coefficient formula, since σ₁^{ψ,φ}(1) = 1. Red-team checks: specialised at ψ = the even character χ₈ mod 8, φ = the trivial character mod 1; the simp attribute fires.

Under the same hypotheses the constant term of E₂^{ψ,φ} is −B_{2,φ}/4 when u = 1 (ψ trivial of modulus 1) and 0 otherwise, B_{2,φ} = v Σ_{a=1}^{v} φ(a) B₂(a/v) the generalized Bernoulli number (Washington (4.1)). Diamond–Shurman's constant term is δ(ψ) L(−1, φ) with L(−1, φ) = −B_{2,φ}/2, halved by the normalization; so −B/(2k) at k = 2. Idea: the constant term of G₂ is ψ(0) Σ_{d≠0} φ̄(d) d⁻²; ψ(0) = 0 for u > 1, and for u = 1 the sum is a Bernoulli number by the functional equation, with g(φ) g(φ̄) = φ(−1) v = v. Red-team checks: end-to-end value test at ψ trivial mod 1, φ = χ₈ (proved primitive): B_{2,χ₈} = 2 computed in Lean, constant term −1/2 = L(−1,χ₈)/2, consistent with ζ_{Q(√2)}(−1) = 1/12; the u ≠ 1 branch specialised at ψ = χ₈.

Correctly stated: the embedding of an exact category into its idempotent completion sends every short exact sequence to a short exact sequence of the induced exact structure, i.e. it is an exact functor in Bühler's sense (Exact categories, Def. 5.1 and Prop. 6.13, 'the inclusion functor preserves exactness'). It holds because the image of a short exact sequence is trivially a retract of itself, and the induced structure consists of such retracts. Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5, checkout 956e3162): no hypotheses beyond the exact structure; only standard axioms; matches the docstring exactly. The converse, that the embedding also reflects exactness (also in Bühler 6.13), is not part of this statement and is recorded separately as missing API.

Correctly stated: given an exact category (an additive category with a Quillen exact structure), this defines the exact structure on its idempotent completion (Karoubi envelope) whose short exact sequences are exactly the retracts, in the category of short sequences, of images of short exact sequences of the original category. This is Bühler's construction (Exact categories, Expo. Math. 28 (2010), §6, Prop. 6.13), which phrases the same class as 'direct summands of sequences in E'; in an idempotent complete category such as the Karoubi envelope (whose short sequences again split idempotents) a retract and a direct summand are the same thing. All six of Bühler's axioms are proved, not assumed: identities are admissible monics and epics, admissible monics and epics are closed under composition, and pushouts of admissible monics and pullbacks of admissible epics along arbitrary maps exist and are again admissible; every member is checked to be a kernel–cokernel pair, and the class is closed under isomorphism. The idea of the proof: the cokernel of a retract of an admissible monic a is the image of the idempotent that the retraction induces on the cokernel of a; a composite of two retracts of admissible maps is a retract of a composite of admissible maps once identity summands are added and a biproduct is twisted by an involution; and a pushout or pullback in the envelope is the image of an idempotent on the corresponding square in the original category. Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5, checkout 956e3162): only the standard axioms are used; the exact-structure definition it targets matches Bühler Def. 2.1 axiom by axiom (E0, E0op, E1, E1op, E2, E2op over kernel–cokernel pairs, closed under isomorphism, in an additive category); specialised to the split exact structure, a compiled probe shows the result is exactly the split exact structure on the Karoubi envelope; no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti construction of it exists. Bühler's further claims that the embedding reflects exactness and is 2-universal are not part of this definition (recorded separately as missing API).

Correctly stated: a short sequence in the idempotent completion is short exact for the induced exact structure exactly when it is a retract, in the category of short sequences, of the image of a short exact sequence of the original exact category. This is the defining description of Bühler's class of exact sequences on the idempotent completion (Exact categories, §6, just before Prop. 6.13, where it is phrased as 'direct summands', equivalent to retracts in an idempotent complete category), and it holds by definition. Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5, checkout 956e3162): simp cannot prove it without itself (simp normal form); same form as the sibling characterisations for the product, transported and chain-complex exact structures; specialised to the split structure it yields the split sequences of the envelope.

Correctly stated: a morphism of the idempotent completion is an admissible epic (deflation) of the induced exact structure exactly when it is a retract, in the arrow category, of the image of an admissible epic of the original exact category. This is the dual of the inflation characterisation: the kernel of a retract of an admissible epic d is the image of the idempotent induced on the kernel of d (Bühler, Exact categories, Prop. 6.13). Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5, checkout 956e3162): simp cannot prove it without itself; both directions are used to build the exact structure; no hypotheses beyond the morphism.

Correctly stated: a morphism of the idempotent completion is an admissible monic (inflation) of the induced exact structure exactly when it is a retract, in the arrow category, of the image of an admissible monic of the original exact category. One direction takes the first map of a witnessing sequence; for the converse, the cokernel of a retract f of an admissible monic a is built as the image of the idempotent that the retraction induces on the cokernel of a, and the resulting sequence is a retract of the image of a's short exact sequence (the argument behind Bühler, Exact categories, Prop. 6.13). Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5, checkout 956e3162): simp cannot prove it without itself; both directions are genuinely used to build the exact structure; no hypotheses beyond the morphism.
Multiplying a section t of O(n) by the O(0)-section corresponding to a structure-sheaf section a is the same as the scalar action of a on t, pointwise. Holds by definition: both are a(x) t(x).

The product of the sections r/1 (degree i) and r'/1 (degree j) is the section rr'/1 of degree i + j, so the map from A to the sections of the twisting sheaves is multiplicative. Correct: (r/1)(r'/1) = rr'/1.
Restricting the section r/1 on U to a smaller open gives the section r/1 there. Holds by definition.

Over every open U, the sections of the structure sheaf of Proj and the sections of O(0) are isomorphic as modules over the structure-sheaf sections, by sending a section to its image in the localizations. Correct: the map from the homogeneous localization A_(x) to A_x is injective and its image is exactly the degree-0 fractions, so a function is locally a degree-0 fraction in A_x exactly when it comes from a structure-sheaf section (isLocallyFraction_val and exists_val_eq). Red-team check: linearity over the structure sheaf (not just additivity) is part of the statement.
The comparison map sends a structure-sheaf section a to the section whose value at x is a(x) viewed in A_x. Holds by definition.
The inverse comparison sends a section of O(0) to the structure-sheaf section with the same values in the localizations. Correct, as the inverse of the comparison map.

For a homogeneous element r of degree j, with j = n, the section r/1 of O(n) over any open U, as an additive map from the degree-j part of A; over all of Proj these are the components of the natural graded map A -> sum over n of Γ(Proj A, O(n)) (Hartshorne II.5). Red-team checks: compiled witness on Proj Q[X,Y]: X and Y give nonzero, distinct global sections of O(1); the hypothesis j = n is exactly the degree condition and cannot be met for negative n.
The section r/1 takes the value r/1 in A_x at every point. Holds by definition.
The section r/1 is the constant fraction section with denominator 1. Holds by definition.

Defines, for an N-graded commutative ring A and any integer n, the twisting sheaf O(n) on Proj A as a sheaf of O_{Proj A}-modules: a section over U is a function sending each point x of U to an element of the localization A_x that is, near every point, a single fraction r/s with r and s homogeneous, deg r = deg s + n, and s outside the primes nearby. This is Hartshorne's O(n) = S(n)~ (II.5) and Stacks 27.10.1: Hartshorne's stalk values are the degree-0 elements m/f of the homogeneous localization of the shifted module S(n), i.e. m of degree deg f + n, which is exactly the convention here. Taking values in the ordinary localization A_x instead of the homogeneous one loses nothing, because the map from the degree-n part of the homogeneous localization to A_x is injective (a homogeneous element killed by some t outside a homogeneous prime is killed by a homogeneous component of t outside it). The sheaf condition is inherited from the subsheaf of sets, and the module structure over the structure sheaf is genuinely given (pointwise multiplication), not just an abelian-group structure. Red-team checks: compiled witnesses on Proj Q[X,Y]: X/1 and Y/1 are nonzero, distinct global sections of O(1), their product is XY in O(2), and 1/X is a section of O(-1) on D+(X), confirming the sign convention and that negative n is allowed; O(0) is isomorphic to the structure sheaf as sheaves of modules (unitIsoTwistingSheafZero). Red-team audit at 956e316250: statement re-read against Hartshorne II.5 and Stacks 27.8-27.10; no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti construction duplicates it (grep, leansearch, leanfinder).
Sections of O(n) add pointwise. Holds by definition.

The section r/s of O(n) over an open U on which the homogeneous element s does not vanish, for r homogeneous of degree deg s + n. This is the standard 'constant fraction' section (compare Mathlib's const for Spec), and it satisfies the local-fraction condition with the single fraction r/s on all of U.
Sections r/s and r'/s with the same denominator add to (r + r')/s. Correct by the corresponding identity in each localization.
The section r/s takes the value r/s in A_x at every point x. Holds by definition.
The sections r/s and r'/s' agree when s'r = sr'. Correct (cross-multiplication); it is a sufficient condition only, as its docstring says ('if', not 'iff').

The difference of sections r/s and r'/s' (both of degree n) is (s'r - sr')/(ss'), again a section of degree n on U, where ss' does not vanish since neither factor does. Correct: the usual fraction identity, with the degree bookkeeping deg(s'r) = deg(sr') = deg s + deg s' + n checked.
The section 0/s is the zero section. Correct since 0/s = 0 in every localization.

Every section of O(n) over U is, near each point x of U, the restriction of a single fraction r/t with r and t homogeneous, deg r = deg t + n, and t nonvanishing on the smaller neighbourhood. This is the definition of the sheaf unfolded, stated in the form used later.
Two sections of O(n) over U are equal if they take the same value in A_x at every point x of U. True because sections are, by construction, functions into the localizations.

Every section of O(n) is, near each point x, of the form r/g on a whole standard open D+(g) containing x, with g homogeneous of positive degree. Correct: from a local fraction r/t on a neighbourhood V, shrink to a basic open D+(a) in V, pick a homogeneous component of a not in x and a homogeneous element p of positive degree not in x, and use g = t * a_m * p, rewriting r/t as (r a_m p)/g. This mirrors Mathlib's locally_const_basicOpen for Spec. Red-team checks: the only hypothesis (x lies in U) is needed; positivity of deg g is genuinely proved.

The multiplication of sections Γ(U, O(m)) x Γ(U, O(n)) -> Γ(U, O(m+n)), (s, t) -> pointwise product in the localizations, packaged as a map that is bilinear over the ring of sections of the structure sheaf. This is the standard multiplication O(m) x O(n) -> O(m+n) (Hartshorne II.5, the map underlying O(m) ⊗ O(n) -> O(m+n)); bilinearity is distributivity and associativity/commutativity in A_x, and its compatibility with restriction is res_mul. Red-team check: on Proj Q[X,Y] the product of the degree-one sections X and Y is the degree-two section XY.
The product of two sections is computed pointwise. Holds by definition.

The multiplication of sections of twisting sheaves is associative, compared pointwise in the localizations (the two sides live in O((l+m)+n) and O(l+(m+n)), which are not literally the same object, hence the pointwise form). Correct by associativity in A_x.
The multiplication of sections is commutative, compared pointwise (O(m+n) and O(n+m) are not literally the same object). Correct by commutativity in A_x.
The product of the sections r/s (degree m) and r'/s' (degree n) is the section rr'/(ss') of degree m + n. Correct by the fraction identity in each localization.
The negative of a section is computed pointwise. Holds by definition.
The negative of the section r/s is (-r)/s. Correct by the corresponding identity in each localization.
Restricting a section to a smaller open V and evaluating at x gives the value of the original section at x. Holds by definition of restriction.
Restricting the section r/s on U to a smaller open V gives the section r/s on V. Holds by definition.
Multiplication of sections commutes with restriction to smaller opens, so the sectionwise products form a morphism of sheaves. Holds by definition, since both are pointwise.
A section a of the structure sheaf acts on a section s of O(n) by (a s)(x) = a(x) s(x), with a(x) viewed in A_x. Holds by definition of the module structure.
The difference of two sections is computed pointwise. Holds by definition.
The zero section takes the value 0 at every point. Holds by definition.

The twisting sheaf O(0) is isomorphic to the structure sheaf of Proj A, as sheaves of O_{Proj A}-modules (the structure sheaf regarded as a module over itself). This is the standard fact O(0) = O_X (Hartshorne II.5, Stacks 27.10); it is assembled from the module isomorphisms on each open set, which are compatible with restriction. Red-team checks: it is an isomorphism in the category of sheaves of modules, not merely of sheaves of sets or abelian groups; its components are the canonical comparison maps.
On sections over U, the isomorphism O -> O(0) is the comparison map sending a to its values in the localizations. Holds by construction.
On sections over U, the inverse isomorphism O(0) -> O is the inverse comparison map. Holds by construction.

A function on an open set U assigning to each point x an element of A_x is a fraction of degree n if it equals one fixed r/s throughout U, with s homogeneous of some degree i, r homogeneous of degree i + n, and s outside every prime of U. This is the defining local condition for sections of the shifted sheaf A(n)~ (Hartshorne II.5): numerator degree minus denominator degree equals n, and the denominator is invertible on U. Red-team checks: sign convention deg r - deg s = n confirmed (degree-one elements give sections of O(1), not O(-1)); degrees are compared in the integers, so no truncated subtraction.

Defines, for a point x of Proj A (a relevant homogeneous prime), the ordinary localization A_x of A at that prime; this is the common ambient ring in which the sections of every twisting sheaf take their values, exactly as Mathlib's Spec structure sheaf uses the localizations A_p. Red-team checks: matches Mathlib's `Localizations` convention for Spec; nothing hidden in it.

Conversely, at each point a local fraction of degree 0 lies in the image of the homogeneous localization A_(x) in A_x. Correct: near the point it is r/s with deg r = deg s, which is an element of A_(x). Red-team check: the degree-0 hypothesis is used (it forces deg r = deg s).

Packages being a fraction of degree n as a prelocal predicate: if a function is a fraction r/s on U it is still the same fraction on any smaller open set. Correct, since the conditions on r, s only get weaker on a smaller open.

The local predicate 'near every point, the function is a fraction r/s of degree n', obtained by sheafifying the previous predicate; the sections of O(n) are exactly the functions satisfying it. This matches the standard definition of the sheaf associated with the graded module A(n) (Hartshorne II.5, Stacks 27.8). Red-team checks: same construction pattern as Mathlib's structure sheaf of Proj, with the degree shift n inserted in the only place it belongs.
The sum of two local fractions of degree n is again one: r/s + r'/s' = (s'r + sr')/(ss'), and both terms of the numerator have degree deg s + deg s' + n. Standard.

The product of a local fraction of degree m and one of degree n is a local fraction of degree m + n: (r/s)(r'/s') = rr'/(ss'), and degrees add. This is the multiplication O(m) x O(n) -> O(m+n) at the level of local sections. Red-team checks: degree bookkeeping verified, no hypotheses beyond the two inputs.
The negative of a local fraction of degree n is one: -(r/s) = (-r)/s. Standard.

A section of the structure sheaf of Proj, viewed through the natural maps from the homogeneous localizations A_(x) into the localizations A_x, is a local fraction of degree 0. Correct: structure-sheaf sections are locally r/s with deg r = deg s.

The zero function is locally a fraction of every degree n, including negative n. Correct: near any point choose a homogeneous s not in the prime, of degree at least -n, and write 0 = 0/s; the proof picks the degree carefully so that the numerator degree deg s + n is a genuine natural number.
Membership in that subgroup is, by definition, being locally a fraction of degree n. Holds by definition.

The local fractions of degree n on U form an additive subgroup of all functions into the localizations (contains 0, closed under addition and negation). This is the abelian group of sections of O(n) over U.

With the pointwise action, the sections of O(n) over U form a module over the ring of sections of the structure sheaf over U: the module axioms reduce to ring identities in A_x. This is what makes O(n) a sheaf of O-modules and not merely of abelian groups. Red-team check: the module structure seen on the sections of the final sheaf of modules is this one, by definition.

Sections of the structure sheaf act on sections of O(n) by pointwise multiplication in the localizations A_x. This is the standard action of O(U) on O(n)(U); the product stays of degree n because 0 + n = n. Red-team check: there is no other action of these rings on these functions to clash with.

O(n) as a presheaf of modules over the structure sheaf of Proj: each group of sections carries the module structure above, and restriction maps are compatible with restricting scalars because both are restriction of functions. Correct.
O(n) as a presheaf of abelian groups: sections over U are the local fractions of degree n, and restriction is restriction of functions, which is additive. Correct.

The presheaf of abelian groups O(n), after forgetting the group structure, is the sheaf of sets O(n); the identification is the identity on each open set. Correct (the two are in fact definitionally the same).

O(n) as a sheaf of sets: the subsheaf of all functions into the localizations given by the local-fraction predicate. A subsheaf cut out by a local predicate is automatically a sheaf, so this is correct; it mirrors Mathlib's construction of the structure sheaf of Proj.

Correctly stated: for an integer D > 0 that is not a perfect square and is congruent to 0 or 1 mod 4, it gives a bijection between the classes of primitive integral binary quadratic forms ax² + bxy + cy² (gcd(a, b, c) = 1) of discriminant b² − 4ac = D under integral changes of variables of determinant 1, and the narrow Picard group of the quadratic order Z[(D + √D)/2] of discriminant D, that is, its invertible fractional ideals modulo principal ideals with a totally positive generator. The map sends a form to the narrow class of the lattice aZ + ((−b + √D)/2)Z, multiplied by √D when a < 0; because √D has negative norm −D, this correction is exactly what makes the class invariant under proper equivalence (without it x² − 3y² and −x² + 3y² would get the same class although they are not properly equivalent). This is the classical form–ideal correspondence in its narrow, positive-discriminant form (Cohen, A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory, §5.2; Cox, Primes of the Form x² + ny², §7). Why it holds: a proper change of variables rescales the corrected ideal by an element of positive norm, and in a real quadratic field such an element is, up to sign, totally positive (well-definedness); every invertible ideal is a positive rational multiple of the ideal of a primitive form with a > 0 (surjectivity); homothetic ideals of two forms with a > 0 and a positive-norm scaling factor come from properly equivalent forms (injectivity). It is a bijection of sets; no group law on form classes is claimed. Red-team checks: only the standard axioms; the hypotheses are satisfiable (D = 5, 12) and each is needed (for D < 0 the statement fails, since negative definite forms double the count); specialised at D = 12, where it sends x² − 3y² to the trivial class and −x² + 3y² to a nontrivial one, so the narrow Picard group of Z[√3] is nontrivial; at D = 5 its injectivity recovers that x² + xy − y² and −x² − xy + y² are properly equivalent, as narrow class number 1 requires; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate found.

Correctly stated: the forward map of the bijection is the sign-corrected form-to-ideal class map; this holds by definition and is the equivalence's evaluation simp lemma. Red-team checks: proved by rfl; its left side is not otherwise simp-reducible.

Correctly stated: for an integer D > 0, not a square, congruent to 0 or 1 mod 4, two primitive forms of discriminant D with the same sign-corrected narrow ideal class are properly equivalent, i.e. related by an integral change of variables of determinant 1. Why: move both forms to proper representatives with positive leading coefficient (an indefinite form properly represents a positive number); there the classes are those of the plain ideals, equal narrow classes give a scaling element of positive norm between the two ideals, and comparing oriented bases of the two lattices gives a determinant-one change of variables. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable and all used; only the standard axioms; at D = 5 it correctly yields that x² + xy − y² and −x² − xy + y² are properly equivalent.

Correctly stated: for an integer D > 0, not a square, congruent to 0 or 1 mod 4, every narrow ideal class of the order of discriminant D is the image of the proper class of some primitive form of discriminant D under the sign-corrected form-to-ideal map. Why: every invertible fractional ideal is a positive rational multiple r of the ideal aZ + ((−b + √D)/2)Z of a primitive form with a > 0, and multiplying by r (norm r² > 0, so totally positive up to sign) does not change the narrow class, so that form's class hits the given class. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (D = 5, 12) and all used; only the standard axioms; no Mathlib duplicate.

Defines when an element x of a Lie algebra L over a field K is regular in Kostant's sense: the centralizer of x, the subspace of all y with [x, y] = 0 (the kernel of ad x), has the smallest dimension among the centralizers of all elements of L. This is the definition of Kostant (1963) and Collingwood–McGovern, Ch. 4: x is regular when dim 𝔤^x equals the minimum of dim 𝔤^y over every y in 𝔤, with the minimum over the whole algebra, not a subset. Dimension is measured as a cardinal, so in infinite dimension an infinite-dimensional centralizer is never treated as having dimension 0 (no junk value), and in finite dimension it agrees with the usual integer dimension (proved in the same file). It is genuinely different from Mathlib's existing notion of a regular element, which asks that the characteristic polynomial of ad x have a nonzero coefficient at the generic rank (over an infinite field: that the Engel subalgebra, the generalised 0-eigenspace of ad x, have minimal dimension). Red-team audit at 956e316250: in 𝔰𝔩₂(ℚ) we proved in Lean that h = diag(1, −1) is regular (its centralizer is ℚ·h), that 0 is not regular (𝔰𝔩₂ is non-abelian), and that the nilpotent e = E₁₂ is regular in this sense but not regular in Mathlib's sense (its Engel subalgebra is everything), which confirms that the two notions differ.

The same statement for integer dimension: two regular elements have centralizers of the same finite dimension. It follows by converting the previous lemma's cardinal equality to integers, and it needs no finiteness assumption. In infinite dimension both sides follow Lean's convention that an infinite dimension counts as 0, which is harmless because the cardinal dimensions are already equal. Red-team audit at 956e316250: checked to be a true consequence of the cardinal statement, not a claim that relies on the junk value.

In finite dimension, given one regular element x₀, an element x is regular exactly when rank(ad x₀) ≤ rank(ad x). It combines the one-inequality criterion with rank–nullity for ad x and ad x₀. This is the rank-lower-bound description that makes the regular set the non-vanishing locus of a minor. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the hypotheses are load-bearing; the inequality goes in the right direction.

Given one regular element x₀, an element x is regular exactly when its centralizer has dimension at most that of the centralizer of x₀. Forward: apply the minimality of x to x₀. Backward: the dimension for x is at most that for x₀, which is at most every centralizer's dimension. This is the standard reduction of regularity to one inequality against the minimal value. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the hypothesis that x₀ is regular is load-bearing.

Any two regular elements have centralizers of the same cardinal dimension: by minimality each dimension is at most the other, so they are equal. This common value is the minimal centralizer dimension, which for a reductive Lie algebra in characteristic zero is the rank. Red-team audit at 956e316250: both hypotheses are used (one for each inequality).

Every Lie algebra over a field has a regular element. Cardinals are well-ordered, so the dimensions of the centralizers reach a minimum, and any element reaching it is regular. As it should be for Kostant's notion, no hypothesis on the field or the dimension is needed. By contrast, Mathlib's existence result for its own regular elements needs an infinite field. Red-team audit at 956e316250: no hypotheses to contradict; the statement is the existence of a minimiser over all of L.

The unfolding lemma: x is regular exactly when, for every y, the centralizer of x has dimension at most that of the centralizer of y. It restates the definition word for word and is proved by reflexivity. Downstream files need it because the definition is not unfolded across modules. Red-team audit at 956e316250: compared with the definition symbol by symbol.

For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra, x is regular exactly when the integer dimension of its centralizer is at most that of every other centralizer. This holds because in finite dimension the cardinal dimension of a subspace is its integer dimension, and passing from integers to cardinals preserves and reflects ≤. The finite-dimensionality hypothesis is needed: Lean gives every infinite-dimensional subspace integer dimension 0, so without it the right-hand side would hold for any element with an infinite-dimensional centralizer. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the hypothesis is load-bearing; this lemma is the form used by the algebraic-group consumer of the definition.

In finite dimension, x is regular exactly when the linear map ad x has the largest rank among all ad y. By rank–nullity, dim ker(ad y) + rank(ad y) = dim L for every y, so minimising the centralizer dimension is the same as maximising the rank of ad. This is the form used to show that the regular set is Zariski-open (Collingwood–McGovern, Ch. 4). Red-team audit at 956e316250: the direction of the inequality was checked (regular means maximal rank of ad x), and finite dimension is needed for rank–nullity in integers.

In an abelian Lie algebra every element is regular: every ad y is zero, so every centralizer is the whole algebra and all have the same dimension. No finiteness assumption is needed. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the only hypothesis is that the algebra is abelian, and it is used.

Multiplying x by a nonzero scalar c does not change whether it is regular: ad(c·x) = c·ad x has the same kernel as ad x because c is invertible. The hypothesis c ≠ 0 is necessary, since c = 0 sends every x to 0, which is regular only in an abelian algebra. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the hypothesis c ≠ 0 is load-bearing; as a simp lemma it fires and discharges c ≠ 0 at a numeral (checked over ℚ).

In a finite-dimensional Lie algebra, 0 is regular exactly when the algebra is abelian. The centralizer of 0 is the whole algebra, so 0 is regular iff every centralizer has full dimension, iff every centralizer is the whole algebra, iff all brackets vanish. Finite dimension is needed: in 𝔰𝔩₂ × A, with A an infinite-dimensional abelian algebra, every centralizer contains A and has the same infinite dimension, so 0 is regular although the algebra is not abelian. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised in Lean to 𝔰𝔩₂(ℚ), which shows that 0 is not regular there.

A Lie algebra isomorphism preserves the finite dimension of centralizers: dim ker(ad e(x)) = dim ker(ad x). This holds because e carries one centralizer linearly and isomorphically onto the other. Red-team audit at 956e316250: correct as stated; works as a simp lemma; also holds over a commutative ring (recorded separately).

Regularity is invariant under Lie algebra isomorphisms: e(x) is regular in L' exactly when x is regular in L. This holds because e matches the centralizers of L and L' while preserving dimension, and e is surjective, so minimising over L' is the same as minimising over L. In particular the regular set is stable under every automorphism, including the adjoint group action, which is the standard fact that the regular set is a union of adjoint orbits (Collingwood–McGovern, Ch. 4). Red-team audit at 956e316250: both directions checked, including the universe lifting between L and L'.

A Lie algebra isomorphism e from L to L' carries the centralizer of x onto the centralizer of e(x), because y commutes with x exactly when e(y) commutes with e(x). The proof writes ad(e x) as the conjugate e ∘ ad x ∘ e⁻¹ (Mathlib's conj_ad_apply) and takes kernels. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the statement is correct as given; it also holds over any commutative ring, not just a field (recorded separately as a minor generality point).

The same invariance for cardinal dimension: an isomorphism e from L to L' carries the centralizer of x onto that of e(x), so the two have equal cardinal dimension. Both sides are lifted to a common universe, since L and L' may live in different universes. Red-team audit at 956e316250: correct as stated; also holds over a commutative ring (recorded separately).

The non-regular elements form a Zariski-closed set. Fix a finite basis of L, which identifies L with Kⁿ. If S consists of non-regular elements, then every x whose coordinates lie in the Zariski closure of S (the common zeros of all polynomials vanishing on S) is also non-regular. Taking S to be the whole non-regular set, that set equals its own Zariski closure, so the regular elements form a Zariski-open set, as in Kostant (1963) and Collingwood–McGovern, Ch. 4. Proof idea: take a regular x₀ and set p = rank(ad x₀). Then y is non-regular exactly when rank(ad y) ≤ p − 1, that is, when all p×p minors of the matrix of ad y vanish. These minors are polynomials in the coordinates of y, because the entries of ad y are linear in y, so the condition passes to the Zariski closure. No assumption on the field (algebraic closure or characteristic) is used, which is correct. Red-team audit at 956e316250: both hypotheses are load-bearing; specialised in Lean to 𝔰𝔩₂(ℚ) with S the full non-regular set.

Over an infinite field the regular elements are Zariski-dense: in the coordinates of a finite basis, the only polynomial vanishing at every regular element is zero. In particular there are regular elements. Proof idea: a regular x₀ has a nonzero p×p minor of ad x₀, which gives a nonzero polynomial q. Every point where q is nonzero is regular, so any f vanishing on the regular set makes f·q vanish on all of Kⁿ. Since K is infinite, f·q is then the zero polynomial, so f = 0. The infinite-field hypothesis is necessary: over a finite field 𝔽_q the nonzero polynomial X^q − X vanishes everywhere. No algebraic closure or characteristic assumption is used, matching the classical statement (Collingwood–McGovern, Ch. 4). Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised in Lean to 𝔰𝔩₂(ℚ) with a finite basis; ⊥ is a genuine conclusion (the vanishing ideal of the empty set is ⊤, not ⊥).

Correctly stated: for a vector bundle E on X and any scheme T with any morphism q : T → X (T need not be affine, q need not be flat), morphisms T → Spec_X(Sym E^∨) over X are in bijection with global sections of the pulled-back sheaf q^*E (module maps O_T → q^*E). This is the functor-of-points description of the total space: EGA II (1.7.9) gives Hom_X(T, Spec Sym F) = Hom(q^*F, O_T); applied to F = E^∨, and using q^*(E^∨) ≅ (q^*E)^∨ and the double-dual identification, both valid because E is locally free of finite rank, it gives Γ(T, q^*E) (Hartshorne II Ex. 5.18(c) is the case of sections over open subsets, stated there for V(E) = Spec S(E) with sections E^∨). The Lean bijection is built exactly this way; its inverse sends a section s to the point whose linear functional is evaluation at s, and it is natural in the bundle (totalSpaceHomEquiv_comp_map); naturality in T is not stated. The finite-local-freeness is needed: for E = Z/2 on Spec Z the dual is 0, so Spec Sym E^∨ = X has a single point over Spec F_2 while Γ(Spec F_2, q^*E) = F_2.
