At `P = (2, 3)`: `ω₂ = 64 + 160 − 8 = 216` and `ψ₂³ = (2y)³ = 216`, so `y(2P) = 1`; the tangent line has slope `λ = 3·4/6 = 2`, giving `x(2P) = 4 − 4 = 0` and `y(2P) = 2(2 − 0) − 3 = 1`. The two agree.

Not checked: the proofs of `ω_spec` and the ZSMul bridge; not re-elaborated locally, the site's dataset marks no `sorry` and CI builds every file.

Defines, for any Lie algebra L over a commutative ring R, the R-linear map from the invariant symmetric bilinear forms on L to the continuous second cohomology of the formal loop algebra R((t)) ⊗ L with trivial coefficients R, sending Φ to the class of the residue cocycle (x⊗f, y⊗g) ↦ Φ(x,y)·Res(f dg). This is the standard cocycle of the affine Kac–Moody central extension (Kac, Infinite-Dimensional Lie Algebras, Ch. 7; Frenkel, Langlands Correspondence for Loop Groups, Lemma 1.3.2, up to the sign convention Res(f dg) versus −Res(f dg)): it is alternating because Φ is symmetric and Res(f dg) = −Res(g df), a cocycle because Φ is invariant, continuous because it vanishes on pairs of power-series currents, and linear in Φ because the residue pairing is. Red-team checks: the cohomology is Mathlib's Chevalley–Eilenberg complex restricted to cochains continuous for the t-adic topology (topology instance checked by rfl, and not discrete); no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Says: for a finite-dimensional Lie algebra g over an algebraically closed field K of characteristic zero whose adjoint representation is irreducible and whose Killing form is nondegenerate (in characteristic zero these are exactly the simple Lie algebras, and for a Lie algebra declared simple in Mathlib both conditions are supplied automatically, which we checked compiles), the map sending an invariant symmetric bilinear form Φ on g to the class of the 2-cocycle (x⊗f, y⊗g) ↦ Φ(x,y)·Res_{t=0}(f dg) is a K-linear isomorphism from the space of invariant symmetric forms onto the continuous second cohomology H²_cont(g((t)), K) with trivial coefficients. This is Frenkel, Langlands Correspondence for Loop Groups, Lemma 1.3.2, which uses the cocycle −κ(x,y)Res(f dg); the two conventions differ by Φ ↦ −Φ, an automorphism of the space of forms. Why it holds: the map is injective because a coboundary (u,v) ↦ −f([u,v]) takes the same value on (t⁻¹⊗x, t⊗y) and (1⊗x, 1⊗y), which have the same bracket, while the residue cocycle of Φ takes the values Φ(x,y) and 0 there; it is surjective because a continuous cocycle restricted to the dense polynomial loop algebra is a multiple of the Killing residue cocycle plus a coboundary, and joint continuity together with perfectness of g makes the primitive vanish on high modes, so it extends continuously. The cohomology is the genuine Chevalley–Eilenberg one (alternating 2-cochains killed by the differential, modulo differentials of 1-cochains), restricted to cochains that vanish on t^N g[[t]] (and, for 2-cochains, on t^N g[[t]] × t^N g[[t]]) for some N, i.e. continuity for the t-adic topology with K discrete; the forward map is by definition the residue class map, so this is a specific isomorphism, not just an abstract one between one-dimensional spaces. Red-team checks at 956e3162: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (simp_all, aesop, grind); not vacuous, since the Killing form maps to a nonzero class and the equivalence reproduces the independent result that the cohomology is one-dimensional; the topology used is the t-adic order topology (checked by rfl) and is not discrete, so continuity is a real restriction; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate. Note: algebraic closure and irreducibility are more than the statement needs (the same proof gives the isomorphism whenever the invariant forms are one-dimensional, e.g. for sl₂ over the rationals, and it should hold for every semisimple g over a characteristic-zero field); recorded as a generality note, not a correctness issue.

States that the classification isomorphism sends a form Φ to the class of its residue cocycle, i.e. the isomorphism is the residue class map itself rather than some other isomorphism between one-dimensional spaces; true by definition. Red-team checks: compiles as a definitional equality.

States that the inverse of the classification isomorphism sends the residue class of an invariant symmetric form Φ back to Φ, which is immediate because the forward map is the residue class map. Red-team checks: compiles, and works as a simp rule together with the forward evaluation lemma (inverse after forward simplifies to the identity).

States that the residue class map applied to a form Φ is, by definition, the class of the residue cocycle of Φ; it holds by unfolding the definition. Red-team checks: compiles as a definitional equality and serves as the simp form.

Over a commutative domain of characteristic zero, and for every Lie algebra L, two invariant symmetric forms with the same residue class are equal. This is the uniqueness half of Frenkel's Lemma 1.3.2: a coboundary with trivial coefficients has the form (u,v) ↦ −f([u,v]), so it takes the same value on (t⁻¹⊗x, t⊗y) and (1⊗x, 1⊗y), which have the same bracket, whereas the residue cocycle of Φ − Ψ takes the values (Φ − Ψ)(x,y) and 0 there. Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent; we proved the same conclusion over an arbitrary commutative ring, so the stated version is correct, only more restrictive than necessary (recorded as a generality note).

For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L with nondegenerate Killing form over a field of characteristic zero, if every invariant bilinear form is a scalar multiple of one invariant symmetric form Ψ that is nonzero on some bracket, then every class in the continuous second cohomology of L((t)) with trivial coefficients is the residue class of an invariant symmetric form (a multiple of Ψ). This is the existence half of Frenkel's Lemma 1.3.2: restricted to the dense polynomial loop algebra, a continuous cocycle is a multiple of the residue cocycle of Ψ plus a coboundary; continuity and perfectness of L make the primitive vanish on high modes, so it extends to a continuous 1-cochain, and continuous cochains agreeing on a dense set agree. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (they hold for every simple Lie algebra with Ψ the Killing form); the conditions that Ψ be invariant, symmetric and nonzero on a bracket already follow from the spanning hypothesis and nondegeneracy of the Killing form (recorded as a generality note), which does not affect correctness.
The cumulant generating function is the logarithm of the finite-sum moment generating function above, which is its definition applied to the previous result.
The characteristic function is E e^{itX}, the sum of P(X = k)·e^{ikt} over k = 0, ..., N-K, the finite-sum form for a law on {0, ..., N-K}.

For every real t the variable e^{tX} is integrable, so the moment generating function is finite on the whole line, as for any finitely supported law; outside the valid range it holds trivially for the zero measure, as the docstring notes.

Every function on the real line is integrable against the law viewed as a distribution on the reals (pushed forward along the inclusion of the natural numbers). This reduces to the previous statement because the inclusion is a measurable embedding.

Every function on the natural numbers (with values in a normed group) is integrable against this law, for all parameters, because the law is a finite combination of point masses with finite weights, or the zero measure. Red-team checks: finiteness of the weights comes from K ≤ N in the valid branch.

Rising factorial moments of the number of draws D = X + r: E[D(D+1)...(D+m-1)] = r(r+1)...(r+m-1)·C(N+m, K+m)/C(N, K), equivalently r(r+1)...(r+m-1)·(N+1)...(N+m)/((K+1)...(K+m)). It follows by dividing by C(N, K) the weighted convolution identity: the sum over k of (k+r)(k+r+1)...(k+r+m-1)·C(k+r-1, k)·C(N-r-k, K-r) equals r(r+1)...(r+m-1)·C(N+m, K+m), which is the unweighted identity for parameters (N+m, K+m, r+m) after absorbing the rising factorial into the first binomial coefficient. Red-team checks: m=1 gives E[X+r] = r(N+1)/(K+1), consistent with the mean; m=2 at N=3, K=2, r=1 gives 10/3, matching direct computation; m=0 is the normalisation.

The mean is E X = r(N-K)/(K+1), the standard formula for the number of failures before the r-th success without replacement: it is the mean n(v+1)/(v+w+2) of Johnson, Kotz and Kemp, Univariate Discrete Distributions, 2nd ed., §6.2.2, eq. (6.11), with n = N-K, v = r-1, w = K-r, and the formula in the Tau Ceti roadmap StandardDistributions §9.3. Proof idea: the first rising factorial moment gives E[X+r] = r(N+1)/(K+1), then subtract r. Red-team checks: 1/3 at N=3, K=2, r=1 and 2 at N=5, K=2, r=2, matching direct computation from the masses; agrees with the Tau Ceti beta-binomial mean with n = N-K and shapes r, K-r+1.

The same finite-sum formula for the law viewed on the real line: E f(X) is the sum of P(X = k)·f(k) over k = 0, ..., N-K. Red-team checks: r ≤ K is needed as for the previous statement; K ≤ N is removable (both sides vanish for K > N).

In the valid range the expectation of any vector-valued f(X) is the finite sum of P(X = k)·f(k) over k = 0, ..., N-K. Red-team checks: r ≤ K is needed (for r > K the measure is zero but the weights are not); K ≤ N turns out to be removable, since for K > N both sides vanish (recorded as a minor generality note).

In the valid range r ≤ K ≤ N the law has total mass 1, so it is a genuine probability distribution; this is the normalisation of the weights. Red-team checks: hypotheses needed, since outside the range the measure is zero.

The law depends measurably on the three parameters (N, K, r). This is automatic because the parameter space of triples of natural numbers is discrete, so every map out of it is measurable. Red-team checks: holds for the discrete structure as stated.

In the valid range the moment generating function is E e^{tX}, the sum of P(X = k)·e^{tk} over k = 0, ..., N-K, the moment generating function of a law supported on {0, ..., N-K} (Johnson-Kotz-Kemp write the corresponding generating function as a ratio of terminating hypergeometric series, eq. (6.9); the finite sum is the same polynomial in e^t). Red-team checks: r ≤ K is needed (for r > K the left side is 0 but the sum is not); K ≤ N is removable since both sides vanish for K > N.

Defines the negative hypergeometric law on the natural numbers: for r ≤ K ≤ N it puts mass C(k+r-1, k)·C(N-r-k, K-r)/C(N, K) on each k = 0, ..., N-K, the law of the number of failures drawn before the r-th success when sampling uniformly at random without replacement from N objects of which K are successes. This is Johnson, Kotz and Kemp, Univariate Discrete Distributions, 2nd ed., §6.2.2, eq. (6.16), p. 241, shifted from total draws to failures, and exactly the specification of the Tau Ceti roadmap StandardDistributions §9.3. Degenerate cases follow the roadmap's conventions: r = 0 gives the point mass at 0 (no draw is needed), K = N gives the point mass at 0 (there are no failures), and outside r ≤ K ≤ N (for example r > K, where the r-th success never comes) it is the zero measure, as the docstring says. The law is defined through its mass function; the sampling description is the standard motivation, and the uniform-permutation construction is a separate roadmap item, not a claim of this definition. As the same section of Johnson-Kotz-Kemp notes (p. 240), for r ≥ 1 this is also the beta-binomial law, here with n = N-K and shapes r and K-r+1 (a bridge this file does not state; recorded as a minor reuse note). Red-team checks: N=3, K=2, r=1 gives masses 2/3 and 1/3, mean 1/3, variance 2/9; N=5, K=2, r=2 gives masses (k+1)/10, mean 2, variance 1; K=N and N=0 give the point mass at 0; mean, variance and the mass at N=3, K=2, r=1 agree with the Tau Ceti beta-binomial law under that substitution.

In the valid range the measure is the finite sum over k = 0, ..., N-K of the weight at k times the point mass at k, its defining formula. Red-team checks: both hypotheses needed, since outside the range the measure is zero while the sum is not.

Outside the range r ≤ K ≤ N the measure is zero, the documented convention for parameters with no valid law (for example r > K, when the r-th success never occurs). Red-team checks: specialised at N=3, K=1, r=2.

In the valid range P(X = k) = C(k+r-1, k)·C(N-r-k, K-r)/C(N, K) for k ≤ N-K and 0 otherwise, as a real number: the negative hypergeometric mass function counting failures (Johnson, Kotz and Kemp, Univariate Discrete Distributions, 2nd ed., §6.2.2, eq. (6.16) shifted by r; roadmap StandardDistributions §9.3). Red-team checks: P(X=0)=2/3, P(X=1)=1/3, P(X=2)=0 for N=3, K=2, r=1, and P(X=3)=4/10 for N=5, K=2, r=2, matching direct counting.

In the valid range the probability of the single value k is the weight at k (0 for k > N-K). Red-team checks: value test at N=3, K=2, r=1; both hypotheses needed, since for N=3, K=1, r=2 the measure is zero but the weight at 0 is 1/3, and for N=0, K=1, r=1 the measure is zero but the weight at 0 is infinite.

In the valid range the law charges k exactly when k ≤ N-K and (k = 0 or r ≥ 1): its support is all of {0, ..., N-K} when r ≥ 1, and just {0} when r = 0, as expected for failures before the r-th success. Red-team checks: r ≤ K is needed, since beyond it the measure is zero.

Waiting for zero successes requires no draw, so the number of failures is 0 almost surely: the law is the point mass at 0 (for any K ≤ N). In the formula, the factor C(k-1, k) is 0 for k ≥ 1 and the k = 0 term is C(N, K)/C(N, K) = 1. Red-team checks: specialised at N = 0.

Defines the chance of seeing k failures before the r-th success when drawing without replacement from N objects of which K are successes: C(k+r-1, k)·C(N-r-k, K-r)/C(N, K) for k ≤ N-K and 0 beyond, as an extended non-negative number. This is the standard mass function in the failure-counting convention: it is Johnson, Kotz and Kemp, Univariate Discrete Distributions, 2nd ed., §6.2.2, eq. (6.15)-(6.16), p. 241 (stated there for the total number of draws x = k+r, with the remark that the name is also used for the number of unsuccessful draws), and the Tau Ceti roadmap StandardDistributions §9.3. Combinatorially, of the C(N, K) equally likely placements of the successes it counts those with r-1 successes among the first k+r-1 draws, a success at draw k+r, and the remaining K-r successes among the last N-k-r positions. The explicit cut-off at N-K is genuinely needed because natural-number subtraction truncates (N=2, K=1, r=1, k=2 would otherwise give 1/2). Outside r ≤ K ≤ N the values are placeholders (positive for r > K, possibly infinite for K > N); the measure, which is zero there, is what should be used. Red-team checks: values 2/3, 1/3, 0 at N=3, K=2, r=1 and 4/10 at k=3 for N=5, K=2, r=2.

When K ≤ N every weight is finite, because the denominator C(N, K) is non-zero. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is needed, since for N=0, K=1, r=1 the weight at 0 is 1/0, which is infinite for extended non-negative numbers.

When K ≤ N, the weight at k is non-zero exactly when k ≤ N-K and either k = 0 or r ≥ 1. With r ≥ 1 both binomial coefficients are positive for every k from 0 to N-K, and with r = 0 the first factor C(k-1, k) vanishes except at k = 0. (For r > K the weight is a placeholder and the statement describes that placeholder rather than a law.) Red-team checks: K ≤ N is needed, since for N=0, K=1, r=0 the weight at 0 is 0 while the right side holds.

For k ≤ N-K the weight is exactly the binomial ratio C(k+r-1, k)·C(N-r-k, K-r)/C(N, K), the defining branch of the mass function. Red-team checks: unfolds the definition; fires as a simplification rule.

For k > N-K (more failures than there are failure objects) the weight is 0, the other branch of the definition. Red-team checks: unfolds the definition; this branch is needed because the bare ratio need not vanish there.

The real value of the weight is the same binomial ratio computed in the real numbers (0 beyond N-K). It holds for all parameters: when C(N, K)=0 both sides are 0, since an infinite extended value has real value 0 and real division by 0 gives 0. Red-team checks: checked at N=3, K=2, r=1.

In the valid range the weights over k = 0, ..., N-K add up to 1. Combinatorially: each of the C(N, K) placements of the K successes among N positions has its r-th success at exactly one position k+r with 0 ≤ k ≤ N-K, and the number of placements with the r-th success there is C(k+r-1, k)·C(N-r-k, K-r); summing gives C(N, K). The file uses this binomial convolution identity from its Tau Ceti combinatorics library. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed; for N=1, K=0, r=1 (so r > K) the sum is 2.

The variance is Var X = r(N+1)(N-K)(K-r+1)/((K+1)^2(K+2)), the standard formula: it is the variance n(v+1)(w+1)(v+w+n+2)/((v+w+2)^2(v+w+3)) of Johnson, Kotz and Kemp, Univariate Discrete Distributions, 2nd ed., §6.2.2, eq. (6.11), with n = N-K, v = r-1, w = K-r, and the formula in the Tau Ceti roadmap StandardDistributions §9.3. Proof idea: combine the first two rising factorial moments and subtract the squared mean. Red-team checks: 2/9 at N=3, K=2, r=1 and 1 at N=5, K=2, r=2, matching direct computation from the masses; agrees with the Tau Ceti beta-binomial variance with n = N-K and shapes r, K-r+1; both hypotheses needed.

A Dehn filling of a knot exterior E along a slope s, recorded inside a given space Y. It consists of closed embeddings of E and of a solid torus V = D²×S¹ into Y, such that the two images cover Y, they meet only in the image of the boundary torus of V, and they agree there through a homeomorphism g of S¹×S¹ (the point q of ∂V is identified with the point g(q) of ∂E) that sends the meridian of V to a curve of slope s. The standard definition (Rolfsen, Knots and Links, Ch. 9) is E ∪_h V, where h: ∂V → ∂E is a homeomorphism taking the meridian of V to a curve of slope s. Because the two pieces are closed and cover Y, Y is exactly this glued space: the file proves the universal property, namely that continuous maps out of Y are the compatible pairs of continuous maps on E and on V. The structure has real constraints: the two embeddings determine the gluing, so they also determine the slope. For example, a filling of the ambient space that uses the inclusion of E and the given neighbourhood must have the meridian slope and cannot have the longitude slope (both compiled). Convention: the classical theorem that Y up to homeomorphism depends only on s is explicitly not formalized. Red-team checks: examples exist (the trivial filling of any knot here, and S¹×S² as 0-surgery on the unknot in a downstream file); no field is left unconstrained.

Continuous maps a on the exterior and b on the filling solid torus that agree along the gluing (a(g(q)) = b(q) for q on the boundary torus) combine into a continuous map on Y. This holds because Y is the union of the two closed images, each homeomorphic to its piece, and a function continuous on each of two closed sets is continuous on their union. Red-team checks: no Mathlib construction replaces it directly (Mathlib's gluing over a cover needs a cover by neighbourhoods, not by closed sets).
The combined map restricts to a on the exterior; this holds by construction.
The combined map restricts to b on the filling solid torus. On the boundary torus this uses the compatibility hypothesis, which is therefore needed.

The combined map is the only continuous map on Y that restricts to a and to b. Together with the existence of the combined map, this is the universal property of the glued space, so Y is the gluing of E and V along the boundary homeomorphism. Red-team checks: every hypothesis is needed (minimal-hypotheses test).

A Dehn filling is determined by its two embeddings. The gluing homeomorphism is forced: on the boundary torus it is read off from where the two embeddings agree, and both embeddings are injective. So the structure carries no data beyond the decomposition. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are used.

A point x of the exterior and a point p of the solid torus have the same image in Y exactly when p = q lies on the boundary torus and x is the point g(q) of ∂E glued to it. So the only identifications are those made by the gluing, which is precisely the equivalence relation defining the glued space E ∪_g V. It follows from the injectivity of the embeddings and the intersection condition. Red-team checks: both directions are proved.
Two continuous maps on Y that agree on the image of the exterior and on the image of the solid torus are equal, because the two images cover Y. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed.

In Y, the image of the exterior and the image of the filling solid torus intersect exactly in the image of the boundary torus of the solid torus. The structure assumes only one inclusion; the other follows because every boundary point of V is glued to a point of E. Red-team checks: both inclusions are proved, matching the standard picture E ∩ V = ∂E = ∂V.

A Dehn filling structure on Y carries over to any space Y′ homeomorphic to Y: compose both embeddings with the homeomorphism and keep the same gluing. Homeomorphisms preserve closed embeddings, covering and the intersection condition, so the result is again a filling, and its slope is unchanged, as it should be.
The transported filling embeds the exterior by the original embedding followed by the homeomorphism; this holds by definition.
Transporting a filling along a homeomorphism keeps the same boundary gluing; this holds by definition.
The transported filling embeds the solid torus by the original embedding followed by the homeomorphism; this holds by definition.

Defines the slope of a Dehn filling. A self-homeomorphism g of the torus S¹×S¹ describes how the boundary torus of the filling solid torus V = D²×S¹ is glued to the boundary torus of the knot exterior, both tori being parametrised by S¹×S¹ through the solid torus neighbourhood. The definition takes the loop t ↦ g(e^{2πit}, 1), the image of the meridian ∂D²×{1} of V, places it on the boundary torus of the exterior, and returns its first homology class up to sign. This is the slope in Rolfsen's sense (Knots and Links, Ch. 9): the isotopy class of the curve that receives the meridian of the attached solid torus, which is the same as a primitive class in H₁(T²; ℤ) up to sign. The class is primitive because the (1,0) curve is primitive and a homeomorphism preserves primitivity. Red-team checks: the meridian is the disc-boundary coordinate circle, as in the framing's own meridian convention; gluing by the identity gives the meridian (slope 1/0 = ∞) and swapping the two factors gives the longitude (slope 0/1 = 0); Lean confirms that these two slopes differ, so the definition does not collapse.

Suppose the gluing carries the meridian loop t ↦ (e^{2πit}, 1) of the filling solid torus, point by point, onto the (p,q) curve t ↦ (e^{2πipt}, e^{2πiqt}), with p and q coprime. Then the filling slope is the slope of the (p,q) curve on the boundary torus of the exterior, that is, the class pμ + qλ up to sign, which has value p/q in the neighbourhood's framing. This holds because the slope depends only on the homology class of the image of the meridian, and equal loops have equal classes. Coprimality is what makes the class primitive, so it is needed even to state the conclusion. Red-team checks: every hypothesis is load-bearing (minimal-hypotheses test); combined with the framing computation it gives slope value exactly p/q (compiled).

Gluing by the homeomorphism that swaps the two circle factors sends the meridian ∂D²×{1} to the circle {1}×S¹, the longitude of the neighbourhood framing. So the slope is the longitude, of value 0/1 = 0. This is the gluing that gives 0-surgery on the unknot. Red-team checks: the slope value in the framing is 0, and it differs from the meridian slope (compiled).

Gluing the solid torus back by the identity of S¹×S¹ has the neighbourhood's meridian as its slope: the curve ∂D²×{1} goes to itself, giving slope 1/0 = ∞. It is the (p,q) = (1,0) case of the (p,q)-curve lemma. Red-team checks: the slope value in the framing is ∞, and it differs from the longitude slope (compiled).

The trivial Dehn filling: the ambient space X is itself a filling of the knot exterior along the meridian slope, with the exterior included as a subspace, the solid torus neighbourhood as the filling solid torus, and the identity as the gluing. This is the standard fact that ∞-surgery, filling along the meridian, gives back the ambient space (Rolfsen, Ch. 9): it amounts to gluing the removed tubular neighbourhood back in by the identity. Convention: this exhibits X as a meridian filling, i.e. it proves that the decomposition exists. The general statement that every meridian filling is homeomorphic to X is the classical well-definedness of Dehn filling, which the file explicitly leaves unformalized. Red-team checks: the exterior and the neighbourhood cover X and meet exactly on the boundary torus (the points with |z| = 1); the slope is computed to be the meridian (∞); any filling of X with these same two embeddings must have the meridian slope (compiled).
The trivial filling embeds the exterior by its inclusion into X; this holds by definition.
The trivial filling glues the boundary tori by the identity; this holds by definition.
The filling solid torus of the trivial filling is the solid torus neighbourhood itself; this holds by definition.

Correctly stated. In words: for every braid word w on n+1 ≥ 1 strands and every unit a of any commutative ring, the braid-route quantity (the Markov trace of the image of the braid under the Temperley–Lieb (Kauffman) representation σᵢ ↦ a·1 + a⁻¹·eᵢ, multiplied by the writhe correction (−a³)^(−e), e the exponent sum) equals δ = −(a²+a⁻²) times the writhe-normalised Kauffman bracket (−a³)^(−writhe)·⟨D⟩ of the closed-braid diagram D of w, with ⟨unknot⟩ = 1. This is the classical agreement of Jones's Markov-trace construction with Kauffman's state-sum construction of the Jones polynomial; the factor δ is just the difference of normalisations, because this Markov trace counts every closed loop (the identity braid on m strands has trace δ^m, so the unknot gets δ) while the bracket gives the unknot 1. These conventions agree with Wikipedia's 'Jones polynomial' article (X(L) = (−A³)^(−w)⟨L⟩ with A = t^(−1/4); the bracket of a closed m-strand braid is δ^(m−1) times the trace normalised to 1 on the identity). Proof idea: uniqueness of skein invariants on closed braids — both sides are unchanged by Markov moves, both satisfy t⁻¹V₊ − tV₋ = (t^(1/2) − t^(−1/2))V₀ with t = a⁻⁴, both are multiplied by δ when an unlinked strand is added, and both equal δ on the one-strand unknot; nothing is divided by δ, so it holds over every commutative ring. Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5 at 956e3162): no hypotheses beyond the unit a and the word, and every strand count n+1 ≥ 1 is covered; computed the normalised bracket of the actual closure directly from its state sum, independently of this theorem (loop counts kernel-checked in Lean): σ₁ in B₂ gives 1 (an unknot with one kink), σ₁² gives −a⁻² − a⁻¹⁰ (positive Hopf link, −t^(1/2) − t^(5/2)), σ₁³ gives a⁻⁴ + a⁻¹² − a⁻¹⁶ (t + t³ − t⁴, the value the skein relation forces for the positive trefoil), and (σ₁σ₂⁻¹)² in B₃ gives a⁸ − a⁴ + 1 − a⁻⁴ + a⁻⁸, the symmetric value of the figure-eight knot; with the braid-side trefoil value δ(a⁻⁴ + a⁻¹² − a⁻¹⁶) computed in the Temperley–Lieb algebra the two sides agree as stated; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated. In words: for every braid word w on n+1 ≥ 1 strands and every unit a of any commutative ring, the writhe-normalised Markov trace of the Temperley–Lieb (Kauffman) representation of the braid equals δ = −(a²+a⁻²) times the Jones polynomial V of the closed braid evaluated at t^(1/2) = a⁻², where V is the integer Laurent polynomial in t^(1/2) obtained from the writhe-normalised bracket by the substitution A = t^(−1/4) (the convention of Wikipedia's 'Jones polynomial' article). It is the previous theorem rewritten through the library's identity that evaluating V at t^(1/2) = a⁻² gives back the normalised bracket at a, valid over every commutative ring, so no division by δ occurs. Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5 at 956e3162): same full-statement and value tests as the bracket form (unknot, Hopf link −t^(1/2) − t^(5/2), right-handed trefoil t + t³ − t⁴, figure-eight on three strands); the variable convention t^(1/2) = a⁻² matches the skein relation t⁻¹V₊ − tV₋ = (t^(1/2) − t^(−1/2))V₀ satisfied by the trace; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. (Its docstring omits the word 'writhe-normalised'; recorded as a documentation finding, the statement itself is right.)

Correctly stated: for every countable index set (finite or countably infinite), the free group on that set admits an injective homomorphism into SL(2, ℤ), i.e. every free group of countable rank is isomorphic to a subgroup of SL(2, ℤ); this is the full countable-rank statement, not only rank two. Why it holds: choose an injection k of the index set into the natural numbers and send the i-th generator to B^k(i) A B^−k(i) with A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [2, 1]]; these conjugates are free by the preceding theorem. Countability cannot be dropped: SL(2, ℤ) is countable, so no free group on an uncountable set embeds in it (proved in Lean for the free group on the subsets of ℕ, via Cantor's theorem). Red-team checks: specialised to the free group on ℕ; the countability assumption is necessary as just shown; only the standard axioms are used; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate found.

Correctly stated: with A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] and B = [[1, 0], [2, 1]] in SL(2, ℤ), for any family of pairwise distinct integers k(i) the conjugates B^k(i) A B^−k(i) freely generate a free subgroup: the homomorphism from the free group on the index set sending the i-th generator to the i-th conjugate is injective. Why it holds: A and B play ping-pong on the cones |x| < |y| and |y| < |x| of ℤ², so B^m A B^−m sends every other translate B^m′(|y| < |x|) into B^m(|y| < |x|), and these translates are pairwise disjoint for distinct m because B^(m′−m) moves the cone |y| < |x| into the opposite cone; the cyclic form of the ping-pong lemma then gives freeness. Distinctness is necessary: equal exponents give equal images, which Lean confirms with a constant family on two indices. Red-team checks: the distinctness hypothesis is the only one and is load-bearing; specialised to the index set {0, …, n−1} with k(i) = i; only the standard axioms are used; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate found.

Correctly stated: in the free group F(a, b) on two generators, for pairwise distinct integers k(i) the elements b^k(i) a b^−k(i) freely generate a free subgroup (the homomorphism from the free group on the index set sending the i-th generator to the i-th such element is injective); in particular the free group of rank n embeds in F(a, b) by sending the i-th generator to bⁱ a b⁻ⁱ, which was checked in Lean as a direct specialisation. Why it holds: following this map by Sanov's embedding a ↦ [[1, 2], [0, 1]], b ↦ [[1, 0], [2, 1]] gives exactly the conjugate-family map into SL(2, ℤ), which is injective by the theorem above, and if a composite is injective so is its first factor. Red-team checks: the distinctness hypothesis is load-bearing (equal exponents identify two generators); only the standard axioms are used; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate found.

Correctly stated: the homomorphism from the free group on two letters a, b to SL(2, ℤ) sending a to A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] and b to B = [[1, 0], [2, 1]] is injective, that is, A and B satisfy no nontrivial relation and freely generate a free subgroup of rank two (Sanov's theorem); the two matrices are exactly these, with off-diagonal entry 2, as checked entry by entry in Lean. The same statement, proved the same way, is the special-linear-group example on Wikipedia's page on the ping-pong lemma. Why it holds: a nonzero power Aⁿ sends an integer vector (x, y) to (x + 2ny, y), so it moves every vector with |x| < |y| into the region |y| < |x|, and every nonzero power of B does the reverse; the two regions are disjoint and nonempty, so by the ping-pong lemma no nonempty reduced word in A and B acts as the identity. Red-team checks: the statement has no hypotheses that could be contradictory; value tests AB ≠ BA and ABA⁻¹B⁻¹ = [[21, −8], [8, −3]] ≠ I computed in Lean, and the word aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is pushed through the theorem; the same map with parameter 1 in place of 2 is shown not injective in Lean ((ab⁻¹a)⁴ goes to the identity), so the 2 is essential and the statement is not vacuous; only the standard axioms are used; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate found.

Correctly stated: a simply connected open subset U of the plane has no holes, that is, every connected component of its complement is unbounded (equivalently U contains its filled hull). Why: on a simply connected open set every zero-free continuous function has a continuous logarithm (Mathlib's lifting theorem); if a point a outside U lay in a bounded complementary component, that component could be enclosed by an open set whose boundary is a compact subset of U surrounding a, and z - a would then have a continuous logarithm on that boundary, which is impossible since it winds once around a. Openness is genuinely needed: the Warsaw circle is simply connected yet bounds a hole. Red-team checks: specialised to the plane minus a point, the punctured disc and the annulus 1<|z|<2, each of which it correctly shows is not simply connected; proof is short and uses only the standard axioms.

Correctly stated: if U is an open subset of the plane with no holes (every connected component of its complement unbounded), then every holomorphic function without zeros on U is the square of a holomorphic function on U. It is the case n = 2 of the library's n-th-root theorem for hole-free open sets, which rests on the homology form of Cauchy's theorem: in a hole-free open set every closed curve has winding number zero about every point outside, so nowhere-zero holomorphic functions have holomorphic logarithms and hence square roots. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are used; the square-root property is the usual one (holomorphic, nowhere zero, squared root agreeing on U); no Mathlib equivalent found.

Correctly stated: a connected open set U in the complex plane is simply connected if and only if it has no holes, that is, every connected component of the complement of U is unbounded. Here 'simply connected' is the genuine homotopy notion (Mathlib's, on U as a subspace: nonempty, path-connected, every loop contractible), which is also the definition in Rudin's Real and Complex Analysis, 10.38, and the 'filled hull' of U is U together with the bounded components of its complement, so 'filled hull contained in U' says exactly that there are no bounded complementary components; this no-holes condition is the usual reformulation of 'the complement in the Riemann sphere is connected', one of the classical characterisations of simply connected plane regions collected in Rudin's Theorem 13.11. Idea of proof: if U is simply connected, z - a has a continuous logarithm on U for every a outside U, which is impossible if a lies in a bounded complementary component, since that component can be enclosed by a compact boundary inside U around which z - a winds once; conversely, with no holes every closed curve in U has winding number zero about every outside point, so by the homology form of Cauchy's theorem nowhere-zero holomorphic functions have holomorphic square roots, and the Koebe square-root argument from the Riemann mapping theorem then shows U is the whole plane or homeomorphic to the disc. Connectedness is needed and excludes the empty set (no holes, but not simply connected) and disjoint unions of discs. Red-team checks: both directions proved with only the standard axioms; specialised to the slit plane and the whole plane (simply connected) and to the plane minus a point, the punctured disc and the annulus 1<|z|<2 (each correctly not simply connected); no contradiction among the hypotheses; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate found.

Correctly stated: a connected open subset of the plane with no holes (every connected component of its complement unbounded) is simply connected in the homotopy sense. The proof chains two classical steps: on such a set every nowhere-zero holomorphic function has a holomorphic square root (homology form of Cauchy's theorem), and a domain with holomorphic square roots is either the whole plane or, by the Koebe square-root argument of the Riemann mapping theorem, homeomorphic to the disc. Both hypotheses are needed: two disjoint discs have no holes but are not connected, and a closed topologist's sine curve is connected with no holes but not path-connected. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (the unit disc); every hypothesis is used; specialised to the slit plane, which it correctly shows is simply connected.

Correctly stated: a connected open subset of the plane whose boundary is connected and whose complement is unbounded is simply connected. Such a set has no holes: an open plane set with connected boundary has connected complement, and that single complementary component is unbounded, so the no-holes criterion applies. It covers the disc, a half-plane and every bounded domain bounded by a Jordan curve; each hypothesis is needed, as the exterior of a closed disc (bounded complement), an annulus (disconnected boundary) and two tangent open discs (connected boundary but disconnected set) show. Red-team checks: specialised to the unit disc, which it correctly shows is simply connected; every hypothesis is used.

Correctly defined. Given a word (a_x) indexed by a finite set s of ordered positions and a map f from positions to labels, this is the grouped word whose letter at a label y is the product a_{x1}…a_{xk} of the letters at the positions x1 < … < xk of s with f(x_i) = y, multiplied in increasing order (the empty product 1 when no position lies over y, a value never read, since cumulants only use the letters at labels that occur). When f is order-preserving on s its fibres are blocks of consecutive positions, so this is exactly the word of products of consecutive letters A_j = a_{i(j-1)+1}…a_{i(j)} of Nica–Speicher, Theorem 11.12, and Krawczyk–Speicher, Combinatorics of free cumulants, Notation 2.1. Red-team checks: value test — grouping positions 0, 1, 2 by labels (0, 0, 1) gives the letters a0a1 and a2, and the cumulant of the grouped word comes out as φ(a0a1a2) − φ(a0a1)φ(a2), Krawczyk–Speicher's worked example; no other construction of this word in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: the unfolding equation of the grouped word — its letter at a label y is the product, in increasing order of position, of the letters at the positions over y — which is the definition itself, stated because other files cannot unfold the definition. Red-team checks: it is what the freeness file uses to show that a grouped letter lies in the subalgebra of its label.

Correctly stated: free cumulants are unchanged by an increasing relabelling of the positions — if e is strictly increasing on the finite set s, the free cumulant of the word x ↦ b(e(x)) along s equals the free cumulant of b along e(s). It is the case of the grouping formula in which every fibre is a single position: the fibre partition is the partition into singletons, so only the one-block partition contributes. This is what identifies cumulants indexed by an arbitrary finite ordered set with the textbook κ_n(a1,…,an). Red-team checks: strict monotonicity is needed (a non-injective e merges letters, and a non-monotone one reorders them, which matters for a noncommutative product); used in the freeness file to relabel a block of a partition by an initial segment of the naturals.

Correctly stated: Nica–Speicher, Theorem 11.12(2) (Krawczyk–Speicher, Remark 2.3, eq. (9)): κ_m(A1,…,Am) = ∑ over π ∈ NC(n) with π ∨ σ = 1_n of κ_π[a1,…,an], where the A_j are products of consecutive blocks of letters and σ is the interval partition into those blocks. Here the blocks are the fibres of a map that is order-preserving on the positions, and the cumulant of the grouped word is taken along the set of labels in increasing order, which is the order of the blocks. It is the one-block case of the general formula, since the pull-back of the one-block partition is the one-block partition. Red-team checks: specialised in Lean to the textbook indexing (letters on Fin n, a monotone surjection onto Fin m); to m = 1 (one group), where it becomes the moment–cumulant formula φ(a1…an) = ∑ over π ∈ NC(n) of κ_π[a]; to m = n (no grouping), where only π = 1_n survives; for the empty word both sides are 1 by the library's convention; a separate computation with random moments confirms the formula for every interval grouping of n ≤ 5 letters.

Correctly stated: the same formula with each κ_π written out as the product, over the blocks B of π, of the free cumulants of the word read along B — the multiplicative form in which Nica–Speicher and Krawczyk–Speicher define κ_π. It follows from the previous theorem and the multiplicativity of free cumulants proved in the basic cumulant file. Red-team checks: one-line derivation, no hypothesis beyond the order-preserving grouping.

Correctly stated: this is Nica–Speicher, Theorem 11.12(1), equivalently Krawczyk–Speicher, Theorem 2.2. For a word a on ordered positions s and a map f order-preserving on s, whose fibres group the letters into consecutive products A_y, and for any noncrossing partition ρ of the labels, the free cumulant κ_ρ[A] equals the sum of κ_π[a] over the noncrossing partitions π of s whose join with the fibre partition σ is the pull-back ρ̂ of ρ; the join is taken in the lattice of noncrossing partitions, as in both sources. Proof idea: as in Nica–Speicher (Remark 11.11), pulling back is a lattice isomorphism from the noncrossing partitions of the labels onto the interval [σ, 1] of NC(s), and it preserves block moments; hence the right-hand sides, as functions of ρ, satisfy the moment–cumulant formula for the grouped word, which determines its cumulants uniquely. It is more general than the book: φ is any function on a monoid (no linearity, unitality or traciality), and positions and labels are arbitrary finite ordered sets. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is satisfiable and needed; a brute-force check over all interval partitions on up to 7 points found that the noncrossing join of a noncrossing partition with an interval partition always equals the join among all partitions, so either reading of the join gives the same theorem; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated. For a word a on ordered positions s, a map f that is order-preserving on s, and any partition P of the set of labels f(s), the block moment of a for the pulled-back partition of s (two positions share a block exactly when their labels share a block of P) equals the block moment of P for the grouped word. Reason: each block of the pull-back is a union of consecutive fibres, so the ordered product of its letters is the ordered product of the corresponding grouped letters (associativity). This is the identity φ_{τ̂}[a1,…,an] = φ_τ[A1,…,Am] used in the second line of the proof of Nica–Speicher, Theorem 11.12. Red-team checks: holds for every partition P, not only noncrossing ones; the order-preserving hypothesis is needed (with labels 0, 1, 0 on three positions and P one block, the two sides would be φ(a0a1a2) and φ(a0a2a1)); no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Says: for a bounded convex open set Ω in dimension n, S ⊆ Ω of positive measure, u integrable on Ω and any A ⊆ Ω, ∫_A |u − u_S| ≤ μ(B(0,1))^(1−1/n) (diam Ω)^n / μ(S) · μ(A)^(1/n) · |Du|(Ω), with u_S the mean over S and |Du|(Ω) the possibly infinite total variation. The factor μ(A)^(1/n) makes it a weak-type L^(n/(n−1)) Poincaré inequality: Hölder's inequality turns a strong L^(n/(n−1)) Sobolev–Poincaré bound (such as the one Evans–Gariepy (1992), §5.6.1 Theorem 1(ii), prove on balls) into this form, and with A = Ω and μ(Ω) ≤ μ(B(0,1)) (diam Ω)^n it recovers the constant of the L¹ inequality. Why it holds: the continuously differentiable case, proved in the Sobolev Poincaré file, is passed to u by mollifying on convex open sets with compact closure in Ω (the mollifications converge in L¹ and eventually do not increase the variation) and then exhausting Ω by such sets, with S replaced by a measurable set of the same measure; its indicator case is the relative isoperimetric inequality. Red-team checks: both sides scale alike under dilations; specialised at Ω = S = (0,1), A = (0,1/2) with u continuously differentiable, where it reads ∫_A |u − ū| ≤ ½∫|u′|; integrability of u could be weakened to local integrability (recorded as a minor generality finding, not a correctness issue).

Says: for a convex open set Ω, S ⊆ Ω of finite positive measure and u locally integrable on Ω, ∫_Ω |u − u_S| ≤ (∫_{Ω−Ω} |h| dh) / μ(S) · |Du|(Ω), where u_S is the mean of u over S and both sides may be infinite. Why: |u(x) − u_S| ≤ (1/μ(S)) ∫_S |u(x) − u(y)| dy ≤ (1/μ(S)) ∫_Ω |u(x) − u(y)| dy, and integrating over x reduces it to the double-integral estimate. S need not be measurable. The two measure conditions are exactly what the mean needs: with μ(S) = ∞ the Lean mean is 0 and the right side would be 0, so the finiteness hypothesis cannot be dropped. Red-team checks: convexity, S ⊆ Ω and both measure conditions are needed (the infinite-measure case checked by hand); instantiated at Ω = S = (0,1); no counterpart in Mathlib.

Says: if Ω is a bounded convex open set in n-dimensional Euclidean space (any finite-dimensional real inner product space, with a Haar measure μ), S ⊆ Ω has positive measure and u is locally integrable on Ω, then ∫_Ω |u − u_S| ≤ μ(B(0,1)) (diam Ω)^(n+1) / μ(S) · |Du|(Ω), where u_S is the mean of u over S and |Du|(Ω) is the total variation of u on Ω (the supremum of ∫ u div φ over smooth compactly supported vector fields with |φ| ≤ 1), which may be infinite. This is the L¹ Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality for functions of bounded variation on convex domains, with an explicit constant; Evans–Gariepy (1992), §5.6.1 Theorem 1(ii), prove the ball case with an unspecified constant (in the stronger L^(n/(n−1)) norm). Why it holds: for each shift h, the integral of |u(x+h) − u(x)| over the points x with x and x+h in Ω is at most |h|·|Du|(Ω), because convexity keeps the segment from x to x+h inside Ω (this translation estimate is proved by duality directly for BV functions, with no detour through Sobolev approximation); integrating over h ∈ Ω − Ω bounds ∫∫_{Ω×Ω} |u(x) − u(y)| by (∫_{Ω−Ω} |h| dh)·|Du|(Ω), averaging over y ∈ S bounds the deviation from u_S, and |h| ≤ diam Ω together with Ω − Ω lying in the closed ball of radius diam Ω, of measure μ(B(0,1)) (diam Ω)^n, gives the constant. Conventions: S need not be measurable and u need not be integrable on Ω; if u is not integrable on S its mean takes Lean's default value 0, but then the variation is infinite and nothing false is asserted. Red-team checks: hypotheses jointly satisfiable (Ω = S = (0,1)); boundedness, convexity, S ⊆ Ω and μ(S) > 0 are each needed (for unbounded Ω the diameter would be the junk value 0; a dumbbell with a thin neck defeats any such constant); specialised to Ω = S = (0,1) in ℝ with u continuously differentiable, where it reads ∫|u − ū| ≤ 2∫|u′|; only the standard axioms.

Says: for a ball B of radius R in n-dimensional Euclidean space and u locally integrable on B, ∫_B |u − u_B| ≤ 2^(n+1) R · |Du|(B), where u_B is the mean of u over the ball and |Du|(B) its total variation on the ball, possibly infinite. It is the bounded convex case with S = Ω = B: diam B ≤ 2R and μ(B) = μ(B(0,1)) R^n, so μ(B(0,1)) (2R)^(n+1) / μ(B) = 2^(n+1) R. Evans–Gariepy (1992), §5.6.1 Theorem 1(ii), prove this ball inequality with an unspecified constant (in the stronger L^(n/(n−1)) norm); here the constant is explicit and proportional to R, as scaling requires. For R ≤ 0 the ball is empty and the left side is 0. Red-team checks: specialised to the interval (−1,1) with u continuously differentiable, where it reads ∫|u − ū| ≤ 4∫|u′|; checked that it is exactly the S = Ω = B case of the convex theorem.

Says: for a convex open set Ω and u locally integrable on Ω, ∫_Ω ∫_Ω |u(x) − u(y)| dy dx ≤ (∫_{Ω−Ω} |h| dh) · |Du|(Ω), where Ω − Ω is the set of differences of points of Ω and |Du|(Ω) the total variation; both sides may be infinite. Why: substitute y = x + h and swap the integrals; for fixed h the inner integral over the x with x, x+h ∈ Ω is at most |h|·|Du|(Ω) by the translation estimate for BV functions, which applies because convexity keeps the segment [x, x+h] in Ω, and it vanishes when h is not in Ω − Ω. A non-measurable u is first replaced by an almost-everywhere equal measurable one, which changes neither side. This is the standard first step of the Poincaré inequality on convex sets. Red-team checks: convexity is needed (a dumbbell with a thin neck has small variation but large oscillation) and local integrability is what makes the variation the distributional one (without it the pairings can take Lean's junk value 0); instantiated at Ω = (0,1); no counterpart in Mathlib.

If B and B' are isomorphic as R-algebras and B is regular over R, then so is B'. This is the expected invariance: flatness, and each fibre κ(p) ⊗ B ≅ κ(p) ⊗ B', is carried along the isomorphism. Red-team audit at 956e316250: B and B' may live in different universes; no extra hypothesis; used for the transport steps in the G-ring file.

Defines when a ring map R → B (R any commutative ring, B an R-algebra) is regular: B is flat over R and, for every prime p of R, the fibre κ(p) ⊗_R B is geometrically regular over the residue field κ(p), where geometrically regular (companion file) means Noetherian with L ⊗ (fibre) a regular ring for every finite purely inseparable extension L of κ(p). This is exactly Stacks, Definition 15.42.1 (Tag 07BZ: flat, with every fibre ring Noetherian and geometrically regular), with geometric regularity in the form of condition (2) of Stacks Lemma 10.166.1 (Tag 0381), which Definition 10.166.2 (Tag 0382) takes as one of the equivalent defining conditions; as in Stacks there is no Noetherian hypothesis on R and no finiteness condition on the map. Conventions: the fibre is written κ(p) ⊗ B instead of B ⊗ κ(p) (canonically isomorphic), and the extensions L are taken in the same universe as R, which loses nothing because every finite extension has an isomorphic copy there (shown by a red-team probe). Red-team audit at 956e316250: non-vacuous in both directions: R over itself, the zero algebra, localizations (ℤ → ℚ, R → R_p, R → R_f), étale algebras and polynomial rings in finitely many variables are regular, while ℤ → ℤ/2 (not flat), the dual numbers over a field and a nontrivial finite purely inseparable field extension are proved not regular (the last agreeing with Stacks Lemma 15.42.6, Tag 07EQ); Noetherianity and regularity of every fibre are derivable from the definition; Mathlib has no regular ring maps or geometric regularity, and no other Tau Ceti file defines them.

The standard localization of R at a multiplicative subset M is a regular R-algebra: the general statement for any localization, applied to the canonical construction. Red-team audit at 956e316250: found automatically for R → R_p and R → R_f.

If R → R' is a bijective ring map and B is an R'-algebra, compatibly with its R-algebra structure, that is regular over R, then B is regular over R'. This holds because flatness over R' is flatness over R (R' is the trivial localization of R), each prime p' of R' pulls back to a prime p of R with isomorphic residue fields, and the fibre κ(p') ⊗_{R'} B is identified with κ(p') ⊗_{κ(p)} (κ(p) ⊗_R B), which is geometrically regular because base change along an isomorphism of fields preserves geometric regularity. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised at R' = R; the bijectivity hypothesis is used. Two minor generality findings are recorded and do not affect correctness: R' must lie in the same universe as R, and the same statement holds for any localization R' of R.

For any multiplicative subset M of R, every localization of R at M is a regular R-algebra. This holds because a localization is flat, and its fibre at a prime p is a localization of the field κ(p), hence either zero or κ(p) itself, both of which are geometrically regular; equivalently, a localization is a directed colimit of the smooth algebras R_f with Noetherian fibres, so Stacks Lemma 15.42.5 (Tag 07EP) applies. It covers every localization, not just a particular model: R → R_p, R → R_f, ℤ → ℚ (not of finite type), and the zero ring when 0 ∈ M. Red-team audit at 956e316250: checked at R_p, R_f and ℤ → ℚ; no extra hypothesis.

Every smooth R-algebra (finitely presented and formally smooth, which is the Stacks notion of a smooth ring map) is regular over R. This holds because a smooth algebra is flat and each of its fibres is smooth over the residue field, hence of finite type (so Noetherian) and geometrically regular; in Stacks it is the trivial case of Lemma 15.42.5 (Tag 07EP: a directed colimit of smooth R-algebras whose fibre rings are Noetherian is regular). Red-team audit at 956e316250: applies to étale algebras and to polynomial rings in finitely many variables, with no extra hypothesis and the algebra in any universe.

Over a field k, a k-algebra B is regular over k exactly when it is geometrically regular over k. This is Stacks Definition 15.42.1 (Tag 07BZ) specialised to a field base: flatness over a field is automatic, the only prime is the zero ideal, its residue field is k itself, and the fibre k ⊗_k B is B; the proof transports geometric regularity along exactly this identification. Red-team audit at 956e316250: no hypotheses beyond k being a field, k and B in independent universes; specialised to show that the dual numbers and nontrivial finite purely inseparable extensions are not regular over k, and that finite separable extensions are, matching Stacks Lemma 15.42.6 (Tag 07EQ).

The noncentral t law has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure, that is, it gives zero mass to every Lebesgue-null set, for every ν and δ. Proof idea: given V = v > 0, the variable is a normal variable divided by the positive constant √(v/ν), which charges no null set because rescaling by a nonzero constant preserves null sets; then integrate over v. Red-team checks: holds with no hypotheses (for ν ≤ 0 the object is zero).

If Z is standard normal, V is chi-squared with ν > 0 degrees of freedom, and Z and V are independent, then (Z + δ)/√(V/ν) has the noncentral t law with parameters ν and δ: the textbook definition in random-variable form (as in the Wikipedia article 'Noncentral t-distribution'). It holds because independence makes the joint law of (Z, V) the product law, and the noncentral t law is by definition the image of that product under the ratio map. Red-team checks: all four hypotheses are load-bearing, and ν > 0 is genuinely needed (at ν = 0 the ratio is identically 0); the hypotheses are satisfiable, witnessed by the coordinate variables on the product space.

A random variable whose law is a noncentral t law has a probability density with respect to Lebesgue measure; this follows from the absolute continuity of the law. Red-team checks: no further hypotheses needed.
The noncentral t object has finite total mass for every ν and δ (mass 1 when ν > 0, mass 0 otherwise). Red-team checks: holds with no hypotheses, as stated.
For ν > 0 the noncentral t law has total mass 1, since it is the image of a product of two probability laws. Red-team checks: ν > 0 is needed (the object is zero otherwise).

The noncentral t object is a probability law exactly when ν > 0; correct because for ν ≤ 0 it is the zero measure by the file's convention. Red-team checks: used it to show the ν = 0 object is not a probability law.

The noncentral t law depends measurably on the pair (ν, δ) jointly, including the invalid region where it is zero. Proof idea: on ν > 0 it is the image of a measurably varying product law under a jointly measurable map, and {ν > 0} is a measurable set. Red-team checks: it composes automatically with measurable parameter functions (in ν alone, in δ alone, and jointly).

Defines the noncentral t distribution with ν degrees of freedom and noncentrality δ as the law of (Z + δ)/√(V/ν), where Z is standard normal and V is an independent chi-squared variable with ν degrees of freedom; independence is built in by taking the product of the two laws. This is exactly the definition in the Wikipedia article 'Noncentral t-distribution', here with ν any positive real number and δ any real number (negative δ allowed). The chi-squared factor is the genuine chi-squared law (the gamma law with shape ν/2 and rate 1/2), and since V > 0 almost surely, the convention that division by zero gives zero never affects the result. Convention: for ν ≤ 0 the object is the zero measure rather than a probability law, which matters because without that guard the formula at ν = 0 would silently give the point mass at 0. The file proves the announced properties: it is a probability law exactly when ν > 0, equals Student's t law at δ = 0, squares to the noncentral F(1, ν; δ²) law, and has a density. Red-team checks: specialised to ν = 1, δ = 0 it is the standard Cauchy law; the downstream mean formula gives the standard value δ√(ν/2)Γ((ν−1)/2)/Γ(ν/2) and separates δ = 1 from δ = 0 at ν = 3; showed the unguarded formula at ν = 0 is the point mass at 0, so the guard is needed; no other construction of this law in Tau Ceti or Mathlib.

For ν > 0, the noncentral t law is a mixture: draw v from the chi-squared law with ν degrees of freedom, then take the law of Y/√(v/ν) with Y normal of mean δ and variance 1. This is conditioning on the chi-squared factor (Fubini's theorem for the independent pair); the values v ≤ 0, where the rescaling degenerates, carry no chi-squared mass. Red-team checks: ν > 0 is needed; this is the representation the library uses downstream to compute the density.

For ν > 0, the noncentral t law is the image of the product of the standard normal law and the chi-squared law with ν degrees of freedom under the map (z, v) ↦ (z + δ)/√(v/ν); this unfolds the definition in its valid range. Red-team checks: the hypothesis ν > 0 is needed, since at ν = 0 the right-hand side is the point mass at 0 while the left-hand side is zero.

For ν > 0, the noncentral t law is the law of Y/√(V/ν), where Y is normal with mean δ and variance 1 and V is an independent chi-squared variable with ν degrees of freedom. This is correct because Z + δ is normal with mean δ and variance 1 when Z is standard normal, and shifting the first coordinate keeps the pair independent. Red-team checks: ν > 0 is needed (at ν = 0 the right side is the point mass at 0).

If T has the noncentral t law with parameters ν and δ, then −T has the noncentral t law with parameters ν and −δ, for every ν and δ. This holds because −Y/√(V/ν), with Y normal of mean δ and variance 1, is the same ratio with a normal numerator of mean −δ. Red-team checks: at δ = 0 it gives the symmetry of Student's t law; no hypotheses needed.

If T has the noncentral t law with ν degrees of freedom and noncentrality δ, then T² has the noncentral F law with numerator degree 1, denominator degree ν and noncentrality δ², as stated in the Wikipedia article 'Noncentral t-distribution'. Proof idea: T² = Y²/(V/ν) almost surely because V > 0 almost surely, and Y² for Y normal of mean δ and variance 1 is noncentral chi-squared with one degree of freedom and noncentrality δ², so T² is exactly the defining ratio (U/1)/(V/ν) of the noncentral F law; that definition, with the noncentral chi-squared law as the Poisson(λ/2) mixture of chi-squared laws, is the standard one. For ν ≤ 0 both sides are zero by convention, as the docstring says. Red-team checks: at δ = 0 it reduces to Fisher's F(1, ν); the second moment ν(1 + δ²)/(ν − 2) derived from it downstream is the standard value.

For ν ≤ 0 the noncentral t object is the zero measure, the file's documented convention for invalid degrees of freedom; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: confirmed it is not a probability law at ν = 0.

With noncentrality δ = 0 the noncentral t law equals Student's t law with the same ν, as an equality of measures, for every ν (for ν ≤ 0 both are the zero measure by convention). This is the standard reduction stated in the Wikipedia article 'Noncentral t-distribution'; the proof uses the library's theorem that Z/√(V/ν) has Student's t law. Red-team checks: specialised to ν = 1 it gives the standard Cauchy law.
The noncentral t law gives zero mass to every single point, for every ν and δ; immediate from absolute continuity, since a point is Lebesgue-null.

For an irreducible, reduced, crystallographic rational root system with finitely many roots, any chosen base, and any admissible Dynkin type t, the system is isomorphic to the model of type t exactly when t is the Dynkin type read off from that base's Cartan matrix; so it is isomorphic to the model of its own type and to no other model, whichever base is used. It holds because the Dynkin type is an isomorphism invariant that does not depend on the base (the Weyl group acts transitively on bases), each model has its own type, and two systems with the same Cartan data are isomorphic by rigidity (Čap, Lie Algebras and Representation Theory, §3.10). Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable by the models; both inputs (the base and admissibility of t) are needed to form the statement; reproved independently from the library's general 'isomorphic iff same Dynkin type' theorem; no Mathlib duplicate; only the standard axioms.

Statement: every irreducible, reduced, crystallographic root system with finitely many roots in a nonzero rational vector space is isomorphic to the model root system of exactly one Dynkin type from the list A_n (n ≥ 1), B_n (n ≥ 2), C_n (n ≥ 3), D_n (n ≥ 4), E6, E7, E8, F4, G2; an isomorphism here is a linear isomorphism carrying roots to roots and coroots to coroots, i.e. preserving every Cartan integer (no inner product is involved, so rescaling a system changes nothing), and the model of each type is its standard root system written in coordinates over ℚ. This is the Cartan–Killing classification as stated in Čap's lecture notes (Lie Algebras and Representation Theory, Wien 2016/17, Theorem 3.10 with the paragraph before it, which give the same list with the same rank ranges and show that the Cartan data of a base determine the root system up to isomorphism), and it is the Layer 5 summit of the Tau Ceti root-systems roadmap. Why it holds: choose a base; the classification of connected positive-definite Cartan matrices attaches one valid type to it, independently of the base because the Weyl group permutes the bases; each model realises its own type; rigidity turns equal Cartan matrices into an isomorphism, and invariance of the type under isomorphism gives uniqueness. The rank ranges are exactly what makes 'exactly one' true: B_1 = C_1 = A_1, C_2 ≅ B_2, D_3 ≅ A_3 and the reducible D_2 = A_1 × A_1 are left out, so no two admissible types name the same system. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (every model meets them); uniqueness has content (from the theorem, the B_3 and C_3 models are not isomorphic, nor the E_7 and E_8 models); reducedness, irreducibility and crystallographicity are each necessary (BC_2, A_1 × A_1, and B_2 with its short roots tripled are counterexamples), while nonemptiness and spanning each follow from the other plus irreducibility (recorded as a minor redundancy, harmless to the statement); the B/C labels checked against the orientation of the standard Cartan matrices; no Mathlib duplicate; only the standard axioms.

If a random angle X has the von Mises law with location m and concentration κ, then the rotated angle X + a has the von Mises law with location m + a and the same concentration; this is the rotation equivariance of the law transferred to random variables.

The density is continuous jointly in the location, the concentration and the angle: the exponent κ cos(θ − m) is continuous in all three, the exponential is continuous, and I₀ is continuous and never zero, so the quotient is continuous.
For a fixed location and concentration the density is continuous in the angle; the specialisation of joint continuity.

For κ ≥ 0 and every integer n, the n-th trigonometric moment of the von Mises law is E[e^{inθ}] = e^{inm} I_{|n|}(κ)/I₀(κ), with |n| so that negative n are covered; this is the standard moment formula of the von Mises distribution (Wikipedia, 'von Mises distribution'). Proof idea: rotating by m produces the phase e^{inm}, and the classical integral (1/2π)∫ e^{κ cos θ} e^{inθ} dθ = I_{|n|}(κ) is DLMF 10.32.3, I_n(κ) = (1/π)∫₀^π e^{κ cos θ} cos(nθ) dθ, the sine part vanishing by symmetry. Convention: e^{inθ} here is Mathlib's n-th Fourier character on ℝ/2πℤ, checked to equal exp(inθ) in real coordinates, so the phase has the textbook sign. Red-team checks: κ = 0 gives moment 0 for n ≠ 0 and 1 for n = 0 (the uniform law); n = −2 gives I₂; the hypothesis κ ≥ 0 is needed only for the zero convention.

The density integrates to one against the normalised circle measure, for every real κ: (1/2π)∫ e^{κ cos(θ − m)} dθ = I₀(κ), the classical integral representation I₀(κ) = (1/π)∫₀^π e^{κ cos θ} dθ (DLMF 10.32.1) after a rotation by m, under which the measure is invariant. Red-team checks: no hypothesis on κ is needed and none is assumed.

For κ ≥ 0 the von Mises law has total mass one: its mass is the integral of the density against the normalised circle measure, I₀(κ)/I₀(κ) = 1 by the integral representation of I₀ (DLMF 10.32.1). This is the check that the normalising constant matches the reference measure (against unnormalised arc length the mass would be 2π). Red-team checks: the hypothesis κ ≥ 0 is needed only because of the zero convention for κ < 0, and it is satisfiable (instantiated at κ = 1); no contradiction derivable.
The von Mises law is a probability measure exactly when κ ≥ 0: for κ ≥ 0 by the normalisation, and for κ < 0 it is the zero measure by convention, which is not a probability measure.

The same normalisation for the extended-valued density: its integral over the circle is 1; it follows from the real statement because the density is positive and continuous on a compact space, hence integrable.

Rotating the circle by a sends the von Mises law with location m to the von Mises law with location m + a and the same concentration, because Haar measure is rotation invariant and the density depends only on θ − m. It holds for every κ, the zero convention for κ < 0 included. Red-team checks: fires as a simplification rule; specialised at m = 0.

The extended-valued density is jointly measurable in the location, the concentration and the angle, as a consequence of joint continuity of the real density; this is what makes the von Mises family a measurable function of its parameters.

The von Mises law depends measurably on the pair (location, concentration), the zero convention for κ < 0 included, which is what is needed to use the family as a Markov kernel or under a prior; it follows from joint measurability of the density and measurability of the set {κ ≥ 0}.
The extended-valued density is a measurable function of the angle, as the extended-real image of a measurable real function.
The real density is a measurable function of the angle, because it is continuous.

For κ ≥ 0 the mean resultant length of the von Mises law, the modulus of its first trigonometric moment E[e^{iθ}], is I₁(κ)/I₀(κ); it follows from the moment formula at n = 1, since |e^{im}| = 1 and I₁(κ) ≥ 0 for κ ≥ 0. This matches the standard value (Wikipedia, 'von Mises distribution', which gives the circular variance 1 − I₁(κ)/I₀(κ)). Red-team checks: κ = 0 gives 0, as for the uniform law.

For κ ≥ 0 the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the von Mises law with respect to the normalised circle measure is the von Mises density, almost everywhere: the standard fact that a measure defined by a density has that density as its derivative.

For κ ≥ 0 the support of the von Mises law (the smallest closed set of full measure) is the whole circle, because its density is continuous and strictly positive and Haar measure gives positive mass to every nonempty open set.

Turning the extended-valued density back into a real number gives the real density; true because the real density is nonnegative (indeed positive), so the round trip through the extended reals is exact.

Defines the von Mises law on the circle ℝ/2πℤ with location m and concentration κ ≥ 0: the normalised circle measure dθ/2π weighted by e^{κ cos(θ − m)}/I₀(κ). This is the standard von Mises distribution, density e^{κ cos(θ − μ)}/(2π I₀(κ)) with respect to dθ (Wikipedia, 'von Mises distribution'); the factor 2π lives in the reference measure, which has total mass 1, so the law has total mass 1 (proved in isProbabilityMeasure_vonMisesMeasure), not 2π. I₀ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order zero, with the power series Σ (κ/2)^{2j}/(j!)² of DLMF 10.25.2. Convention: for κ < 0, outside the standard range κ ≥ 0, the definition returns the zero measure, as the library's other parametric families (e.g. the von Mises–Fisher law) do. Red-team checks: κ = 0 gives the uniform (Haar) law; for κ ≥ 0 the law equals Mathlib's exponential tilt of Haar measure by κ cos(θ − m) (compiled); I₀(0) = 1 and I₁(0) = 0 evaluated.
For κ < 0 the von Mises law is the zero measure, the documented convention for concentrations outside the standard range κ ≥ 0.
For κ ≥ 0 the von Mises law is the normalised circle measure weighted by the von Mises density; this is the defining branch of the definition.

At κ = 0 the von Mises law is the uniform law (normalised Haar measure) on the circle, since the density is e⁰/I₀(0) = 1; this matches the standard statement that the von Mises distribution with κ = 0 is the circular uniform distribution (Wikipedia, 'von Mises distribution').

The same von Mises density viewed as a function with values in the extended nonnegative reals, the form measure theory uses for densities; since the real density is positive, nothing is lost in the conversion. Red-team checks: converting back recovers the real density exactly (toReal_vonMisesPDF).

Defines the von Mises density on the circle: for a location m and a concentration κ, the angle θ gets weight e^{κ cos(θ − m)} divided by I₀(κ), the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order zero. This is the standard density e^{κ cos(θ − μ)}/(2π I₀(κ)) with respect to dθ (Wikipedia, 'von Mises distribution') written against the normalised circle measure dθ/2π, which absorbs the factor 2π. The cosine of a point of the circle is taken through any real representative, which is well defined because cosine has period 2π, and I₀ is the library's Bessel function, whose power series Σ (κ/2)^{2j}/(j!)² (DLMF 10.25.2) is proved for it. Red-team checks: value tests at θ = m, κ = 1 (gives e/I₀(1)) and at θ = m + π (gives e^{−κ}/I₀(κ)); I₀(0) = 1, so κ = 0 gives the constant density 1.

When the location and the angle are given by real numbers μ and x, the density equals e^{κ cos(x − μ)}/I₀(κ), the textbook formula in real coordinates; it holds because the circle's cosine is computed from real representatives and the image of x minus the image of μ is the image of x − μ. Red-team checks: it fires as a simplification rule; specialised at μ = x = 0, κ = 1.
The defining equation of the von Mises density, θ ↦ e^{κ cos(θ − m)}/I₀(κ); correct by construction, and needed because the definition's body is hidden from files that import this one.

The von Mises density is strictly positive at every angle and for every real concentration: it is an exponential divided by I₀(κ), and I₀(κ) ≥ 1 because its power series has nonnegative terms and leading term 1. No hypothesis is assumed.
The defining equation of the extended-valued density: it is the extended-real image of the real von Mises density; correct by construction.

If a random angle X has the wrapped Cauchy law with location m and scale γ, then the rotated angle X + a has the wrapped Cauchy law with location m + a and the same scale. This is the rotation property of the law, restated for random variables: the law of X + a is the image of the law of X under rotation by a. Red-team checks: the hypothesis can be met (by the identity variable on the circle with this law).

If a real random variable X is Cauchy with centre r and scale γ, then X reduced modulo 2π has the wrapped Cauchy law with location r (as a point of the circle) and scale γ. This is the defining description of the wrapped Cauchy law, and it follows from the representation of the law at a real location. Red-team checks: the hypothesis can be met (by the identity on the line under the Cauchy law); the underlying measure is not assumed to be a probability measure, since that follows from the hypothesis.

If two random angles X and Y are independent, with wrapped Cauchy laws of parameters (m₁, γ₁) and (m₂, γ₂), then X + Y, added on the circle, has the wrapped Cauchy law with parameters (m₁ + m₂, γ₁ + γ₂). It follows from the convolution theorem, since the law of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their laws. Red-team checks: the hypotheses can be met (by the two coordinates under the product law); independence cannot be dropped, since for a Cauchy variable x of positive scale a probe takes X = x mod 2π and Y = −x mod 2π, each with the right law, but X + Y = 0, which is not wrapped Cauchy.

The wrapped Cauchy law, viewed as a probability measure on the circle with the topology of weak convergence, depends continuously on the pair (location, scale). This includes scale zero, where the law is a point mass. It holds because every law in the family is the image of the standard Cauchy law under x ↦ m + (γx mod 2π), which is jointly continuous in (m, γ, x), so by dominated convergence the integrals of bounded continuous functions vary continuously. Red-team checks: the topology is weak convergence of probability measures, and the zero-scale boundary is included, consistent with the zero-scale lemma.

For every integer n, the n-th trigonometric moment E[e^{inθ}] of the wrapped Cauchy law with location m and scale γ equals e^{inm}·e^{−γ|n|}. The Wikipedia article 'Wrapped Cauchy distribution' gives the same circular moments e^{inμ − |n|γ}. These are the characteristic function e^{itμ − γ|t|} of the Cauchy law evaluated at the integers, and that is how the proof goes: since e^{inθ} is 2π-periodic, the moment of a wrapped law at n is the characteristic function of the real law at n. Convention: the moment uses e^{+inθ} with no complex conjugate, and the |n| makes the moment at −n the conjugate of the moment at n. Red-team checks: n = 0 gives total mass 1; n = −1 gives e^{−im}e^{−γ}; n = 2 gives e^{2im}e^{−2γ}; scale 0 gives the moments of the point mass; a probe shows these moments determine the law.

Every wrapped Cauchy law has total mass one. This holds because the law is the image, under a measurable map, of a probability law (the Cauchy law, or the point mass at zero scale), and images preserve total mass. Red-team checks: it holds for every location and every scale including zero, and it agrees with the zeroth trigonometric moment being 1.

Rotating the circle by an angle a carries the wrapped Cauchy law with location m to the wrapped Cauchy law with location m + a and the same scale. This holds because the law is the image of a Cauchy variable under x ↦ m + (x mod 2π), and following that by rotation by a gives x ↦ (m + a) + (x mod 2π). Red-team checks: there are no hypotheses, and the rewriting rule fires as stated.

The wrapped Cauchy law depends measurably on the pair (location, scale), as a map into the space of measures with its usual measurable structure, generated by evaluation on measurable sets. This holds because every law in the family is the image of one fixed law, the standard Cauchy law, under maps x ↦ m + (γx mod 2π) that are jointly measurable in (m, γ, x). Red-team checks: all scales are covered, including zero.

The mean resultant length of the wrapped Cauchy law, the modulus of its first trigonometric moment E[e^{iθ}], equals e^{−γ}, so its circular variance is 1 − e^{−γ}. The Wikipedia article 'Wrapped Cauchy distribution' gives the same mean resultant length e^{−γ} and circular variance 1 − e^{−γ}. It is the moment formula at n = 1, since |e^{im}| = 1. Red-team checks: it does not depend on the location; it equals 1 at scale 0 (a point mass) and is below 1 at every positive scale; the scale is recovered from it.

As the scale tends to 0, the wrapped Cauchy laws with a fixed location m converge weakly to the point mass at m. This is the degenerate limit ρ = e^{−γ} → 1. It follows from the joint continuity theorem at scale 0 together with the zero-scale formula. Red-team checks: the limit is taken along nonnegative scales, in the weak topology on probability measures, and it agrees with every Fourier moment tending to e^{inm}.

Defines the wrapped Cauchy law with location m, a point of the circle ℝ/2πℤ, and scale γ ≥ 0. Take a real Cauchy variable with centre 0 and scale γ, reduce it modulo 2π and rotate by m. The Cauchy law has density γ/(π(x² + γ²)), the convention of the underlying Cauchy law. This is the wrapping construction of the wrapped Cauchy distribution described in the Wikipedia article 'Wrapped Cauchy distribution', parametrised by the scale γ of the unwrapped law, so the mean resultant length is ρ = e^{−γ}. Convention: γ = 0 gives the point mass at m (the limit ρ → 1), which the file states and proves separately; the uniform law (γ = ∞) is not a member. Red-team checks: the file's moments e^{inm}e^{−γ|n|} match the article's circular moments e^{inμ−|n|γ}, and a probe proves that any probability law on the circle with these moments equals this one, so the definition is the standard law; a positive scale never gives a point mass; the scale can be read off the law; Mathlib and Tau Ceti have no other construction of this law.

If the location is the class of a real number r, the wrapped Cauchy law is the image on the circle of the Cauchy law centred at r with the same scale; that is, it is the law of X mod 2π for X Cauchy with centre r and scale γ. This is the usual description of wrapping a Cauchy variable with location r. It holds because shifting a Cauchy law by r shifts its centre by r, and reduction mod 2π turns adding r into rotating by the class of r. Red-team checks: there are no hypotheses, and at r = 0 the formula is the definition.

Convolving, on the circle group, the wrapped Cauchy laws with parameters (m₁, γ₁) and (m₂, γ₂) gives the wrapped Cauchy law with parameters (m₁ + m₂, γ₁ + γ₂). It is stated as an equality of measures on the circle, for all locations and all nonnegative scales. Proof idea: the real Cauchy family is closed under convolution, with locations and scales adding, because the characteristic functions multiply (e^{itx₁ − γ₁|t|}·e^{itx₂ − γ₂|t|}). Reduction modulo 2π is a group homomorphism, so it carries convolution on the line to convolution on the circle. Red-team checks: at zero scales it gives δ_{m₁} ∗ δ_{m₂} = δ_{m₁+m₂}; it agrees with the Fourier moments multiplying; there are no hypotheses.
