States the defining formula: the wrapped Cauchy law with location m and scale γ is the image of the centred Cauchy law of scale γ under x ↦ m + (x mod 2π). It restates the definition, so it holds by construction. It is the interface other files use, since the definition's body is not unfolded outside this file. Red-team checks: the statement matches the definition term for term.

Every wrapped Cauchy law is the image of the standard Cauchy law (centre 0, scale 1) under x ↦ m + (γx mod 2π). This is the location–scale representation of the Cauchy family (γX has scale γ when X is standard Cauchy), read on the circle. At γ = 0 the map is constant and both sides are the point mass at m. Red-team checks: it holds for every scale including zero, and it agrees with the definition and the zero-scale lemma.

At scale zero the wrapped Cauchy law is the point mass at its location m. This carries to the circle the convention that the Cauchy law of scale 0 is the point mass at its centre, the weak limit of Cauchy laws as the scale shrinks. Red-team checks: it agrees with the Fourier moments at γ = 0 (all equal to e^{inm}, the moments of the point mass) and with the weak limit as γ → 0 proved in the same file.

Two metric-measure spaces (complete separable metric spaces with a Borel measure finite on bounded sets) related by a measure-preserving isometry are at Gromov–Prokhorov distance 0, because the second measure is the image of the first under an isometry. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the assumptions are exactly those of the structures involved.

If two metric-measure spaces are related by a measure-preserving isometry, their measures are at the same Gromov–Prokhorov distance from any measure on any space; this is the invariance under isomorphism that makes the distance well defined on isomorphism classes, as Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter require. Red-team audit at 956e316250: no assumption on the third space.

Restricting a metric-measure space to the support of its measure does not change its Gromov–Prokhorov distance to any measure. Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter define isomorphism of metric measure spaces through isometries between supports (Definition 2.1), and this lemma is what makes that convention harmless. Red-team audit at 956e316250: follows from the isomorphism invariance applied to the measure-preserving inclusion of the support; no assumption on the third space.

Converse criterion: if the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is less than δ, some admissible gluing f makes every measurable set of X have μ-mass at most δ plus the ν-mass of its cross δ-neighbourhood in Y, and symmetrically. It holds because the infimum is attained below δ by some gluing, whose Lévy–Prokhorov inequalities are tested on the copies of the set. Red-team audit at 956e316250: used to prove compiled lower bounds (a unit point mass against the uniform measure on two points at distance 1 is at distance at least 1/4; a measure of infinite mass is at infinite distance from the zero measure), so it carries real content.

Defines the Gromov–Prokhorov distance between a measure μ on a space X and a measure ν on a space Y: put X and Y side by side in their disjoint union, choose any distance on the union that restricts to the given distances on X and on Y (it is fixed by the cross distances from points of X to points of Y), take the Lévy–Prokhorov distance between the two copies of the measures there (the least ε such that each set's mass under one measure is at most the other measure's mass of its open ε-neighbourhood plus ε, both ways round), and minimise over all such gluings. This is Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter's Definition 5.1 (Probab. Theory Related Fields 145, 2009) in the disjoint-union form of their Remark 5.2(ii), eq. (5.10), and the Lévy–Prokhorov distance used is Mathlib's, whose two-sided condition agrees with the one-sided Prokhorov condition (5.2) for probability measures. Lean also admits gluings with zero or infinite cross distances and tests sets measurable in the disjoint union rather than closed sets of the glued space; for probability measures on Borel spaces this changes nothing, because adding a small constant to the cross distances gives a genuine metric at that small cost, the infinitely-far gluing only gives the trivial value max(μ(X), ν(Y)), and a measurable set can be replaced by its closure without changing its neighbourhoods. The value lies in [0, ∞] and the definition makes sense for arbitrary measures. Red-team audit at 956e316250: d(μ, μ) = 0 and two unit point masses on one-point spaces are at distance 0, while a unit point mass and the uniform measure on two points at distance 1 are at distance at least 1/4, and a unit and a double point mass at distance at least 1 (all compiled), so the definition is not degenerate; no construction of this distance in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Symmetry: the Gromov–Prokhorov distance from μ to ν equals that from ν to μ, for arbitrary measures on any two spaces and with no hypotheses; a gluing of X with Y read backwards is a gluing of Y with X, and the Lévy–Prokhorov condition is symmetric. Symmetry is part of Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter's Lemma 5.4 (the distance is a metric). Red-team audit at 956e316250: no hypotheses to weaken; exact equality.

For 0 < p < ∞, an admissible gluing f and a coupling π of μ and ν, the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most (the L^p(π)-norm of f) raised to the power p/(p+1): by Markov's inequality the π-mass of {f ≥ ε} is at most ‖f‖_p^p / ε^p, which is at most ε as soon as ε^(p+1) ≥ ‖f‖_p^p. This is the standard bound of a Prokhorov distance by a power of a Wasserstein distance (exponent 1/2 for p = 1). Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised at p = 1 through the Sturm-distance corollary (compiled); the exponent range matches the docstring.

For an admissible gluing f and a coupling π of μ and ν, the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most the π-essential supremum of f, since above the essential supremum the set where f ≥ ε is π-null. Red-team audit at 956e316250: no further hypotheses; it is the p = ∞ end of the previous bound.

For two measures on the same space, the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most their Lévy–Prokhorov distance: glue the space to itself using its own metric as the cross distance. No measurability assumption on open sets is needed. Red-team audit at 956e316250: hypothesis-free; it gives d(μ, μ) = 0.

Common embeddings give upper bounds: if T and S embed X and Y isometrically into a space Z whose open sets are measurable, with T and S measurable up to null sets, then the Gromov–Prokhorov distance of μ and ν is at most the Lévy–Prokhorov distance of their images in Z. So restricting Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter's infimum over all common spaces (Definition 5.1) to the disjoint union does not raise it. Proof idea: the cross distances d_Z(T x, S y) form an admissible gluing, and the Lévy–Prokhorov inequalities in Z transfer to it through closures of image sets. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised at the identity embeddings of the real line it gives the single-space bound (compiled); hypotheses consistent.

The distance never exceeds the larger of the two total masses: glue the spaces infinitely far apart, so that no neighbourhood reaches the other side, and the Lévy–Prokhorov condition holds at ε = max(μ(X), ν(Y)); for probability measures this is the familiar bound by 1. Red-team audit at 956e316250: holds for arbitrary measures; specialised to give the bound 1 for a unit point mass against the uniform measure on two points (compiled).

Coupling bound: if for some admissible gluing f a coupling π of μ and ν (a measure on X × Y with marginals μ and ν) gives mass at most δ to the pairs at cross distance at least δ, then the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most δ. This is the easy half of the coupling description of the Prokhorov distance (Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter, eq. (5.4)) applied in the glued space. Red-team audit at 956e316250: hypotheses satisfiable and all used; no measurability of f is needed.

Upper-bound criterion: if for some admissible gluing (cross distances f obeying the triangle inequality together with the metrics of X and Y) every measurable set A of X has μ-mass at most δ plus the ν-mass of the points of Y at cross distance less than δ from A, and symmetrically for measurable sets of Y, then the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most δ. This is the Lévy–Prokhorov condition in the glued space, checked only on sets lying in one of the two sides, which suffices because the two copies of the measures live on different sides. Red-team audit at 956e316250: each hypothesis is used and they are jointly satisfiable (the infinitely-far gluing with δ the larger mass); used to prove all the upper bounds in the file.

For 0 < p < ∞, the Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most D_p(μ, ν)^(p/(p+1)), where D_p is Sturm's transportation distance (the infimum over gluings and couplings of the L^p norm of the cross distance), by taking the infimum of the previous Markov bound; so convergence in Sturm's distance implies Gromov–Prokhorov convergence. Red-team audit at 956e316250: holds for arbitrary measures (with no coupling D_p is infinite and the bound trivial); specialised at p = 1 to the bound by the square root of D_1 (compiled).

The Gromov–Prokhorov distance is at most Sturm's transportation distance D_∞ (the infimum over gluings and couplings of the essential supremum of the cross distance), by taking the infimum of the essential-supremum bound. Red-team audit at 956e316250: no hypotheses.

A measure and its image under an isometry T into another space (T measurable up to null sets) are at Gromov–Prokhorov distance 0: glue the spaces by the cross distance d(T x, y), under which each set of X is at distance 0 from its image. This is the fact behind Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter's Remark 5.2(i) that the distance only depends on isometry classes. Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to two unit point masses on one-point spaces (compiled); hypotheses consistent and both used.

Isometry invariance: replacing μ by its image under an isometry T (measurable up to null sets) does not change its Gromov–Prokhorov distance to any measure on any space, when the open sets of the source and target spaces are measurable. It follows from the triangle inequality and the zero distance between a measure and its isometric image, and expresses that the distance is well defined on isometry classes (Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter, Remark 5.2(i)). Red-team audit at 956e316250: specialised to the embedding of the real line as an axis of the plane (compiled); the assumption on the source space is removable (recorded as a minor generality finding), which does not affect correctness.

Two finite measures are at finite Gromov–Prokhorov distance, immediately from the bound by the larger total mass. Red-team audit at 956e316250: finiteness is needed: a measure of infinite mass on the real line is at infinite distance from the zero measure (compiled).

Every measure is at Gromov–Prokhorov distance 0 from itself, from the previous bound and the vanishing of the Lévy–Prokhorov distance on the diagonal. Red-team audit at 956e316250: holds for all measures, finite or not; specialised on the real line (compiled).

The triangle inequality: the distance from μ to ρ is at most the distance from μ to ν plus that from ν to ρ, for arbitrary measures on three spaces, assuming only that the open sets of the middle space are measurable (true for Borel σ-algebras). Proof: amalgamate the two gluings along the middle space (the cross distance from x to z is the shortest path through Y), and chain the two Lévy–Prokhorov inequalities through the cross neighbourhoods in Y, which are open and hence measurable. This is the triangle inequality of Greven–Pfaffelhuber–Winter's Lemma 5.4, here for arbitrary measures on extended pseudometric spaces. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the measurability hypothesis cannot be dropped: compiled counterexample with the middle space the real line under the trivial σ-algebra, where a point mass there is at distance 0 from both a unit point mass and the uniform measure on {0, 1}, which are at distance at least 1/4; specialised to three different Borel spaces (compiled).

Correctly stated: the cellular chain complex of the CW structure on the realization |K| (one n-cell for each n-simplex) is isomorphic, as a chain complex of R-modules, to the oriented simplicial chain complex of K with the alternating deleted-vertex boundary. In degree n the isomorphism sends the cellular basis vector of a simplex to that simplex times the unit s_n = e_(n-1)...e_0, where e_k is the cellular incidence number of the 0-th face of the standard (k+1)-simplex; because the cellular boundary coefficient of the j-th face of an (n+1)-cell is (-1)^j e_n and s_(n+1) = e_n s_n, the rescaled cellular boundary is exactly the simplicial one. Red-team checks: the chain-map identity was rechecked by hand from the incidence formula; each degreewise map is a change of basis, hence an isomorphism; no finiteness of K and no commutativity of R is assumed.

Correctly stated: in degree n, the chain isomorphism from cellular to simplicial chains is the degreewise linear isomorphism, up to the identification of each chain group with its defining module; true by definition.

Correctly stated: in degree n, the inverse chain isomorphism is the inverse of the degreewise linear isomorphism, up to the identification of each chain group with its defining module; true by definition.

Correctly stated: in each degree n, the R-linear isomorphism from the cellular chain group of |K| (free on the n-cells, with basis given by the characteristic maps) to the free R-module on the n-simplices of K that sends the basis vector of each cell to its simplex multiplied by the unit s_n; it is the change of basis between the cellular basis and the rescaled standard basis, matched through the bijection between n-cells and n-simplices. Red-team checks: agrees with its docstring and with the companion formula on basis vectors.

Correctly stated: the degreewise isomorphism sends the cellular basis vector of the cell of an n-simplex c to s_n times c, as the docstring says; this is immediate from its definition as a change of basis.

Correctly stated: the inverse of the degreewise isomorphism sends r times the simplex c to (r times the inverse of s_n) times the cellular basis vector of c, which inverts the previous formula since s_n is a unit. Red-team checks: as a simplification rule its left side is not rewritten by any other rule (checked).
Correctly stated: viewed in the ring, the scale in degree n+1 is e_n times the scale in degree n, by definition.

Correctly stated: for a simplicial complex K whose vertices are linearly ordered, any ring R (not necessarily commutative) and every degree n, the n-th homology of the simplicial chain complex of K (the free R-module on the n-simplices, each oriented by listing its vertices in increasing order, with boundary the alternating sum of the faces obtained by deleting one vertex) is isomorphic as an R-module to the n-th singular homology of the geometric realization |K| with coefficients in R. This is the absolute case (A empty) of Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2.27 (Section 2.1, p. 128); Hatcher explains on p. 107 that a simplicial complex becomes a Delta-complex once its vertices are ordered (for instance by a linear order on all vertices), and its simplicial chain complex is then exactly this one. The proof goes through cellular homology: |K| is a CW complex with one n-cell per n-simplex, the cellular boundary coefficient of the j-th face of a cell is (-1)^j times a unit depending only on the dimension, so rescaling the cellular basis by a unit in each degree identifies the cellular chain complex with the simplicial one, and cellular homology is singular homology (Hatcher, Theorem 2.35). Conventions: |K| carries the weak topology (a set is closed exactly when it meets every closed simplex in a closed set), so infinite and non-locally-finite complexes are included and no finiteness is assumed; the chains are the oriented simplicial chains, not Munkres' ordered chains on all vertex tuples; the isomorphism is the composite through cellular homology and is not claimed to be natural or to equal Hatcher's canonical map; the coefficient ring lives in the same set-theoretic universe as the vertex set. Red-team checks: only the vertex order and the ring structure are assumed, so there is no hypothesis to contradict; the topology used on |K| was checked to be the weak topology; specialised to the infinite full simplex on the natural numbers, where it yields vanishing integral singular homology of the realization in every positive degree; also instantiated with the (non-commutative) rational quaternions as coefficients; uses only the standard axioms.

Correctly defined: the sequence of units s_0 = 1, s_(n+1) = e_n s_n of the coefficient ring, where e_n is the cellular incidence number of the 0-th face of the standard (n+1)-simplex (proved to be a unit), so s_n = e_(n-1)...e_0; this is exactly the degreewise rescaling that turns the cellular boundary coefficients (-1)^j e_n into the simplicial signs (-1)^j.
Correctly stated: the scale in degree 0 is 1, by definition.

Correctly stated: if f is smooth and the band c - delta <= f <= c + delta (delta > 0) is compact, then for some epsilon strictly between 0 and delta the covering number (by open sets contractible in M) of {f <= c + epsilon} is at most that of {f <= c - epsilon} plus the number of critical points in the band, which is infinity, making the bound vacuous as it should be, when there are infinitely many. This is the second deformation lemma: outside a small neighbourhood U of the critical points of the band the flow pushes {f <= c + epsilon} below the level c - epsilon, and since manifolds are locally contractible U can be taken to be a union of one open set contractible in M per critical point; subadditivity of the count then gives the bound. Degenerate critical points are allowed. Red-team checks: every hypothesis needed; statement matches its docstring; no counterpart in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: if f is smooth, t < b, the sublevel set {f <= b} is compact and contains only finitely many critical points, then {f <= t} can be covered by at most as many open sets contractible in M as there are critical points of f in {f <= t}. Proof by strong induction on the number of critical values at most t: if there is no critical point the compact sublevel set is empty (a continuous function attains its minimum on a nonempty compact set, at a critical point); otherwise cross the largest critical value with the second deformation lemma and use the first deformation lemma for the critical-point-free band above it. The auxiliary b > t only provides a compact margin above t. Red-team checks: every hypothesis needed; taking b = t + 1 for t a bound of f on a compact manifold recovers the main Lusternik-Schnirelmann theorem; statement matches its docstring.

Correctly stated: let f be a smooth function on a boundaryless manifold M; if the band of points with a <= f <= b is compact and contains no critical point of f, then the sublevel set {f <= b} needs no more open sets contractible in M to cover it than {f <= a}. This is the first deformation lemma of Lusternik-Schnirelmann theory: flowing down a descending vector field gives a deformation of M, homotopic to the identity, carrying {f <= b} into {f <= a}, and the relative category cannot increase along such a deformation. When a > b it holds trivially by monotonicity, consistent with the statement. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (e.g. an empty band) and each one needed; statement matches its docstring; no counterpart in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: for a smooth function f on a compact smooth manifold M without boundary (finite-dimensional, Hausdorff), the number of critical points of f (points where the derivative vanishes, degenerate ones included, and counted as infinity when there are infinitely many) is at least the least number of open sets, each contractible inside M (inclusion homotopic to a constant map, the sets themselves need not be contractible), needed to cover M. This is the classical Lusternik-Schnirelmann theorem as stated by Kundu-Rudyak (arXiv:2306.07942, Theorem 3.3 with Definition 3.1): #Crit(f) >= 1 + cat M for the normalised category, where a cover U_0,...,U_k gives cat M <= k; the count used here is the unnormalised one (a point has count 1, a lemma in the library), so the two inequalities are the same and there is no off-by-one. Proof idea: if there are infinitely many critical points the bound is trivial; otherwise induct over the finitely many critical values, flowing sublevel sets down along a descending flow, which costs nothing across bands without critical points and at most one contractible-in-M open neighbourhood per critical point when crossing a critical level (manifolds are locally contractible). Connectedness is not assumed, which is harmless; the boundary hypothesis is genuinely needed (the identity function on [0,1] has no critical point). Red-team checks at 956e316250: specialised to the circle, where I proved in Lean that the count is at least 2 (from the non-contractibility of the circle), so the theorem yields at least two critical points for every smooth function on the circle, and the hypotheses are satisfiable there; an infinite critical set gives infinity, not a junk 0; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Says: let u be a convex function (it may take +∞, never −∞) that is finite and differentiable at P-almost every point, and let the law of U have a density. If U = ∇u ∘ s almost everywhere for some s of law P, then s = ∇u* ∘ U almost everywhere, where u* is the Legendre–Fenchel conjugate. So once the convex factor of a polar factorization is fixed, the measure-preserving factor is determined. This is the argument for uniqueness of s in Brenier's Theorem 1.2 (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 1991, Step 2 of the proof, pp. 409–410), where s' is shown to equal ∇u* ∘ ∇u ∘ s' = ∇u* ∘ U. Why it holds: ∇u(x) lies in the subdifferential of u at x, so x lies in the subdifferential of u* at ∇u(x). The conjugate is differentiable almost everywhere for the law of U, so ∇u*(∇u(x)) = x for P-almost every x; then read this identity along s. Red-team checks: it needs no assumption on the measure m beyond the laws; every hypothesis is used. Its hypotheses are met by the output of the polar factorization theorem, and combined with Brenier's uniqueness of the monotone rearrangement it gives uniqueness of the whole factorization (checked in Lean).

Says: on a finite measure space, let P and the law of U have finite second moments, the law of U having a density, and let U = T ∘ s with T an optimal quadratic transport map from P to the law of U and s of law P. Then any map s' of law P whose correlation ∫⟨s', U⟩ with U is at least that of s equals s almost everywhere. So s is the unique correlation maximiser: Brenier's Theorem 1.2(b) (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 1991) in a general form. Why it holds: with finite second moments the quadratic distance equals a second-moment term, fixed by the laws, minus the correlation. So a larger correlation means a quadratic distance no larger, and the unique-minimiser theorem in the same file applies. Red-team checks: specialised to T the identity and s = U on the real line, it gives the equality case of the rearrangement inequality (a map with the law of U whose correlation with U reaches ∫ U² is U itself); every hypothesis is used.

Says: on a finite measure space, let T be an optimal transport map for the cost |x − y|²/2 from P to the law of U, at finite optimal cost, the law of U having a density. If U = T ∘ s with s of law P, then any map s' of law P whose quadratic distance ∫|s' − U|²/2 to U is at most that of s equals s almost everywhere. So s is the unique map of law P closest to U, the projection of U onto the measure-preserving maps in Brenier's polar factorization. Why it holds: the joint law of (s', U) is then an optimal plan. The quadratic cost is symmetric, so exchanging the coordinates gives an optimal plan out of the law of U. That law has a density, so the optimal plan is unique and carried by the graph of a single map V (Brenier's theorem); hence s' = V ∘ U = s. Red-team checks: the finite-cost hypothesis is necessary, since without it the comparison of distances is vacuous; every hypothesis is used. With the companion fact that s minimises this distance, it gives existence and uniqueness of the projection (checked in Lean).

Brenier's polar factorization. Let (α, m) be a probability space and U a measurable map into a finite-dimensional real inner product space such as ℝⁿ, whose law has a density. Let P be a probability law with a density, at finite quadratic transport cost from the law of U. Then there is a convex function u (it may take the value +∞; it is lower semicontinuous, and finite and differentiable around P-almost every point) with three properties: its gradient is the optimal transport map from P to the law of U; the map s = ∇u* ∘ U, where u* is the Legendre–Fenchel conjugate, has law P; and U = ∇u ∘ s for m-almost every point. This is the existence part of Brenier, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 44 (1991), Theorem 1.2. Brenier states it on a bounded domain, with P having the same null sets as Lebesgue measure and U in Lᵖ. Here the domain may be unbounded and the probability space arbitrary, but finite quadratic cost forces U to be square-integrable on a bounded domain, whereas Brenier also allows 1 ≤ p < 2 (recorded as a generality note). Proof idea, as in Brenier: apply the optimal-transport form of Brenier's theorem in both directions between P and the law of U. The gradients of u and of u* are inverse to each other almost everywhere, so s has law P and ∇u ∘ s = U. Uniqueness of s, and the fact that s is the map of law P closest to U, are the companion theorems in the same file. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (U the identity on the uniform law of [0,1]); every hypothesis is used by the proof, though two of them (P being a probability measure, and U being measurable) follow from the others, recorded as a minor note. For m-almost every point ω, u is finite near s(ω) and differentiable there (derived from the conclusion), so the junk value of the gradient never enters. Together with the file's companion results it gives the full theorem, with uniqueness of the pair and the minimising property (checked in Lean).

Says: let μ and the law of U have finite second moments, and let T be an optimal transport map for the cost |x − y|²/2 from μ to the law of U. If U = T ∘ s almost everywhere with s of law μ, then among all maps s' of law μ, s has the largest correlation ∫⟨s', U⟩ with U. This is the maximal-correlation property (b) of Brenier's polar factorization theorem (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 1991, Theorem 1.2), in a general form. Why it holds: the pair (s, U) has the optimal plan of T as its joint law, so its quadratic cost is the least among all pairs (s', U). Expanding |s' − U|² = |s'|² + |U|² − 2⟨s', U⟩, the squared-norm terms depend only on the laws, so least cost means greatest correlation. Red-team checks: specialised to T the identity and s = U, it gives the rearrangement inequality ∫ s'U ≤ ∫ U² for every s' with the law of U. The correlation integrals are genuine: finite second moments make the integrands integrable, so no junk zero enters. Every hypothesis is used.

Uniqueness of the trace: any bounded linear operator from W^{1,p}(Ω) to L^p(∂Ω) that sends the restriction to Ω of every smooth compactly supported function on the whole space to that function's restriction to ∂Ω is the trace operator. This is stronger than textbook uniqueness, since it only asks for agreement on restrictions of test functions (which are continuous up to the boundary), so it implies that the trace is the only bounded operator with the boundary-value property for all functions continuous on the closure. The proof is the standard density argument: restrictions of whole-space test functions are dense in W^{1,p}(Ω) for a bounded Lipschitz domain and p < ∞ (proved, via the bounded extension operator, in the extension file), and two continuous linear maps that agree on a dense set are equal. Red-team checks: the closure-continuous form of uniqueness was derived from it in three lines (compiled); the density theorem it uses is a proved theorem, not a hypothesis.

Existence half of the trace theorem: for a bounded Lipschitz domain and 1 ≤ p < ∞ there is a bounded linear operator W^{1,p}(Ω) → L^p(∂Ω, (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure) whose value on every function with a representative continuous on the closure of Ω is that representative restricted to ∂Ω, almost everywhere. The operator is built by gluing local chart traces with a finite smooth partition of unity whose interior piece vanishes on the boundary, so the boundary pieces sum to one there. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable non-trivially (the interval (−1,1) in dimension one (E zero-dimensional), which is a bounded Lipschitz domain whose boundary measure is counting measure on the two endpoints, compiled); the conclusion is not vacuous, since there the boundary measure gives each endpoint mass one.

Defines the trace operator of a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω in a Euclidean space ℝ × E of dimension n ≥ 1, for 1 ≤ p < ∞: a bounded (continuous) linear map from the Sobolev space W^{1,p}(Ω) to L^p(∂Ω), where ∂Ω carries the (n−1)-dimensional Euclidean Hausdorff measure (Mathlib's normalised Hausdorff measure, a fixed positive multiple of the raw one, so the same L^p space up to an equivalent norm). It is chosen as an operator with the boundary-value property — a Sobolev function with a representative continuous on the closure of Ω has trace equal to that representative restricted to ∂Ω — whose existence is the companion existence theorem; the choice is harmless because the companion uniqueness theorem shows there is only one such operator. This is the classical trace theorem, usually stated for C¹ boundaries and here proved for Lipschitz ones, with p = ∞ excluded as in the classical statement. The Lipschitz-domain hypothesis is the genuine notion: an open set which near every boundary point, after a rigid motion, is the part of a cylinder strictly above the graph of a Lipschitz function, all with one Lipschitz constant. Red-team checks: hypotheses jointly satisfiable, and non-trivially so — on the interval (−1,1) in dimension one (E zero-dimensional), which is a bounded Lipschitz domain whose boundary measure is counting measure on the two endpoints, compiled, the trace of every function continuous on [−1,1] evaluates to its value at the endpoint 1, so the operator is not zero; uniqueness among all operators with the boundary-value property for functions continuous on the closure derived from the uniqueness theorem in three lines (compiled); axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

The defining boundary-value property of the trace: if u in W^{1,p}(Ω) agrees almost everywhere in Ω with a function f continuous on the closure of Ω, then the trace of u equals f almost everywhere on ∂Ω for (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Continuity is required on the closure, not merely in Ω, which is the classical hypothesis u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) ∩ C(Ω̄). It holds because the trace was chosen with this property and such an operator exists: in each Lipschitz boundary chart the localized trace agrees with the classical boundary value, surface measure on the graph patch has the same null sets as tangential Lebesgue measure, and the chart pieces add up to f because the boundary cutoffs of the partition of unity sum to one on ∂Ω. Red-team checks: specialised to the interval (−1,1) in dimension one (E zero-dimensional), which is a bounded Lipschitz domain whose boundary measure is counting measure on the two endpoints, where it gives trace value f(1) at the endpoint 1 (compiled); hypotheses satisfiable; no contradiction derivable.

The trace commutes with multiplication by a smooth function ψ which is bounded together with its gradient on Ω: the trace of ψu is ψ times the trace of u, almost everywhere on ∂Ω. Correct: both sides are continuous and linear in u (multiplication by ψ is bounded on L^p(∂Ω) because |ψ| ≤ M persists on the closure), and they agree on the dense set of restrictions of test functions by the boundary-value property.

The kernel of the trace operator is exactly W^{1,p}_0(Ω), stated as an equality of subspaces; it repackages the preceding equivalence and is the roadmap's target of a trace operator with kernel W^{1,p}_0 for Lipschitz boundaries. Red-team checks: one-line consequence of the equivalence; docstring accurate.

Defines, for one Lipschitz boundary chart and a smooth cutoff ψ supported in the chart cylinder, the localized trace as an L^p function on ∂Ω for surface measure: the chart trace (an L^p function of the tangential variable) is read at the tangential coordinate of each boundary point in the chart, and taken to be zero on the rest of ∂Ω. It is a well-defined bounded operator because surface measure on the graph patch pushes forward to at most (L+1)^{dim E} times tangential Lebesgue measure. Red-team checks: its pointwise formula and its identification with the trace of ψu are proved in this file, so it is the intended object.

Unfolds the previous definition: almost everywhere on ∂Ω, the boundary version of a chart trace equals the chart trace evaluated at the tangential coordinate on the chart's boundary patch, and zero off that patch. Correct, as the composite of reading at the tangential coordinate and extension by zero.

For a Sobolev function with a representative f continuous on the closure of Ω, the boundary version of a chart trace with cutoff ψ is ψ·f almost everywhere on ∂Ω. Correct: inside the chart it reduces to the chart trace agreeing with the classical value ψf at graph points, and outside the chart cylinder both sides vanish because ψ does.

The boundary version of a chart trace with cutoff ψ equals the global trace composed with multiplication by ψ, as operators. Correct: both are continuous and both send the restriction of a test function φ to ψφ on ∂Ω, and these restrictions are dense.

The chart trace, a function of the tangential variable y, vanishes for almost every y whose graph point lies outside the chart cylinder. Correct: the cutoff vanishes at such graph points, so the claim holds for restrictions of test functions, and it passes to all of W^{1,p}(Ω) by density and continuity of restricting to that set of parameters.

If the trace of u on ∂Ω is zero then every chart trace of u is zero. Correct: the boundary version of the chart trace is the trace of ψu, which is ψ times zero; parameters inside the cylinder where the chart trace is nonzero would map to a surface-null set, hence form a Lebesgue-null set by the null-set correspondence, and outside the cylinder the preceding lemma applies.

On a bounded Lipschitz domain and for 1 ≤ p < ∞, a function of W^{1,p}(Ω) lies in W^{1,p}_0(Ω) (the closure of the test functions supported in Ω) exactly when its trace on ∂Ω is zero — the classical trace-zero theorem, usually stated for C¹ boundaries. One direction is the preceding lemma. Conversely, zero trace forces every localized chart trace to vanish (the boundary version of a chart trace is the trace of the cutoff product, and surface and tangential null sets correspond), and a function whose chart traces all vanish lies in W^{1,p}_0 by the chart characterisation proved in the kernel file. Red-team checks: both directions stated; no hypotheses beyond those of the trace operator; axioms only the standard three.

If chart cutoffs ψ_i sum to one on ∂Ω, the sum of the boundary versions of the chart traces of a function with a representative f continuous on the closure is f almost everywhere on ∂Ω. Correct: by the previous lemma the sum is (Σψ_i)·f, which is f on ∂Ω; the summation hypothesis is asked only on the boundary, the weakest form.

Functions in W^{1,p}_0(Ω), the closure of the smooth functions compactly supported in Ω, have zero trace. Correct: a test function supported in the open set Ω vanishes on ∂Ω, so its trace is zero by the boundary-value property, and the kernel of a continuous operator is closed. Red-team checks: statement matches the docstring; the subspace is the standard W^{1,p}_0.

Correctly stated. It says: for a linear functional phi from a module M to a commutative ring R, any x in R, and the functional phi' on M + R sending (m, r) to phi(m) + r x, if the Koszul complex of phi has zero homology in degrees k+2 and k+1, then the Koszul complex of phi' has zero homology in degree k+2. This holds because the Koszul complex of phi' is the cone of multiplication by x on the Koszul complex of phi (Stacks Project, Tag 0628), so H_{k+2} of the new complex sits between H_{k+2} and H_{k+1} of the old one in a long exact sequence, and both of those vanish; the proof does this by hand, writing an element of the (k+2)-nd exterior power of M + R as a + e wedge b. Red-team checks: neither hypothesis can be dropped, since for x = 0 the cone splits and the new H_{k+2} is the direct sum of the old H_{k+2} and H_{k+1}; it is the higher-degree inductive step of the acyclicity theorem for regular sequences and is exercised by that theorem's compiled instances.

Correctly stated. It says: for a linear functional phi from M to a commutative ring R, an element x of R and the functional phi' on M + R sending (m, r) to phi(m) + r x, if the Koszul complex of phi has zero homology in degree 1 and x is a nonzerodivisor on R/phi(M) (which is H_0 of that complex), then the Koszul complex of phi' has zero homology in degree 1. This follows from the cone description (Stacks Project, Tag 0628): a degree-one cycle (m, r) satisfies x r = -phi(m), which lies in phi(M), so r lies in phi(M) by regularity, and the cycle is then corrected to a boundary using exactness of the old complex in degree 1. Red-team checks: the regularity hypothesis is needed (x = 0 on M = 0 gives H_1 = R, the compiled non-example of the main theorem) and so is exactness in degree 1; this is the step of the acyclicity theorem that consumes the regular-sequence hypothesis.

Correctly stated. It says: if x_1, ..., x_n in a commutative ring R form a weakly regular sequence (each x_i is a nonzerodivisor on R/(x_1, ..., x_{i-1}), with no requirement that R/(x) be nonzero), then the Koszul complex K(x) -- the exterior powers of R^n, with K_k the k-th exterior power and differential the contraction sending the i-th basis vector to x_i -- has zero homology in every degree k >= 1. This is the Stacks Project, Tag 062F (such a sequence is Koszul-regular, which by Tag 062E means H_i(K(x)) = 0 for all i other than 0), which, like the Lean statement, needs no nonvanishing condition on R/(x). Why it holds: by induction on n, K(x_1, ..., x_n) is the cone of multiplication by x_n on K(x_1, ..., x_{n-1}) (Stacks Tag 0628); the higher homology then vanishes by the inductive hypothesis, and in degree one the only input needed is that x_n is a nonzerodivisor on R/(x_1, ..., x_{n-1}), which is H_0 of the shorter complex. Together with the isomorphism H_0(K(x)) = R/(x_1, ..., x_n) proved in the Koszul complex's basic file, this says K(x) is a finite free resolution of R/(x); that resolution is not packaged as a single object. Red-team checks: the complex matches Stacks Definition 0622 (the sign (-1)^i with 0-based indexing is Stacks' (-1)^(i+1) with 1-based); every positive degree is covered, including the top degree n, where it says no nonzero r has x_i r = 0 for all i; witnessed at the sequence (2) and at (2, 1) in the integers (weakly regular, though R/(x) = 0); the hypothesis is needed, since for x = (0) in the integers H_1 is nonzero (compiled); no hypothesis is redundant; no Koszul complex in Mathlib at the pinned version and no second one in Tau Ceti.

Under the same hypotheses (a Banach algebra A with a bounded left approximate identity, acting boundedly and associatively on the left of a Banach space E), the set A·E of single products a·z equals the closed linear span of A·E, so A·E is already a closed linear subspace of E. This is the clause 'In particular, A·L is a closed linear subspace of L' of Theorem 2 in W. L. Paschke, Pacific J. Math. 46 (1973) 249–251, which restates Hewitt–Ross (32.22). Proof: products lie in their closed linear span, and conversely every element of that span is a single product a·y by the factorization theorem above, applied with any ε. Red-team audit at 956e316250: every hypothesis is needed (lean_minimal_hypotheses); for A acting on itself it gives A·A = A, i.e. every element of A is a product of two elements.

This is the Cohen–Hewitt factorization theorem. Let A be a real or complex Banach algebra, not necessarily unital, with a left approximate identity (e·b → b for every b) whose elements eventually have norm at most C, acting on a Banach space E on the left through a bounded bilinear, associative action. Then every x in the closed linear span of the products a·z (the essential part of E) can be written x = a·y with ‖a‖ ≤ C, y in the closure of A·x, and ‖y − x‖ < ε for any prescribed ε > 0. This is exactly Theorem 2 of W. L. Paschke, Pacific J. Math. 46 (1973) 249–251, which restates Hewitt–Ross (32.22): there the conclusion reads ‖y − z‖ ≤ δ and the module is a left Banach module, while the Lean version allows any bounded action and gives the strict inequality. It also matches the statement asked for in the Tau Ceti BanachAlgebras roadmap, §A4. The proof is the classical one: in the ℓ¹-unitization of A put a_n = (1 − t)^n + Σ_{k<n} t(1 − t)^k e_k with t(1 + C) = 1/2 and each e_k taken from the approximate identity. Each a_n is invertible with ‖a_n⁻¹‖ ≤ 4^n, the vectors y_n = a_n⁻¹·x form a Cauchy sequence inside the closure of A·x, and in the limit a = Σ t(1 − t)^k e_k satisfies ‖a‖ ≤ C and a·y = x. Conventions: the approximate identity is a proper filter on A (for a net, the filter of its tails), and 'bounded by C' means eventually bounded. After passing to a tail this is the usual uniformly bounded net. No hypothesis C > 0 is needed, since C ≥ 0 follows. Red-team audit at 956e316250: every hypothesis is needed (lean_minimal_hypotheses); the hypotheses can all hold at once (ℝ acting on itself with the approximate identity {1}), so the statement is not vacuous; for A acting on itself it gives the classical Cohen factorization A = A·A with ‖a‖ ≤ C; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Says: if f and g are smooth embeddings of a finite-dimensional real vector space E (the open n-disc ℝⁿ) into a boundaryless smooth manifold M of the same dimension, with the same centre f(0) = g(0), and the Jacobian determinants at 0 of f and of g, both read in the chart of M at that centre, have positive product (the two derivatives give the same orientation), then there is a map H from [0,1] × E to M, smooth jointly in time and space, with H(0,·) = f, H(1,·) = g, every time slice a smooth embedding (an immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image), and H(t,0) = f(0) for all t. This is Hirsch, Differential Topology, Chapter 4, Theorem 6.6 (p. 117) for Eⁿ = ℝⁿ: Hirsch asks that Det D(f₁⁻¹f₀)(0) > 0, and in the chart φ this derivative is D(φg)(0)⁻¹·D(φf)(0) with both factors invertible, so the quotient of the two determinants and their product have the same sign; changing the chart multiplies both determinants by the same nonzero number, so the condition does not depend on the chart. The proof follows Hirsch: shrink both embeddings radially until they land in a Euclidean ball inside the chart at the centre, join them there by the Euclidean disc theorem (rescale each to its derivative at 0, then a path of linear maps of positive relative determinant), and carry the motion back through the inverse chart. Conventions: an isotopy is a jointly smooth family whose time slices are smooth embeddings, the definition Hirsch recalls at the start of Chapter 8 (p. 177); his Chapter 4 wording (p. 111) also asks the track (x,t) ↦ (H(t,x),t) to be an embedding, which is automatic on compact pieces such as closed discs. Dimension 0 is included. Moving the centre and extending to an ambient isotopy (Hirsch 8.3.1) are not claimed, as the file says. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (f = g = identity of ℝ²) and discriminating (the identity and x ↦ -x on ℝ fail them); both hypotheses needed (the conclusion at t = 1 forces f(0) = g(0)); the derivative in the hypothesis is a genuine derivative, not a junk value; M = E recovers the Euclidean disc theorem; in dimension 0 the hypothesis is 0 < 1·1; no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti version.

Correctly stated: for u a limit in operator norm of continuous finite-rank operators on a Banach space over a complete nontrivially normed field, and μ a nonzero scalar, μ is an eigenvalue of u (u x = μ x for some nonzero x) exactly when μ lies in the spectrum of u, i.e. u − μ has no bounded inverse; the spectrum is taken in the algebra of bounded operators, as the docstring says. This is the Riesz–Schauder description of the nonzero spectrum. Mathlib proves the same statement for compact operators (IsCompactOperator.hasEigenvalue_iff_mem_spectrum), but that does not cover this one: over a field that is not locally compact, such as the completed algebraic closure of the p-adics, no nonzero finite-rank operator is compact, and that is exactly the setting of Serre 1962. Proof idea: rescale to 1 − μ⁻¹u, whose kernel is the μ-eigenspace, and apply the Fredholm alternative (1 − μ⁻¹u is invertible exactly when injective). The hypothesis μ ≠ 0 is needed: an injective completely continuous operator on an infinite-dimensional space has 0 in its spectrum without 0 being an eigenvalue. Red-team audit at 956e3162: checked on the identity of the p-adic numbers (eigenvalue 1, in the spectrum).

Correctly stated: for u a limit in operator norm of continuous finite-rank operators on a Banach space over a complete nontrivially normed field, the index of 1 − u, the dimension of its kernel minus the codimension of its range, is 0. Since the companion result shows 1 − u is Fredholm, both dimensions are finite and the zero is genuine rather than the default value given to infinite dimensions; together they are exactly the corollary to Proposition 12 in Serre 1962 (§7): the image of 1 − u has finite codimension equal to the dimension of the kernel. Proof idea: 1 − u is an invertible operator plus a finite-rank one; invertible operators have index 0 and finite-rank perturbations do not change the index. Red-team audit at 956e3162: complete continuity is needed (u = 1 − S with S the unilateral shift on a Hilbert space gives index −1); checked on u = 0 and on a rank-one projection; the simp attribute fires once the hypothesis is supplied.

Correctly stated: if u is a bounded operator on a Banach space E over a complete nontrivially normed field and u is a limit, in operator norm, of continuous operators of finite rank (Serre's 'completely continuous' operators, Serre 1962, §3), then 1 − u is a Fredholm operator in the strong sense of Mathlib's definition: its range is closed and of finite codimension, its kernel is finite-dimensional and has a closed complement, and it is open onto its range. This is the Fredholm half of the corollary to Proposition 12 of Serre, Endomorphismes complètement continus des espaces de Banach p-adiques (1962, §7, 'alternative de Fredholm'), which Serre proves over a complete non-archimedean field for spaces with an orthonormal basis; here neither restriction is imposed, so real and complex Banach spaces are covered too. Proof idea: choose a finite-rank v with ‖u − v‖ ≤ 1/2; the Neumann series makes 1 − (u − v) invertible, so 1 − u is an invertible operator plus a finite-rank one, and adding a finite-rank operator to a Fredholm operator keeps it Fredholm. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the hypotheses are satisfiable (u = 0); the complete-continuity hypothesis is needed (u = identity of an infinite-dimensional space gives 1 − u = 0); checked on u = 0 and on a rank-one projection; the file elaborates in under 1 s.

Correctly stated: the Fredholm alternative. If u is a limit in operator norm of continuous finite-rank operators on a Banach space E over a complete nontrivially normed field, then 1 − u has a bounded two-sided inverse exactly when it is injective. Serre 1962 (§7, corollary to Proposition 12, 'alternative de Fredholm') proves this for 1 − au and every scalar a, over a complete non-archimedean field and for spaces with an orthonormal basis; the Lean statement gives Serre's form by applying it to au (still completely continuous; checked in Lean), and needs neither an orthonormal basis nor a non-archimedean norm, so it is a full and more general version of the cited result. Proof idea: 1 − u is Fredholm of index 0, so an injective 1 − u has cokernel of dimension 0, i.e. is onto, and the open mapping theorem makes a bounded bijection on a Banach space invertible. Red-team audit at 956e3162: hypotheses satisfiable (u = 0, where 1 − u is the identity); for a rank-one projection P both sides fail, since 1 − P kills the image vector; complete continuity is needed (u = 1 − S with S the unilateral shift gives an injective, non-invertible 1 − u); completeness of E is needed for the open mapping step. Completeness of the field turns out not to be needed for this statement (recorded as a minor generality note, not a correctness issue).

Correctly stated: for u a limit in operator norm of continuous finite-rank operators on a Banach space over a complete nontrivially normed field, 1 − u has a bounded inverse exactly when it is surjective. This is the other half of the Fredholm alternative in Serre 1962 (§7, corollary to Proposition 12: the codimension of the image of 1 − au equals the dimension of its kernel), again without Serre's orthonormal-basis and non-archimedean assumptions. Proof idea: 1 − u is Fredholm of index 0, so a surjective 1 − u has kernel of dimension 0, hence is bijective, and the open mapping theorem gives a bounded inverse. Red-team audit at 956e3162: hypotheses satisfiable (u = 0); for a rank-one projection P, 1 − P is neither onto nor invertible, as both sides predict; complete continuity is needed (u = 1 − T with T the backward shift gives a surjective, non-invertible 1 − u).

Says: let L be a finite extension of the nonarchimedean local field K, embedded in an algebraic closure of K, over which the curve acquires good reduction (after a change of coordinates over L the equation has integral coefficients and unit discriminant); if σ is an element of the inertia group of K that fixes L, n is an integer not divisible by the residue characteristic, and P is a point over the algebraic closure with σ(nP) = nP, then σ(P) = P, and in particular σ fixes every n-torsion point. This is Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, VII.4.1(a) (torsion of order prime to p is unramified at good reduction) applied over L, in the form its proof gives: such a σ lies in the inertia group of L, σ(P) − P is n-torsion and reduces to the identity because inertia acts trivially on the residue field, and reduction is injective on torsion of order prime to p. The proof passes to a finite normal extension M containing L and the coordinates of P, where σ restricts into the inertia group of M over L, and applies the good-reduction result there. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): docstring matches the statement clause by clause; it is the forward lemma's engine and is exercised by the compiled good-reduction specialisation of the forward theorem; only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: if the curve has potential good reduction, there is a finite extension M of K inside the algebraic closure such that every inertia element fixing M acts trivially on T_ℓ(E) for every prime ℓ different from the residue characteristic. This is the first step of Silverman's proof of VII.7.3: take a finite extension over which E has good reduction; by VII.7.1 (or VII.4.1) its inertia acts trivially on T_ℓ(E), and the inertia of that extension is the set of inertia elements of K fixing it. Potential good reduction is Silverman's definition (VII §5: good reduction over some finite extension), here with a minimal model taken after the base change. Red-team checks: the single hypothesis is the potential-good-reduction assumption; exercised, through the forward theorem, by a compiled specialisation at a curve with good reduction over K; only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: if the curve has potential good reduction and ℓ is a prime different from the residue characteristic, then the image of the inertia group of K in the automorphisms of T_ℓ(E) is a finite set, i.e. inertia acts through a finite quotient. This is the forward implication of Silverman, AEC VII.7.3. Proof idea, as in Silverman: by the previous lemma the inertia elements fixing a finite extension M act trivially, so the action of an inertia element depends only on its restriction to the normal closure of M, whose Galois group over K is finite. It is the image of the inertia group, not of the whole Galois group (which is infinite in general), and no elliptic-curve hypothesis is needed since potential good reduction already forces a nonzero discriminant. Red-team checks: compiled specialisation: a curve with good reduction over K gets a finite inertia image; the condition ℓ ≠ p cannot be dropped (for ℓ = p and good ordinary reduction inertia acts on the p-adic Tate module through the infinite cyclotomic character); only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: let W be an elliptic curve and ℓ a prime invertible in K (a weaker condition than being different from the residue characteristic); if the image of the inertia group in the automorphisms of T_ℓ(E) is finite, then there is a finite extension M of K inside the algebraic closure such that every inertia element fixing M acts trivially on T_ℓ(E). Proof idea: take M generated by the ℓ²-torsion points; an inertia element fixing M fixes E[ℓ²], and an automorphism of the Tate module of finite order that is trivial modulo ℓ² with ℓ² ≥ 3 is the identity (Serre's lemma), so it acts trivially. Silverman's proof of VII.7.3 makes the same reduction with the fixed field of the kernel of the finite quotient. Red-team checks: both explicit hypotheses load-bearing (minimal-hypotheses tool); the elliptic-curve hypothesis is used (the proof fails without it); only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: for an elliptic curve E over a nonarchimedean local field K (locally compact, nontrivially valued, so complete with finite residue field) and any prime ℓ different from the residue characteristic, E has potential good reduction exactly when the image of the inertia group of K acting on the ℓ-adic Tate module T_ℓ(E) = lim E[ℓ^n] is finite, that is, inertia acts through a finite quotient. This is Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves (2nd ed.), Corollary VII.7.3, read in the text: "E has potential good reduction if and only if the inertia group acts on the Tate module through a finite quotient for some (all) primes ℓ ≠ char(k)"; the Lean statement holds for each such ℓ, which gives both "some" and "all". Silverman's chapter VII assumes K and its residue field perfect; here the residue field is finite (so perfect) and K may also be a Laurent-series field over a finite field (positive characteristic), where automorphisms of the algebraic closure are the same as those of the separable closure and the ℓ-power torsion points lie in the separable closure, so nothing changes. Proof: forward via good reduction over a finite extension and the finite Galois group of its normal closure; converse via the ℓ²-division field, Serre's lemma and the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion VII.7.1 over that field. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (simp_all, grind, aesop fail); the residue-characteristic hypothesis is load-bearing (minimal-hypotheses tool); compiled specialisations: multiplicative reduction gives an infinite inertia image, good reduction a finite one; the statement elaborates at the 5-adic numbers with ℓ = 2; only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: for an elliptic curve over a nonarchimedean local field K and a prime ℓ different from the residue characteristic, if inertia acts on T_ℓ(E) through a finite quotient (finite image), then the curve has potential good reduction. This is the converse implication of Silverman, AEC VII.7.3. It chains the two previous results: a finite image makes the inertia of a finite extension act trivially, and that gives good reduction over the extension by the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion (VII.7.1). Red-team checks: both explicit hypotheses load-bearing (minimal-hypotheses tool); compiled specialisation: a curve with multiplicative reduction gets an infinite inertia image; only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: let W be an elliptic curve (nonzero discriminant; the section assumes this), M a finite extension of K inside the algebraic closure, ℓ a prime different from the residue characteristic; if every inertia element of K fixing M acts trivially on T_ℓ(E), then W has potential good reduction (indeed good reduction over M). This is the converse step of Silverman's proof of VII.7.3: the inertia group of M consists of the inertia elements of K fixing M, so the Tate module is unramified over M and the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion (Silverman VII.7.1, (c) implies (a)) gives good reduction over M. The elliptic-curve hypothesis is necessary: for the nodal cubic the nonsingular points form the multiplicative group, whose Tate module is unramified, yet there is no potential good reduction. Red-team checks: every explicit hypothesis load-bearing (minimal-hypotheses tool); only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Says: under the same hypotheses (W acquires good reduction over a finite extension L embedded in the algebraic closure), every element of the inertia group of K that fixes L acts trivially on the ℓ-adic Tate module T_ℓ(E) = lim E[ℓ^n], for every prime ℓ different from the residue characteristic. It is the previous lemma applied to the ℓ^n-torsion points for every n, which is exactly how Silverman VII.4.1(b) deduces that T_ℓ(E) is unramified from (a). Red-team checks: each explicit hypothesis needed (minimal-hypotheses tool); docstring matches; only the standard axioms (propext, choice, quotient soundness).

Correctly stated. It says: if E is a complex normed space (not necessarily complete) and every continuous linear functional applied to f gives a complex-differentiable function on an open set U of the plane, then f is continuous in norm on U. This is part (a) of Rudin, Functional Analysis (2nd ed.), Theorem 3.31, and Rudin remarks after its proof (p. 84) that this part uses neither metrizability nor completeness, matching the absence of a completeness assumption here. Why it holds: on a small closed disc in U each scalar function is bounded, so by the uniform boundedness principle f is norm-bounded there; the Cauchy estimate then makes each scalar function Lipschitz with constant proportional to the norm of the functional, and Hahn-Banach turns this into a Lipschitz bound for f itself. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; specialised at E = C; the openness of U turns out to be unnecessary (recorded separately as a generality improvement), which makes the statement weaker than it could be but not incorrect.

Correctly stated. For a function into a complex Banach space and an open set U of the plane, f is holomorphic on U exactly when every continuous linear functional applied to f is holomorphic on U. One direction is the chain rule (a continuous linear map composed with a holomorphic map is holomorphic); the other is Dunford's theorem, the preceding declaration. Red-team checks: completeness and openness are both needed for the converse (same counterexamples as for Dunford's theorem), and no contradiction is derivable from the hypotheses.

Correctly stated (Dunford's theorem). It says: let E be a complete normed complex vector space (a complex Banach space), U an open subset of the complex plane, and f a function such that applying any continuous linear functional to f gives an ordinary holomorphic scalar function on U; then f itself is holomorphic on U, i.e. complex differentiable in the norm of E. Rudin, Functional Analysis (2nd ed.), Definition 3.30 and Theorem 3.31(c) (pp. 82-83) prove this for complex Fréchet spaces, and Haak-Haase, arXiv:2403.11712, Remark 2.3(3a), state exactly this Banach-space form, so the Lean statement is the Banach-space case of Rudin's theorem with nothing added. Why it holds: the uniform boundedness principle makes f locally bounded and then continuous; a continuous Banach-valued f has a Cauchy integral over each small circle, which is analytic inside it, and since every functional takes the same value on f and on that integral (scalar Cauchy formula) and functionals separate points, f equals an analytic function near each point. Both hypotheses are genuinely needed: without completeness, the span of the vectors (z^n)_n (|z|<1) inside l^2 carries a weakly holomorphic map whose derivative at 0, the unit vector e_1, lies outside that span; without openness, on U = {0} together with the points 1/n, the map with f(1/n) = e_n/n in l^2 and f(0) = 0 is weakly but not strongly differentiable at 0. Red-team checks (claude-opus-5-5 at 956e3162): no separability, reflexivity or local-boundedness assumption is smuggled in; the hypothesis quantifies over all continuous functionals; no contradiction is derivable from the hypotheses (f = 0 meets them); specialised at E = C and at E = C x C with f(z) = (z, z^2); no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (grep of the pinned Mathlib, exact?, Loogle, LeanSearch, LeanFinder).

Correctly stated. A function from the complex plane into a complex Banach space is entire (complex differentiable everywhere) exactly when every continuous linear functional applied to it is entire; it is the preceding equivalence with U the whole plane. Red-team checks: completeness is needed (f(z) = (z^n/n!)_n, viewed in the span of its own values inside l^2, is weakly entire but its derivative at 0, the unit vector e_1, leaves that span); checked on the vector-valued example z -> (z, z^2).

Correct: if a bounded set s (not necessarily measurable) has outer volume at least that of a closed ball of radius diam s / 2, then s lies inside some closed ball of radius diam s / 2. Together with the isodiametric inequality this says an extremal set fits in a ball of the same diameter, which fails for general sets (an equilateral triangle of side d lies in no disc of radius d/2). The proof passes to the closed convex hull H, which has the same diameter and therefore exactly the ball's volume; Brunn-Minkowski for H and its reflection with weight 1/2 is then an equality, and the equality case for convex bodies (equality only for translates and dilates; Gardner, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 39 (2002), eq. (2) and the sentence after it) makes the reflection a translate of H, so H is centrally symmetric, and a centrally symmetric set of diameter d lies in the ball of radius d/2 about its centre. A set of volume zero is handled separately: it must have diameter 0. Red-team checks at 956e3162: both hypotheses needed (an unbounded set is assigned diameter 0 and fits in no single point; without the volume condition, the triangle); standard axioms only.

Correct: a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set s has the volume of a closed ball of radius diam s / 2 if and only if s agrees, up to a null set, with some closed ball of that radius. This is the equality case of the isodiametric inequality as in Maggi, Ponsiglione and Pratelli, 'Quantitative stability in the isodiametric inequality via the isoperimetric inequality', eq. (1.1) ('equality holds if and only if E is (equivalent to) a ball'), with the radius tied to the diameter of s itself, so a null modification cannot enlarge the allowed ball. The forward direction combines the containment theorem (s lies in a ball of radius diam s / 2) with the fact that a measurable subset of a ball with the ball's volume differs from it by a null set; the converse is invariance of volume under null modifications and translations. Measurability is needed for the forward direction, since a non-measurable subset of a ball can have full outer measure without filling the ball up to a null set. Red-team checks at 956e3162: checked on closed and open discs; boundedness is removable only through the zero-diameter convention for unbounded sets (recorded as a nit); standard axioms only.

Correct: a nonempty closed bounded set s (a compact set, for instance a convex body) has the volume of a closed ball of radius diam s / 2 exactly when s is itself a closed ball of radius diam s / 2, i.e. closed balls are the only compact volume maximisers at fixed diameter. This is the equality case in Maggi, Ponsiglione and Pratelli, 'Quantitative stability in the isodiametric inequality via the isoperimetric inequality', eq. (1.1), sharpened from 'equivalent to a ball' to literal equality by closedness. Proof: s lies in a closed ball B of radius diam s / 2 with the same volume; the open ball minus s is then an open null set, hence empty, so s contains the open ball and, being closed, its closure B; radius 0 (a single point) is handled directly. Each hypothesis is needed in positive dimension: the empty set has the volume of a radius-0 ball but is no ball, the open unit disc has the closed disc's volume but is not closed, and a line has (by convention) diameter 0 and volume 0 without being a point; in dimension 0 the space is a point and both sides hold. Red-team checks at 956e3162: the closed unit disc satisfies it; a two-point set correctly fails both sides; the open disc, empty set and dimension-0 cases compiled; standard axioms only.

Correct: for every set s, bounded or not, the outer volume of s is at most (extended diameter of s / 2)^n times the volume of the unit ball, where the extended diameter of an unbounded set is infinite. For bounded sets this is the isodiametric inequality of this file (Maggi, Ponsiglione and Pratelli, 'Quantitative stability in the isodiametric inequality via the isoperimetric inequality', eq. (1.1)); for an unbounded set in positive dimension the right side is infinite, so the bound holds trivially, and in dimension 0 every set is bounded. This form avoids the convention that an unbounded set has real diameter 0. Red-team checks at 956e3162: both cases checked (the whole space gives infinity <= infinity); dimension 0 handled separately in the proof; standard axioms only.

Correct: a bounded set s in an n-dimensional real inner product space has outer volume at most (diam s / 2)^n times the volume of the unit ball, i.e. omega_n (diam s / 2)^n, which is the isodiametric inequality in the normalized form of Maggi, Ponsiglione and Pratelli, 'Quantitative stability in the isodiametric inequality via the isoperimetric inequality', eq. (1.1) (written there as (diam E / 2)^n |B| >= |E|). It follows from the closed-ball form in this file by the scaling law that a closed ball of radius r has r^n times the volume of the unit ball. On Euclidean n-space the constant omega_n is the familiar pi^(n/2)/Gamma(n/2+1). Boundedness is needed because an unbounded set is assigned diameter 0; no measurability is required, since the bound is on outer volume. Red-team checks at 956e3162: specialised to Euclidean n-space through Mathlib's ball-volume formula; sharp for the closed unit disc (pi = 1 times pi); the whole line confirms boundedness is needed; the pinned Mathlib has only the sup-norm analogue (volume at most diameter^n), not this Euclidean statement.

Correct: in a finite-dimensional real inner product space (for example Euclidean n-space with Lebesgue measure), every bounded set, measurable or not, has outer volume at most the volume of a closed ball whose radius is half the set's diameter, wherever that ball is centred. This is the isodiametric inequality as stated in Maggi, Ponsiglione and Pratelli, 'Quantitative stability in the isodiametric inequality via the isoperimetric inequality', eq. (1.1). The proof is the classical one: replace the set by its closure (same diameter, at least the same outer volume), apply the Brunn-Minkowski inequality to half the closure and half its reflection through the origin, which shows that half the difference body has at least the closure's volume, and observe that half the difference body lies in the ball of radius diameter/2 about the origin. Boundedness is genuinely needed, since the diameter of an unbounded set is recorded as 0 and the whole space would then violate the bound; in dimension 0 both sides equal 1 for a nonempty set. Red-team checks at 956e3162: every hypothesis needed (the whole space is a counterexample without boundedness); specialised to Euclidean n-space it gives exactly volume <= (pi^(n/2)/Gamma(n/2+1)) (diam/2)^n; equality for the closed unit disc; no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti; standard axioms only.

Correct: the isodiametric bound in real numbers: for a bounded set s, its (finite) outer volume is at most (diam s / 2)^n times the volume of the unit ball. Bounded sets have finite outer volume, so passing from extended to real values loses nothing. Boundedness is needed, since an unbounded set of finite positive area would otherwise be bounded by 0. Red-team checks at 956e3162: derived from the extended-valued form by monotonicity of the conversion to reals on finite values; no further hypotheses.

Defines the Frobenius characteristic in d ≥ n variables: the complex-linear isomorphism from the complex class functions on the symmetric group Sₙ onto the symmetric polynomials of degree n in d variables that sends the character of each Specht module S^μ to the Schur polynomial s_μ. It is built by matching two bases indexed by the partitions of n: the irreducible (Specht) characters, a basis of the class functions, and the Schur polynomials, a basis of the degree-n symmetric polynomials once d ≥ n (with fewer variables the Schur polynomials of partitions with more than d parts vanish and no such isomorphism exists, so the hypothesis d ≥ n is the right one). Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7 defines the characteristic map by ch(f) = (1/n!) Σ_w f(w) p_ρ(w) (7.2), shows ch(χ^λ) = s_λ (7.5) and that ch is an isometric isomorphism (7.3); in this file the formula (frobeniusCharacteristic_eq_sum_psumPart) and the isometry (hallInner_frobeniusCharacteristic) are proved, so this basis-defined map is Macdonald's. The labelling agrees with his: the Specht character of (n) is the trivial character and that of (1ⁿ) the sign (his §7 Example 1), and s_(n) = h_n, s_(1ⁿ) = e_n. Red-team checks: d ≥ n needed for the map to exist; Frobenius's formula specialised at n = 2 gives the textbook p_(2) = s_(2) − s_(1,1) and p_(1,1) = s_(2) + s_(1,1); no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; only standard axioms.

Gives the explicit formula ch(f) = Σ_μ ⟨χ^μ, f⟩ s_μ, summed over all partitions μ of n, for a complex class function f and d ≥ n variables. Correct: expand f in the orthonormal basis of Specht characters, whose coefficients are the pairings ⟨χ^μ, f⟩, and apply ch, which sends χ^μ to s_μ; with d ≥ n every partition of n indexes a Schur basis vector, so nothing is lost.

The cycle-type formula: ch(f) = (1/n!) Σ over π in Sₙ of f(π) p_ρ(π) for every complex class function f, in d ≥ n variables. This is exactly Macdonald's definition of the characteristic map, (7.2) in Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7, so it identifies the basis-defined map of this file with the classical one. Both sides are linear in f, and on the Specht characters the identity is the inverse Frobenius formula.

Says that the Frobenius characteristic sends the character of the complex Specht module S^μ to the Schur polynomial s_μ in d ≥ n variables, which is (7.5) ch(χ^μ) = s_μ in Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7. It holds by construction, the map matching the basis of Specht characters with the Schur basis partition by partition. Red-team checks: a simp lemma whose left side is in simp normal form (simp without it makes no progress); no duplicate.

The Frobenius characteristic is an isometry: for complex class functions f, g on Sₙ and d ≥ n variables, the Hall inner product of ch(f) and ch(g) equals (1/n!) Σ_π f(π) g(π⁻¹). That is exactly the scalar product on class functions with which Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7 opens, and his isometry statement (7.3); the pairing is bilinear rather than Hermitian, as in Macdonald, and on Sₙ it equals (1/n!) Σ f(π) g(π) since every permutation is conjugate to its inverse. The Hall inner product is defined here by making the Schur polynomials orthonormal, which is Macdonald's (4.8); his defining property ⟨h_μ, m_ν⟩ = δ_μν (4.5) is a theorem in the Hall inner product file and ⟨p_ρ, p_σ⟩ = z_ρ δ_ρσ (4.7) is hallInner_psumPart here. The proof checks the identity on the basis of Specht characters, where both sides are δ_μν by orthonormality. Red-team checks: d ≥ n needed for the map; simp lemma in normal form; only standard axioms.

The power sums are orthogonal for the Hall inner product: ⟨p_ρ, p_ρ'⟩ is z_ρ if ρ = ρ' and 0 otherwise, where z_ρ = Π_i i^(m_i) m_i! with m_i the number of parts of ρ equal to i, in at least n variables and over any commutative ring. This is (4.7) in Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §4, with his z_λ from §2. It follows from ⟨p_ρ, s_μ⟩ = χ^μ(ρ) and the column orthogonality of the character table of Sₙ. Red-team checks: the hypothesis of at least n variables is needed (with one variable, ⟨p_(2), p_(1,1)⟩ = 1 over ℚ, checked in Lean); simp lemma in normal form.

Says that ⟨p_ρ, s_μ⟩ = χ^μ(ρ) for the Hall inner product, for every partition μ of n with at most as many parts as there are variables, over any commutative ring. This is (7.7), χ^λ_ρ = ⟨s_λ, p_ρ⟩, in Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7; here it is Frobenius's formula read in the Schur basis, in which the Hall product pairs a polynomial with s_μ by taking its s_μ-coefficient.

Frobenius's formula: for a partition ρ of n, the power-sum product p_ρ = p_ρ1 p_ρ2 ⋯ equals Σ_λ χ^λ(ρ) s_λ over the partitions λ of n, where χ^λ(ρ) is the value of the irreducible character of Sₙ indexed by λ on permutations of cycle type ρ. This is (7.8) in Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7: the transition matrix from the Schur functions to the power sums is the character table of Sₙ. It is stated in any finite set of variables and over any commutative ring, with integer coefficients; when there are fewer variables than parts the extra Schur polynomials are zero, so nothing breaks. The proof expands both sides in the monomial symmetric polynomials (p_ρ through fixed points of a permutation of cycle type ρ on tabloids, s_λ through Kostka numbers) and matches the coefficients by Young's rule. Red-team checks: specialised at n = 2 in two variables over ℚ it gives p_(2) = s_(2) − s_(1,1) and p_(1,1) = s_(2) + s_(1,1), with s_(2) = h_2 and s_(1,1) = e_2, the textbook values (checked in Lean); the character labelling (trivial for (n), sign for (1ⁿ)) matches Macdonald §7 Example 1; no Mathlib duplicate.

Says that the coefficient of s_μ in the Schur expansion of ch(f) is the character pairing ⟨χ^μ, f⟩ = (1/n!) Σ_π χ^μ(π) f(π⁻¹). Correct because the Specht characters are orthonormal for this pairing, so ⟨χ^μ, f⟩ is the χ^μ-coordinate of f, and ch sends χ^μ to s_μ. Red-team checks: simp lemma in normal form; d ≥ n is needed for the map itself.

The inverse of Frobenius's formula: Σ over π in Sₙ of χ^μ(π) p_ρ(π) equals n!·s_μ, where ρ(π) is the cycle type of π with fixed points counted as parts 1. Grouping permutations by cycle type (n!/z_ρ of them have type ρ) this is s_μ = Σ_ρ z_ρ⁻¹ χ^μ(ρ) p_ρ, which is (7.2) combined with (7.5) in Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I §7; it is stated without dividing by n!, so it holds over every commutative ring and in any finite set of variables. It is proved by the same monomial expansion as Frobenius's formula, using Young's rule in its character-pairing form.

Says: for any ring R, commutative or not, and any left R-module M, there is an injective R-module Q and an injective linear map from M into Q whose image is essential in Q (every nonzero submodule of Q meets the image in a nonzero element); that is, Q is an injective envelope (injective hull) of M. Q is produced in the same universe (size class) as M, which is why the statement assumes the ring is small relative to that universe; this is automatic when R and M live in the same universe, and for arbitrary universes the envelope still exists one universe up (checked: derived from this theorem by lifting M). The Stacks Project proves the same statement for commutative rings (Lemma 47.5.2, Tag 08Y3: embed M in an injective module and take a maximal essential extension inside it by Zorn's lemma), with 'essential' defined exactly as here (Definition 47.2.1, Tag 08XJ); nothing in that argument uses commutativity, and the Lean proof is that argument: embed M in an injective module (Mathlib: module categories have enough injectives), then apply the companion result that a maximal essential extension of M inside an injective module is injective. Red-team checks: no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses (only a ring and a module); instantiated at the noncommutative ring of 2x2 rational matrices acting on column vectors; the predicate produced is not vacuous (Z -> Q over Z checked to be an injective envelope, the identity of Z checked not to be one); no duplicate in Mathlib (no injective hulls at the pin) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti; standard axioms only.

Says: if Q is an injective module over a ring R (commutative or not) and i is an injective linear map from M into Q, then some submodule P of Q containing the image of M is itself an injective module in which the image of M is essential, so the corestriction of i to P is an injective envelope of M; in words, an injective envelope of M can be found inside any injective module containing M. The Stacks Project states this for commutative rings: the proof of Lemma 47.5.2 (Tag 08Y3) builds the hull as a maximal essential extension inside a given injective module, and Lemma 47.5.3(5) (Tag 08Y4) makes the hull a direct summand of any injective module containing M; the argument does not use commutativity. Proof idea: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal essential extension E of the image inside Q, and again a submodule K maximal with K meeting E only in 0; E then embeds essentially into Q/K, the inclusion of E into Q extends to a map Q/K -> Q, which is injective by essentiality and has image exactly E by maximality, so Q -> Q/K -> E retracts Q onto E and E is injective as a retract of an injective module.
