Red-team checks: hypotheses consistent (instantiated at Z inside Q over Z); both explicit hypotheses are needed; injectivity of P and essentiality of the image are proved, not assumed; the ring-smallness assumption turns out to be unnecessary (recorded as a generality finding) but is automatic in the usual same-universe case, so it excludes no standard case.

The report is right about the prose, and the Lean is correct. The hypothesis `hmax` quantifies over `K` with `K ≤ I`, and, as the module docstring and the docstring of `eq_of_le_of_finrank_quotientLie_le` say, `K ≤ I` means the subgroup cut out by `K` contains the one cut out by `I`. So in the subgroup language of the first sentence, the members that must be dimension-dominated are those containing the given subgroup, not those contained in it; the family {1, 𝔾ₐ} shows the stated version would be false. The fix replaces "contained in" by "containing" and notes the ideal-side reading (`K ≤ I`) for clarity.

Correctly stated: under the hypotheses of Newman's Tauberian theorem (f measurable and bounded by M on [0,∞), its Laplace transform on Re z > 0 agreeing with a function G holomorphic on an open set containing Re z ≥ 0), for every radius R > 0 and every ε > 0 one has |G(0) − ∫₀^T f(t) dt| ≤ 2M/R + ε for all sufficiently large T. This is the central estimate in Zagier's proof of the Analytic Theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly 104 (1997), 705–708): after division by 2πi the right and left semicircles each contribute at most M/R (Zagier's B/R), and the detour integral tends to 0 as T → ∞ because the kernel e^{Tz} decays where Re z < 0; the detour width is allowed to depend on R, as in Zagier. Red-team checks: every hypothesis used; it implies the main theorem on letting R → ∞, and its hypotheses hold for f(t) = e^{−t}; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: for R, δ > 0, a function G holomorphic on an open convex set containing the right semicircle |z| = R, Re z ≥ 0 and Newman's parabolic detour from iR to −iR through the left half-plane, the truncated transform G_T(z) = ∫₀^T f(t)e^{−zt} dt of a function f integrable on [0, T], and Newman's kernel k_T(z) = e^{Tz}(1 + z²/R²)/z, it states that the integral of (G − G_T)k_T over the right semicircle (from −iR to iR) plus the integral of G k_T over the detour (from iR back to −iR) equals 2πi(G(0) − ∫₀^T f(t) dt) plus the integral of G_T k_T over the left semicircle (from iR to −iR), each integral including the velocity of its parametrisation. This is Cauchy's integral formula for (G − G_T)e^{Tz}(1 + z²/R²) on the closed contour formed by the right semicircle and the detour (the factor e^{Tz}(1 + z²/R²) equals 1 at 0, and G_T(0) = ∫₀^T f), combined with replacing the left semicircle by the detour for the entire function G_T: the contour step of Zagier's proof of the Analytic Theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly 104 (1997), 705–708). Red-team checks: docstring matches the statement (orientations, endpoints, velocity factors); every hypothesis used; hypotheses satisfiable (the whole plane as the convex set, any entire G); only the standard axioms; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: this is Newman's Tauberian theorem. If f is a complex-valued function on [0,∞) that is measurable there (up to a null set) and bounded by M, and its Laplace transform ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^{−zt} dt, which converges for Re z > 0, agrees on that open half-plane with a function G holomorphic on an open set containing the closed half-plane Re z ≥ 0, then the truncated integrals ∫₀^T f(t) dt converge to G(0) as T → ∞. This is clause for clause the Analytic Theorem of D. Zagier, Newman's short proof of the prime number theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly 104 (1997), 705–708): f bounded and locally integrable (here boundedness plus measurability gives local integrability), g(z) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^{−zt} dt for Re z > 0 extends holomorphically to Re z ≥ 0, and then ∫₀^∞ f(t) dt exists and equals g(0); the Lean conclusion is exactly this improper integral, G(0) is the value of the extension, and values of f at negative t play no role. The proof is Newman's: for each R, Cauchy's formula with the kernel e^{Tz}(1 + z²/R²)/z on the right semicircle of radius R closed by a detour through the left half-plane inside the domain of holomorphy bounds |G(0) − ∫₀^T f| by 2M/R plus a term tending to 0, and then R → ∞. For Re z > 0 the Laplace integral genuinely converges (bounded times exponentially decaying), so the hypothesis never uses the default value of a divergent integral. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): Zagier's statement read in the paper itself; specialised to f(t) = e^{−t}, G(z) = 1/(z + 1) on Re z > −1/2, giving ∫₀^T e^{−t} dt → 1 (compiles), so the hypotheses hold for nonzero data and are not contradictory; f = 1 has transform 1/z, which does not extend holomorphically to 0, consistent with ∫₀^T 1 = T diverging; every hypothesis is used; only the standard axioms; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti (five-way search, git grep).

Correctly stated: for each nonzero integer D there is a finite list of integral binary quadratic forms such that every form of discriminant D, primitive or not, definite or indefinite, is carried to a form on the list by an integer change of variables of determinant 1. Why: for nonsquare D, Lagrange reduction gives an equivalent form with |b| ≤ |a| ≤ |c|, and then 3|a||c| ≤ |D| with a, c nonzero bounds all three coefficients; for D = s² ≠ 0 every form is equivalent to sxy + cy² with 0 ≤ c < |s|. The hypothesis D ≠ 0 is genuinely needed: the forms nx² (n = 1, 2, 3, …) all have discriminant 0 and pairwise different gcds of coefficients, a class invariant, so no finite list meets all their classes (proved in Lean). Red-team audit at 956e3162: the action is the proper SL₂(ℤ) action f ↦ f∘γ⁻¹; hypothesis satisfiable (D = 5); necessity of D ≠ 0 compiled; no Mathlib counterpart (exact?, loogle, leansearch, leanfinder, grep); used by the finiteness of classes of rank-two lattices.

Correctly stated: if a collection of integral binary quadratic forms, all of one nonzero discriminant D, is closed under integer changes of variables of determinant 1, then it splits into finitely many equivalence classes under those changes of variables. It follows from the finite list of representatives for discriminant D: the listed forms lying in the collection meet every class. Taking the collection to be all forms of discriminant D, the primitive ones, or the positive definite ones gives the usual finiteness of class numbers, for definite and indefinite D and for square D. D ≠ 0 is needed: the forms of discriminant 0 fall into infinitely many classes (nx² for n = 1, 2, …, told apart by the gcd of coefficients), proved in Lean. Red-team audit at 956e3162: both hypotheses load-bearing (D ≠ 0 by that counterexample; without the discriminant condition the discriminant itself separates infinitely many classes); specialised to all forms of the square discriminant 4; classes are SL₂(ℤ) orbits within the collection; no Mathlib counterpart found.

Correctly stated: for every nonzero integer D, the primitive integral binary quadratic forms ax² + bxy + cy² (coefficients with no common factor) of discriminant b² − 4ac = D fall into finitely many classes under proper equivalence, that is, under integer changes of variables of determinant 1. This is Lagrange's classical finiteness of the class number (Wikipedia's 'Binary quadratic form' records it as Lagrange's theorem), here for definite and indefinite D alike and for square D too. Why it holds: for nonsquare D every class contains a form with |b| ≤ |a| ≤ |c|, which forces 3|a||c| ≤ |D| with a, c nonzero and leaves finitely many candidates; for D = s² every class contains a form sxy + cy² with 0 ≤ c < |s|. Conventions: for D < 0 positive and negative definite classes are counted together, and for D not congruent to 0 or 1 mod 4 there are no forms, so the statement is trivially (and rightly) true there. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the classes are orbits of SL₂(ℤ) acting by f ↦ f∘γ⁻¹ (proper, not GL₂ equivalence) on forms of discriminant exactly D with content 1; hypotheses satisfiable and the statement specialised at D = 5, −4 and the square 9; no junk values (a plain finiteness statement); axioms only propext, choice, Quot.sound. The nonzero assumption is not actually needed for primitive forms (D = 0 has just the two classes ±y², compiled), recorded as a minor generality finding; the statement as written is correct.

Correctly stated: take a smooth metric-compatible connection on the tangent bundle of a smooth Riemannian manifold whose curvature has the pointwise constant-curvature form R(w,u)v = κ(y)(⟨u,v⟩w − ⟨w,v⟩u) at every point y, and smooth vector fields X, Y, Z, σ. At any point x where κ is differentiable, the covariant derivative of the curvature, (∇_X R)(Y,Z)σ = ∇_X(R(Y,Z)σ) − R(∇_X Y,Z)σ − R(Y,∇_X Z)σ − R(Y,Z)∇_Xσ, equals dκ(X)(⟨Z,σ⟩Y − ⟨Y,σ⟩Z), as its docstring says. Why: R(Y,Z)σ = κ·P with P = ⟨Z,σ⟩Y − ⟨Y,σ⟩Z, and the Leibniz rule splits off dκ(X)P. Metric compatibility (X⟨A,B⟩ = ⟨∇_X A,B⟩ + ⟨A,∇_X B⟩) then shows that ∇_X P is the sum of the three terms obtained by differentiating one of Y, Z, σ at a time, and these cancel the three correction terms. This is the standard computation behind Schur's theorem; no torsion hypothesis is needed and none is assumed. Red-team checks (at 956e316250): all hypotheses are used (differentiability of κ at x is needed for the Leibniz step); it still compiles with the curvature form assumed only near x (a generality note, not an overstatement); the library's locally-symmetric-space file uses it.

Correctly stated: this is Schur's theorem. Take a smooth Riemannian manifold M of dimension at least 3 that is connected (the empty manifold is allowed), and a smooth connection on its tangent bundle that preserves the metric and has no torsion, i.e. the Levi-Civita connection. If there is a real function κ on M such that, at every point p, every tangent 2-plane at p has sectional curvature κ(p), then κ takes the same value at any two points; nothing is assumed about the regularity of κ. Sectional curvature is the usual quotient ⟨R(u,v)v,u⟩/(|u|²|v|² − ⟨u,v⟩²) over linearly independent u, v, with R(X,Y) = ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_Y∇_X − ∇_[X,Y], the convention under which the library proves that the round sphere has curvature +1. Wikipedia's 'Schur's lemma (Riemannian geometry)' states the same result for connected manifolds of dimension other than 2. Here the bound is dimension at least 3 because the hypothesis on κ says nothing in dimension 1, where there are no 2-planes, and in dimension 2 every metric satisfies it, so the bound is essential. Why it holds: if the curvature is the same on every plane at a point, then R(w,u)v = κ(⟨u,v⟩w − ⟨w,v⟩u) there, so the scalar curvature is n(n−1)κ and κ is smooth. Because the model tensor is parallel, ∇R = dκ ⊗ (model tensor), and the second Bianchi identity, evaluated on three orthonormal vectors, forces dκ = 0, so κ is constant on a connected manifold. The second Bianchi identity is proved in the library, not assumed. Red-team checks (at 956e316250): applied to the round 3-sphere with its Levi-Civita connection, so the hypotheses can all hold at once; each hypothesis (dimension, connectedness, torsion-free, metric-compatible, pointwise isotropy) is mathematically needed and used; no junk-value shortcut, since the smoothness of κ is derived, not assumed; only the three standard axioms; no Mathlib counterpart (Mathlib has no curvature tensor).

Correctly stated: this is the global form of Schur's theorem. Under the same hypotheses as the main theorem (smooth metric-compatible torsion-free connection, connected manifold of dimension at least 3, every tangent 2-plane at each point p having the same sectional curvature κ(p)), for any chosen point x₀ every tangent 2-plane at every point has sectional curvature κ(x₀), i.e. the manifold has constant sectional curvature. It follows at once from the main theorem, which gives κ(x) = κ(x₀) for every x. Red-team checks (at 956e316250): applied to the round 3-sphere it returns constant sectional curvature 1, the known value; the hypotheses are consistent and the conclusion is exactly the standard notion of constant curvature.

Correctly stated: this is the pointwise (differential) half of Schur's theorem. Take a smooth metric-compatible torsion-free connection on the tangent bundle of a smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension at least 3. Suppose that at every point y the curvature has the constant-curvature form R(w,u)v = κ(y)(⟨u,v⟩w − ⟨w,v⟩u) for some real function κ. Then at each point x where κ is differentiable, its differential dκ(x) is zero; no connectedness is needed. Why: the model tensor (Y,Z,σ) ↦ ⟨Z,σ⟩Y − ⟨Y,σ⟩Z is parallel for a metric connection, so ∇_X R = dκ(X) times the model tensor. Now evaluate the second Bianchi identity at X = e_i and Y = σ = e_j, Z = e_k, for three distinct orthonormal vectors, and take the inner product with e_k: only −dκ(e_i) is left, so it vanishes. This is where dimension at least 3 is used. The differentiability hypothesis does honest work: the zero is never obtained from Lean's convention that a non-differentiable function has derivative zero. It is also automatic, since κ equals the smooth scalar curvature divided by n(n−1); this is recorded as a generality note. Red-team checks (at 956e316250): every hypothesis is used by the proof; versions without the differentiability hypothesis, and with the curvature form assumed only near x, also compile, so the statement claims less than is true, never more; its hypotheses hold for the round sphere (curvature form with κ = 1, proved in the library).

Correctly stated: the diagram-indexed character formula for the Weyl module packaged as a finite-dimensional representation of GLₙ(k). Over a field of characteristic zero its character at an invertible diagonal matrix diag(t) is the tableau Schur polynomial of the diagram evaluated at t. It is the unbundled statement, the packaged character being the trace of the same action. Red-team checks: instantiated over ℚ at μ = (1), (2), (1,1) and the empty diagram, giving t₁+…+tₙ, h₂, e₂ and 1.

Correctly stated: the one-row character formula (Weyl module ≅ symmetric power, character h_d = Schur polynomial of one row) for the Weyl module packaged as a finite-dimensional representation of GLₙ(k), over a field of characteristic zero. Red-team checks: agrees with the general diagram theorem; a special case of it (minor generality finding).

Correctly stated: the one-column character formula (Weyl module ≅ exterior power, character e_d = Schur polynomial of one column) for the Weyl module packaged as a finite-dimensional representation of GLₙ(k), over a field of characteristic zero. Red-team checks: agrees with the general diagram theorem; a special case of it (minor generality finding).

Correctly stated: the same character formula for the Weyl module packaged as a finite-dimensional representation of GLₙ(k). For a field of characteristic zero and every partition μ, its character at diag(t₁,…,tₙ) is the Schur polynomial s_μ(t₁,…,tₙ), both sides vanishing when μ has more than n parts. It follows from the unbundled theorem, since the character of the packaged representation is by definition the trace of the same action. Red-team checks: instantiated over ℚ; agrees with the unbundled form and with the extreme-shape cases (Sym, Λ) proved independently; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; file elaborates in about 2 s.

Correctly stated: the Weyl-module character formula indexed by Young diagrams rather than partitions. For a field of characteristic zero, every Young diagram μ and every invertible diagonal matrix diag(t₁,…,tₙ), the trace on the Weyl module 𝕊^μ(kⁿ) is the Schur polynomial of the diagram, the sum over semistandard tableaux of shape μ with entries below n of the monomials recording each entry's multiplicity (Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I (5.12)). It is the partition version applied to the partition of row lengths of μ, whose diagram is μ itself and whose Schur polynomial is the diagram's. Red-team checks: specialised to one-row and one-column shapes, giving Mathlib's h_d and e_d; for shapes with more than n rows both sides are zero, checked independently; holds in every universe; it is the form used by the branching and Laurent-character files; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; file elaborates in about 2 s.

Correctly stated: for a Young diagram with at most one row, of length d, over a field of characteristic zero, the character of the Weyl module at diag(t) is the Schur polynomial of that shape. Such a Weyl module is isomorphic to the d-th symmetric power of kⁿ, on which diag(t) has trace the sum of all degree-d monomials in t, the complete homogeneous polynomial h_d(t). For a one-row shape the semistandard tableaux are the weakly increasing words of length d, so the Schur polynomial is also h_d. Red-team checks: agrees with the file's general theorem, proved by a different route; specialised to d = 1, giving t₁+…+tₙ. It is a special case of that general theorem (recorded as a minor generality finding), not an error.

Correctly stated: for a Young diagram with at most one column, of length d, over a field of characteristic zero, the character of the Weyl module at diag(t) is the Schur polynomial of that shape. Such a Weyl module is isomorphic to the d-th exterior power of kⁿ, on which diag(t) has trace the elementary symmetric polynomial e_d(t), the sum of products of d distinct tᵢ. For a one-column shape the semistandard tableaux are the strictly increasing words of length d, so the Schur polynomial is also e_d; for d > n both are zero. Red-team checks: agrees with the file's general theorem, proved by a different route; specialised to d = 2, giving Mathlib's e₂. It is a special case of that general theorem (recorded as a minor generality finding), not an error.

Correctly stated, and it is the full classical theorem. Over any field k of characteristic zero, for every n and every partition μ of any d, the trace of the diagonal matrix diag(t₁,…,tₙ) (all tᵢ nonzero, so that it lies in GLₙ(k)) on the Weyl module 𝕊^μ(kⁿ) equals the Schur polynomial s_μ(t₁,…,tₙ). Here 𝕊^μ(kⁿ) is the image of the Young symmetrizer of μ (row symmetrizer times column antisymmetrizer) acting on the d-th tensor power of kⁿ by permuting factors, with GLₙ acting diagonally; s_μ is the sum over semistandard tableaux of shape μ with entries from n letters of the monomial counting each letter, which is Macdonald's (5.12) in Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Ch. I. Macdonald's Appendix A to Ch. I, (7.2) and (8.4)(i), states the same over a field of characteristic 0: the trace of the irreducible polynomial functor F_λ on a diagonal map is s_λ of the eigenvalues, where F_λ(kⁿ) is the space of S_d-maps from the irreducible S_d-module of λ into the tensor power, a representation isomorphic to the Young-symmetrizer image. The proof writes the character as (1/d!) Σ_σ χ^μ(σ) p_{cycle type of σ}(t) and applies the inverse of Frobenius's formula. Every partition is covered: with more than n parts the Weyl module is zero and s_μ in n variables is zero, so both sides vanish (each checked on its own). Characteristic zero is the right hypothesis here, since in characteristic p the symmetrizer image can be too small: for one row of length p and n = 1 the symmetrizer acts by p! = 0, while s_(p)(t) = t^p. Red-team checks: no contradiction (instantiated over ℚ); no explicit hypotheses to drop; specialised to μ = (1) giving t₁+…+tₙ, μ = (2) giving Mathlib's complete homogeneous h₂, μ = (1,1) giving Mathlib's elementary e₂, μ = ∅ giving 1, and dimensions 3 for Sym²(ℚ²) and Λ²(ℚ³), all compiled; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; simp lemma in simp normal form; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; file elaborates in about 2 s.

Correctly stated: over a field of characteristic zero, the dimension of the Weyl module 𝕊^μ(kⁿ) of a Young diagram μ is the number of semistandard tableaux of shape μ with entries in {0,…,n−1}. This is the character formula at the identity matrix: the trace of the identity is the dimension, and the Schur polynomial at (1,…,1) counts the tableaux, one monomial each. Macdonald's proof of (8.2) in Appendix A to Ch. I of Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., uses the same fact, that dim F_λ(V) is s_λ(1,…,1). When μ has more than n rows there is no tableau and the module is zero, so both sides are 0. Red-team checks: the count is of a finite type, so no zero-cardinality junk is involved; dimensions n for μ = (1), 3 for Sym²(ℚ²) and 3 for Λ²(ℚ³) come out of the same route, all compiled; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti; axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; file elaborates in about 2 s.

The global norm index theorem. For a finite abelian extension L/K of number fields, the group of norms of idele classes N_{L/K}(C_L) has index exactly [L:K] in the idele class group C_K: the quotient C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L) has [L:K] elements. Since [L:K] ≥ 1, the statement also asserts that the quotient is finite, so the convention that an infinite set has size 0 cannot make it true vacuously. This is Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Theorem 5.3(b): for finite abelian L/K the Artin map gives C_K/Nm(C_L) ≅ Gal(L/K), a group of order [L:K]. Proof idea: finite global reciprocity identifies the quotient with Gal(L/K)^ab, which is Gal(L/K) itself for abelian L/K and has order [L:K] by Galois theory. Reciprocity comes from the global class formation whose invariant is the sum of the local invariants (Milne VIII §4). The objects are the genuine ones: Mathlib's idele class group (all places, archimedean included, modulo principal ideles), and the norm whose v-component is the product over w | v of the local norms (Milne V §4, p. 177). Red-team checks: compiled the cases L = K (index 1) and K = ℚ, L = ℚ(ζ₅) (index 4), and derived finiteness of the quotient from the statement. Both hypotheses are needed: by norm limitation (Milne VIII, Theorem 4.8) an S₃-extension of ℚ has index 2, not 6, and a non-normal cubic field has index 1, not 3. Only the standard axioms are used.

Defines finite global reciprocity for a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields: an isomorphism from C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L) (the idele class group of K modulo norms of idele classes of L) onto the abelianized Galois group Gal(L/K)^ab, written additively. It is the reciprocity isomorphism of the global class formation of idele classes, whose invariant is the sum of the local invariants. The formation's norm quotient is identified with C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L), and its Galois group with Gal(L/K) by restriction along a chosen embedding of L into a separable closure of K. Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, VIII §4 (Theorem 4.7 and the paragraph after it) uses the same construction: Tate's theorem applied to the global fundamental class gives Gal(L/K)^ab ≅ C_K/Nm(C_L), the inverse of the global Artin map. Convention: the embedding is only an auxiliary choice; this file proves the isomorphism does not depend on it. Sibling files prove that its local factors are the local Artin maps, which is how Milne V §5, Prop. 5.2 characterizes the global Artin map, and that a uniformizer at an unramified prime goes to the arithmetic Frobenius. Red-team checks: C_K is Mathlib's idele class group (ideles over all places, archimedean included, modulo the principal ideles). The norm map has v-component equal to the product over w | v of the local norms N_{L_w/K_v}, which is Milne's idele norm (V §4, p. 177), and it is proved compatible with the global norm on L^×. The construction uses only the standard axioms.

Says that finite global reciprocity does not depend on the embedding of L into the separable closure of K. The layer of L (the subgroup of the absolute Galois group fixing L) is the same for every embedding. Two embeddings differ by an element of the absolute Galois group, so the two identifications of the layer's Galois group with Gal(L/K) differ by an inner automorphism, which is trivial on the abelianization. Red-team checks: it asserts equality of the two isomorphisms themselves, not merely of their images, and it assumes nothing beyond the Galois setting.

Says how finite global reciprocity acts on the class of an idele class c. The image is the Artin symbol of c in the global class formation, with c viewed in the ground level of the layer of L, carried to Gal(L/K)^ab by restriction along the embedding. This is the defining formula of the construction, since the reciprocity isomorphism applied to the class of c modulo norms is by definition the Artin symbol of c. Red-team checks: as a simplification rule it fires on its own left side (compiled test).

Defines the global Artin map C_K → Gal(L/K)^ab of a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields: reduce an idele class modulo N_{L/K}(C_L), then apply finite global reciprocity. For abelian L/K this is Milne's Artin map on idele classes composed with the quotient map, i.e. the map C_K/Nm(C_L) → Gal(L/K) of Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Theorem 5.3(b). Red-team checks: this file proves that its kernel is exactly the norm group, that it is surjective and that it kills principal ideles; sibling files identify its local factors with the local Artin maps.
Says that the global Artin symbol of an idele class c is finite global reciprocity applied to the class of c modulo norms from L. This holds by definition.

Compatibility in towers. Let M/K be a finite Galois extension with a K-embedding f : M → L into the finite Galois extension L/K. Restricting the Artin symbol of an idele class from Gal(L/K)^ab to Gal(M/K)^ab along f gives its Artin symbol for M/K, where M is embedded in the separable closure through f. This is the standard compatibility of the Artin map with restriction (Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, proof of Prop. 5.2: for L ⊂ L′ the Artin symbol for L′/K restricts to the Artin symbol for L/K). Proof idea: both symbols are restrictions of one representative of the absolute Artin symbol. Red-team checks: it assumes only that both extensions are Galois, and only the standard axioms are used.

Says that the global Artin map does not depend on the embedding of L into the separable closure of K. It follows at once from the same statement for finite global reciprocity, since the Artin map is the quotient map followed by that isomorphism.

Suppose an element g of the absolute Galois group of K represents the absolute Artin symbol of an idele class c, i.e. its image in the abelianized absolute Galois group is the Artin symbol of c. Then for every finite Galois L/K the Artin symbol of c in Gal(L/K)^ab is the class of the restriction of g to L. This is correct because the Artin maps of the finite layers of a class formation are the restrictions of its absolute Artin map. Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Prop. 5.2 characterizes the global Artin map to Gal(K^ab/K) by the same compatibility, φ(a)|_L = φ_{L/K}(a) for every finite L ⊂ K^ab. Red-team checks: every hypothesis is needed (each removal breaks the proof), and the hypothesis on g can always be met, since every absolute Artin symbol has a representative.

Says that the global Artin symbol of an idele class c ∈ C_K is trivial exactly when c is the norm of an idele class of L, i.e. the kernel of the global Artin map is N_{L/K}(C_L). This is the injectivity half of the reciprocity isomorphism C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L) ≅ Gal(L/K)^ab: Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Theorem 5.3(b) for abelian L/K, and VIII §4 with the abelianization for Galois L/K. It holds because the Artin map is the quotient map followed by an isomorphism. Red-team checks: the right-hand side is the image of the genuine idele-class norm (product of the local norms over the places above), not a larger or smaller group. As a simplification rule it fires (compiled test).

Says that the global Artin symbol of the class of a principal idele (the diagonal image of some x ∈ K^×) is trivial. This holds because the global Artin map is defined on C_K, the ideles modulo the principal ideles, where that class is the identity. Convention: since the map is defined on C_K from the start, this is the formal half of Milne's reciprocity law (Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Theorem 5.3(a)). The substantive half, that the map is the product of the local Artin maps, is the local-global compatibility proved in the sibling Compatibility file. Red-team checks: as a simplification rule it fires on its own left side, and plain simplification without it does not close the goal, so it is not redundant (both compiled).

Says that the kernel of the global Artin map C_K → Gal(L/K)^ab is exactly the norm group N_{L/K}(C_L) (in additive notation). It has the same content as the companion 'equals zero iff' statement, stated as an equality of subgroups: part (b) of the reciprocity law, Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Theorem 5.3(b).

Says that the global Artin map C_K → Gal(L/K)^ab is surjective: every element of the abelianized Galois group is the Artin symbol of some idele class. This holds because the map is the surjective quotient map C_K → C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L) followed by the reciprocity isomorphism. It matches Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V §5, Theorem 5.3(b) and Remark 5.7(a), which notes that in the number-field case the Artin map is surjective.

Correctly stated. It says: two symmetric bilinear forms over the 2-adic integers on free modules of the same finite rank, each unimodular (unit Gram determinant) and odd (some vector has unit norm), are isometric over the 2-adic integers exactly when the product of their determinants is a square (for units, the same as the determinants agreeing up to a unit square) and the norms of characteristic vectors (w with B(w,x) congruent to B(x,x) mod 2 for all x) agree mod 8, i.e. their oddities agree. This is the odd (type I) case of Allcock, Gal and Mark, The Conway-Sloane calculus for 2-adic lattices (arXiv:1511.04614), Theorem 5.1: a unimodular 2-adic lattice is characterized by its dimension, type, sign and oddity, with no rank restriction. Their sign records the determinant only up to sign (1 or 7 versus 3 or 5 mod 8), but for an odd form with unit diagonal entries d_1..d_n, k of them congruent to 3 mod 4, the determinant is (-1)^k mod 4 and the oddity is n + 2k mod 4, so for a fixed rank the pairs (sign, oddity) and (determinant square class, oddity) carry the same information. The proof diagonalizes each form with unit entries, uses that the sum of an orthogonal basis is characteristic with norm equal to the trace, and realizes any unit diagonal with the same product class and the same sum mod 8 by induction on the rank (a 2-adic unit is a square exactly when it is 1 mod 8). Rank zero is excluded automatically because the zero form represents no unit, and ranks one and two agree with a direct enumeration of the diagonal forms with entries 1, 3, 5, 7. Red-team audit at 956e316250: the theorem was specialised to show that the diagonal forms (1,1) and (3,3) are not isometric and that (1,1) and (5,5) are, so its hypotheses can all be met and both directions have content; neither oddness hypothesis can be dropped (the hyperbolic plane and the diagonal form (1,7) have determinant product -7, a square, and oddity 0, yet only the second is odd); only the standard axioms; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Correctly stated. It says: if not every self-pairing B(x,x) of a bilinear form over the 2-adic integers is divisible by 2, then some B(x,x) is a unit. This holds because the 2-adic integers form a local ring whose non-units are exactly the multiples of 2; it is the step from not even to odd in the unimodular classification. Red-team audit at 956e316250: hypothesis satisfiable (the form (1)) and needed; no Mathlib duplicate.

Correctly stated. It says: if B and C have orthogonal bases of the same size whose self-pairings d_1..d_n and e_1..e_n are 2-adic units, then B and C are isometric exactly when the product of all the d_i and e_i is a square and the sums of the e_i and of the d_i agree mod 8. This is the classification of odd unimodular 2-adic forms by rank, determinant square class and oddity, in the form of Allcock-Gal-Mark (arXiv:1511.04614) Theorem 5.1 for unit diagonal forms: the forward direction is invariance of the determinant up to unit squares and of the trace mod 8, which is the norm of the characteristic vector given by the sum of the basis; the converse realizes the diagonal e inside B with the companion realization theorem and matches Gram matrices. Red-team audit at 956e316250: hypotheses met by the diagonal forms (1,1), (3,3), (5,5); the unit hypotheses are needed (a zero diagonal entry makes the square condition hold vacuously); rank zero and rank one come out right; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Correctly stated. It says: if a bilinear form over the 2-adic integers has an orthogonal basis with unit self-pairings d_i, then for any units v_1..v_n whose product times the product of the d_i is a square and whose sum agrees with the sum of the d_i mod 8, the form has an orthogonal basis with self-pairings exactly v_1..v_n. This is the realization step behind the 2-adic unimodular classification (Allcock-Gal-Mark, arXiv:1511.04614, Theorem 5.1); since a 2-adic unit is a square exactly when it is 1 mod 8, only residues mod 8 matter, and the proof inducts on rank, finding a vector that represents some v_j up to a unit square and has a unit-norm vector orthogonal to it (b_i + 2b_k represents 5d_i mod 8, and b_0 + b_1 + b_2, possibly plus 2b_3, supplies the other residues mod 4), splitting it off and recursing. No symmetry hypothesis is needed because a form with an orthogonal basis is automatically symmetric. Red-team audit at 956e316250: every hypothesis is needed (for the diagonal form (1,7) the non-unit target (0,0) passes both congruence conditions but cannot be realized); rank zero is trivial; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.
The class [s] has order exactly two: it is nonzero and twice it vanishes, and 2 is prime.
The half-lattice K is contained in the Leech lattice.
The shift has norm B(s, s) = (9/4 + 23·1/4)/2 = 4, the minimal norm of the Leech lattice. Red-team checks: value recomputed by hand.

With the halved dot product B(x, y) = (x·y)/2 that the Golay Construction B lattice carries, B(s, x) = (x_0 + … + x_23)/4 − x_0 for every rational vector x: half of the dot-product identity for s. Red-team checks: identity verified by hand.
The discriminant quadratic form of the even lattice K, q([x]) = B(x, x)/2 mod 1, vanishes at [s], because B(s, s)/2 = 2 is an integer.
The Gram determinant of the Leech lattice has absolute value 1, a restatement of unimodularity.
The Leech lattice is a free abelian group of rank 24: it is a full lattice in rational 24-space.
The form of the Leech lattice, the halved dot product on rational 24-space, is nondegenerate.

Every vector of the Leech lattice has even norm (x·x)/2, because it is glued from the even lattice K along a subgroup isotropic for the discriminant quadratic form. Red-team checks: s and (2,2,0,…,0) have norm 4.

The glue subgroup {0, [s]} is isotropic for the discriminant quadratic form of K (the form vanishes on both elements); this is the standard criterion for the overlattice it defines to be even. Red-team checks: no hypotheses; both elements checked.

The glue subgroup is Lagrangian: it is isotropic, the discriminant form of K is nondegenerate, and its order squared, 2² = 4, equals the order of the discriminant group (K has discriminant 4, being of index two in the unimodular Golay Construction A lattice). This is the standard criterion for the glued lattice to be unimodular. Red-team checks: cardinalities 2 and 4 confirmed from the library's lemmas.
The form (x·x)/2 is positive at every nonzero rational vector, so the Leech lattice is positive definite.
The Leech lattice equals its own dual with respect to the halved dot product, because it is glued from K along a Lagrangian subgroup of K*/K.

Defines the Leech lattice as K ∪ (s + K) in rational 24-space with the form B(x, y) = (x·y)/2, where K is the Construction B lattice of the extended binary Golay code (integer vectors whose reduction mod 2 is a codeword and whose coordinate sum is divisible by 4) and s = (−3/2, 1/2, …, 1/2). Writing x = a/2, this is the standard congruence description of the Leech lattice as given on Wikipedia's 'Leech lattice' page: vectors 2^(−3/2)·a with a integral, a_1 + … + a_24 ≡ 4a_j (mod 8) for every j, and each mod-4 residue class of coordinates supported on a Golay codeword; the scaling agrees because B(x, x) = (a·a)/8 = |2^(−3/2)·a|². The Golay code used is proved in the library to have length 24, dimension 12 and minimum distance 8 (weight distribution 1, 759, 2576, 759, 1), so it is the extended binary Golay code. This file proves the lattice positive definite, even, unimodular and of rank 24; its congruence description, minimum norm 4 and the absence of roots are proved in the companion file on the Leech minimum. Red-team checks: witnesses (2,2,0,…,0) in K, s and s + (2,2,0,…,0) in the lattice, and non-witnesses (2,0,…,0) and (1,1,0,…,0) (norms 2 and 1) and the all-halves vector (norm 3, ruling out the shift (1/2,…,1/2)) not in it, all compiled; standard axioms only; no other Leech construction in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.
The underlying group of the Leech lattice is the preimage in the dual lattice K* of the glue subgroup {0, [s]}, i.e. the overlattice of K that this subgroup determines.
The Leech lattice carries the halved dot product (x·y)/2, the same form as K, so a vector's norm is (x·x)/2.
The lattice vector s has norm 4, so the minimum norm 4 of the Leech lattice is attained.

Defines the vector s = (−3/2, 1/2, …, 1/2) of rational 24-space, with −3/2 in coordinate 0. It is half of the classical odd Leech vector (−3, 1, …, 1), which is the right normalisation because this Leech model uses coordinates x = a/2 with the halved dot product. Red-team checks: coordinate values evaluated; 2s lies in the Golay Construction B half-lattice K and s does not (both proved in this file); s has norm 4.

The class [s] of the shift in the discriminant group K*/K of the half-lattice K, which is defined because s pairs integrally with K. Red-team checks: it is nonzero and of order two (proved in this file).
Unfolding lemma: [s] is the image of s in K*/K.
The class [s] is nonzero in K*/K, because s itself is not in K.

The subgroup of the discriminant group K*/K generated by [s]; since [s] has order two it is {0, [s]}. This is the glue subgroup of the Construction B description of the Leech lattice. Red-team checks: membership and order two proved in this file.
For every rational vector x, the dot product s·x equals (x_0 + … + x_23)/2 − 2x_0, since s·x = −(3/2)x_0 + (1/2)·(sum of the other coordinates). Red-team checks: identity verified by hand.

The shift pairs integrally with the half-lattice K (integer vectors whose reduction mod 2 is a Golay codeword and whose coordinate sum is divisible by 4): for x in K, B(s, x) = (sum of coordinates)/4 − x_0 is an integer, so s lies in the dual lattice of K. Red-team checks: statement matches the module docstring; no hypotheses.
The shift s is a vector of the Leech lattice (the coset s + K contains it).
The shift s is not the zero vector (its coordinate 1 is 1/2).
The shift is not in K, because K consists of integer vectors and s has half-integer coordinates.
Every coordinate of s other than coordinate 0 equals 1/2; the hypothesis that the index is not 0 is needed, since coordinate 0 is −3/2.
Coordinate 0 of the shift s is −3/2, directly from the definition.

A rational vector lies in the Leech lattice exactly when it lies in K or its difference with s lies in K: the lattice is K ∪ (s + K), the Construction B description. Red-team checks: witness and non-witness vectors ((2,2,0,…,0), s, (2,0,…,0), (1,1,0,…,0), all-halves) tested through this lemma.
An element of K*/K lies in the subgroup generated by [s] exactly when it is 0 or [s], because 2[s] = 0.
The glue subgroup has exactly two elements, since [s] has order two.
K has index two in the Leech lattice, because the glue subgroup has two elements.
Twice the class [s] is zero, because 2s = (−3, 1, …, 1) lies in K.

Twice the shift, (−3, 1, …, 1), lies in K: it is an integer vector reducing mod 2 to the all-ones word, which lies in the Golay code because a self-dual binary code contains the all-ones word, and its coordinate sum 20 is divisible by 4.

Says: if q is a nonzero complex number that is not a root of unity, the centre of the quantum enveloping algebra U_q(sl2), generated by E, F, K, K^-1 with KK^-1 = K^-1K = 1, KE = q^2 EK, KF = q^-2 FK and EF - FE = (K - K^-1)/(q - q^-1), is exactly the subalgebra generated by the Casimir element Omega = FE + (qK + q^-1 K^-1)/(q - q^-1)^2. Pandzic and Somberg (arXiv:1702.02435, Section 2) give the same presentation in their relations (2.1) and state, just before (2.5), that for q not a root of unity the centre is generated by EF + (qK^-1 + q^-1 K)/(q - q^-1)^2, which the library proves equal to Omega; the Tau Ceti roadmap (QuantumGroups, Q8 item 3) asks for exactly this element and result. The proof works in the basis of ordered monomials F^a K^b E^c: commuting with K forces a = c, commuting with E removes the monomials of top E-degree n that carry a nonzero power of K, and Omega^n has top part F^n E^n with coefficient 1, so subtracting a multiple of Omega^n lowers the degree and induction finishes. This theorem states generation only; that Omega satisfies no polynomial relation, so the centre is a polynomial ring in Omega, is the companion result transcendental_casimir, and the two are combined in polynomialAlgEquivCenter. Red-team checks at 956e3162: the hypotheses are satisfiable (specialised at q = 2); genericity cannot be dropped (at q = 1 the algebra is commutative, so K is central, yet K is not in the subalgebra generated by Omega: compiled counterexample); E is not central at generic q, so the centre is a proper subalgebra; the algebra is nontrivial (PBW basis); the standard 2-dimensional representation satisfies the relations and Omega acts on it by (q^2 + q^-2)/(q - q^-1)^2, the expected value; only the standard axioms are used.

Says that the isomorphism from C[X] onto the centre of U_q(sl2) sends a polynomial p to p(Omega), regarded as an element of U_q(sl2); this is what identifies the isomorphism with evaluation at the Casimir element. Red-team checks: the automatic simplifier uses it as a rewrite rule and cannot prove the equation without it; specialised to p = X it gives Omega.

Defines, for q nonzero and not a root of unity, the isomorphism of complex algebras from the polynomial ring C[X] onto the centre of U_q(sl2) given by evaluating a polynomial at the Casimir element Omega. It is assembled from the two results of the same file: evaluation at Omega is injective because Omega is transcendental, and its image, the subalgebra generated by Omega, is the whole centre; together they say the centre is a polynomial algebra in one variable on Omega, as the Tau Ceti roadmap (QuantumGroups, Q8 item 3) requires. Red-team checks: the map is evaluation at Omega (see coe_polynomialAlgEquivCenter_apply), so X goes to Omega rather than to an arbitrary generator; only the standard axioms are used.

Says: for every nonzero complex q, the Casimir element Omega = FE + (qK + q^-1 K^-1)/(q - q^-1)^2 of U_q(sl2) satisfies no nonzero polynomial equation with complex coefficients, that is, its powers 1, Omega, Omega^2, ... are linearly independent. Proof: in the PBW basis F^a K^b E^c, the power Omega^n only involves E-exponents at most n and has coefficient 1 on F^n E^n, so for a polynomial p of degree d the coefficient of F^d E^d in p(Omega) is the leading coefficient of p, which is nonzero. No root-of-unity condition is needed, matching the argument. Red-team checks at 956e3162: the hypothesis q nonzero is necessary (at q = 0 the relations force E = F = 0 and, with the library's convention that 1/0 = 0, Omega = 0: compiled); only the standard axioms are used.

Defines the sphere symmetric sequence S: its level n is the n-fold smash power (S¹)^∧n of the simplicial circle S¹ = Δ[1]/∂Δ[1] (Mathlib's circle, the quotient of the interval identifying its two vertices, which Tau Ceti also shows is the pushout collapsing the boundary), the symmetric group Σ_n acts by permuting the smash factors, the multiplication S^p ∧ S^q → S^(p+q) concatenates coordinates, and the unit is the identification of the 0-sphere with the empty smash power; with these it is a commutative monoid for the Day convolution product of symmetric sequences. This is the object of Hovey-Shipley-Smith, Symmetric spectra (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 2000): Section 1.2 takes S¹ = Δ[1]/∂Δ[1] and S^p = (S¹)^∧p with the left permutation action of Σ_p, and Section 2.2 states that this sequence of spheres is a commutative monoid in symmetric sequences. Commutativity is proved, not assumed: the block swap in Σ_(p+q) corresponds under concatenation to swapping the two factors of S^p ∧ S^q, which makes the sequence a braided monoidal functor out of the groupoid of finite sets and bijections, and such a functor gives a commutative Day convolution monoid. Red-team checks: level n is definitionally (S¹)^∧n and a permutation acts on a family of simplices by reindexing its coordinates; the action is genuinely non-trivial (compiled witness: the transposition in Σ₂ moves a 2-simplex of S² = S¹ ∧ S¹, detected by mapping the circle to the nerve of the group of order 2); the monoid and commutativity structures found are the block-concatenation ones; no duplicate in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Defines the category of symmetric spectra of pointed simplicial sets as the category of left modules over the sphere symmetric sequence S: an object is a symmetric sequence X (pointed simplicial sets X_n with a basepoint-preserving action of Σ_n, i.e. a functor out of the groupoid of the finite sets {1,...,n} and their bijections) with a unital, associative action map S ⊗ X → X for the Day convolution tensor product, and a morphism is a map of symmetric sequences commuting with the actions. This is exactly Hovey-Shipley-Smith, Symmetric spectra (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 2000), Proposition 2.2.1, which identifies symmetric spectra in the sense of their Definition 1.2.2 with left S-modules; their Definition 2.1.1 uses the same index groupoid, and their tensor product of symmetric sequences (Definition 2.1.3, with the universal property of Proposition 2.1.4: maps out of X ⊗ Y are families of Σ_p × Σ_q-equivariant maps X_p ∧ Y_q → Z_(p+q)) is the Day convolution used here. The action is on the left, as in Hovey-Shipley-Smith; since S is commutative, right modules would give an equivalent category anyway. Convention: simplicial sets are taken in the smallest universe, as in the source. Red-team checks: the module action was confirmed to be tensoring on the left (S ⊗ X → X); the sphere spectrum, S acting on itself by its multiplication, was built as a witness; the monoid structure used is the block-concatenation one and its commutativity is a proof; no comparable definition in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Defines the coproduct Δ : Γ → Γ ⊗_L Γ of the Hopf algebroid (L, Γ), Γ = L[b₁, b₂, …] (L the Lazard ring), as the ring map classifying the composite f₂∘f₁ of the universal composable pair of strict isomorphisms. Here f₁ has coefficients bᵢ ⊗ 1 (left factor), f₂ has coefficients 1 ⊗ bᵢ (right factor), and the source of the composite is the source of f₁. This is exactly Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres, Theorem A2.1.16. Its proof sets f(x) = f₂(f₁(x)) ('since f₂ follows f₁') to get Σ Δ(bᵢ) = Σⱼ (Σᵢ bᵢ)^(j+1) ⊗ bⱼ with b₀ = 1. Formal group laws are commutative, as in Ravenel's Definition A2.1.1; the ring is ungraded here, and Ravenel's grading |bᵢ| = 2i plays no role in the identities. Red-team checks (compiled Lean witnesses, read against the text of A2.1.16): Δ(b₁) = b₁⊗1 + 1⊗b₁, Δ(b₂) = b₂⊗1 + 2b₁⊗b₁ + 1⊗b₂, and Δ(b₃) = b₃⊗1 + (2b₂ + b₁²)⊗b₁ + 3b₁⊗b₂ + 1⊗b₃. These are Ravenel's formula, and the last rules out the reversed order of composition. All Hopf algebroid identities of Ravenel A1.1.1(a)-(f) are proved, (a) in the Lazard coordinate-change file and (b)-(f) here.
