Correctly stated: substituting the coordinate z into a complex polynomial p gives a meromorphic function on the sphere whose value at every finite point a is p(a). It follows by induction on p from the rule that the sum and the product of two meromorphic functions take the sum and the product of their values at points where both are finite. Red-team checks: value test z² + 1 vanishes at the finite point i; the same induction proves the rule for any meromorphic function in place of z (recorded as a generalisation, not a correctness issue).

Correctly defined: the coordinate z of the Riemann sphere, that is the identity map of the sphere (the complex plane with one point ∞ added) regarded as a meromorphic function, i.e. as a holomorphic map from the sphere to itself that is not identically ∞. This is the standard generator of the function field of the sphere: it takes the value a at each finite point a and has a pole (value ∞) at ∞. Red-team checks (built at 956e316250): the sphere carries the standard complex structure, with the two charts z on the plane and 1/z near ∞; the value at ∞ is ∞ and the value at a finite point a is a; the identity map is holomorphic in these charts.

Correctly stated: the coordinate function takes the value x at every point x of the Riemann sphere, including the value ∞ at ∞; this holds by definition, since the coordinate is the identity map. Red-team checks: holds definitionally and is used by simp.

Correctly stated: a meromorphic function on the Riemann sphere with no zeros and no poles at finite points is constant. If it has a pole at ∞, its reciprocal has no poles anywhere; otherwise it has none itself; either way one gets a holomorphic function on the compact connected sphere, which is constant by the maximum principle. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are satisfiable (nonzero constants) and both are needed, since z (a zero at 0) and 1/z (a pole at 0) are nonconstant functions satisfying all but one of them; the proof uses each hypothesis.

Correctly stated: every point of the Riemann sphere is a zero of some nonzero meromorphic function, namely a finite point t is a zero of z − t and the point ∞ is a zero of 1/z. Red-team checks: both witnesses are nonzero (z − t takes the value 1 at t + 1, and z is ∞ at ∞, so neither is the zero function).

Correctly stated: evaluation at the coordinate z is an isomorphism of complex algebras, hence of fields, from the field ℂ(X) of complex rational functions onto the field of meromorphic functions on the Riemann sphere, sending X to z; this is the classical theorem that the meromorphic functions on the sphere are exactly the rational functions of z. A meromorphic function on the sphere is here a holomorphic map from the sphere to itself that is not identically ∞, holomorphy being tested in the standard charts z and 1/z, so meromorphy at ∞ is required and essential singularities are excluded; the zero function is the constant map 0, and the field structure on these functions is proved in the library rather than assumed. Injectivity is automatic for a ring map out of a field, and surjectivity is the classical argument: dividing f by the product of the (z − u) raised to the order of f at u, over its finitely many finite zeros and poles u, leaves a function without zeros or poles in the plane, which is constant by the maximum principle. Red-team checks: built and axiom-checked locally at 956e316250 (only the three standard axioms); X goes to z, which has a pole at ∞; 1/X has a pole at 0 and a zero at ∞; (X² + 1)/(X − 1) takes the value 5 at 2; proved in Lean that no meromorphic function on the sphere agrees with e^z on the plane (its value at ∞ would have to be both 0 and ∞), so the definition really excludes essential singularities at ∞; no other construction of this isomorphism in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: the isomorphism sends the variable X to the coordinate function z, the case p = X of the polynomial rule; together with being a complex algebra map this determines the isomorphism as evaluation at z. Red-team checks: used by simp; the image has its pole at ∞, as z should.

Correctly stated: on polynomials the isomorphism is substitution of the coordinate, i.e. a polynomial p, viewed as a rational function, goes to the meromorphic function p(z); this is how the isomorphism is built, as the extension of polynomial evaluation at z to the field of fractions. Red-team checks: used by simp; specialises to X going to z.

Correctly stated: the meromorphic function attached to a rational function r takes the value r(a) at every finite point a where the reduced denominator of r does not vanish; at the other finite points r has a pole, the value there is ∞ and the quotient formula has no meaning, which is why the hypothesis is needed. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is necessary (for r = 1/X the value at 0 is ∞, checked in Lean); specialised to r = X, giving value a at a.

Correctly stated: for a real-valued distribution T on an open set Ω of a finite-dimensional real normed space (for example any open subset of R^n, the empty set and the whole space included), T has order zero, meaning that for every compact K inside Ω there is a constant C with |T(φ)| ≤ C·sup|φ| for all test functions φ supported in K, if and only if there are two positive Borel measures ν₁ and ν₂ on Ω, each regular and finite on compact subsets of Ω but possibly of infinite total mass, with T(φ) = ∫φ dν₁ − ∫φ dν₂ for every test function φ. This is the classical identification of real distributions of order zero with signed Radon measures, written as the difference of a positive and a negative part, and the docstring says exactly this; no uniqueness of the pair is claimed (it is not unique), and only real-valued distributions are covered. Because both measures are finite on compact sets, every test function is genuinely integrable against them, so the integrals are never a conventional zero value. The proof extends T, by uniform approximation with test functions supported in one fixed compact subset of Ω (mollification), to all compactly supported continuous functions on Ω, checks that the extension is linear and bounded above on every order interval [0, f], and applies the Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem for such functionals (Tau Ceti's signed form of Mathlib's theorem for positive functionals), which yields the two measures; the converse is the estimate |∫φ dν| ≤ ν(K)·sup|φ| for φ supported in K. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the Dirac mass at a point of Ω is represented by the pair (that Dirac mass, 0) and so has order zero; the derivative of the Dirac mass at 0 on the real line provably fails the order-zero bound (the test functions sin(nx) times a bump equal to 1 near 0 have sup at most 1 and derivative n at 0), so the condition is not vacuous; the empty domain and the whole space were instantiated; the only assumptions are the setting, so nothing contradictory can be derived; and the proof never uses the continuity of T, so the equivalence even holds for merely linear T.

Correctly stated: over a field with a valuation taking integer values on nonzero elements, if f has nonzero constant term and all slopes of its Newton polygon equal a rational number with denominator e, then e times the number of irreducible factors of f, counted with multiplicity, is at most deg f; that is, f has at most deg f / e irreducible factors. Reason: each irreducible factor has positive degree divisible by e (by the divisibility lemma of this file), and the degrees of the irreducible factors add up to deg f. For a nonzero constant both sides are 0. Red-team checks at 956e3162: every hypothesis is used; no Mathlib counterpart.

Correctly stated: over any ring with a valuation taking integer values on nonzero elements, if f has nonzero constant term and every slope of its Newton polygon equals the rational number q, then the denominator of q divides the degree of every divisor g of f. Reason: g also has nonzero constant term and its slopes are among those of f, so g's polygon is a single segment of slope q over [0, deg g] whose end heights are integers, hence q times deg g is an integer. Red-team checks at 956e3162: every hypothesis is used; the nonzero-constant-term hypothesis is needed (for f = X(X^2 - p) with the p-adic valuation both slopes are -1/2, but the factor X has degree 1); no Mathlib counterpart.

Correctly stated: over a field with a valuation taking integer values on nonzero elements, a polynomial f with nonzero constant term whose Newton polygon slopes all equal one rational number q, and whose degree equals the denominator of q, is irreducible. With a nonzero constant term the polygon covers [0, deg f], so it is then a single segment of slope q; any factor g has its slopes among those of f and integer end heights, so q times deg g is an integer, i.e. the denominator of q (= deg f) divides deg g, leaving deg g = 0 or deg g = deg f. It is the same criterion as the coprime form, with q = a/d written in lowest terms. Red-team checks at 956e3162: positive degree is automatic because a denominator is positive; the nonzero-constant-term hypothesis cannot be dropped (X^2 has no finite slopes, so q = 1/2 would otherwise apply, checked in Lean); removing any hypothesis breaks the proof; the coprime form and Eisenstein's criterion follow from it in Lean; no Mathlib counterpart.

Correctly stated: this is the Eisenstein-Dumas criterion. Let K be a field with a valuation v taking integer values on nonzero elements (a discrete valuation normalised at a uniformiser is the main case; the trivial valuation is also allowed), and let f = a_0 + a_1 X + ... + a_d X^d have degree d >= 1 and a_0 nonzero; if every edge of the Newton polygon of f (the lower convex hull of the points (i, v(a_i)), zero coefficients omitted) has slope a/d for an integer a with gcd(|a|, d) = 1, then f is irreducible over K. Because a_0 is nonzero the polygon spans all of [0, d] and every unit step is counted, so 'every slope equals a/d' says exactly that the polygon is the single segment from (0, v(a_0)) to (d, v(a_d)), and it forces a = v(a_d) - v(a_0); this matches the corollary in the Wikipedia article 'Newton polygon' (section Corollaries and applications: discrete normalised valuation, one segment of slope a/n with a coprime to n, then f is irreducible over K, with no completeness assumption). Why it holds: the slopes of any factor g of f are among those of f, so g's polygon is again one segment of slope a/d with integer end heights, hence d divides a times deg g, so d divides deg g and g is constant or of degree d. Conventions: slopes increase from left to right and a root of valuation r gives slope -r, so an Eisenstein polynomial has a = -1; only gcd(|a|, d) enters, so the sign of a is immaterial, and a/d is an honest real quotient. Red-team checks at 956e3162: Eisenstein's criterion over a field (v(a_0) = 1, v(a_d) = 0, v(a_i) >= 1 in between) derived in Lean as a corollary with a = -1, by showing the polygon is the single segment of slope -1/d; each hypothesis is needed (X^2 meets all the others vacuously with a/d = 1/2, a nonzero constant meets all but d >= 1, and neither is irreducible, both checked in Lean; X^2 - p^2 under half the p-adic valuation has one segment of slope -1/2 and is reducible, so integrality is needed); no contradiction among the hypotheses; no Mathlib counterpart (Mathlib has no Newton polygons); only the standard axioms.

Correctly stated: for every point q of G with values in a commutative R-algebra B, q lies in the centralizer subscheme Z_G(D(X)) if and only if q lies in the fixed-point subscheme of the conjugation action of D(X) on G. Both subschemes are characterised on points over all algebras: q is in the centralizer when it commutes with every point of D(X) after every extension of B, and q is a fixed point when pushing the coaction forward along q gives the trivial coaction; testing at the universal point of D(X) over B ⊗ R[X] shows the two conditions are the same. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): both universal properties read; it is a one-line consequence of the equality of ideals that follows it (a minor API note, not a defect in the statement).

Correctly stated: the ideal of H cutting out the scheme-theoretic centralizer Z_G(D(X)) equals the fixed-point ideal of the conjugation action of D(X) on G, the ideal generated by all coordinate functions of nontrivial weight for that action. So the centralizer of a homomorphism from a diagonalizable group is the fixed-point subscheme of its conjugation action, the standard reduction for proving centralizers smooth. Proof: two ideals are equal when exactly the same algebra maps kill them, which the previous lemma shows point by point. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): both definitions read (centralizer ideal spanned by the coefficients of the conjugation defect, fixed-point ideal spanned by the nontrivial weight spaces); both point characterisations quantify over all algebras, so this is an identity of closed subschemes, not of rational points.

Correctly stated: for every commutative R-algebra B and every B-point of G × D(X), i.e. a pair (g, t) of a B-point g of G and a B-point t of D(X), the conjugation coaction evaluated at that point is the B-point φ(t)·g·φ(t)⁻¹ of G, the product being taken in the group G(B). This is the defining property of the comorphism of the conjugation morphism under the Yoneda description of morphisms of affine schemes, and the proof reduces it to the evaluation formula of the universal conjugation map of H. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): the roles of the two tensor factors (acted-on point of G, acting point of D(X)) match the docstring.

Correctly defined: given a homomorphism φ from the diagonalizable group D(X) to an affine group G = Spec H (encoded by its comorphism H → R[X]), this is the comorphism H → H ⊗ R[X] of the conjugation morphism G × D(X) → G, (g, t) ↦ φ(t) g φ(t)⁻¹. It is built as the universal conjugation map of H followed by the comorphism of φ on the conjugating factor and a swap of tensor factors, which is how the comorphism of such a composite of morphisms of affine schemes is written; the next lemma in the file confirms that on every point it is conjugation by the image of the D(X)-point. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): formula read against its evaluation lemma and the comodule axioms proved for it; no Tau Ceti or Mathlib copy of this action found.

Correctly defined: the conjugation action of D(X) on G written in coordinates, making H a comodule algebra over the Hopf algebra R[X] (the coaction is an algebra map, coassociative and counital). Coassociativity is the action law φ(t₂)(φ(t₁) g φ(t₁)⁻¹)φ(t₂)⁻¹ = φ(t₁t₂) g φ(t₁t₂)⁻¹, which holds because D(X) is commutative, and counitality says the identity of D(X) acts trivially; both are proved against every test algebra, so this is the genuine action of the diagonalizable group on G, not only on rational points. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): no existing Tau Ceti or Mathlib construction of this action to reuse (the corestriction construction would need a conjugation coaction of H on itself, which the library lacks).

Correctly stated: the coaction of the conjugation comodule-algebra structure is the conjugation coaction map defined earlier in the file; it holds by definition. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): holds by unfolding, as stated.

Correctly stated: over any commutative ring R, if the coordinate ring of an affine group G is formally smooth, then so is the coordinate ring of the centralizer Z_G(D(X)) of any homomorphism from any diagonalizable group D(X) (X an arbitrary abelian group). Proof: the centralizer is the fixed-point subscheme of the conjugation action of D(X) (previous lemma), and fixed points of a diagonalizable group acting on a formally smooth affine scheme are formally smooth by the infinitesimal lifting criterion: lift a fixed point over a square-zero thickening arbitrarily, then keep its weight-one component, which is again an algebra map because the errors in nontrivial weights multiply to zero. This is the formal-smoothness part of SGA 3, Exp. XI, Cor. 5.3, here with no finiteness assumption on X, R or G. Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): formal smoothness of H is the only hypothesis and it is needed (for the trivial homomorphism the centralizer is all of G).

Correctly stated: over a Noetherian commutative ring R, if G = Spec H is a smooth affine group scheme of finite type and φ : D(X) → G is any homomorphism from the diagonalizable group of an abelian group X, then the scheme-theoretic centralizer of φ (the closed subgroup scheme of points of G commuting with every point of D(X) after every base change) is smooth over R, in the full sense: formally smooth and of finite presentation, not merely flat. This is the diagonalizable case of SGA 3, Exp. XI, Cor. 5.3 together with Cor. 4.2 (G smooth affine over any base, u : H → G a homomorphism from a group of multiplicative type and of finite type; then Centr_G(u) is a closed subgroup scheme smooth over the base), here with X not required to be finitely generated and φ not required to be a closed immersion. Proof: formal smoothness from the fixed-point description of the centralizer, finite presentation from finite type over a Noetherian base. Convention: the Noetherian hypothesis is stronger than needed, since the centralizer ideal is finitely generated over any base (recorded as a minor generality finding, with a compiled proof). Red-team checks (audit at 956e316250): hypotheses satisfiable, compiled at μ₂ = D(ℤ/2) over ℚ with the identity map and at 𝔾ₐ over ℤ with the trivial map from 𝔾ₘ; standard axioms only.

A Zipf-distributed variable is positive with probability one: the only natural number that is not positive is 0, which has mass zero for every s (trivially for the zero measure at s <= 1). Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): holds with no hypotheses, as stated.

For s > 1 the Zipf masses k^(-s)/zeta(s) over all natural numbers k sum to 1: this is the p-series identity sum over k >= 1 of k^(-s) = zeta(s) (the k = 0 term being 0), divided by zeta(s) > 0. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is needed (the series diverges for s <= 1); the zeta identity is Tau Ceti's real form of Mathlib's Dirichlet-series formula for zeta.

For s > 1 the Zipf law has total mass 1, so it is a probability distribution, as the zeta distribution is in the Wikipedia article 'Zeta distribution'. It holds because the masses k^(-s)/zeta(s) are nonnegative and sum to 1 by the identity sum of k^(-s) = zeta(s). Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): specialised at s = 2 to total mass 1; the hypothesis is needed, since for s <= 1 the law is zero.

The map sending an exponent s to the Zipf law (the zero measure for s <= 1) is measurable for the standard sigma-algebra on measures, generated by evaluation at measurable sets. Each mass k^(-s)/zeta(s) is measurable in s because the zeta function is measurable (continuous away from its pole), a countable weighted sum of point masses with measurable weights is measurable, and the two branches are glued along the measurable set s > 1. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the statement covers the whole parameter line including the zero branch, as the docstring says.

The zeta (Zipf) law with exponent s: for s > 1 it is the measure on the natural numbers giving each point k the mass k^(-s)/zeta(s), hence no mass at 0 and positive mass at every k >= 1; for s <= 1, where no such law exists, it is defined to be the zero measure, as its docstring says. This is the zeta distribution of the Wikipedia article 'Zeta distribution' (support the positive integers, parameter s > 1, mass k^(-s)/zeta(s)), whose n-th raw moment is zeta(s - n)/zeta(s) for n < s - 1 and infinite otherwise; the companion Moments file proves exactly this for natural n, with existence stated as an integrability equivalence and the formula only under n < s - 1, so neither the arbitrary value Lean gives zeta at its pole s = 1 nor the zero value of a divergent integral enters. Total mass 1 comes from the p-series identity sum over k >= 1 of k^(-s) = zeta(s) for s > 1. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): derived P(X = 1) = 6/pi^2 at s = 2 from zeta(2) = pi^2/6; derived that the mean is not integrable at s = 2; the point 0 has mass 0 for every s; s = 1 and s = 1/2 give the zero measure; no duplicate in Mathlib (five-way search) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

For s > 1 and a positive integer N, the set {0, 1, ..., N} has nonzero Zipf probability, since it contains the point 1, which has positive mass. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): both hypotheses are needed (for N = 0 the set is {0}, of mass 0; for s <= 1 the law is zero).

For s > 1 the Zipf law is the countable sum over k of point masses at k with weights k^(-s)/zeta(s); immediate from the definition, which takes this branch exactly when s > 1. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is needed: at s = -3 the law is zero by convention while the weights are positive (zeta(-3) = 1/120), checked in Lean.

For s <= 1 the Zipf law is the zero measure, the documented convention for exponents at which k^(-s) is not summable and no zeta law exists; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): specialised at s = 1 and s = 1/2.

Real-valued form: for s > 1 the probability of {k} under the Zipf law is the real number k^(-s)/zeta(s). Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): specialised at s = 2, k = 1 to 6/pi^2 from zeta(2) = pi^2/6.

For s > 1 the Zipf law gives the one-point set {k} the mass k^(-s)/zeta(s), i.e. P(X = k) = k^(-s)/zeta(s), the defining property of the zeta distribution (Wikipedia, 'Zeta distribution'). It follows by evaluating a countable sum of weighted point masses at a point. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): specialised at s = 2, k = 1 to 6/pi^2; the hypothesis is needed (at s = -3 the law is zero but the formula gives 120, checked in Lean).

For s > 1 the point k has nonzero Zipf probability exactly when k >= 1: the support of the zeta distribution is the positive integers, as in its standard definition. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is needed (for s <= 1 the law is zero).

Every Zipf law, including the zero measure used for s <= 1, gives the point 0 probability zero, so the law lives on the positive integers. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): holds for all s, as stated; checked at s = 2.

Defines the Zipf mass as an extended nonnegative real by taking the real mass k^(-s)/zeta(s) and truncating negative values to 0; for s > 1 the real mass is nonnegative, so nothing is truncated, and this is the weight put on the point k. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): agrees with the real mass for s > 1 and is finite at every k.

Defines, for a real exponent s and a natural number k, the number k^(-s)/zeta(s), where zeta(s) is the real part of the Riemann zeta function at s; for s > 1 this is the probability that a zeta (Zipf) distributed variable equals k, matching the Wikipedia article 'Zeta distribution' (P(X = k) = k^(-s)/zeta(s), s > 1). At k = 0 the convention that 0 raised to a negative power is 0 gives mass 0, so the law sits on the positive integers; for s <= 1 the formula is only an auxiliary value, and the measure built from it is set to zero. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): value at s = 2, k = 1 computed as 6/pi^2 from zeta(2) = pi^2/6; at s = 0 the value at k = 1 is -2 (zeta(0) = -1/2), which is why the positivity lemmas assume s > 1; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

States the defining formula: the real Zipf mass at k is k^(-s) divided by the real part of zeta(s); it holds by definition. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): matches the definition verbatim; it is the unfolding lemma the Cdf, Quantile, Finite and Moments files use.

For s > 1 every Zipf mass k^(-s)/zeta(s) is nonnegative, because k^(-s) >= 0 and zeta(s) > 0 for real s > 1. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is needed (at s = 0 the mass at k = 1 is -2, checked in Lean).

For s > 1 the mass k^(-s)/zeta(s) is strictly positive exactly when k is a positive integer: k^(-s) > 0 for k >= 1, it is 0 at k = 0, and zeta(s) > 0 for real s > 1 (a Mathlib theorem). Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is needed (at s = 0 the mass at k = 1 is -2, checked in Lean).

For s different from 0 the Zipf mass at k = 0 is 0, because 0 raised to the nonzero power -s is 0 under the real-power convention. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is necessary: at s = 0 the mass at 0 is 1/zeta(0) = -2, checked in Lean.

For s > 1 the extended-real Zipf mass at k vanishes exactly when k = 0, restating that the masses are positive on the positive integers and zero at 0. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): the hypothesis is needed (at s = 0 the mass at k = 1 truncates to 0, checked in Lean).
The extended-real Zipf mass is never infinite, since it is the truncation of a real number. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): holds for every s and k with no hypotheses, as stated.

Out of an even column the horizontal map is 1 - λ; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
Out of an odd column the horizontal map is the cyclic norm N; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Two consecutive horizontal maps compose to zero, N(1 - λ) = 0 = (1 - λ)N, because λ has order dividing q+1 on q-cochains so that λN = Nλ = N; this makes each row a complex, as in Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1. Red-team checks: both parities of the column covered; simp cannot prove it without this lemma and its left side is in simp normal form.

Defines the vertical map of the cyclic bicomplex: the Hochschild coboundary b in even columns and minus the bar coboundary b' (b without its last, wrap-around term) in odd columns. This matches Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1, whose even columns are Hochschild complexes and odd columns acyclic Hochschild complexes with the sign of the differential changed; b and b' agree with Connes, Noncommutative Geometry, III.1 (the formula for b, and b' in Lemma 6). Red-team checks: b and b' unfolded and compared with both sources; the degree-one total differential computed explicitly (compiled).

The vertical maps depend only on the parity of the column, so moving two columns to the right changes nothing. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; simp cannot prove it without this lemma and its left side is in simp normal form.

Adjacent squares of the cyclic bicomplex anticommute: going right then up is minus going up then right. In even columns this is (1 - λ)b = b'(1 - λ) and in odd columns bN = Nb', the cochain transposes of Lemma 1.1 of Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1 (b(1 - t) = (1 - t)b' and b'N = Nb); the second is also Lemma 6 of Connes, Noncommutative Geometry, III.1. Red-team checks: both parities compared with the sources; the signs are consistent with the total differential squaring to zero, which the file proves.
Two consecutive vertical maps compose to zero, as maps of cochains (b∘b = 0 and b'∘b' = 0). Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
The anticommutation of adjacent squares, evaluated at a cochain. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Two consecutive vertical maps send every cochain to zero: b(b φ) = 0 and b'(b' φ) = 0 for an associative, possibly nonunital algebra. Red-team checks: associativity is assumed where it is needed; simp cannot prove it without this lemma and its left side is in simp normal form.
In an even column the vertical map is the Hochschild coboundary b; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
In an odd column the vertical map is minus the bar coboundary, -b'; immediate from the definition. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Defines the cochain map from Connes' cyclic cochain complex (cyclic cochains with the Hochschild coboundary) to the total complex of the cyclic bicomplex, given in each degree by the inclusion into column zero; compatibility with the differentials is the commutation proved above. Red-team checks: componentwise equal to the inclusion (proved); compared with the transpose of the augmentation in Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1.
The components of the cochain map into the total complex are the inclusions into column zero. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Defines the inclusion of cyclic m-cochains into column zero, row m, of the total complex in degree m. Column zero carries the Hochschild coboundary, and the cyclic cochains (Connes, Noncommutative Geometry, III.1: φ(a1,...,an,a0) = (-1)^n φ(a0,...,an)) are exactly the kernel of 1 - λ there, so this is the transpose of the augmentation of the total complex onto the cyclic complex in Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1. Red-team checks: the cyclicity condition compared with Connes' (equivalent form with the rotation inverted); injective (proved in the file).
The inclusion of cyclic cochains into column zero is injective. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

A cyclic cocycle placed in column zero is a total cocycle, since D of the inclusion is the inclusion of b φ = 0. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Defines the degree-m term of the total complex, the direct sum over p + q = m of the q-cochains, as the families (x_q) of q-cochains with x_q = 0 for q > m, the component x_q sitting in column m - q. Each total degree has finitely many terms, so this is the term of the total complex of Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1, transposed. Red-team checks: exactly the rows 0,...,m occur; the degree-zero term is the 0-cochains in column zero (degree-zero tests compiled).

A total cochain of degree m is also one of every degree n >= m, both being families vanishing above the given row; immediate. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Assembles the total complex of the cyclic bicomplex as a cochain complex of modules indexed by the natural numbers, with the terms and differential defined above. Red-team checks: built with the standard cochain-complex constructor from the proved D^2 = 0; its degree-zero cohomology is the traces (compiled).

Identifies the degree-m term of the total complex with the module of total cochains of degree m (an identity isomorphism). Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
Under that identification the differential of the total complex is the total differential D. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Defines the total differential D = d_h + d_v from degree m to degree m+1: row 0 receives the horizontal map out of column m, and row q+1 receives the vertical map of the row-q component plus the horizontal map of the row-(q+1) component. The squares anticommute, so no further signs are needed, as in Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1, where the total differential is the sum of the horizontal and vertical ones. Red-team checks: in degree one the components are N x0, -b' x0 + (1 - λ) x1 and b x1 (compiled), matching that double complex transposed; D squares to zero (proved); the truncated subtraction in the column indices only meets components that are zero.

In row q+1 the total differential is the vertical map of the row-q component plus the horizontal map of the row-(q+1) component. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; simp cannot prove it without this lemma.

In row zero the total differential is the horizontal map out of column m applied to the row-zero component. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; simp cannot prove it without this lemma and plain simp uses it.
The total differential squares to zero, as a composite of linear maps. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

The inclusion commutes with the differentials: D of a cyclic cochain φ in column zero is (1 - λ)φ = 0 in column one plus bφ in column zero, that is, the inclusion of the cyclic coboundary bφ (b preserves cyclic cochains: Connes, Noncommutative Geometry, III.1, Corollary 7). Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses; simp cannot prove it without this lemma and its left side is in simp normal form.

The total differential squares to zero, from d_h^2 = 0, d_v^2 = 0 and the anticommuting squares, as stated for the total complex in Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1. Red-team checks: associativity of the algebra is assumed exactly here; simp cannot prove it without this lemma and its left side is in simp normal form.

Defines the linear map sending a total cocycle (an element of the kernel of D) to its cohomology class in the cohomology of the total complex. Red-team checks: agrees with the homology class of any cycle with the same underlying cochain (proved), surjective (proved).

The class of a total cocycle equals the cohomology class of any cycle of the total complex whose underlying total cochain is that cocycle. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
In degree n+1 a total cocycle has zero class exactly when it is D of a total cochain of degree n. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
Every cohomology class of the total complex is the class of a total cocycle. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.
In degree zero there are no coboundaries, so a total cocycle has zero class exactly when it is zero. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

The map on cohomology induced by the inclusion sends the cyclic cohomology class of a cyclic cocycle to the class of the same cochain placed in column zero of the total complex. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

A family of cochains lies in total degree m exactly when it vanishes above row m; restates the definition. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

A total cochain is a total cocycle exactly when the differential of the total complex kills it; transports D through the identification of terms. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

In cohomological degree m, the inclusion of Connes' cyclic cochain complex into the total complex of the cyclic bicomplex induces an isomorphism on m-th cohomology, provided 1, 2, ..., m are invertible in the base ring. This is the cochain form of Proposition 1.2 of Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1 together with its Remark that an isomorphism in degree n needs only n! invertible. The proof kills the components of a total cocycle column by column using row exactness, which moves cocycles and coboundaries into column zero, where they are cyclic cocycles and cyclic coboundaries. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is used and is needed for row exactness (fails over the field with two elements, compiled); in degree zero no hypothesis is needed and both sides are the traces (compiled).

Over a commutative ring containing the rationals, the inclusion of Connes' cyclic cochain complex (multilinear maps φ from A^(n+1) to the coefficient module with φ(a1,...,an,a0) = (-1)^n φ(a0,...,an), with the Hochschild coboundary b) into column zero of the total complex of the cyclic bicomplex (columns b and -b', rows 1 - λ and N) is a quasi-isomorphism: it induces an isomorphism on cohomology in every degree. This is the cochain (transposed) form of Proposition 1.2 of Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1, which states that for a ground ring containing the rationals the augmentation of the total complex onto the cyclic complex (A^(*+1)/(1 - t), b) is a quasi-isomorphism; the cyclic cochains and b are those of Connes, Noncommutative Geometry, III.1, where Corollary 7 shows they form a subcomplex whose degree-zero cohomology is the traces. It holds because each row 1 - λ, N, 1 - λ, ... is exact away from column zero once q+1 is invertible, so every total cocycle and coboundary can be pushed into column zero. The algebra here may be nonunital and the coefficients any module, which is more general than the sources (unital algebra, scalar coefficients) and needs no extra argument since row exactness uses no unit. Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (instantiated at the rationals and at 2x2 rational matrices, compiled); degree-zero cohomology of both sides is the traces (compiled); the explicit degree-one total differential matches the transposed Loday-Quillen double complex (compiled); invertibility is needed for row exactness (fails over the field with two elements, compiled); only the three standard axioms.

When q+1 is invertible in the base ring, every row of the cyclic bicomplex is exact at each column p+1 >= 1: the image of the horizontal map into column p+1 is the kernel of the map out of it. This is exactness of the periodic resolution 1 - λ, N, 1 - λ, ... for the cyclic group of order q+1 away from degree zero, the input of Proposition 1.2 of Loday-Quillen, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984), section 1, which uses that the homology of that cyclic group vanishes in positive degrees in characteristic zero. Red-team checks: the hypothesis cannot be dropped: over the field with two elements and q = 1, λ is the identity on 1-cochains, so 1 - λ has zero image while N = 0 kills the nonzero cochain (a0,a1) -> a0 a1 (compiled).
A cochain placed alone in a row k <= m is a total cochain of degree m. Red-team checks: read against the definitions; no contradiction derivable from the hypotheses.

Says that g_r is holomorphic (complex differentiable) on the upper half-plane, for every real pair r. True because the prefactor is an entire function of τ, and each half product ∏(1 − qⁿv) is a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions, hence holomorphic by Weierstrass's theorem. Red-team checks: it is stated on the open set {Im τ > 0}, the usual meaning of holomorphic on ℍ; it rightly has no hypothesis on r, since for integral r the function is identically 0 and still holomorphic.

Says that the partial products of ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿw)(1 − qⁿw⁻¹), as functions of τ with q = e^{2πiτ} and w = e^{2πi(r₁τ+r₂)}, converge locally uniformly on the upper half-plane to the infinite product. This is the Weierstrass M-test: on a compact subset of the upper half-plane |q| ≤ c < 1 and |w|, |w⁻¹| are bounded, so Σ(|qⁿw| + |qⁿw⁻¹|) converges uniformly there. It is a genuine convergence statement, so the infinite product in the definition is a true limit, not Lean's placeholder value 1 for a divergent product. Red-team checks: specialised at a point, it gives convergence of the product there (compiled).

Defines, for a real pair r = (r₁, r₂) and τ in the upper half-plane, the Siegel function g_r(τ) = −e^{πi B₂(r₁)τ} e^{πi r₂(r₁−1)} (1 − w) ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿw)(1 − qⁿw⁻¹), where q = e^{2πiτ}, w = e^{2πi(r₁τ+r₂)} and B₂(x) = x² − x + 1/6 is the second Bernoulli polynomial. This is term for term the product formula in Koo–Shin–Yoon (arXiv:1007.2307, eq. (2.3)) and, once the n = 0 factor is split off, in Bilu–Parent (arXiv:0907.3306, eq. (7)); both cite Kubert–Lang, Modular Units, Ch. 2 §1. The leading minus sign, the exponent ½B₂(r₁) of q and the phase e^{πi r₂(r₁−1)} all agree. On the upper half-plane the product converges absolutely, which the file proves, so no placeholder value enters. Off it the value is a documented placeholder. For integral r one factor vanishes, so g_r is identically 0, which is why nonvanishing is stated only for r ∉ ℤ². Red-team checks: value test g_{(0,0)} = 0 (compiled); B₂ checked against x² − x + 1/6; a numerical evaluation of the defining product satisfies the translation laws below for random r, s, τ to relative error 1e-14; it also satisfies the inversion law g_r(−1/τ) = ζ₁₂⁹ g_{(r₂,−r₁)}(τ) of Koo–Shin–Yoon Lemma 3.1(iii), a test that is sensitive to the sign and phase normalisation; Mathlib and the rest of Tau Ceti have no Siegel function, Klein form or Jacobi triple product.

Says that for s = (s₁, s₂) ∈ ℤ² and τ in the upper half-plane, g_{r+s}(τ) = (−1)^{s₁s₂+s₁+s₂} e^{−πi(s₁r₂ − s₂r₁)} g_r(τ). Streng (arXiv:1503.08127, Lemma 2.13(3)) states exactly this law for h_a, which he notes is −i times Kubert–Lang's g_a, so it holds for g_a too; it is the Siegel-function form of Kubert–Lang's translation law for Klein forms. Proof idea: shifting r₂ by 1 leaves w unchanged and changes only the phase. Shifting r₁ by 1 replaces w by qw; the quasi-periodicity θ_q(qw) = −w⁻¹θ_q(w), together with B₂(x+1) = B₂(x) + 2x, then gives the factor −e^{−πi r₂}. Red-team checks: confirmed numerically for 20 random choices of r, s and τ (relative error below 1e-14); the cases s = (0,1) and s = (1,0) checked by hand; the upper-half-plane hypothesis is needed for the r₁-shift, which uses convergence of the product.

Says that g_r(τ + 1) = e^{πi/6} g_{(r₁, r₁+r₂)}(τ) for every τ, where (r₁, r₁+r₂) is the row vector r multiplied by T = [[1,1],[0,1]]. Koo–Shin–Yoon (arXiv:1007.2307, Lemma 3.1(iii)) state this T-transformation as g_r∘T = ζ₁₂ g_{rT}, with ζ₁₂ = e^{2πi/12} = e^{πi/6}. Proof: q is unchanged, w at τ + 1 is the w of (r₁, r₁+r₂) at τ, and the prefactors differ by e^{πi(B₂(r₁) − r₁² + r₁)} = e^{πi/6}. Red-team checks: no hypothesis on τ is needed, since the identity holds factor by factor; confirmed numerically for random r and τ; consistent with the level-two formulas, since g_{(½,0)}(τ+1) = e^{πi/6} g_{(½,½)}(τ) (checked by hand).

Spells out the defining product g_r(τ) = −e^{πi B₂(r₁)τ} e^{πi r₂(r₁−1)} (1 − w) ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿw)(1 − qⁿw⁻¹). It holds by definition. It is the unfolding lemma that other files need, because the definition's body is not exposed to them. Red-team checks: the right-hand side is literally the body of the definition.

For τ in the upper half-plane, splits the defining product into two half products: g_r(τ) = −e^{πi B₂(r₁)τ} e^{πi r₂(r₁−1)} (1 − w) · ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿw) · ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿw⁻¹). This is correct because each half product converges absolutely when |q| < 1 (the series Σ|qⁿv| converges), and the product of two convergent infinite products is the infinite product of the termwise products. Red-team checks: the hypothesis Im τ > 0 is load-bearing (it gives |q| < 1).

Writes g_r(τ) as the phase −e^{πi B₂(r₁)τ} e^{πi r₂(r₁−1)} times the theta product θ_q(w) = (1 − w) ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿw)(1 − qⁿw⁻¹), with q = e^{2πiτ} and w = e^{2πi(r₁τ+r₂)}. It holds for every τ: θ_q(w) is defined by the same product with w⁻¹ where the definition has e^{−2πi(r₁τ+r₂)}, and e^{−z} = (e^z)⁻¹. Red-team checks: it holds with no hypothesis, as a rewriting of the definition should; both sides are the same infinite product, so no convergence question arises.

Says that g_{(½,½)}(τ) = −e^{−πi/4} e^{−πiτ/12} (∏_{n≥0} (1 + s^{2n+1}))² on the upper half-plane, where s = e^{πiτ}. From the definition: B₂(½) = −1/12, the phase is e^{πi·½·(−½)} = e^{−πi/4}, w = −s, and (1 + s) ∏_{n≥1} (1 + s^{2n+1})(1 + s^{2n−1}) is the square of ∏_{n≥0} (1 + s^{2n+1}). Red-team checks: recomputed by hand; consistent with the T-law, since g_{(½,0)}(τ+1) = e^{πi/6} g_{(½,½)}(τ).

Says that g_{(½,0)}(τ) = −e^{−πiτ/12} (∏_{n≥0} (1 − s^{2n+1}))² on the upper half-plane, where s = e^{πiτ}, so that q = s². Directly from the definition: B₂(½) = −1/12, the phase is 1, w = s, and (1 − s) ∏_{n≥1} (1 − s^{2n+1})(1 − s^{2n−1}) regroups as the square of the odd product. Red-team checks: recomputed by hand; Im τ > 0 is needed for the products to converge.

Says that if r = (r₁, r₂) is not in ℤ², then g_r(τ) ≠ 0 at every τ in the upper half-plane. An absolutely convergent product with no zero factor is nonzero. A factor 1 − e^{2πi((n+r₁)τ+r₂)} or 1 − e^{2πi((n−r₁)τ−r₂)} vanishes at a point of ℍ only if n ± r₁ = 0 and r₂ ∈ ℤ, which means r ∈ ℤ². Koo–Shin–Yoon (arXiv:1007.2307, after (2.3)) state that g_r has no zeros on ℍ. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is exactly r ∉ ℤ² (proved equivalent to: not both r₁ and r₂ integers), not the stronger r₁ ∉ ℤ; the theorem applies to r = (0, ½) (compiled); the hypothesis is needed, since g_{(0,0)} = 0 identically (compiled); both hypotheses are load-bearing; nonvanishing of the infinite product comes from Mathlib's theorem on absolutely convergent products, not from a placeholder value.

Says that g_{(0,½)}(τ) = 2i e^{πiτ/6} (∏_{n≥1} (1 + qⁿ))² on the upper half-plane. Directly from the definition: B₂(0) = 1/6, the phase is e^{−πi/2} = −i, and w = e^{πi} = −1, so 1 − w = 2 and each factor (1 − qⁿw)(1 − qⁿw⁻¹) equals (1 + qⁿ)². Red-team checks: recomputed by hand; Im τ > 0 is needed to evaluate the product.

Says that g_{(0,½)}(τ) g_{(½,0)}(τ) g_{(½,½)}(τ) = 2ζ₈, where ζ₈ = e^{2πi/8}, for every τ in the upper half-plane. By the three product formulas, the prefactors multiply to 2i·e^{−πi/4} = 2e^{πi/4}. The products combine to (∏_{n≥1} (1 + qⁿ) · ∏_{n≥0} (1 − s^{2n+1})(1 + s^{2n+1}))² = (∏_{n≥1} (1 + qⁿ) ∏_{n≥0} (1 − q^{2n+1}))², which is 1 by Euler's identity ∏_{n≥1} (1 + qⁿ) ∏_{n≥0} (1 − q^{2n+1}) = 1. This is the Siegel-function form of Weber's identity 𝔣𝔣₁𝔣₂ = √2. Red-team checks: numerically g₀g₁g₂ = 1.41421356 + 1.41421356i = 2ζ₈ at τ = 0.2 + 0.7i; the hypothesis Im τ > 0 is needed for the products to converge.

Says the Koszul differential, viewed inside the full exterior algebra, is the contraction by φ there; this holds by definition, since the differential is that contraction restricted to one degree. Red-team checks: definitional, matches the definition clause by clause.

If g : M → N has a linear left inverse h (h ∘ g = id) and ψ = φ ∘ h, so that also ψ ∘ g = φ, then exactness of the Koszul complex of ψ at the (n+1)-st exterior power implies exactness of the Koszul complex of φ there. This holds because the maps induced by g and h exhibit K(φ) as a retract of K(ψ) as complexes, and a retract of an exact sequence is exact. Red-team checks: each of the hypotheses h ∘ g = id, φ ∘ h = ψ and the exactness hypothesis is needed (removing any breaks the proof); the hypotheses are jointly satisfiable (g = h = identity); the degrees (exactness at the (n+1)-st term between d from degree n+2 and d to degree n) are right.

The Koszul complex K(φ) of a linear functional φ : M → R, for any module M over a commutative ring R: the chain complex indexed by the natural numbers whose degree-n term is the n-th exterior power of M (so R in degree 0 and M in degree 1) and whose differential from degree n+1 to degree n is contraction by φ. This is the complex underlying the Koszul complex of the Stacks Project, Definition 15.29.1 (Tag 0622), homologically indexed, with the same differential; the Koszul complex of a sequence (Definition 15.29.2, Tag 0623) is the case of the functional Rⁿ → R sending the i-th basis vector to xᵢ. The multiplicative (differential graded algebra) structure of Stacks' definition is not part of this object. Red-team checks: the degree-n term is definitionally the n-th exterior power; differentials into negative degrees are zero; witness M = R, φ = multiplication by x gives 0 → R → R → 0 with H₀ ≅ R/(x), and H₁ = 0 exactly when x is a nonzerodivisor (proved); over ℤ, H₀ of the Koszul complex of (2, 3) is zero; d∘d = 0 is proved, not assumed; pinned Mathlib has no Koszul complex (mathlib4#43708 is upstream work, not merged there).

The Koszul complex is exact in degree k+1, i.e. its (k+1)-st homology vanishes, if and only if the two Koszul differentials from degree k+2 to k+1 and from k+1 to k form an exact sequence (the kernel of the second equals the image of the first). This is the definition of homology vanishing at an interior term, translated from the category of modules to the elementwise statement. Red-team checks: specialised at M = R, φ = multiplication by x, where it gives H₁ = 0 if and only if x is a nonzerodivisor; the degrees match.

The zeroth Koszul homology is R/φ(M): an isomorphism of R-modules from H₀(K(φ)) to the quotient of R by the image ideal of φ. Since H₀ of a complex concentrated in nonnegative degrees is the cokernel of the first differential, and the first differential is φ under the identifications of the 0th and 1st exterior powers with R and M, the cokernel is R/φ(M). It is an R-module isomorphism (the complex is a complex of modules, so H₀ carries no ring structure here). Red-team checks: specialised at M = R, φ = multiplication by x, giving H₀ ≅ R/(x); the class of 1 goes to the class of 1 (proved by simp from the next lemma).

For a finite family x = (xᵢ) of elements of R, the Koszul complex of the functional Rⁿ → R sending v to Σᵢ vᵢxᵢ (which sends the i-th basis vector to xᵢ) is the Koszul complex K(x₁, …, xₙ) of Stacks Project Definition 15.29.2 (Tag 0623), and its zeroth homology is R/(x₁, …, xₙ) as an R-module. This is the general H₀ isomorphism together with the fact that the image of that functional is the ideal generated by the xᵢ. Red-team checks: checked the functional sends the i-th basis vector to xᵢ; over ℤ with x = (2, 3) it shows H₀ = 0, as (2, 3) = ℤ.

The isomorphism H₀(K(x)) ≅ R/(x₁, …, xₙ) sends the class of an element of the 0th exterior power to the class of the corresponding scalar modulo (x₁, …, xₙ). Immediate from the general formula. Red-team checks: direct specialisation of the general evaluation lemma.

The isomorphism H₀(K(φ)) ≅ R/φ(M) sends the homology class of an element of the 0th exterior power to the class modulo φ(M) of the corresponding scalar, i.e. it is the expected map. Red-team checks: evaluated on the class of 1, which goes to the class of 1.

The chain map K(φ) → K(ψ) induced by a linear map g : M → N with ψ ∘ g = φ, given in degree n by the n-th exterior power of g. This is the map of Stacks Project Lemma 15.29.3 (Tag 0624), on underlying complexes; that it commutes with the differentials is the naturality of contraction. Red-team checks: hypothesis ψ ∘ g = φ is exactly Stacks'; functoriality proved below.

A linear isomorphism e : M ≅ N with ψ ∘ e = φ induces an isomorphism of Koszul complexes K(φ) ≅ K(ψ), with inverse induced by the inverse of e; this is the functoriality of Stacks Lemma 15.29.3 applied to e and its inverse. Red-team checks: both round trips are proved to be identities via map_comp and map_id.
The forward map of the isomorphism induced by e is the chain map induced by e; true by definition. Red-team checks: definitional.
The inverse of the isomorphism induced by e is the chain map induced by the inverse of e; true by definition. Red-team checks: definitional.

The chain map induced by a composite g' ∘ g equals the composite of the induced chain maps, because exterior powers are functorial. Red-team checks: the compatibility hypotheses compose as they should; functoriality check.
In degree n, the chain map induced by g is the n-th exterior power of g; true by definition. Red-team checks: definitional.
The identity map of M induces the identity of the Koszul complex, because the exterior powers of the identity are identities. Red-team checks: functoriality check.

For m in M, left exterior multiplication by m is a null-homotopy of multiplication by φ(m) on the Koszul complex. This is Stacks Project Lemma 15.29.5 (Tag 0626), f = de + ed with f = φ(e), packaged as a chain homotopy from φ(m)·id to 0; its two identities are the degree-zero and positive-degree homotopy lemmas above. Red-team checks: the homotopy is built from those two identities, which match Stacks' signs; the components are exterior multiplication by m (next lemma).
The component of the Koszul homotopy from degree n to degree n+1 is exterior multiplication by m; true by construction. Red-team checks: definitional unfolding of the construction.

Every value φ(m) of the functional annihilates every Koszul homology module: φ(m)·z = 0 for every class z in every Hₙ(K(φ)). Equivalently the ideal φ(M) annihilates the Koszul homology; for a sequence x₁, …, xᵣ this is Stacks Project Lemma 15.29.6 (Tag 0663), that (x₁, …, xᵣ) annihilates Hᵢ(K(x)). It follows because homotopic maps induce the same map on homology, and multiplication by φ(m) is null-homotopic. Red-team checks: specialised at M = R, φ = multiplication by x, giving x·Hₙ = 0; no hypotheses on R or M beyond commutativity.
The degree-n term of the Koszul complex is the n-th exterior power of M; true by definition. Red-team checks: definitional.

The differential of the Koszul complex from degree n+1 to degree n is the Koszul differential (contraction by φ); true by construction of the complex from its consecutive differentials. Red-team checks: checked against the definition; the other components are zero by the shape of a chain complex.

Defines the Koszul differential of a linear functional φ : M → R on a module M over a commutative ring R: the map from the (n+1)-st to the n-th exterior power of M given by contraction with φ, which on a wedge v₀ ∧ ⋯ ∧ vₙ is the alternating sum Σᵢ (−1)ⁱ φ(vᵢ) v₀ ∧ ⋯ ∧ v̂ᵢ ∧ ⋯ ∧ vₙ. This is exactly the differential of the Stacks Project, Section 15.29 (Tag 0621), d(e₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ eₙ) = Σᵢ (−1)^{i+1} φ(eᵢ) e₁ ∧ ⋯ ê_i ⋯ ∧ eₙ: indexing from 0 with sign (−1)ⁱ is the same sign as indexing from 1 with (−1)^{i+1}. It is obtained by restricting the contraction on the whole exterior algebra to the degree-(n+1) part, which contraction maps into degree n. Red-team checks: evaluated on two and three vectors, giving φ(v₀)v₁ − φ(v₁)v₀ and φ(v₀) v₁∧v₂ − φ(v₁) v₀∧v₂ + φ(v₂) v₀∧v₁ as Stacks' formula predicts; no general module (free or finite) hypothesis; Mathlib (pinned) has no Koszul differential.

The Koszul differential squares to zero: applying it twice, from degree n+2 to degree n, gives the zero map. This is the standard fact that contraction by a functional is a square-zero antiderivation (the condition that makes the Koszul complex a complex, Stacks Project Section 15.29); it is deduced from the corresponding identity for contraction on the exterior algebra. Red-team checks: no hypotheses beyond φ; the statement is the composite equals zero, not a weaker pointwise claim.

Naturality: if g : M → N is linear and ψ ∘ g = φ, then the map induced by g on exterior powers intertwines the Koszul differentials of φ and ψ. This is the content of Stacks Project Lemma 15.29.3 (Tag 0624), which says such a g induces a map of Koszul complexes; it follows from the compatibility of contraction with the induced algebra map. Red-team checks: the hypothesis ψ ∘ g = φ is needed (removing it breaks the proof), and is exactly Stacks' hypothesis.

The Koszul homotopy identity in the lowest degree: for m in M and r in the 0th exterior power, d(m ∧ r) = φ(m) r. This is the degree-0 case of Stacks Project Lemma 15.29.5 (Tag 0626), f = de + ed with f = φ(e), where the term ed vanishes because d is zero out of degree 0. Red-team checks: matches Stacks' identity with e = m.

Elementwise form of d ∘ d = 0: for every x in the (n+2)-nd exterior power, d(d x) = 0. Immediate from the composite version. Red-team checks: simp cannot derive it from the composite form alone, so the elementwise lemma is not redundant.

Elementwise naturality with the compatibility built in: applying the Koszul differential of ψ after the map induced by g equals applying the map induced by g after the Koszul differential of the pulled-back functional ψ ∘ g. Immediate from the composite version with φ = ψ ∘ g. Red-team checks: no hypotheses; a direct specialisation.

The alternating-deletion formula: the Koszul differential sends v₀ ∧ ⋯ ∧ vₙ to Σᵢ (−1)ⁱ φ(vᵢ) times the wedge with vᵢ deleted. This is the explicit formula in the Stacks Project, Section 15.29 (Tag 0621), with 0-based indexing (so the sign (−1)ⁱ here is Stacks' (−1)^{i+1}); it follows from the corresponding formula for contraction on the exterior algebra. Red-team checks: specialised to two and three vectors, reproducing the expected signed sums term by term.

For the functional (m, r) ↦ φ(m) + r x on M × R (φ with one scalar x adjoined), it computes the M-part of the Koszul differential: projecting d z to the exterior powers of M gives the Koszul differential of φ on the projection of z, plus x times the projection of the contraction of z with the second coordinate. Writing z = a + e ∧ b with e = (0,1), this is d(a) + x·b, the familiar formula behind the inductive (mapping-cone) description of K(x₁,…,xₙ,x). It follows from the corresponding identity for contraction on exterior algebras. Red-team checks: checked the decomposition by hand (the projection kills e, and contraction with the second coordinate sends e ∧ b to b); its consumer is the regular-sequence exactness proof.

The image of the first Koszul differential, transported to R along the identification of the 0th exterior power with R, is the image φ(M) of φ, an ideal of R. This follows from the identification of the first differential with φ, since the identification of the 1st exterior power with M is surjective. Red-team checks: it is what makes H₀ = R/φ(M) below; specialised at M = R, φ = multiplication by x, giving the ideal (x).

The Koszul homotopy identity in positive degrees: for m in M and v in the (n+1)-st exterior power, m ∧ d(v) + d(m ∧ v) = φ(m) v. This is Stacks Project Lemma 15.29.5 (Tag 0626), f = de + ed as endomorphisms of K(φ) where e is left multiplication by an element e of M and f = φ(e); it is the statement that contraction is an antiderivation, d(m ∧ v) = φ(m) v − m ∧ d(v). Red-team checks: sign and degree conventions match Stacks exactly.

Identifies the first Koszul differential: under the standard identifications of the 0th exterior power with R and the 1st with M, the differential from degree 1 to degree 0 is the functional φ itself. This is the defining property d(e) = φ(e) of Stacks Project Definition 15.29.1 (Tag 0622); it follows from the alternating-deletion formula with a single vector. Red-team checks: checked against the alternating-deletion formula in degree 1; the identifications are Mathlib's standard ones (sending the empty wedge to 1 and a one-vector wedge to that vector).

Elementwise form: for x in the first exterior power, the scalar corresponding to d x is φ applied to the vector corresponding to x. Immediate from the composite version. Red-team checks: direct consequence, no extra hypotheses.

**How the row defines a group, for a reader who does not use Lean.** `GroupPresentation.Group` is Mathlib's `PresentedGroup` on the compiled relators: the free group on the listed generators modulo the normal subgroup generated by the relator words. Only the generator list and the relator expressions affect the group; the source, locator, notes and expected counts are documentation, and `…_matchesMetadata` checks the counts against the data. A relator `r` stands for the relation `r = 1`; a source equation `x = y` is stored as `x⁻¹y`; `rⁿ` is `n` copies of `r`; the literature's commutator `[r, s] = r⁻¹s⁻¹rs` is stored as `Relator.commInvInv r s`, since Mathlib's `⁅r, s⁆` is `r s r⁻¹ s⁻¹`; and `Relator.conj r s` is `s⁻¹ r s`. A relator that the source calls redundant does not change the group.

**Independent check on the compiled words.** I evaluated `relatorLetters` for this row in Lean at commit `36f24f5` and ran the 34 words in GAP 4.16.1 with ACE 5.7.0.
- Coset enumeration over the subgroup generated by `a, …, f` closes at index 1782, the degree of the rank-three action of Suz on the cosets of `G₂(4)`. The permutation action on those cosets has image of order exactly `448345497600 = |Suz|`, simple. So the presented group maps onto Suz, the only simple group of that order.
- Dropping the last generator at each step and enumerating each sub-presentation over the next gives indices `1782, 416, 280, 36, 12, 5, 2`, whose product is `2·|Suz|`. So the presented group is Suz or a group of twice its order mapping onto it. The sub-presentations are bigger than the subgroups they map onto, so the bound is not tight; it does not decide between the two.

**What this leaves open.** Suz has Schur multiplier of order 6, so the double cover `2·Suz` is the one alternative the bound allows; I did not rule it out. The relator count matches the source (`suzPresentation_matchesMetadata`), and the source's construction is the argument that its six extra relations kill the centre.

Not checked: whether the order is `|Suz|` or `2·|Suz|`; the Lean proofs, which Lean checks.

**For a reader who does not use Lean.** A `GroupPresentation` is a record: a list of generator names, a list of relator expressions, and documentation fields (source, locator, conventions, notes, expected counts). The group it defines is the free group on the generators modulo the normal subgroup generated by the relators, `GroupPresentation.Group`; the documentation does not affect it. `SporadicName.presentation` is a plain case split, so the group attached to `.Co2`, for instance, is literally the group of `Sporadic.co2Presentation`.

**Why the choice of presentation matters.** The roadmap requires an actual presentation, proved in the literature to define the group, not a semi-presentation, which only recognises standard generators inside a group built elsewhere. The rows draw on ATLAS v3 presentations on standard generators, Coxeter-type presentations on involutions, symmetric-generation presentations, the computer-proved presentations of Lyons and Thompson, and the `Y₄₄₃` and `Y₄₃₃` presentations of the Monster and Baby Monster.

**What I verified.** I evaluated all twenty-six compiled relator lists (`relatorLetters`) in Lean at the commit and ran them in GAP 4.16.1 with ACE 5.7.0 and AtlasRep 2.1.12.
- **Presented group proved to be the named group** (an upper bound from coset enumeration equals the order, and the group maps onto the named group): M₁₁, M₁₂, M₂₂, M₂₃, M₂₄, J₁, J₂, J₃, HS, Fi₂₃.
- **Presented group maps onto the named group**: McL, He, Co₂, Fi₂₂ and J₄, whose relators hold on ATLAS standard generators; Suz, O'N, Co₃, Co₁, Fi₂₄' and Ru, where a coset action has image of exactly the right order and is simple; HN, where it is primitive and perfect of the right order. For Suz the order is also at most `2·|Suz|`.
- **Ly**: the relators without `z` present exactly `G₂(5)`, and `⟨a, b, c, d⟩` has the source's index 8835156, so the presented group has order at most `|Ly|`; the lower bound is the source's theorem.
- **Th**: the relators without `u` present a group mapping onto `³D₄(2):3`, the subgroup of the source's final enumeration, which I could not complete.
- **Literature**: M and B, compared with Bray, Ivanov, Kitazume and Breuer–Magaard–Wilson, with an exact GAP computation showing their extra relators are central and nontrivial.
A surjection rules out a trivial or wrong presentation but not a missing relator; for those rows, and for Th, the source's proof is the argument for sufficiency, and for Ly it is the argument for the lower bound.

Correctly stated: it is the classification of finite simple groups, in the form "every finite simple group is isomorphic to one on the list", with the list built from explicit groups. I checked the statement, the index and every branch at commit `36f24f5`, the sporadic branch by computation. Each constituent has its own review on the site. No earlier review of this declaration.

**What it says, for a reader who does not use Lean.** For every finite simple group `G`, there is an index `i` and an isomorphism of groups `G ≅ i.Group`. The index ranges over four kinds:
- primes `p`, with `i.Group` the cyclic group of order `p`;
- `n ≥ 5`, with the alternating group `Aₙ`;
- the valid Lie-type parameters, with the simple group of Lie type, the Tits group included;
- the twenty-six sporadic names, each with the group of a recorded presentation.

`[Finite G]` and `[IsSimpleGroup G]` are hypotheses. Mathlib's simplicity requires `G` nontrivial with no normal subgroups but `⊥` and `⊤`, so the cyclic groups of prime order count, as in the textbooks. `Nonempty (G ≃* i.Group)` means an isomorphism exists. The statement is universe-polymorphic; `classificationStatement_of_zero` shows the universe makes no difference.

**What it does not say, and why that is right.** It is a definition of a proposition, not a theorem: proving it is the classification itself. It claims only the hard direction. That every listed group is finite and simple is the subject of the separate roadmap CFSGBasicProperties, just as it is a separate fact classically. Uniqueness of the index is not claimed. The ranges and the six removed duplicates (`A₁(4)`, `A₁(5)`, `A₁(9)`, `A₂(2)`, `A₃(2)`, `B₂(3)`) make the list irredundant anyway, and dropping a name never drops a group.

**A subtlety for reviewers.** The proposition depends only on the set of isomorphism types `{i.Group}`, so it cannot tell which index carries which group. A wrong sporadic carrier would make it false, since the group meant would then be isomorphic to nothing on the list. So correctness rests on the carriers, which I checked as follows.
- **Lie type.** All seventeen families audited: each carrier is the right simply connected group over `𝔽̄_p`, each Steinberg map the standard one, and the recipe `[H,H]/Z([H,H])` gives the simple group, `²F₄(2)'` for Tits. Some identifications rest on classical theorems that are not formalized, notably Chevalley's on the points of the integral carriers.
- **Sporadic.** I ran the twenty-six Lean-compiled relator lists in GAP 4.16.1 with ACE and AtlasRep. Ten rows (M₁₁, M₁₂, M₂₂, M₂₃, M₂₄, J₁, J₂, J₃, HS, Fi₂₃) are proved to present the named group. Twelve (McL, He, Co₂, Fi₂₂, J₄, Suz, O'N, Co₃, Co₁, Fi₂₄', Ru, HN) are shown to map onto it, which rules out a trivial or wrong group but not a missing relator. For Ly the source's enumeration is reproduced and bounds the order by `|Ly|`; for Th the subgroup its proof rests on checks out; and M and B agree with Bray, Ivanov and Breuer–Magaard–Wilson, with their central relators confirmed central by an exact computation.

**No junk values.** Invalid Lie-type parameters have no carrier, and every carrier is an honest construction, not a choice from an existence theorem. The roadmap lists no tagged Check for this declaration; its A0 completion criteria (no stand-in carrier, no invalid index reaching a carrier, no `Finite` or `IsSimpleGroup` instance assumed for `i.Group`) hold at the commit.

**For a reader who does not use Lean.** `PresentedGroup R` is the quotient of the free group on the generators by the normal closure of the set `R` of relator words, the usual meaning of `⟨X | R⟩`. Nothing about the result is assumed: it could in principle be trivial, infinite, or a cover of the intended group if a relator were wrong or missing. That is why the definition is only as good as the transcription, and why the rows were checked by computation as well as against their sources. `abbrev` makes it transparent, so Lean sees each branch as the presented group of its row.

**The four branches, for a reader who does not use Lean.**
- `cyclic p`: `Multiplicative (ZMod p)`. `ZMod p` is `ℤ/pℤ`, an additive group, and `Multiplicative` reads its addition as multiplication so that it is a `Group`; this is the cyclic group of order `p`.
- `alternating n`: `alternatingGroup (Fin n)`, the even permutations of `{0, …, n − 1}`, which is `Aₙ`, with `n ≥ 5`.
- `lie d`: `ValidLieTypeIndex.Group d`, the derived subgroup of the Steinberg fixed points modulo its centre, on an explicit simply connected carrier; this is the simple group of Lie type named by `d`, the Tits group included.
- `sporadic s`: `SporadicName.Group s`, the group defined by the recorded presentation for `s`.

**`abbrev` and the `Group` instance.** `abbrev` makes the definition transparent, so Lean sees each branch as the concrete type it names. The instance `Group i.Group` is found by cases on `i`; nothing about finiteness or simplicity is assumed or provided, as the roadmap requires.

**Evidence on the branches.** The cyclic and alternating branches are Mathlib's standard groups. For the Lie-type branch I audited all seventeen families: each carrier is the right simply connected group over `𝔽̄_p` and each Steinberg map the standard one, with some identifications resting on classical theorems not yet formalized (see `TauCeti.ValidLieTypeIndex.Group`). For the sporadic branch I ran the Lean-compiled relators in GAP: ten rows are proved to present their group, twelve to map onto it, Ly is bounded above by `|Ly|`, and Th, B and M were checked on the subgroups their sources' proofs rest on and against the literature (see `TauCeti.SporadicName.presentation`).

**Only the image matters.** The classification statement uses only the set of isomorphism types `{i.Group}`, so swapping two sporadic presentations would leave it unchanged.
