For every choice of parameters, almost every point under the inverse Gaussian law is strictly positive; this restates that (−∞, 0] has mass 0.

For μ > 0 and λ > 0 the distribution function of the inverse Gaussian law is 0 for x ≤ 0 and Φ(√(λ/x)(x/μ − 1)) + e^(2λ/μ)·Φ(−√(λ/x)(x/μ + 1)) for x > 0, combining the two one-sided statements into one formula.

For μ > 0 and λ > 0 the distribution function of the inverse Gaussian law is 0 at every x ≤ 0, since the law gives no mass to (−∞, 0]. The parameter hypotheses make the law a probability measure, which the distribution function requires.

For μ > 0, λ > 0 and x > 0, the distribution function P(X ≤ x) of the inverse Gaussian law is Φ(√(λ/x)(x/μ − 1)) + e^(2λ/μ)·Φ(−√(λ/x)(x/μ + 1)), with Φ the standard normal distribution function; this is the cdf in the Wikipedia article on the inverse Gaussian distribution. Proof: the right side has the density as derivative on (0, ∞) and tends to 1 at infinity, so 1 minus it equals the integral of the density over (x, ∞), the upper tail. Red-team checks: specialised at μ = λ = x = 1 to Φ(0) + e²·Φ(−2) ≈ 0.6681; numerical integration of the density agrees with the formula at (μ, λ, x) = (1, 1, 1), (2, 3, 1.5) and (0.5, 4, 0.7) to 9 digits; all three hypotheses are needed.
If a random variable X has law IG(μ, λ) and b > 0, then bX has law IG(bμ, bλ), the random-variable form of the scaling rule.
A random variable whose law is inverse Gaussian has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure (its law is absolutely continuous), since the law is defined by a density.

For all parameters, a (vector-valued) function is integrable against the inverse Gaussian law exactly when its product with the density is Lebesgue integrable, the standard criterion for a law given by a density.

The real density is Lebesgue integrable on the whole line for every choice of parameters: at valid parameters it is 0 on (−∞, 0] and integrable on (0, ∞) because it is the nonnegative derivative of the closed-form cdf, which has finite limits at 0 and at infinity; at invalid parameters it is identically 0.
For all parameters, the integral of a function against the inverse Gaussian law equals the Lebesgue integral of its product with the density, the standard formula for a law given by a density.

Normalisation: for μ > 0 and λ > 0 the inverse Gaussian density integrates to 1 over the real line, the fact that the density in the Wikipedia article on the inverse Gaussian distribution is a probability density. The proof uses the explicit antiderivative F(x) = Φ(√(λ/x)(x/μ − 1)) + e^(2λ/μ)·Φ(−√(λ/x)(x/μ + 1)) on (0, ∞), Φ the standard normal cdf: its derivative is the density (the two Gaussian arguments w₁, w₂ satisfy w₂² − w₁² = 4λ/μ, so the factor e^(2λ/μ) turns the second chain-rule term into a multiple of the first), F tends to 0 at 0 from the right and to 1 at infinity, and the improper fundamental theorem of calculus gives total integral 1. At invalid parameters the integral is 0 by the zero-density convention, so both hypotheses are needed. Red-team checks: numerical quadrature at μ = 2, λ = 3 gives 0.99999999999; specialised at μ = 2, λ = 3.

Defines the inverse Gaussian law IG(μ, λ) as Lebesgue measure on the real line weighted by the density √(λ/(2πx³))·exp(−λ(x−μ)²/(2μ²x)) on x > 0 (zero on x ≤ 0), and the zero measure when μ ≤ 0 or λ ≤ 0. The Wikipedia article on the inverse Gaussian distribution gives exactly this density on (0, ∞) with μ > 0 the mean and λ > 0 the shape, the same closed-form cdf Φ(√(λ/x)(x/μ − 1)) + e^(2λ/μ)·Φ(−√(λ/x)(x/μ + 1)), and the scaling rule tX ∼ IG(tμ, tλ) for t > 0. The file proves all three facts the Voyager announcement attributes to it, in full and under no hypotheses beyond μ, λ > 0 (and b > 0 for scaling): the law is a probability measure exactly when μ, λ > 0 (the nontrivial normalisation is proved through an explicit antiderivative), its cdf is that formula for x > 0 and 0 for x ≤ 0, and its image under x ↦ bx is IG(bμ, bλ). The zero-measure convention at invalid parameters is stated in the docstring and characterised by its own theorem. Red-team checks: the law is by definition Lebesgue measure with this density; the cdf theorem at μ = λ = x = 1 gives Φ(0) + e²·Φ(−2) ≈ 0.6681, matching numerical integration of the density (0.668102), and two more points agree to 9 digits; scaling fails, as it must, for every b ≤ 0; no construction of this law (or of the Wald law) in pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti, searched by name and by formula.
For all parameters the inverse Gaussian law gives the half-line (−∞, 0] mass 0, since its density vanishes there.
The inverse Gaussian law is Lebesgue measure weighted by the extended-real inverse Gaussian density; it holds by definition.

For b > 0, the image of IG(μ, λ) under x ↦ bx is IG(bμ, bλ): if X is inverse Gaussian with mean μ and shape λ then bX is inverse Gaussian with mean bμ and shape bλ. The Wikipedia article on the inverse Gaussian distribution states this scaling rule for t > 0. Proof: the image of a law with density f under x ↦ bx has density b⁻¹·f(x/b), which is the IG(bμ, bλ) density by the density scaling identity; at invalid parameters both sides are the zero measure. Red-team checks: for every b ≤ 0 the identity fails at μ = λ = 1 (the image is a probability measure, the right side is the zero measure), so b > 0 is necessary; specialised at b = 2, μ = 1, λ = 3.
If μ ≤ 0 or λ ≤ 0 the inverse Gaussian law is the zero measure, because the density vanishes identically there; this is the documented convention.

The same inverse Gaussian density viewed as an extended nonnegative real-valued function (the real density, which is never negative, read in [0, ∞]), the form needed to weight Lebesgue measure. Red-team checks: converting back to real numbers recovers the real density exactly.

Defines the inverse Gaussian density with mean μ and shape λ: the real function equal to √(λ/(2πx³))·exp(−λ(x−μ)²/(2μ²x)) at x > 0 when μ > 0 and λ > 0, and 0 otherwise. This is term by term the density in the Wikipedia article on the inverse Gaussian distribution (support x > 0, mean μ > 0, shape λ > 0): λ over 2πx³ under the root, and exponent −λ(x−μ)²/(2μ²x). Setting it to 0 off the valid parameters is the library's documented convention, which makes the associated law the zero measure there. Red-team checks: evaluated at μ = λ = x = 1 to √(1/(2π)); compared clause by clause with the source; numerical quadrature of the formula at μ = 2, λ = 3 gives total mass 1 to 11 digits.

For b > 0, the density of IG(bμ, bλ) at x equals b⁻¹ times the density of IG(μ, λ) at x/b, for all μ, λ and x: the change-of-variables identity behind scaling, checked by direct algebra (the square root gains the factor b⁻¹ and the exponent is unchanged), with both sides 0 off the valid range.
The density is nonnegative everywhere and for all parameters, since it is either 0 or a square root times an exponential.
The density is 0 at every x ≤ 0, for all parameters, reflecting that the inverse Gaussian law lives on the positive half-line; immediate from the definition.
The density vanishes identically unless μ > 0 and λ > 0, the documented invalid-parameter convention; immediate from the definition.

For μ > 0, λ > 0 and x > 0 the density equals the classical formula √(λ/(2πx³))·exp(−λ(x−μ)²/(2μ²x)), straight from the definition. Each of the three positivity hypotheses is needed, since the density is 0 by definition when any fails.
At positive parameters the density is strictly positive at every x > 0, being a positive square root times an exponential.
The extended-real inverse Gaussian density is, by definition, the real density read as an extended nonnegative real; it holds by unfolding the definition.
The extended-real density is 0 at every x ≤ 0, for all parameters.
The extended-real density vanishes identically unless both μ and λ are positive.
At positive parameters and x > 0 the extended-real density is the classical formula √(λ/(2πx³))·exp(−λ(x−μ)²/(2μ²x)) read as an extended nonnegative real.

For μ > 0 and λ > 0 the inverse Gaussian law has total mass 1, by the normalisation of its density. Red-team checks: specialised at μ = λ = 1; both hypotheses are needed, since the law is the zero measure otherwise.

The inverse Gaussian law is a probability measure if and only if μ > 0 and λ > 0: one direction is the normalisation of the density, and conversely at invalid parameters the law is the zero measure, of mass 0. Red-team checks: used to show that the law with μ = 1, λ = 0 is not a probability measure.
At positive parameters the extended-real density also has total integral 1, from the real normalisation together with integrability and nonnegativity.

The map sending (μ, λ) to the inverse Gaussian law (the zero measure at invalid parameters) is measurable into the space of measures with its standard σ-algebra, because the density is jointly measurable in the parameters and the point.
For fixed parameters the extended-real density is a measurable function of x.
For fixed parameters the real density is a measurable function of x, being a section of the jointly measurable density.
The extended-real density is jointly measurable in (μ, λ, x), as a measurable function of the jointly measurable real density.
The real density is jointly measurable as a function of (μ, λ, x): it is a measurable formula on the measurable set where μ, λ and x are all positive, and 0 elsewhere.
The density of a random variable with inverse Gaussian law is the inverse Gaussian density, up to a Lebesgue-null set (densities are only determined almost everywhere).
For all parameters, the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the inverse Gaussian law with respect to Lebesgue measure is its density, almost everywhere.

At positive parameters the topological support of the inverse Gaussian law (the smallest closed set of full measure) is [0, ∞): the density is positive exactly on (0, ∞), whose closure is [0, ∞); the point 0 lies in the support though it carries no mass. Both hypotheses are needed, since the support is empty at invalid parameters.
The support of the inverse Gaussian law is [0, ∞) at valid parameters and empty otherwise, the zero measure having empty support.
Converting the extended-real density back to a real number recovers the real density, because the real density is nonnegative.

Correctly stated: a continuous injective map from one manifold without boundary to another of the same finite dimension (each locally homeomorphic to open subsets of a real n-dimensional space) is an open embedding, that is, a homeomorphism onto an open subset of the target. This is the global form of invariance of domain: by the open-set version (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2B.3, transported through charts) every open set has open image, so the map is open, and a continuous open injection is a homeomorphism onto its image, which is open. Red-team checks: only the standard axioms; specialised to continuous injections R^n -> R^n and C -> R x R; the equal-dimension hypothesis is needed, since the inclusion of R as the x-axis of R^2 is a continuous injection whose image is not open.

Correctly stated: with A, B and the homeomorphism e as in the interior statement (subsets of boundaryless manifolds of the same finite dimension), a point x of A lies in the frontier of A (its closure minus its interior) exactly when e(x) lies in the frontier of B. Every point of a set lies in its closure, so for points of A, lying in the frontier just means not being interior, and the statement is the invariance of interior points negated. Red-team checks: only the standard axioms; the reduction to the interior statement is exactly the definition of the frontier; the equal-dimension hypothesis is needed for the same reason as there (a segment in R versus the same segment on the x-axis of R^2).

Correctly stated: if A and B are subsets of manifolds without boundary of the same finite dimension and e is a homeomorphism from A onto B (both with the subspace topology), then a point x of A is an interior point of A exactly when e(x) is an interior point of B; this is the classical invariance of interior points, a consequence of invariance of domain. Why: on the interior of A, e is a continuous injection into the ambient manifold of B, so it carries the interior of A to an open set, which lies in B and contains e(x); applying the same argument to the inverse homeomorphism gives the converse. Red-team checks: only the standard axioms; specialised to prove that the intervals [0,1) and (0,1) are not homeomorphic (0 is not interior in [0,1), while every point of the open interval is interior); the equal-dimension hypothesis is needed, since 1/2 is interior to [0,1] in R but its copy on the x-axis of R^2 is not interior to the segment there.

Correctly stated: if M and N are spaces locally homeomorphic to open subsets of real vector spaces of the same finite dimension n (manifolds without boundary; no Hausdorff condition, smoothness or chart compatibility is required, which is harmless because the statement is local), U is open in M, and f is continuous and injective on U, then f(U) is open in N. For M = N = R^n this is exactly Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 2B.3 ('If U is an open set in R^n and h : U -> R^n is an embedding, or more generally just a continuous injection, then the image h(U) is an open set in R^n'), and the general case follows by reading f in a chart around a point of U and a chart around its image. The proof is Hatcher's: regard the target as sitting in its one-point compactification S^n; for a small closed ball D around a point of U, the complement of the image of its boundary sphere is disconnected by the Jordan-Brouwer separation theorem, while it is the disjoint union of the complement of f(D), which is path connected (it is acyclic), and the image of the open ball, which is path connected; so the latter is a path component of an open subset of S^n and therefore open. Dimension 0 is allowed: both spaces are then discrete and every subset is open. Red-team checks: only the standard axioms, no sorry; specialised to show that a continuous injection R^n -> R^n is an open map, and to maps C -> R x R; every hypothesis is needed (U = {0} with the identity; a constant map; the transposition of 1/2 and 5 on (0,1), which is injective but not continuous; the inclusion of R as the x-axis of R^2, whose image is not open and which only the equal-dimension hypothesis excludes); no duplicate in Mathlib (pinned 2cabef97) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated. It says: if K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and P is a polynomial of positive degree whose coefficients are Laurent series in X over K (the zero polynomial is also allowed, trivially), then for some positive integer n, substituting X ↦ Xⁿ in every coefficient of P gives a polynomial with a root in the Laurent series field K((X)). Identifying K((X)) with K((X^{1/n})) through X ↦ X^{1/n}, this is exactly the statement that P has a root in K((X^{1/n})), i.e. the Newton–Puiseux theorem; Mannaa and Coquand (Dynamic Newton–Puiseux Theorem, arXiv:1304.6770, Introduction) state it for monic F in K[[X]][Y] with roots in K[[X^{1/m}]], and note that it is usually stated as algebraic closedness of the union of the K((X^{1/m})), which Tau Ceti derives from this theorem (puiseuxField.instIsAlgClosed). The proof is the classical algorithm: make P monic, remove the Y^{m-1} term by a translation (characteristic zero allows dividing by m), ramify and rescale along the smallest slope to get a monic polynomial over K[[X]] whose reduction mod X is not a single power (Y-b)^m, split that reduction into coprime factors (K algebraically closed), lift the splitting by Hensel's lemma, and recurse on a factor of smaller degree. The ramification index n is a positive integer by construction, so the degenerate substitution n = 0 cannot occur. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): hypotheses satisfiable; the positive-degree hypothesis is needed (a nonzero constant has no root after any substitution); algebraic closedness is needed (over the reals, Y²+1 has no root after any ramification, checked in Lean); ramification is genuinely needed (Y²-X has no root in K((X)) itself, checked in Lean, while the theorem yields n and y with y² = Xⁿ, and n = 2, y = X works by hand); characteristic zero is used in the translation step and is necessary (Artin–Schreier equations); no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti statement of this theorem (the analytic Puiseux files concern convergent families, a different statement).

Correctly stated. It says: for K algebraically closed of characteristic zero, a polynomial P of positive degree over the Laurent series field K((X)), and any level n, if the coefficients of P are embedded into the Puiseux field by X ↦ t^{1/n}, the resulting polynomial has a root in the Puiseux field, and that root already lies in a single level K((t^{1/(nm)})) for some positive integer m. For n = 1 the embedding is the standard inclusion X ↦ t of K((X)) into the Puiseux field, so the statement is that P has a Puiseux-series root with bounded denominators, the form in which Mannaa and Coquand (arXiv:1304.6770, Introduction) describe the union of the K((X^{1/m})) as algebraically closed. It follows from the Newton–Puiseux root theorem exists_isRoot_map_expand: a root y in K((X)) of P with X ↦ X^m substituted is carried by the level-nm embedding to a root, because the level-nm embedding after X ↦ X^m is the level-n embedding. It is the input to the proof that the Puiseux field is algebraically closed, which uses it at every level n. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): hypotheses satisfiable; the positive-degree hypothesis is needed; no duplicate in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Defines one step of the shortest-augmenting-path method of Dinits and Edmonds–Karp for flows with lower and upper bounds: g arises from f when g is obtained from f by pushing, along an s–t walk in the residual network of f that uses only arcs of positive residual capacity and has the least possible number of arcs, an amount equal to the smallest residual capacity on that walk (its bottleneck); the walk must use at least one arc. This is the augmentation step of Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), §4.4, Theorem 4.4, where a shortest s–t path in the residual graph is chosen at every iteration; a walk of least length is automatically a path, so no arc is pushed twice. Residual capacities are the usual ones (forward copy of an arc: upper bound minus flow; reverse copy: flow minus lower bound) and the update adds the push on forward copies and subtracts it on reverse copies. Red-team audit at 956e3162: compared clause by clause with the residual definitions; steps exist exactly when an augmenting path exists (exists_shortestAugmentationStep_iff), so the relation is not vacuous; with equal terminals no step exists, as it should.

Monotonicity of residual distances, the key lemma of Dinits and Edmonds–Karp: after a shortest-augmentation step, the distance from s to every vertex v in the residual network, counted in arcs of positive residual capacity (infinite when v is unreachable), does not decrease. Arcs that gain residual capacity are reverses of arcs of the shortest walk, along which the old distance drops by one, and all other arcs can only lose capacity; so the old distance rises by at most one along every positive arc of the new residual network and vanishes at s, which makes it a lower bound for the new distance. The proof of Theorem 4.4 in Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), §4.4, uses the same fact for the distance to t. Red-team audit at 956e3162: stated for every vertex, infinite distances included; only the step is assumed.

Integrality of a single step: if the lower bounds, the upper bounds and the current assignment all take values in an additive subgroup H of the coefficients (for instance the integers inside the reals), then so does the assignment after a shortest-augmentation step. Residual capacities are differences of elements of H, the bottleneck is one of them, and the step adds or subtracts it on each arc. Red-team audit at 956e3162: each of the three membership hypotheses is needed; only a linear order on the coefficients is assumed.

Each shortest-augmentation step strictly increases the value (the net flow into the sink): the value rises by the bottleneck, which is positive because every arc of the walk has positive residual capacity. This is the usual increase value(f') = value(f) + α with α > 0 of augmenting-path methods (Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), §4.3). Red-team audit at 956e3162: a step forces s ≠ t, which the increase needs; no other hypothesis.

Existence of maximum flows with lower and upper bounds: if at least one bounded s–t assignment exists (values between the bounds, conservation at every vertex other than s and t), then one of largest value exists. Over the reals this is often proved by compactness; here it holds over any linearly ordered abelian group, by running shortest-path augmentation from the given assignment. The feasibility hypothesis is necessary: with incompatible bounds there is no assignment at all. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the hypothesis is load-bearing and satisfiable (the zero flow for nonnegative capacities).

Integrality of maximum flows with bounds: if the lower and upper bounds lie in an additive subgroup H of the coefficients and some bounded s–t assignment has all its values in H, then some maximum bounded s–t assignment has all its values in H. Start shortest-path augmentation from that assignment: each step keeps the values in H (toFun_mem) and finitely many steps reach a maximum. For integer bounds inside the reals this gives an integer-valued maximum flow, generalising the integrity theorem (Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), Corollary 4.2a). Red-team audit at 956e3162: every hypothesis is needed; arbitrary linearly ordered abelian coefficients.

From any bounded s–t assignment, finitely many shortest-augmentation steps lead to a maximum one, i.e. one of largest value among all bounded s–t assignments with the same bounds. This follows from termination by well-founded induction: an assignment that is not maximum admits a step (previous criterion), and the induction hypothesis applies to the result. Red-team audit at 956e3162: covers s = t, where the starting assignment is already maximum; 'finitely many steps' is the reflexive-transitive closure of the step relation.

For distinct source s and sink t, a shortest-augmentation step starts from a bounded assignment f exactly when t can be reached from s along residual arcs of positive capacity, that is, exactly when f has an augmenting path. One direction is immediate, since the walk of a step is augmenting; for the other, a reachable t is reached by a walk of least length, which is a path with positive bottleneck, and pushing the bottleneck along it is a step. The hypothesis s ≠ t is necessary: for s = t the sink is trivially reachable but no step exists, since a step uses at least one arc. Red-team audit at 956e3162: s ≠ t is load-bearing (minimal-hypotheses check and the s = t case); both sides are satisfiable.

Max-flow/min-cut with lower bounds: for distinct terminals s and t, if some bounded s–t assignment exists, then some bounded s–t assignment has value equal to u(δ⁺S) − l(δ⁻S) for some vertex set S containing s but not t, where u(δ⁺S) is the total upper bound on arcs leaving S and l(δ⁻S) the total lower bound on arcs entering S. Since every bounded assignment has value at most this quantity for every such S (weak duality, val_le_cutBound), this says that the maximum value equals the minimum cut bound. Proof: take a maximum assignment (exists_isMaximum); it has no augmenting path, and no arc of positive residual capacity leaves the set S of vertices reachable from s in its residual network, which is exactly equality in weak duality. With zero lower bounds this is the classical max-flow min-cut theorem (Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), Theorem 4.2). Red-team audit at 956e3162: s ≠ t and feasibility are both load-bearing; for s = t no such S exists.

A bounded s–t assignment has the largest value among all bounded s–t assignments with the same bounds exactly when no shortest-augmentation step starts from it. For s ≠ t this is the augmenting-path optimality criterion of Ford and Fulkerson (a flow is maximum exactly when it has no augmenting path) combined with the previous lemma; for s = t every assignment has value zero, hence is maximum, and no step exists, so both sides hold and no hypothesis is needed. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the degenerate case s = t is handled, not excluded; no extra hypotheses.

The unfolding lemma for a shortest-augmentation step: a step from f to g holds exactly when there is a shortest augmenting walk of positive residual capacities whose bottleneck push turns f into g. It restates the definition word for word (proved by reflexivity), so files that cannot see the definition's body can still use it. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the two sides are identical clause by clause.

Termination of shortest-path augmentation: there is no infinite sequence of bounded s–t assignments each obtained from the previous one by a shortest-augmentation step, for coefficients in any linearly ordered abelian group, with no Archimedean, discreteness or rationality assumption. This is the theorem of Dinits (1970) and Edmonds–Karp (1972), stated as Theorem 4.4 of Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), §4.4, for real capacities together with the bound |V|·|A| on the number of iterations; the Lean statement claims termination only, not the bound. Proof: residual distances from s never decrease, and while they all stay the same the set of arcs u → v of positive residual capacity with d(v) = d(u) + 1 strictly shrinks (the bottleneck arc leaves it and no new arc enters), so a lexicographic pair of natural numbers drops at every step, whatever the sizes of the capacities; by contrast, augmentation along arbitrary paths need not terminate for real capacities (same notes, §4.3, after Theorem 4.3). Red-team audit at 956e3162: the measure counts only vertices and arcs; the proof uses only the three standard axioms; applied through the main theorem at the non-Archimedean group ℤ × ℤ with the lexicographic order.

For nonnegative capacities on a finite directed network (parallel arcs and loops allowed), a maximum s–t flow exists: some flow has value at least that of every other flow. Over the reals this is usually obtained by compactness; here it holds over any linearly ordered abelian group, as the case H = everything of the integrality theorem. Nonnegativity is necessary, since a negative capacity admits no flow at all. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the hypothesis is load-bearing; no s ≠ t needed (for s = t every flow has value zero).

Integrality for ordinary flows: for nonnegative capacities that lie in an additive subgroup H of the coefficients, some maximum s–t flow (0 ≤ f ≤ c on every arc, conservation away from s and t) takes all its values in H. With integer capacities inside the reals this is the integrity theorem, Corollary 4.2a of Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes): there is an integer-valued maximum flow. Proof: augment from the zero flow, which lies in H; the maximum reached has value at least zero, so it is an ordinary flow, and it is maximum among ordinary flows. No distinctness of s and t is needed. Red-team audit at 956e3162: nonnegativity of the capacities is load-bearing (otherwise no flow exists); used downstream for Hoffman's theorem, mixed capacities and flows between vertex sets.

The max-flow min-cut theorem: in a finite directed network with nonnegative capacities in any linearly ordered abelian group (the reals included), and distinct source s and sink t, there are an s–t flow f (0 ≤ f ≤ c on every arc, conservation at every vertex other than s and t) and a vertex set S with s ∈ S, t ∉ S such that the value of f equals the total capacity of the arcs leaving S. The value is the net flow into t, which equals the net flow out of s, as in Schrijver, A Course in Combinatorial Optimization (CWI lecture notes), §4.2, definitions (4)–(7); the cut capacity counts only arcs from S to its complement, each parallel arc separately and no loops, as there. Together with weak duality (Flow.val_le_arrowSum, Proposition 2 of the same notes) this is exactly Theorem 4.2 there: the maximum value of an s–t flow equals the minimum capacity of an s–t cut, and both extrema are attained. Proof: a maximum flow exists by shortest-path augmentation (exists_isMaximum) and has no augmenting path, so the set of vertices reachable from s in its residual network is a saturated cut. Tau Ceti's flows also require nonnegative value; this changes nothing, since the zero flow is a flow and the witness found is a flow in the usual sense. Red-team audit at 956e3162: s ≠ t and nonnegativity are both load-bearing (at s = t the conclusion is false, as no S contains s and omits it); specialised over the reals to the path s → v → t with capacities 3 and 5, where it yields a maximum flow of value exactly 3 = min(3, 5); with two parallel arcs s → t of capacities 1 and 2 and loops of capacity 7 at both ends it yields value 3, confirming that parallel arcs add and loops never cross a cut; instantiated at ℤ × ℤ with the lexicographic order; only the three standard axioms.

Correctly stated: if u is locally Lipschitz on the open set Ω (in particular if u is C¹ there), then against an additive Haar measure the integral over all real levels t of the perimeter in Ω of {u > t} equals ∫_Ω |∇u|, where ∇u is the classical derivative, which exists almost everywhere by Rademacher's theorem, and its norm as a linear functional is the Euclidean length of the gradient. Together with the identity |Du|(Ω) = ∫_Ω |∇u| for locally Lipschitz u this is the coarea formula for Lipschitz functions. The direction ≥ is the coarea inequality; for ≤, the indicator of {u > t} is the pointwise limit of ψ((n+1)(u − t)) for a smooth transition function ψ, lower semicontinuity of perimeter bounds P({u > t}; Ω) by the liminf of their variations ∫_Ω (n+1)ψ'((n+1)(u − t))|∇u|, and Fatou's lemma and Tonelli's theorem integrate over t using ∫_ℝ (n+1)ψ'((n+1)(a − t)) dt = 1. The derivative's default value 0 at points of non-differentiability only affects a null set. Red-team checks: the Lipschitz hypothesis is used throughout the proof; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Correctly stated: if u is locally integrable on the open set Ω and has finite total variation there (against an additive Haar measure), then {u > t} has finite perimeter in Ω for almost every real level t. It follows from the coarea formula: the integral over t of these perimeters equals the finite total variation, and a measurable [0, ∞]-valued function with finite integral is finite almost everywhere, the measurability being the lemma above; this is the almost-every-level finite-perimeter part of the BV coarea theorem. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed by the proof; the docstring omits the local-integrability hypothesis (recorded as a wording nit only).

Correctly stated: for u locally integrable on the open set Ω and any smooth vector field φ with compact support in Ω, against an additive Haar measure, ∫ u div φ equals the integral over all real levels t of ∫_{u > t} div φ (the layer-cake formula for the distributional pairing). It holds because every real number satisfies u(x) = ∫_ℝ (1_{t<u(x)} − 1_{t<0}) dt, the function div φ(x)·(1_{t<u(x)} − 1_{t<0}) is integrable on Ω × ℝ (div φ is bounded with compact support in Ω and u is integrable there), so Fubini's theorem swaps the integrals, and the subtracted term contributes nothing because a compactly supported divergence integrates to 0. Both sides are genuine integrals: the left integrand is integrable by local integrability and the level integrand is integrable by Fubini, so no default value for non-integrable functions enters. Red-team checks: no contradiction in the hypotheses (satisfied by u = 0 on ℝ²); dropping either hypothesis breaks the proof; the same statement and proof also hold without the inner product (recorded as a minor generality note, not a correctness issue).

Correctly stated: for u almost-everywhere measurable on the open set Ω and a locally finite measure, the map t ↦ P({u > t}; Ω) from ℝ to [0, ∞] is Borel measurable. After replacing u by a measurable representative (the perimeter in Ω only sees sets up to null sets in Ω), the map is lower semicontinuous at every level t whose level set {u = t} is null in Ω, by lower semicontinuity of perimeter under local convergence in measure; only countably many levels have positive measure for a σ-finite measure, and a function lower semicontinuous off a countable set is measurable. This is what makes the integral in the coarea formula a genuine Lebesgue integral rather than a lower integral of a non-measurable function. Red-team checks: the measurability hypothesis is needed; the statement also holds with an opens-measurable σ-algebra in place of the Borel one (recorded as a minor generality note).

Correctly stated: for every real function u that is locally integrable on an open set Ω of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the total variation of u on Ω (the supremum, in [0, ∞], of ∫ u div φ over smooth compactly supported vector fields φ in Ω with |φ(x)| ≤ 1 at every point, Euclidean norm) equals the integral over all real levels t, against Lebesgue measure on ℝ, of the perimeter in Ω of the superlevel set {u > t}, where the perimeter of a set is the total variation of its indicator; both sides may be infinite and no bounded-variation assumption is made. This is the scalar BV coarea formula |Du|(Ω) = ∫_ℝ P({x | u(x) > t}; Ω) dt exactly as the Tau Ceti Geometric Measure Theory roadmap (milestone G4) states it, and allowing infinite values makes it cover both the BV case and its converse (finite level integral forces finite variation). The inequality ≤ follows from writing u(x) = ∫_ℝ (1_{t<u(x)} − 1_{t<0}) dt, Fubini, and ∫ div φ = 0; the reverse is proved first for locally Lipschitz u (smooth approximations of each indicator, lower semicontinuity of perimeter, Fatou and Tonelli), then on subdomains with compact closure via mollification and almost-every-level convergence of superlevel sets, and finally on Ω by an exhaustion and monotone convergence. The level function t ↦ P({u > t}; Ω) is separately proved measurable, so the right side is a genuine Lebesgue integral, and the pairing ∫ u div φ is a genuine integral because u is locally integrable; any Haar measure may replace Lebesgue measure on the space since both sides scale by the same factor. Red-team checks (Lean, at 956e3162): the hypotheses are satisfiable (ℝ² with u = |x|) and the local-integrability hypothesis is needed by the proof; u = 0 gives 0 = 0; for u the indicator of any set s the right side reduces to P(s)·|[0,1)| = P(s); for the tent function max(0, 1 − |x|) on ℝ it yields total variation exactly 2 from the perimeter 2 of the intervals (t−1, 1−t); in dimension 0 every u has zero variation; axioms are only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: for u locally integrable on the open set Ω, against an additive Haar measure, the total variation of u on Ω is at most the integral over all real levels t of the perimeter in Ω of {u > t} (the easy half of the coarea formula). For each admissible field φ (smooth, compactly supported in Ω, pointwise norm at most 1) the layer-cake formula rewrites ∫ u div φ as ∫_ℝ (∫_{u>t} div φ) dt, each inner pairing is at most P({u > t}; Ω) because the perimeter is the supremum of exactly these pairings, and taking the supremum over φ gives the bound in [0, ∞]. Red-team checks: the local-integrability hypothesis is needed by the proof; consistent with the equality case checked on the tent function and on indicators.

Correctly stated Noether finiteness theorem: for a Noetherian commutative ring R, a commutative R-algebra A of finite type and a finite group G acting on A by R-algebra automorphisms (not necessarily faithfully), the invariant subalgebra A^G is of finite type over R, in every characteristic including the modular case. Proof idea: A is integral over A^G through the monic orbit polynomials and finitely generated over it, hence a finite A^G-module; the Artin-Tate lemma for the tower R, A^G, A (R Noetherian, A of finite type over R and finite over A^G) then makes A^G of finite type over R, and this is the only place Noetherianity is used (the companion statement over a Q-algebra removes it). Red-team checks beyond the existing answer: rebuilt locally at 956e3162 with only the standard axioms; instantiated with S2 swapping the variables of F2[x,y] (modular case) and of Z[x,y]; the same goal cannot be closed from Mathlib alone and the pinned Mathlib has no such theorem.

Correctly stated: over an algebra R over the rationals, Noetherian or not, the invariants of a finite group acting by R-algebra automorphisms on a commutative R-algebra of finite type form an R-algebra of finite type. It follows from the degree bound: after choosing finitely many generators there are only finitely many monomials of degree at most |G|, and their orbit sums generate the invariants. It complements the Noetherian version, trading Noetherianity of the base for invertibility of the integers. Red-team checks: instantiated with S2 swapping the variables of Q[x,y]; hypotheses consistent; only the standard axioms are used.

Correctly stated: if a finite group G acts by R-algebra automorphisms on a commutative algebra A of finite type over a commutative ring R, then A is a finitely generated module over its invariant subalgebra A^G, with no Noetherian or characteristic hypothesis, as the docstring says. Why it holds: each a in A is a root of the monic orbit polynomial, the product of (T - g·a) over g in G, whose coefficients are invariant, so A is integral over A^G; any finite set of R-algebra generators of A also generates it over A^G, and an integral extension of finite type is module-finite. The action need not be faithful, only compatible with R. Red-team checks (audit at 956e3162): instantiated with the symmetric group S2 swapping the variables of F2[x,y] (a modular case, where |G| is not invertible) and found there automatically; a library search of the pinned Mathlib finds no finiteness statement for fixed subalgebras; only the standard axioms are used.

Correctly stated Noether degree bound: if R is an algebra over the rationals, A a commutative R-algebra generated by a finite family x, and G a finite group acting on A by R-algebra automorphisms, then the invariant subalgebra A^G is exactly the R-subalgebra generated by the orbit sums of the monomials x^d of total degree at most |G|. For a polynomial ring with a linear action and x a basis of linear forms these generators are invariants of degree at most |G|, which is Noether's a priori bound for the degrees of generating polynomial invariants in characteristic zero as recalled by Fogarty (Electron. Res. Announc. AMS 7 (2001)), who extends it to characteristic prime to |G| (not claimed here). For a non-linear action the statement remains true as written, the degree being measured in the chosen generators rather than in a grading, as the module docstring explains. Proof: an invariant f = P(x) equals |G|^-1 times the sum of g·f over G, a combination of orbit sums of monomials, each of which lies in the subalgebra by the preceding lemma; conversely each orbit sum is invariant. Red-team checks: instantiated at S2 swapping the variables of Q[x,y]; the characteristic hypothesis is necessary, since over F2 the same S2 example fails (xy is invariant, yet every orbit sum takes the value 0 at both (0,0) and (1,1)), proved in Lean; finiteness of the family is removable (a generality remark).

Correctly stated: if R is an algebra over the rationals, A an R-algebra, G a finite monoid acting on A by ring endomorphisms and x a finite family in A, then for every monomial x^d the orbit sum, the sum of g·x^d over g in G, is a polynomial over R in the orbit sums of the monomials of total degree at most |G|. This is the key step of Noether's proof of her degree bound: with y_g = sum_i (g·x_i) u_i in A[u], the coefficient of u^d in the power sum of the k-th powers of the y_g is the multinomial coefficient of d times the orbit sum of x^d (k = deg d), Newton's identities for the |G| elements y_g express every power sum through the first |G| ones (dividing by integers up to |G|!), and one finally divides by the multinomial coefficient. The argument is purely polynomial, so it needs neither linearity of the action nor compatibility with R. Red-team checks: specialised to S2 swapping x and y in Q[x,y], it yields x^3 + y^3 from the orbit sums of degree at most 2; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; finiteness of the family is removable, which is a generality remark, not a correctness one.

If (R, I) is already a henselian pair, its henselization is R: an R-algebra isomorphism from the henselization to R, given by the universal map to R (taking J = I) with the structure map as inverse. Going R -> R^h -> R gives the identity, because the identity is the only R-algebra map R -> R. Going R^h -> R -> R^h gives the identity by uniqueness of maps out of R^h, because I R^h lies in the Jacobson radical of R^h. This is the standard consequence of the adjunction in Stacks Lemma 15.12.1 (tag 0A02), since henselian pairs form a full subcategory of pairs. Red-team checks: compiled at the 5-adic integers with their maximal ideal; the file also checks the zero ideal of any ring (always a henselian pair) and the field with five elements.
The inverse of the isomorphism above is the structure map from R to its henselization, which is how the inverse is built; this lemma records that as a simplification rule.

Says that two R-algebra maps from the henselization of (R, I) to an R-algebra S are equal whenever the ideal generated by the image of I in S lies in the Jacobson radical of S. Every element of the henselization comes from an étale neighbourhood B (an étale R-algebra with R/I = B/IB). Two maps B -> S agree modulo IS because B/IB is generated by the image of R, and maps out of an étale algebra that agree modulo an ideal inside the Jacobson radical are equal: the diagonal splits off by an idempotent, and an idempotent lying in that ideal is 0. This is the argument at the end of the proof of Stacks Lemma 15.12.1 (tag 0A02). Red-team checks: the Jacobson hypothesis is used (minimal-hypotheses test); with S the henselization itself (allowed because I R^h lies in its Jacobson radical) it says the identity is the only R-algebra endomorphism (compiled).

If (R, I) is a henselian pair, the structure map from R to its henselization along I is bijective, a restatement of the isomorphism above. Red-team check: the henselian hypothesis cannot be dropped. For (Z, (5)) the structure map is not bijective, because the henselization contains a square root of -1 (a root of X^2 + 1 lifting 2 mod 5) and Z does not (compiled).

Every R-algebra map from the henselization of (R, I) to S equals the chosen map, for a henselian pair (S, J) receiving a map of pairs from (R, I). So uniqueness holds among all R-algebra maps, with no condition on the extended ideal, as in the proof of Stacks Lemma 15.12.1 (tag 0A02). It is the Jacobson-radical uniqueness theorem in this file, applied because J lies in the Jacobson radical of S.

States the universal property of the henselization of a pair: for a ring R with an ideal I, a henselian pair (S, J) and a ring map R -> S sending I into J, there is exactly one R-algebra map from the henselization R^h to S that sends the extended ideal I R^h into J. This is Stacks Lemma 15.12.1 (tag 0A02), which says (A, I) |-> (A^h, I^h) is left adjoint to the inclusion of henselian pairs into pairs; its proof builds A^h as here, as the colimit of the étale A-algebras B with A/I = B/IB, takes I^h = I A^h, and shows the factorisation is unique among all A-algebra maps. The Lean file proves that stronger uniqueness as well (every R-algebra map to S is the chosen one), so the condition on the extended ideal holds automatically. 'Henselian' is Mathlib's notion (J lies in the Jacobson radical, and a simple root modulo J of a monic polynomial lifts to a root), which is equivalent to Stacks Definition 15.11.1: it implies Gabber's criterion, condition (5) of Lemma 15.11.6 (tag 09XI), and follows from that lemma's condition (2) on étale sections. A sibling file proves that the henselization is itself henselian along I R^h, so the property is about the right object. The proof idea: each étale neighbourhood B base-changes to an étale neighbourhood of (S, J), which has a section because (S, J) is henselian; two maps out of B agree because they agree modulo an ideal inside the Jacobson radical; so the sections are compatible and pass to the colimit. Red-team checks: only the standard axioms; the hypotheses are satisfiable (S = R^h with J = I R^h, where the identity is the only map); specialised to Z -> Z_5 with the maximal ideal; the construction is not degenerate, since the henselization of (Z, (5)) contains a square root of -1 and so is not Z (compiled); the condition on the extended ideal holds for every R-algebra map, matching the uniqueness in Stacks.

The chosen R-algebra map from the henselization of (R, I) to S, for a henselian pair (S, J) and a ring map R -> S sending I into J. On each étale neighbourhood B it is an R-algebra map B -> S, which exists because the base change S (x)_R B has a section over the henselian pair (S, J). These maps are compatible and glue on the colimit, as in the proof of Stacks Lemma 15.12.1 (tag 0A02). Red-team checks: every R-algebra map to S equals it, so the choices made in the construction do not matter; only the standard axioms.

On an étale neighbourhood B of (R, I), the chosen map composed with the canonical map from B to the henselization equals any given R-algebra map B -> S. This holds because there is at most one R-algebra map B -> S: two such maps agree modulo IS, which lies in J and hence in the Jacobson radical of S.
The elementwise form of the previous statement: the chosen map sends the image in the henselization of an element b of an étale neighbourhood B to phi(b), for any R-algebra map phi from B to S.

The ring-map version: two ring maps from the henselization of (R, I) to a commutative ring T that agree on the image of R are equal, provided the ideal generated by the image of I in T lies in the Jacobson radical of T. It follows from the algebra-map version by making T an R-algebra through the common restriction to R. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are used (minimal-hypotheses test); a sibling file uses it to show that the induced map of henselizations is unique.

Correctly stated: this is the second (differential) Bianchi identity. Given a smooth connection ∇ on a real vector bundle V over a smooth manifold (modelled on a complete normed space, so finite dimension is not assumed), a smooth torsion-free connection ∇ᵀ on the tangent bundle, smooth vector fields X, Y, Z and a smooth section s of V, it says that at every point (∇_X R)(Y,Z)s + (∇_Y R)(Z,X)s + (∇_Z R)(X,Y)s = 0, where R(X,Y) = ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_Y∇_X − ∇_[X,Y] with [X,Y] = DY·X − DX·Y in a chart (the convention of Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed., p. 196), and (∇_X R)(Y,Z)s = ∇_X(R(Y,Z)s) − R(∇ᵀ_X Y, Z)s − R(Y, ∇ᵀ_X Z)s − R(Y,Z)(∇_X s), with all four terms and these signs in each of the three cyclic summands. For the tangent bundle with ∇ = ∇ᵀ the Levi-Civita connection, pairing with the metric gives exactly Lee's differential Bianchi identity in its form (7.8) (Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature, 1997, Prop. 7.5, p. 123); for a general bundle it is d_∇R = 0 for the curvature 2-form. Proof idea: for any connection the cyclic sum of [∇_X, R(Y,Z)] + R(X,[Y,Z]) vanishes (the third-order terms by the Jacobi identity for commutators of operators, the rest by the Jacobi identity for vector fields), and torsion-freeness ∇ᵀ_X Y − ∇ᵀ_Y X = [X,Y] turns the three bracket terms into the six correction terms of ∇R; with torsion, extra terms appear, so that hypothesis is genuinely needed. Red-team checks at 956e3162: dropping any hypothesis (torsion-freeness, smoothness of X, Y, Z or s) breaks the proof; the hypotheses are jointly satisfiable (the theorem was instantiated and compiled on the Euclidean plane with its Levi-Civita connection as both connections and constant fields); the pinned Mathlib (2cabef97) has no curvature or Bianchi identity (text search, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle); downstream, the pointwise tensor form of the identity and Schur's theorem (constant pointwise curvature in dimension at least 3 is locally constant) are derived from it in exactly this form; only the standard axioms are used.

Correctly stated: for any smooth connection ∇ on a real vector bundle (no torsion condition, no tangent connection involved), smooth vector fields X, Y, Z and a smooth section s, the cyclic sum over (X, Y, Z) of ∇_X(R(Y,Z)s) − R(Y,Z)(∇_X s) + R(X,[Y,Z])s vanishes at every point, that is, the cyclic sum of [∇_X, R(Y,Z)] + R(X,[Y,Z]) is zero as an operator, with Lee's curvature R(X,Y) = ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_Y∇_X − ∇_[X,Y]. It holds because [∇_X, R(Y,Z)] + R(X,[Y,Z]) = [∇_X,[∇_Y,∇_Z]] − ∇_[X,[Y,Z]] (the two [∇_X, ∇_[Y,Z]] terms cancel); the cyclic sum of the first term vanishes by the Jacobi identity for commutators, and that of the second by the Jacobi identity for vector fields and linearity of ∇ in the direction. It is the torsion-independent core from which this file's second Bianchi identity follows. Red-team checks at 956e3162: dropping any of the four smoothness hypotheses breaks the proof; its hypotheses are a subset of the main theorem's, which were instantiated and compiled on the Euclidean plane; no counterpart in the pinned Mathlib; only the standard axioms are used.

The Pietsch factorization theorem: for 1 ≤ p < ∞, C ≥ 0 and a Banach target F, the p-summing norm of T : E → F is at most C if and only if there are a regular Borel probability measure ν on the closed unit ball of the dual with its weak-star topology (compact by Banach–Alaoglu) and an operator S of norm at most C on the closure of j_p(E) in L^p(ν) with T = S ∘ j_p, where j_p sends x to the class of f ↦ f(x). This is the factorization stated in Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda (arXiv:1210.3332, Section 1) (the factor lives on the closure X_p of the canonical image and is extended by continuity) and in the Tau Ceti roadmap (BanachSpaceTheory README, item B6), with the norm bound in both directions. Proof idea: Pietsch domination gives ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖j_p(x)‖; the factor S(j_p x) := Tx on the image is then well defined with norm at most C and extends to the closure because F is complete; conversely any such factorization gives the domination bound. Conventions: the summing norm takes values in [0, ∞]; C must be nonnegative, and that assumption is present and essential — without it the equivalence fails at T = 0, C = −1 (left side true, right side false; compiled). Red-team checks: the measure lives on the weak-star (not norm) topology of the ball, is a probability measure, and the factor's domain is the closure (each read off the statement and checked in Lean); the finiteness of p and C ≥ 0 are both needed; the factorization recovers ‖T‖ ≤ C because ‖j_p‖ ≤ 1 (compiled); the source may be merely seminormed, scalars real or complex; no duplicate in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Pietsch factorization through the canonical image: for 1 ≤ p < ∞, C ≥ 0 and a normed target, the p-summing norm of T is at most C if and only if, for some regular Borel probability measure ν on the weak-star dual unit ball, T = S ∘ j_p for an operator S of norm at most C defined on the image j_p(E) inside L^p(ν). This is the form the roadmap (BanachSpaceTheory README, item B6) asks for when the target need not be complete. Why it holds: a domination bound ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖j_p(x)‖ makes T vanish on the kernel of j_p, so S(j_p x) := Tx is well defined with norm at most C (the argument spelled out in Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda (arXiv:1210.3332, Section 1)); conversely ‖Tx‖ = ‖S j_p x‖ ≤ C‖j_p x‖ and domination applies. Red-team checks: at C = 0 it forces T = 0 (compiled); C ≥ 0 and the finiteness of p are needed; the target is assumed normed rather than seminormed, which is what makes T vanish on the kernel of j_p and the factor well defined.

Pietsch domination phrased with j_p: for 1 ≤ p < ∞ and C ≥ 0, the p-summing norm of T is at most C if and only if there is a regular Borel probability measure ν on the weak-star compact closed unit ball of the dual with ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖j_p(x)‖ for every x. Here the p-summing norm is the least C with (Σ‖Tx_i‖^p)^{1/p} ≤ C · sup_{‖φ‖≤1} (Σ|φ(x_i)|^p)^{1/p} for all finite families, valued in [0, ∞] so that an operator that is not p-summing has norm ∞. Since ‖j_p(x)‖ = (∫ |f(x)|^p dν(f))^{1/p}, this is the Pietsch domination theorem as stated in the Tau Ceti roadmap (BanachSpaceTheory README, item B6) and in Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda (arXiv:1210.3332, Section 1), display (1), with the sharp constant; the statement reduces to the library's domination theorem (easy direction by integrating the pointwise bound, hard direction by Hahn–Banach separation and the Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem) by rewriting that norm. Red-team checks: both the finiteness of p and C ≥ 0 are needed; the source space may be merely seminormed and the target seminormed; real or complex scalars.

Says that j_p(x), as an element of L^p(ν), is represented almost everywhere by the evaluation function f ↦ f(x) on the dual unit ball, which is the defining property of the canonical map. It holds because the inclusion of continuous functions into L^p sends a continuous function to its own almost-everywhere class. Red-team checks: no hypotheses beyond the setting; it is the input to the norm formula for j_p.

Defines the canonical operator j_p from E into L^p(ν), for p ≥ 1 and a finite Borel measure ν on the closed unit ball of the dual of E with its weak-star topology: a vector x goes to the class of the function f ↦ f(x) on the ball. It is the composite of the evaluation map x ↦ (f ↦ f(x)), a bounded operator into the continuous functions on the ball (compact by Banach–Alaoglu), with the standard inclusion of continuous functions on a compact space into L^p of a finite measure, which is exactly the map j_p ∘ e of the Pietsch factorization diagram in Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda (arXiv:1210.3332, Section 1). Red-team checks: the ball carries the subspace topology of the weak-star dual (verified in Lean to be literally the induced topology from pointwise evaluation) with its Borel structure, and is compact; for a Dirac mass at a functional φ in the ball the norm of j_p(x) computes to |φ(x)| (compiled).

For 1 ≤ p < ∞, the L^p(ν) norm of j_p(x) equals (∫ |f(x)|^p dν(f))^{1/p}, the right-hand side of Pietsch's domination inequality. It is the usual integral formula for the L^p norm, applied to the representative f ↦ f(x). Red-team checks: finiteness of p is needed and assumed (the integral formula is for finite exponents only); for a Dirac mass at φ the formula gives |φ(x)| (compiled).

When ν is a probability measure, j_p has operator norm at most 1: every f in the unit ball satisfies |f(x)| ≤ ‖x‖, so the L^p(ν) norm of f ↦ f(x) is at most ‖x‖ · ν(ball)^{1/p} = ‖x‖. This is the standard fact that the Pietsch map is a contraction. Red-team checks: compiled; the statement carries a finite-measure assumption already implied by the probability assumption (recorded as a minor generality finding), which does not affect its correctness.

Correctly stated: every naturality square of the chart structure maps (for a basic open D(f) ⊆ V) is cartesian, which is the base-change lemma (Stacks Lemma 27.15.2) and exactly the hypothesis relative gluing needs. Red-team audit at 956e3162: proved from quasi-coherence, not assumed.

Correctly stated: for an affine open U of X and a function f on U, every positive-degree element of the graded ring of sections over the basic open D(f) lies in the ideal generated by the restrictions of the positive-degree sections over U, which is exactly what is needed for restriction of sections to induce a morphism from the projective spectrum over D(f) to the one over U (a graded map induces a morphism of Proj on the locus where the image of the irrelevant ideal generates, Stacks Lemma 27.11.1). It holds because quasi-coherence makes the sections over D(f) the localization at f of the sections over U, that is their base change along Γ(U) → Γ(D(f)), and base change carries generators of the irrelevant ideal to generators. Red-team audit at 956e3162: both hypotheses (U affine, every component quasi-coherent) are used by the proof; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; axioms are the standard three.

Correctly stated: the same containment of irrelevant ideals as for a basic open, phrased for an arrow U → V of the category of affine opens of X used for the gluing; such an arrow exists only when U is a basic open D(f) of V, so the statement reduces to the basic-open case. Red-team audit at 956e3162: a direct specialisation, claiming nothing more.

Correct: the diagram of charts is locally directed, the technical condition under which Mathlib glues schemes along a diagram; it is Mathlib's general fact for relative gluing data over a thin index category. Red-team audit at 956e3162: not redundant — with this named instance switched off, instance search fails to find the condition.

Correct: each chart Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) → Proj_X(A) is an open immersion, as for the members of any open cover. Red-team audit at 956e3162: not redundant — instance search does not find it without this named instance.

Correctly stated: for an affine open U, a function f on U and the basic open D(f) ⊆ U, the square formed by the morphism Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(D(f), Aₙ)) → Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) induced by restriction, the two structure maps to Spec Γ(D(f)) and Spec Γ(U), and Spec of the restriction Γ(U) → Γ(D(f)), is cartesian: the chart over D(f) is the base change of the chart over U. This is Stacks Lemma 27.15.2 (tag 01NO) for the inclusion D(f) ⊆ U, and Stacks proves it the same way: quasi-coherence makes the graded ring over the smaller open the base change of the one over the larger, and Proj commutes with base change of the coefficient ring. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the cartesian square is the full Stacks statement for basic opens, with only affineness and quasi-coherence assumed (both used); it is the input that makes every transition square of the gluing cartesian.

Correctly stated, the main theorem: for every affine open U of X, the square formed by the chart Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) → Proj_X(A), its structure map to U, the inclusion U → X and π is cartesian, that is π⁻¹(U) ≅ Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) as schemes over U. This is the property of Stacks Lemma 27.15.4 ('for every affine open U ⊂ S there exists an isomorphism i_U : π⁻¹(U) → Proj(A) with A = A(U)'), stated for all affine opens, not only those of a chosen cover. It follows from Mathlib's relative gluing theorem, whose only input, that the transition squares are cartesian, is proved here from quasi-coherence. Red-team audit at 956e3162: specialised to an affine X and U = X, the chart is an isomorphism over X (compiled), recovering Proj of the global graded sections; no contradiction possible from the hypotheses (instantiated on the Rees algebra of an ideal sheaf); the properness file uses it to reduce properties of π to the charts; axioms are the standard three.

Correct definition of the relative Proj: for any scheme X and a commutative graded 𝒪_X-algebra A = ⨁_{n≥0} Aₙ (a unit 𝒪_X → A₀ and associative, commutative multiplications Aᵢ ⊗ Aⱼ → Aᵢ₊ⱼ) whose components are all quasi-coherent, it is the scheme glued from the projective spectra Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) over all affine opens U of X along the open immersions induced by restriction to basic opens. This is Stacks Situation 27.15.1 and Lemma 27.15.4 (Section 27.15 'Relative Proj via glueing', tags 01NM and 01NQ; the tag 01NS attached in the file is Section 27.16, the functor-of-points construction of the same scheme), which likewise assumes only a quasi-coherent graded algebra, with no condition on A₀ and no generation in degree one. It is correct because the gluing data are exactly Stacks' (charts over affines, transition maps from restriction, cartesian squares from quasi-coherence), and the companion theorem shows its part over each affine open U is Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) over U, which characterises it. Red-team audit at 956e3162: the graded-algebra notion is a commutative monoid in ℕ-graded 𝒪_X-modules for the tensor (A ⊗ B)ₙ = ⨁_{i+j=n} Aᵢ ⊗ Bⱼ with the sign-free symmetry (checked which structures are used); specialised to an affine base X, the chart over X is an isomorphism compatible with the maps to X (compiled), so Proj_X(A) ≅ Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(X, Aₙ)), which for the sheaf associated to a graded R-algebra S on Spec R is Proj S; instantiated on the Rees algebra of an ideal sheaf; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (pinned Mathlib glues only relative spectra); axioms are the standard three.

Correct definition: the open cover of Proj_X(A) by the charts Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)), U ranging over the affine opens of X. Red-team audit at 956e3162: each chart map is an open immersion and the chart over U is the full preimage of U under π.
Correctly stated: the chart over the affine open U is Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) itself (by definition). Red-team audit at 956e3162: holds by definition, as stated.

Identities and composites go to identities and composites because restriction and Proj are both functorial, which is the transitivity Stacks Lemma 27.15.3 records. Red-team audit at 956e3162: functoriality is proved, not assumed.

Red-team audit at 956e3162: no cocycle condition is taken as input: Mathlib's relative gluing needs only a functor and cartesian naturality squares, both proved in this file.

Correctly stated: the transition maps of the gluing datum are the morphisms of projective spectra induced by restriction of sections (true by definition). Red-team audit at 956e3162: holds by definition, as stated.

Correctly stated: the map from the chart over U to U is the structure map Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) → Spec Γ(U) followed by the identification Spec Γ(U) ≅ U (by definition). Red-team audit at 956e3162: holds by definition, as stated.

Correct definition: the structure morphism π: Proj_X(A) → X, induced on the glued scheme by the chart maps Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) → Spec Γ(U) ≅ U ⊆ X; this is the π of Stacks Lemma 27.15.4. Red-team audit at 956e3162: its restriction to each chart is the expected one (relativeProjCover_f_relativeProjToBase), and over each affine open it is the chart's structure map (isPullback_relativeProjCover).

Correctly stated: the preimage under π of an affine open U is exactly the image of the chart over U, so π⁻¹(U) is the open subscheme identified with Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) as in Stacks Lemma 27.15.4. Red-team audit at 956e3162: follows from Mathlib's preimage lemma for relative gluing; no hypothesis beyond the definition's.

Correct definition: the structure maps Proj(⨁ₙ Γ(U, Aₙ)) → Spec Γ(U) of the charts, induced by the map from Γ(U) to the degree-zero sections given by the unit of A, form a natural family, commuting with the transition maps because the squares of the base-change lemma commute.
