Correctly stated: for positive semidefinite U and V, entries (i,j) and (k,l) of X ~ MN(M,U,V) have covariance U_ik V_jl, that is, the row covariance at the two row indices times the column covariance at the two column indices, as the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) specifies. It is the ((j,i),(l,k)) entry of the Kronecker covariance V ⊗ U of the column-stacked vectorisation. Red-team checks: specialised to U = diag(1,2), V = diag(3,5) on 2×2 matrices it gives Cov(X₁₂,X₁₂) = 5 = U₁₁V₂₂ and Cov(X₂₁,X₂₁) = 6 = U₂₂V₁₁ (a reversed Kronecker order would swap these); the hypotheses are consistent (zero and identity satisfy them) and needed (at U = −1, V = 1 the law is a point mass, whose covariance is 0, not −1).

Correctly stated: for every choice of parameters, the expectation of entry X_ij under MN(M,U,V) is M_ij. Gaussian entries have mean M_ij, and the point-mass fallback sits at M. This matches E[X] = M in Wikipedia's 'Matrix normal distribution' (revision of 25 July 2025).

Correctly stated: for every choice of parameters, valid or not, the matrix normal law has total mass one. In the valid case it is the image of a Gaussian probability law under a measurable bijection, and otherwise it is a point mass.

Correctly stated: for positive semidefinite U and V, the entry X_ij of X ~ MN(M,U,V) is normal with mean M_ij and variance U_ii V_jj. This is the diagonal case of the entry covariance U_ik V_jl, and the variance is nonnegative, so no truncation occurs. It is a coordinate marginal of the vectorised Gaussian N(vec M, V ⊗ U), coordinate (j,i). Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; it agrees with the entry-covariance theorem at (i,j) = (k,l).

Correctly stated: for positive semidefinite U and V, column j of X ~ MN(M,U,V) is multivariate normal with mean the j-th column of M and covariance V_jj·U, which is the entry covariance U_ik V_jj restricted to one column. the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) asks for these column marginals. It is a coordinate selection of the vectorised Gaussian. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; the covariance agrees with the entry-covariance theorem.

Correctly stated: for positive semidefinite U and V and arbitrary, possibly rectangular or singular, A, B, C of compatible shapes, if X ~ MN(M,U,V) then AXB + C ~ MN(AMB + C, AUAᵀ, BᵀVB). Wikipedia's 'Matrix normal distribution' (revision of 25 July 2025) gives DXC ~ MN(DMC, DUDᵀ, CᵀVC) for full-rank D and C, and the rank conditions are needed there only to keep the covariances positive definite. Since this library allows semidefinite covariances, dropping them is right, and the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) asks for exactly these parameters. Proof idea: vec(AXB) = (Bᵀ ⊗ A) vec X, so the vectorised law is an affine image of N(vec M, V ⊗ U), with covariance (Bᵀ ⊗ A)(V ⊗ U)(B ⊗ Aᵀ) = (BᵀVB) ⊗ (AUAᵀ). Red-team checks: the map is continuous, so the image law is meaningful; the hypotheses are consistent and needed (with U = diag(1,−1), A = [1 0], V = B = 1, the left side is a point mass but the right side has variance 1); with A = [1 1] and U = V = 1 it gives row covariance 2, the variance of the sum of two independent standard normals.

Correctly stated: for positive semidefinite U and V, row i of X ~ MN(M,U,V) is multivariate normal with mean the i-th row of M and covariance U_ii·V, which is the entry covariance U_ii V_jl restricted to one row. the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) asks for these row marginals. It is a coordinate selection of the vectorised Gaussian. Red-team checks: no contradiction from the hypotheses; the covariance agrees with the entry-covariance theorem.

Correctly stated: if X ~ MN(M,U,V), its transpose has law MN(Mᵀ,V,U), with the row and column covariances exchanged; Wikipedia's 'Matrix normal distribution' (revision of 25 July 2025) states the same transpose property. It holds for all parameters. For valid ones, transposition permutes the vectorised coordinates and turns V ⊗ U into U ⊗ V; for invalid ones both sides are the point mass at Mᵀ. Red-team checks: in the 2×2 example, entry (2,1) of the transpose has variance 5 = Var(X₁₂); transposition is measurable, so the image law is meaningful.

Correctly stated: for positive semidefinite U and V, the column-stacked vectorisation vec X of X ~ MN(M,U,V) has law N(vec M, V ⊗ U), which is the defining property in Wikipedia's 'Matrix normal distribution' (revision of 25 July 2025). It follows from the definition because vectorisation and its inverse are mutually inverse measurable maps. Red-team checks: the hypotheses are consistent (zero and identity covariances satisfy them) and needed (for two negative definite covariances the left side is a point mass while the right side is a nondegenerate Gaussian); the column-stacking and Kronecker order were checked numerically on 2×2 matrices.

Correctly stated: for an n×p mean matrix M, a row covariance U (n×n) and a column covariance V (p×p), both positive semidefinite, this is the law of the random matrix whose column-stacked vectorisation vec X is multivariate normal with mean vec M and covariance V ⊗ U (Kronecker product, column covariance first); equivalently, entries (i,j) and (k,l) have covariance U_ik V_jl. Wikipedia's 'Matrix normal distribution' (revision of 25 July 2025) defines MN(M,U,V) by exactly vec X ~ N(vec M, V ⊗ U) with U n×n and V p×p, and the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) asks for this law with semidefinite covariances and entry covariance U_ik V_jl. Conventions: positive definiteness is relaxed to semidefiniteness, so singular laws are included; if U or V is not positive semidefinite the law is the point mass at M, an explicit branch that is needed because two negative definite matrices have a positive definite Kronecker product. Red-team checks at ab0153c6: on 2×2 matrices with U = diag(1,2), V = diag(3,5), the variance of entry (1,2) computed straight from the definition and Mathlib's multivariate Gaussian is 5 = U₁₁V₂₂ (the reversed Kronecker order would give 6), and the covariance theorem gives 6 = U₂₂V₁₁ for entry (2,1); the law was proved equal to the roadmap's row-stacking construction (a Gaussian on (row, column) pairs with covariance U ⊗ V); it reuses Mathlib's multivariate Gaussian and vectorisation, and neither Mathlib nor Tau Ceti has another matrix normal construction.

Correctly stated: if the row or the column covariance is not positive semidefinite, the law is the point mass at the mean M. This is the definition's documented fallback branch, and the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) asks for exactly this Dirac fallback for invalid parameters. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is satisfiable (U = −1), so the statement is not vacuous.

Correctly stated: when both covariances are positive semidefinite, the matrix normal law is the multivariate normal law N(vec M, V ⊗ U) on column-stacked vectors, read back as a matrix. This is the defining branch, as the docstring says. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed to select this branch, since for two negative definite covariances the definition gives the point mass while the right side is a nondegenerate Gaussian.

Correctly stated: if there is only one matrix of the given shape, which happens exactly when there are no rows or no columns, every matrix normal law is the point mass at it, because a probability measure on a one-point space is that point mass. the Tau Ceti roadmap (StandardDistributions §11.2) asks for this empty-shape Dirac law.

Correctly stated: a zero row covariance makes the matrix normal law the point mass at its mean, for every column covariance V. If V is positive semidefinite, the Kronecker covariance V ⊗ 0 vanishes and the Gaussian degenerates to the point mass; otherwise the fallback is the point mass anyway.

Correctly stated: a zero column covariance makes the matrix normal law the point mass at its mean, for every row covariance U. If U is positive semidefinite, the Kronecker covariance 0 ⊗ U vanishes; otherwise the fallback is the point mass anyway.

Correctly stated: for all parameters, every entry of a matrix normal matrix has finite moments of every finite order p. Gaussian entries have all moments, and the point-mass fallback trivially does. Only finite p is claimed, which is right, since a nondegenerate Gaussian entry is unbounded.

If X and Y are independent with exponential laws of rates r > 0 and l > 0, then m + X − Y has the asymmetric Laplace law with left rate l and right rate r. Independence means the pair (X, Y) has the product of the two exponential laws as its law, and m + X − Y is the image of that pair under (x, y) ↦ m + x − y, which is how the law is defined. This is the standard representation of the asymmetric Laplace law as a shifted difference of exponentials, with the right tail coming from X and the left from Y, which the file's density computation confirms (the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution' states the representation with the two rates swapped relative to its own density). Red-team checks (ab0153c6): the hypotheses are consistent (l = r = 1); no extra assumption such as a probability space is required.

Defines the asymmetric Laplace law with location m, left rate l and right rate r as the law of m + X − Y for independent X ~ Exp(r) and Y ~ Exp(l), namely the image of the product of the two exponential laws under the measurable map (x, y) ↦ m + x − y, and as the zero measure when l ≤ 0 or r ≤ 0 (documented, not a probability law). The file proves what the announcement lists: this law is Lebesgue measure weighted by lr/(l+r)·e^{l(x−m)} for x ≤ m and lr/(l+r)·e^{−r(x−m)} for x > m (so the right tail has the rate r of X, as convolution shows), with characteristic function e^{imt}·rl/((r−it)(l+it)), mean m + 1/r − 1/l and variance 1/r² + 1/l². With r = λκ and l = λ/κ these density, distribution-function, characteristic-function, mean and variance formulas are exactly those of the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution'; that article's separate sentence on differences of exponentials assigns the two rates the other way round, inconsistently with its own density, and the file's assignment is the correct one. With equal rates it is the Laplace law of scale 1/r. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): full-statement test passed; compiled values at m = 0, l = 2, r = 1: density (2/3)e^{−1} ∈ (0.2452, 0.2453) at 1 and (2/3)e^{−2} ∈ (0.0902, 0.0903) at −1, mean 1/2, variance 5/4, distribution function 1/3 at the location; no Mathlib counterpart (pinned Mathlib has no Laplace family; loogle, leansearch, leanfinder, grep).

For every choice of parameters the law equals Lebesgue measure weighted by the glued density (both sides are zero at invalid rates). For positive rates the proof computes the characteristic function of both sides, from the exponential construction and by integrating the density on each half-line, and concludes by uniqueness of characteristic functions; this is the standard fact that X − Y for independent X ~ Exp(r), Y ~ Exp(l) has density rl/(r+l)·e^{−rz} for z > 0 and rl/(r+l)·e^{lz} for z < 0, and it machine-checks that the right tail has the rate of X. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): no hypotheses; degenerate rates checked against the zero measure.
For a nonpositive left rate the law is the zero measure, the file's documented convention for parameters with no asymmetric Laplace law.
For a nonpositive right rate the law is the zero measure, the file's documented convention for parameters with no asymmetric Laplace law.

For positive rates the law is the image of the product of the exponential laws of rates r and l under (x, y) ↦ m + x − y, that is the law of m + X − Y for independent X ~ Exp(r), Y ~ Exp(l); this is the definition.

With equal rates l = r the asymmetric Laplace law is the Laplace law with location m and scale b = 1/r: the density r²/(2r)·e^{−r|x−m|} equals (2b)⁻¹e^{−|x−m|/b}. It holds for every r: for r ≤ 0 both sides are the zero measure, the Laplace scale 1/r being invalid too.

The same density as a function with values in the extended nonnegative reals (the real density, which is already nonnegative, converted), the form used to weight Lebesgue measure; it matches the standard density for the reasons given for the real-valued version. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): converting back gives the real density at every parameter; measurable.

Defines the asymmetric Laplace density with location m, left rate l and right rate r: f(x) = lr/(l+r)·e^{l(x−m)} for x ≤ m and lr/(l+r)·e^{−r(x−m)} for x > m, and f = 0 when l ≤ 0 or r ≤ 0, where there is no such law (documented). This is the density of m + X − Y for independent X ~ Exp(r), Y ~ Exp(l): convolution gives rl/(r+l)·e^{−rz} for z = x − m > 0 and rl/(r+l)·e^{lz} for z < 0, so the right tail carries the rate of X, as here. With r = λκ and l = λ/κ it is the density λ/(κ+1/κ)·exp(−(x−m)λsκ^s), s = sgn(x−m), of the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution'. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): compiled values at m = 0, l = 2, r = 1: f(1) = (2/3)e^{−1} ∈ (0.2452, 0.2453) and f(−1) = (2/3)e^{−2} ∈ (0.0902, 0.0903); right-tail ratio f(x+1)/f(x) = e^{−r} for x > m compiled; the branches agree at x = m.
The density is nonnegative for every choice of parameters, valid or not: it is a positive constant times an exponential, or zero.

For positive rates and x ≤ m the density equals lr/(l+r)·e^{l(x−m)}, the rising left branch, by the definition. Both rate hypotheses are needed: at l = −2, r = 1 the density is 0 while the formula is positive.

For positive rates and x > m the density equals lr/(l+r)·e^{−r(x−m)}, the decaying right branch governed by the right rate r, by the definition; the rate hypotheses are needed since the density is 0 at invalid rates.
For a nonpositive left rate the density is identically zero, the documented convention for parameters with no asymmetric Laplace law; immediate from the definition.
For a nonpositive right rate the density is identically zero, the documented convention for parameters with no asymmetric Laplace law; immediate from the definition.
For positive rates the density is strictly positive at every point, being the positive constant lr/(l+r) times an exponential; the hypotheses are needed since the density vanishes otherwise.
The extended-real density is the real density converted to an extended nonnegative real; this is the definition.
For positive rates and x ≤ m the extended-real density is the left branch lr/(l+r)·e^{l(x−m)}, converted; follows from the real version.
For positive rates and x > m the extended-real density is the right branch lr/(l+r)·e^{−r(x−m)}, converted; follows from the real version.
For a nonpositive left rate the extended-real density is identically zero (documented convention), from the real version.
For a nonpositive right rate the extended-real density is identically zero (documented convention), from the real version.

For positive rates the distribution function is F(x) = r/(l+r)·e^{l(x−m)} for x ≤ m and 1 − l/(l+r)·e^{−r(x−m)} for x > m, from integrating the density below x (or subtracting the upper tail). With r = λκ, l = λ/κ this is the distribution function in the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution' (κ²/(1+κ²)·e^{(λ/κ)(x−m)} up to m, 1 − e^{−λκ(x−m)}/(1+κ²) above); the branches agree at m with value r/(l+r) = P(X ≤ Y). Red-team checks (ab0153c6): F = 1/3 at the location for l = 2, r = 1, compiled.

For positive rates the characteristic function t ↦ E e^{itZ} of Z = m + X − Y is e^{imt}·rl/((r − it)(l + it)): independence factorizes it as e^{imt}·E e^{itX}·E e^{−itY}, with E e^{itX} = r/(r − it) for X ~ Exp(r) and E e^{−itY} = l/(l + it) for Y ~ Exp(l). With r = λκ, l = λ/κ this is e^{imt}/((1 + iκt/λ)(1 − it/(κλ))), the characteristic function in the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution'; at l = r = 1/b it reduces to the Laplace characteristic function e^{imt}/(1 + b²t²). The sign convention is E e^{+itZ}. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): the file reaches the same value a second way, by integrating the density against e^{itx} on each half-line; the rate hypotheses are needed (at l = −1, r = 1, t = 0 the left side is 0 and the right side 1, compiled).
For positive rates the distribution function is continuous, since the law has a density and so gives no mass to single points.

A random variable whose law is asymmetric Laplace has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure, because the law is Lebesgue measure weighted by an integrable density. No hypotheses: at invalid rates the law is zero, which forces the probability space to be null.
The density is Lebesgue integrable on every lower half-line (−∞, x], for every parameter, as a restriction of its integrability on the whole line.
The density is Lebesgue integrable on every upper half-line (x, ∞), for every parameter, as a restriction of its integrability on the whole line.

For every parameter, a vector-valued function g is integrable for the asymmetric Laplace law exactly when f·g is Lebesgue integrable, f the density: the standard transfer for a measure given by a density.
For every choice of parameters the density is Lebesgue integrable on the whole line: two exponentially decaying tails at positive rates, the zero function otherwise.
For every parameter the law has a finite first moment, a consequence of the finite second moment on a finite measure.
For every parameter, the integral of g against the asymmetric Laplace law equals the Lebesgue integral of f·g, f the density: change of variables for a measure given by a density.
For positive rates the density has total integral 1: its masses below and above the location are r/(l+r) and l/(l+r). The rate hypotheses are needed since the density is 0 otherwise.

For positive rates and x ≤ m the density integrates over (−∞, x] to r/(l+r)·e^{l(x−m)}, the elementary integral of lr/(l+r)·e^{l(y−m)}. At x = m this is r/(l+r), which is P(X ≤ Y) for independent X ~ Exp(r), Y ~ Exp(l), as it must be. The hypothesis x ≤ m is needed (above m the formula changes) and so are the rate hypotheses.
For positive rates and x ≥ m the density integrates over (x, ∞) to l/(l+r)·e^{−r(x−m)}, the elementary integral of the right branch; at x = m the two half-line masses r/(l+r) and l/(l+r) add up to 1.

For positive rates the mean is m + 1/r − 1/l, since E[m + X − Y] = m + E X − E Y with E X = 1/r and E Y = 1/l. With r = λκ, l = λ/κ it equals the mean m + (1 − κ²)/(λκ) given in the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution'. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): value 1/2 at m = 0, l = 2, r = 1 compiled; the hypotheses are needed (at l = −1, r = 1 the mean of the zero measure is 0, not 2, compiled).
For positive rates the law has total mass 1, being the image of a product of two probability measures (exponential laws of positive rate). The hypotheses are needed: otherwise it is the zero measure.
For positive rates the extended-real density has total mass 1, the normalization of the real density transferred to the extended-real integral.

The map from the parameters (m, l, r) to the asymmetric Laplace law is measurable for the standard σ-algebra on measures, so the family is a measurable kernel; it follows from joint measurability of the density.
For fixed parameters the extended-real density is Borel measurable, as the conversion of a measurable real function.
For fixed parameters the real density is a Borel-measurable function of the point: it is piecewise exponential, cut at the location by a half-line.
The density is jointly measurable in the location, both rates and the point, being built from measurable comparisons and exponentials.
For every parameter the law has a finite second moment: m + X − Y is square-integrable when X and Y are exponential, and the zero measure trivially.
For a random variable with asymmetric Laplace law, its density agrees with the asymmetric Laplace density at almost every point, the right notion since densities are defined only up to null sets.
For every parameter, the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the asymmetric Laplace law with respect to Lebesgue measure is the asymmetric Laplace density, almost everywhere.
For positive rates the distribution function is strictly increasing on the whole line, because the density is strictly positive everywhere.
The support of the law is the whole real line for positive rates (its distribution function increases strictly) and empty otherwise (the zero measure); both cases are covered.
Converting the extended-real density back to a real number returns the real density, at every parameter, because the real density is nonnegative.

For positive rates the variance is 1/r² + 1/l², the sum of the variances of the independent parts X ~ Exp(r) and −Y with Y ~ Exp(l). With r = λκ, l = λ/κ this is the variance (1 + κ⁴)/(κ²λ²) given in the Wikipedia article 'Asymmetric Laplace distribution'. Red-team checks (ab0153c6): value 5/4 at l = 2, r = 1 compiled; the hypotheses are needed (zero-measure counterexample at l = −1 compiled).

Correctly stated: for finite families x = (x_i) and y = (y_j) in a commutative semiring S, the formal power series in t whose t^n coefficient is the sum over all partitions λ of n of s_λ(x)·s_λ(y) equals the product over all pairs (i, j) of the geometric series Σ_m (x_i y_j)^m t^m; that is, Σ_λ s_λ(x)s_λ(y) t^|λ| = ∏_{i,j} (1 − x_i y_j t)^(-1). This is the Cauchy identity for Schur polynomials as stated in the Wikipedia article 'Schur polynomial' (summed over all partitions; those with more parts than letters contribute zero), with t recording degree, and taking x and y to be independent indeterminates gives the identity of polynomials in the two alphabets. Each factor (1 − x_i y_j t)^(-1) is written explicitly as a geometric series, which over a commutative ring is the true inverse of 1 − x_i y_j t, so the statement involves no division and no junk value, and it makes sense over semirings, where 1 − x_i y_j t is not defined. The proof compares coefficients: the t^n coefficient of the product is h_n evaluated at the products x_i y_j, and the companion degree-n theorem identifies that with Σ_{λ ⊢ n} s_λ(x)s_λ(y). Red-team checks: with one letter on each side it gives Σ_n (xy)^n t^n = (1 − xyt)^(-1), only one-row partitions surviving; the geometric factor was checked to invert 1 − a t over any commutative ring; an empty alphabet gives 1 on both sides; the generic specialisation to independent indeterminates compiles; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate was found; it uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: for finite families x = (x_i) and y = (y_j) in a commutative semiring and every n, the sum over all partitions λ of n of s_λ(x)·s_λ(y) equals the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial h_n in variables indexed by the pairs (i, j), evaluated at the products x_i y_j. This is the degree-n part of the Cauchy identity Σ_λ s_λ(x)s_λ(y) = ∏_{i,j}(1 − x_i y_j)^(-1) as stated in the Wikipedia article 'Schur polynomial', because the product of the geometric series ∏_{i,j}(1 − x_i y_j t)^(-1) is the generating function Σ_n h_n(x_i y_j) t^n. The proof groups the pairs by their first letter, writing h_n(xy) as a sum over exponent vectors l of total degree n of x^l ∏_i h_{l_i}(y); it expands ∏_i h_{l_i} in Schur polynomials, whose coefficients are the Kostka numbers K_{λl}, and recognises Σ_l K_{λl} x^l as s_λ(x), since s_λ is homogeneous of degree n. Conventions: s_λ is the tableau generating function (semistandard tableaux of shape λ, rows weakly increasing and columns strictly increasing, entries from the alphabet), h_n is Mathlib's sum over multisets of size n, and the sum is over all partitions of n, those with more parts than letters giving s_λ = 0. Red-team checks: there are no hypotheses beyond finite alphabets with decidable equality, which are needed to form h_n; in two letters s_(1) = x_0 + x_1, s_(1,1) = x_0 x_1 = e_2 and s_(2) = h_2, and in one letter s_(1,1) = 0, all compiled; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate was found (pinned Mathlib has no Schur polynomials; leansearch, leanfinder, loogle and git grep); every import is needed; it uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated. It says: on a finite-dimensional real inner product space E of dimension n ≥ 2 with a Haar measure μ, and with p = n/(n−1) (written as 1/n + 1/p = 1, which itself forces n ≥ 2), every integrable real function u satisfies ‖u‖_{L^p(μ)} ≤ C·|Du|(E), where |Du|(E) is the total variation of u over the whole space defined by duality (the supremum of ∫ u div φ over smooth compactly supported vector fields φ with Euclidean length at most 1), possibly infinite, and C is exactly the constant of Mathlib's Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality for compactly supported C¹ functions (MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_fderiv_one), so this is the extension of that inequality to functions of bounded variation that the Geometric Measure Theory roadmap asks for in item G4. Why it holds: the mollifications ρ_ε ⋆ u are C¹ and integrable, so ‖ρ_ε ⋆ u‖_p ≤ C ∫|∇(ρ_ε ⋆ u)| = C |D(ρ_ε ⋆ u)|(E) ≤ C |Du|(E), because convolving with a probability density does not increase variation; they converge to u in L¹, and Fatou's lemma along an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence passes the bound to u. Conventions: when |Du|(E) = ∞ the bound holds trivially (C is positive); integrability is essential, since a nonzero constant has zero variation and infinite L^p norm, and it is excluded because it is not integrable on E; C depends on μ, as it must when the Haar measure is not normalised. Red-team checks (Lean, at ab0153c6): hypotheses satisfiable (dimension 2, p = 2) and both load-bearing; with only local integrability the inequality fails for u ≡ 1, and nonzero constants are not integrable under the hypotheses (both compiled); for a compactly supported C¹ real function it gives back Mathlib's inequality with the same constant, since the variation of a C¹ function is ∫|∇u| for the matching Euclidean/operator norm (compiled); for the indicator of a ball the right-hand side is finite (compiled); only the standard axioms; no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti; elaborates in well under a second.

Correctly stated. It says: on a finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension n ≥ 2 with a Haar measure μ, every null-measurable set s of finite measure satisfies μ(s)^((n−1)/n) ≤ C·P(s), where P(s) is the perimeter of s in the whole space (the total variation of its indicator function, possibly infinite) and C is the constant of Mathlib's Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality; this is the isoperimetric inequality with a non-optimal constant. It follows by applying the Sobolev inequality for functions of bounded variation to the indicator of s, which is integrable because μ(s) is finite and whose L^p norm, for p = n/(n−1), is μ(s)^(1/p) with 1/p = 1 − 1/n. The finiteness of μ(s) cannot be dropped: the complement of a ball has infinite measure but the same finite perimeter as the ball. Red-team checks (Lean, at ab0153c6): every hypothesis load-bearing; the complement-of-the-ball counterexample to the statement without finite measure compiled; specialised to a ball of radius r it gives the finite, nontrivial bound μ(B_r)^((n−1)/n) ≤ C·n·r^(n−1)·μ(B_1) (compiled); only the standard axioms; no duplicate in the pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: with G, M, K as above, the dimension of the degree-n part of the invariant ring Sym(M)^G, read in K, equals (1/|G|) Σ_g tr(g | Symⁿ M). This is the standard formula 'dimension of the invariants = average of the character', equation (2) in Stanley's proof of Theorem 2.1 (Bull. AMS 1979) for the trivial character, applied to the representation of G on Symⁿ M; it follows from the trace of the Reynolds projection by linearity of the trace. In characteristic p it determines the dimension only modulo p, as the docstring says. Red-team checks at ab0153c6: independently re-derived (compiled) from Mathlib's general character formula for the dimension of invariants; hypotheses satisfiable; finite-dimensionality needed; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: the formal power series Σ_n dim(Sym(M)^G ∩ Symⁿ M) tⁿ, with dimensions read in K, equals (1/|G|) Σ_g Σ_n tr(g | Symⁿ M) tⁿ in K[[t]] — Molien's formula before the graded traces are evaluated. It is the degreewise dimension formula assembled coefficient by coefficient, exactly the step from (2) to (3) in Stanley's proof of Theorem 2.1 (Bull. AMS 1979). Red-team checks at ab0153c6: coefficients agree by construction with the degreewise lemma; hypotheses satisfiable (ℚ with {±1}); finite-dimensionality needed; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: for a finite group G acting linearly on a finite-dimensional space M over a field K in which |G| is invertible, the series Σ_n dim((Sym M)^G ∩ Symⁿ M) tⁿ, with dimensions read in K, equals (1/|G|) Σ_g det(1 − t g)⁻¹ in K[[t]], where det(1 − t g) is written as the reversed characteristic polynomial t^d χ_g(1/t) of g. This is Molien's theorem as in Stanley (Bull. AMS 1979), Theorem 2.1 with the trivial character, stated there over ℂ for a subgroup of GL(V) acting on the polynomial ring whose linear forms are V; here any field with |G| invertible and any (possibly non-faithful) action is allowed, and in characteristic p the identity determines the dimensions only modulo p, as the docstring says. The proof averages the traces of the degree-n Reynolds projections and then uses the graded trace identity (Σ_n tr(g | Symⁿ M) tⁿ)·det(1 − t g) = 1, valid because g has finite order invertible in K and so is diagonalisable over an algebraic closure. The reversed characteristic polynomial has constant term 1, so its inverse is a genuine power-series inverse. Red-team checks at ab0153c6, all compiled: reversal gives (1 − 2t)(1 − 3t) for diag(2,3); specialised at the trivial group on ℚ (every degree has dimension 1, series 1/(1 − t)) and at {±1} acting on ℚ by sign (degree-n dimension (1 + (−1)ⁿ)/2, series 1/(1 − t²)); hypotheses satisfiable; finite-dimensionality needed; no Molien formula in pinned Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: for a finite group G acting linearly on a finite-dimensional vector space M over a field K in which |G| is invertible, the averaging (Reynolds) operator (1/|G|) Σ_g g on the degree-n part Symⁿ M of the symmetric algebra has trace equal, in K, to the dimension of the G-invariant elements of degree n. This holds because the averaging operator is an idempotent projection of Symⁿ M onto its invariants, and the trace of a projection of a finite-dimensional space is the dimension of its image (read in K); the invariants of Symⁿ M are identified with the degree-n part of the invariant ring. Red-team checks at ab0153c6: no contradiction from the hypotheses (instantiated at ℚ with {±1} acting by sign); finite-dimensionality is needed (the file does not compile without it); axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; elaborates in well under a second.

Says: if every capacity and every arrow value of the current flow is an integer multiple of d, and s ≠ t, then one augmentation step raises the flow value by at least d. Why: residual capacities are then multiples of d, so the bottleneck is a positive multiple k·d with k ≥ 1, and the value rises by exactly the bottleneck; if d ≤ 0 the bound is implied by the strict increase. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (two vertices, capacity 2, d = 1); s ≠ t is needed (with s = t an augmenting cycle leaves the value at 0); every hypothesis is used; no positivity of d is assumed.

Termination of the Ford–Fulkerson method for capacities in a cyclic subgroup. Says: if every capacity is an integer multiple of some d > 0 and s ≠ t, then from any flow whose arrow values are multiples of d, every sequence of augmentation steps is finite, whichever augmenting walks are chosen at each step. Why: each step keeps all arrow values multiples of d (residual capacities and bottlenecks are differences of multiples of d) and raises the value by at least d, while values are bounded by the capacity leaving s; this is the classical termination argument for integer capacities, here for any discrete cyclic subgroup of an ordered group. It is stated as accessibility of the starting flow for the one-step relation, which means exactly that no infinite chain of steps starts there. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) It does not follow from the library's separate termination theorem for shortest augmenting paths, which only constrains steps along walks of least length. Red-team checks: direction of the step relation checked against its definition; s ≠ t is genuinely needed (with s = t one can augment around a 2-cycle through s and back forever); d > 0 is removable (recorded separately); hypotheses satisfiable.

Says: for integer capacities and s ≠ t, every sequence of augmentation steps from any flow is finite, whatever augmenting walks are chosen. Why: the case d = 1 of the cyclic-subgroup termination theorem, since every integer is a multiple of 1; each step raises the integer value by at least 1 and values are bounded by the capacity leaving s. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: s ≠ t is genuinely needed (with s = t, augmenting around a cycle through s and back never stops); every starting flow is covered.

Says: for rational capacities and s ≠ t, every sequence of augmentation steps from any flow is finite, whatever augmenting walks are chosen. Why: the finitely many capacities and the arrow values of the starting flow have a common denominator D, so all are integer multiples of 1/D, and the cyclic-subgroup termination theorem applies with d = 1/D. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: the common denominator is taken over the starting flow's values as well as the capacities, so arbitrary rational starting flows are covered; s ≠ t is needed.

Says: for nonnegative integer capacities and s ≠ t, a maximum flow exists. Why: augmentation from the zero flow terminates, by the case d = 1 of the cyclic-subgroup results. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: nonnegativity needed (otherwise no flow exists). It is also a special case of the library's general existence theorem for maximum flows, which needs neither integrality nor s ≠ t (duplication recorded separately; not a correctness issue).

Says: for nonnegative capacities that are integer multiples of some d > 0, with s ≠ t, some maximum flow has every arrow value an integer multiple of d (integrality of maximum flows). Why: augment from the zero flow until no augmenting walk is left; termination and preservation of the multiples of d come from the results above. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable (two vertices, capacity 2, d = 1); nonnegative capacities are needed, since otherwise no flow exists. The library's general integrality theorem for an arbitrary additive subgroup, proved via shortest augmenting paths, already implies this without d > 0 and s ≠ t; that duplication is recorded separately and is not a correctness problem.

Says: for nonnegative rational capacities and s ≠ t, a maximum flow exists. Why: the capacities are integer multiples of 1/D for a common denominator D, and augmentation from the zero flow terminates by the cyclic-subgroup results with d = 1/D. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: nonnegativity needed. It is also a special case of the library's general existence theorem for maximum flows, which needs neither rational coefficients nor s ≠ t (duplication recorded separately; not a correctness issue).

Says: if the capacities are integer multiples of some d > 0 and s ≠ t, then from any flow with arrow values in the multiples of d, finitely many augmentation steps reach a maximum flow, again with arrow values in the multiples of d. Why: by the termination theorem one may keep augmenting until no step applies; between distinct terminals a flow admits no augmentation step exactly when it is maximum (the augmenting-path optimality criterion), and each step preserves the multiples of d. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable; s ≠ t needed for the optimality criterion; d > 0 removable (recorded separately).

Integral max-flow/min-cut. Says: in a finite network whose capacities are nonnegative integer multiples of some d > 0, with distinct source s and sink t, there is a single flow all of whose arrow values are integer multiples of d, together with a vertex set S containing s but not t, such that the value of the flow equals the total capacity of the arrows from S to its complement. Since no flow exceeds the capacity of any such cut (weak duality), this flow is maximum and this cut minimum: maximum flow value equals minimum cut capacity, attained by a flow with values in the multiples of d. Proof idea: run Ford–Fulkerson from the zero flow; it terminates because each augmentation raises the value by at least d and values are bounded, and once no augmenting walk is left, the vertices reachable from s in the residual network form a saturated cut. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) The statement claims only that some maximum flow is integral, as the classical theorem does; the termination of every augmentation sequence is the separate theorem on accessibility for augmentation steps in the same file. Red-team checks: specialised to rational capacities that are integers (d = 1), giving a maximum flow with integer arrow values whose value is a cut capacity; hypotheses satisfiable; s ≠ t and nonnegativity are needed; d > 0 is not needed, and the integral conclusion also follows from the library's general integrality theorem for an arbitrary subgroup (recorded separately as a duplication, not a correctness issue).

Says: if the capacities are integer multiples of some d > 0 and s ≠ t, there is no infinite sequence of flows with arrow values in the multiples of d whose values strictly increase. Why: such a flow has value n·d for a natural number n, and by weak duality n·d is at most the total capacity leaving s, itself a multiple m·d, so the values lie among the finitely many multiples 0, d, …, m·d. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: hypotheses satisfiable; the well-founded relation is 'has larger value', the increasing direction, as the docstring says; the hypotheses d > 0 and s ≠ t turn out to be unnecessary (a generality point recorded separately, not a correctness issue).

Says: for integer capacities and s ≠ t, there is no infinite sequence of flows of strictly increasing value. Why: every integer is a multiple of 1, so this is the case d = 1 of the cyclic-subgroup result: values are integers between 0 and the capacity leaving s. (Setting throughout: a finite directed network, possibly with parallel arrows and loops, with capacities in a linearly ordered abelian group; a flow has 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ cap(e) on every arrow, is conserved at every vertex other than the source s and sink t, and has nonnegative value, its net inflow at t; an augmentation step pushes the bottleneck amount along a walk from s to t in the residual network that uses no arrow twice and only arrows of positive residual capacity.) Red-team checks: no nonnegativity assumption is needed (with a negative capacity there are no flows at all); s ≠ t is unnecessary, since all values are 0 when s = t (recorded separately as a generality point).

For 1 ≤ p < ∞ and C ≥ 0: if the p-summing norm of T is at most C, there is a regular Borel probability measure ν on the closed unit ball of the dual, compact in its weak-star topology, with ‖Tx‖ ≤ C (∫ |f(x)|^p dν(f))^{1/p} for every x. This is the hard half of the Pietsch domination theorem (Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda, arXiv:1210.3332, Introduction, display (1)), with the sharp constant. It is proved, not assumed: rescaling a finite family by weights, the summing inequality keeps the cone spanned by the functions f ↦ ‖Tx‖^p − C^p|f(x)|^p away from the open cone of functions bounded below by a positive constant; Hahn–Banach separates the two, the separating functional is negative on positive functions, and the Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem represents its negative by a regular measure, which is then normalised to mass one. Red-team checks: the conclusion asserts probability, regularity and the domination inequality together, each read off the statement; specialised, it gives ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖x‖ (compiled); finiteness of p is needed; C ≥ 0 is not (compiled, recorded as a minor generality note).

An operator with finite p-summing norm πₚ(T), for 1 ≤ p < ∞, is dominated with the constant πₚ(T) itself by a regular Borel probability measure on the weak-star closed unit ball of the dual: ‖Tx‖ ≤ πₚ(T) (∫ |f(x)|^p dν(f))^{1/p} for every x. It is the hard direction of Pietsch domination at C = πₚ(T), so a Pietsch measure exists with the optimal constant. Red-team checks: the finiteness hypothesis is needed, since without it an operator of infinite summing norm would receive the constant 0 (the real value assigned to ∞) and the conclusion would force it to vanish; the one-line derivation from the previous theorem was checked.

For 1 ≤ p < ∞ and C ≥ 0, an operator T between seminormed spaces over the real or complex numbers has absolutely p-summing norm πₚ(T) ≤ C (the norm takes values in [0, ∞], so an operator that is not p-summing has πₚ = ∞) exactly when some regular Borel probability measure ν on the closed unit ball of the dual, with its weak-star topology, satisfies ‖Tx‖ ≤ C (∫ |f(x)|^p dν(f))^{1/p} for every x. This is the Pietsch domination theorem as stated by Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda (arXiv:1210.3332, Introduction, display (1)), in the sharper form with the exact constant; their qualitative form (T is p-summing iff such a constant C > 0 and such a ν exist) follows from it in a few lines (compiled). Why it holds: the easy direction integrates against ν the pointwise bound Σ|f(xᵢ)|^p ≤ (weak p-norm of the family)^p, valid for every functional f of norm at most 1; the hard direction uses Hahn–Banach in the continuous functions on the (compact) ball to separate the cone spanned by the functions f ↦ ‖Txᵢ‖^p − C^p|f(xᵢ)|^p from the functions bounded below by a positive constant, and represents the resulting positive functional by a regular measure via the Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem, normalised to total mass one. The integral is a genuine one: f ↦ |f(x)|^p is continuous on the weak-star compact ball, hence integrable for every finite measure (compiled), so the convention that a non-integrable function integrates to 0 never enters. Red-team checks: both directions are proved, using only the three standard axioms; finiteness of p is needed (at p = ∞ the integrand degenerates to the constant 1 and the forward direction fails for the identity of the scalar field, compiled); the hypothesis C ≥ 0 turns out not to be needed here, unlike in the factorization theorem (for C < 0 both sides say T has zero norm, the Dirac mass at the zero functional witnessing the right side; compiled, recorded as a minor generality note); specialised to the rank-one operator x ↦ φ(x)y with ‖φ‖ ≤ 1, the Dirac mass at φ dominates with constant ‖y‖, matching πₚ = ‖φ‖‖y‖ (compiled); the forward direction recovers ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖x‖ (compiled); no duplicate in Mathlib, which has no summing operators, or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

For 1 ≤ p < ∞ and C ≥ 0: if some probability measure ν on the closed unit ball of the dual, with its weak-star topology, satisfies ‖Tx‖ ≤ C (∫ |f(x)|^p dν(f))^{1/p} for every x, then the p-summing norm of T is at most C. This is the easy half of the Pietsch domination theorem (Botelho, Pellegrino and Rueda, arXiv:1210.3332, Introduction, display (1)); proof: for a finite family xᵢ, raise the bound to the p-th power, sum, exchange sum and integral, and bound Σ|f(xᵢ)|^p at each functional f of norm at most 1 by the p-th power of the weak p-norm of the family. Regularity of ν is rightly not assumed, and only open sets need to be measurable. Red-team checks: the integrand is integrable for every finite measure on the ball, so the hypothesis is not distorted by the zero value given to non-integrable integrals (compiled); nonzero witness: for the rank-one operator x ↦ φ(x)y with ‖φ‖ ≤ 1, the Dirac mass at φ gives πₚ ≤ ‖y‖ (compiled), sharp when ‖φ‖ = 1; two minor generality notes recorded (C ≥ 0 is not needed, and the statement holds over any locally compact nontrivially normed scalar field; both compiled).

Defines, for a graded algebra H (an A-infinity algebra with no differential and no operations above arity two), the vanishing of the bigraded Hochschild cohomology HH^{n,2-n}(H,H): every Hochschild cocycle that is an n-ary operation of internal degree 2-n is the Hochschild coboundary of an (n-1)-ary operation of the same internal degree. Cochains are written on the suspension, where internal degree 2-n in arity n and in arity n-1 become suspended degrees one and zero. The differential is the Gerstenhaber bracket with the product, which is the classical Hochschild differential (outer terms from the product, inner terms from composing with it). For a graded algebra it raises arity by one and preserves internal degree, so this is exactly cocycles modulo coboundaries in that bidegree. Asking for a primitive concentrated in one bidegree loses nothing, since any primitive can be projected there. It is the hypothesis HH^q(A, A[2-q]) = 0 of Seidel-Thomas, Braid group actions on derived categories of coherent sheaves, Theorem 4.7. The complex here is the nonunital one on all of H, which for a unital algebra computes the usual Hochschild cohomology in the degrees n >= 3 used. Red-team checks: it holds for every graded algebra concentrated in degree zero and every n >= 3 (proved in Lean: the cochains vanish because 2-n is not 0). It fails at n = 4 for zigzag algebras with four edges into one vertex, such as affine D4 (an existing library theorem with standard axioms only), so it is neither vacuous nor automatic.

Over any commutative ring, let H be a graded algebra (an A-infinity algebra with m1 = 0 and mn = 0 for n >= 3) with HH^{n,2-n}(H,H) = 0 for every n >= 3. Then every A-infinity structure on the same graded module with m1 = 0 and the same product m2 is A-infinity isomorphic to H, via an A-infinity morphism with a two-sided A-infinity inverse. This is the form in which Kadeishvili's obstruction theory proves intrinsic formality. The proof is the classical one. If the structure agrees with H up to arity n, its arity-(n+1) part is a Hochschild cocycle of degree 2-(n+1), hence a coboundary by hypothesis. Gauge-transforming by the negative of the primitive removes it without touching lower arities. Each gauge morphism is the identity below arity n, so the infinite composite stabilises arity by arity. Its limit is a genuine A-infinity morphism with identity linear part, hence an isomorphism. Seidel-Thomas prove their Theorem 4.7 by the same arity-by-arity induction (Lemma 4.9), noting that each step changes a single component. No field is needed because everything happens on H itself. Red-team checks: standard axioms only; removing any of minimality, equal grading or equal product breaks the proof; the hypotheses hold for every graded algebra concentrated in degree zero.

Unfolds the definition of the vanishing of HH^{n,2-n}(H,H) and repeats it word for word, proved by reflexivity. Other files have no other way to see inside the definition (it is used so in the zigzag-algebra computation).

Kadeishvili's criterion: over a field, a graded algebra H with HH^{n,2-n}(H,H) = 0 for every n >= 3 is intrinsically formal. That is, every A-infinity algebra whose cohomology algebra is isomorphic to H as a graded algebra is formal: A-infinity quasi-isomorphic to its cohomology, equipped with the product alone. This is the definition of Keller, Introduction to A-infinity algebras and modules, Section 3.3, which credits the sufficient condition to Kadeishvili (1988) and to Seidel-Thomas 4.7. It is the statement of Seidel-Thomas, Braid group actions on derived categories of coherent sheaves, Theorem 4.7, whose hypothesis is HH^q(A, A[2-q]) = 0 for q > 2. Proof: over a field every A-infinity algebra is quasi-isomorphic to a minimal model on its cohomology. Transported along the given isomorphism, it suffices that every minimal structure on H with the same product be A-infinity isomorphic to H, which is the obstruction-theoretic theorem proved just before it. Conventions: A-infinity algebras are nonunital, as in Keller Section 3 (Seidel-Thomas use augmented algebras). The algebras quantified over have underlying modules in the same universe as H, which is size bookkeeping only. Red-team checks: specialised in Lean to an arbitrary graded algebra concentrated in degree zero, it recovers the library's degree-zero intrinsic formality theorem. All three hypotheses are needed, and the first two also appear in the conclusion. The hypothesis is not automatic: HH^{4,-2} is nonzero for the affine D4 zigzag algebra. Standard axioms only.

Defines when a tower of modules A₀ ← A₁ ← A₂ ← ⋯ is Mittag-Leffler: for every n there is an index beyond which the images of the composite maps A_k → A_n all coincide, i.e. the decreasing images in A_n stabilise. It is taken to be the Mittag-Leffler condition for inverse systems of sets applied to the underlying sets, which is exactly how Stacks Definition 10.86.1 (Tag 0595) defines it for modules (a system of modules is Mittag-Leffler when its underlying system of sets is). Red-team checks: the file proves it equivalent to Stacks' explicit form; a tower with surjective maps and the tower with all maps zero (not surjective) both satisfy it, so it is strictly weaker than surjectivity; the tower ℤ ← ℤ ← ⋯ with multiplication by 2 does not satisfy it, as the library proves.

States that a tower is Mittag-Leffler exactly when for every n there is m ≥ n such that for all k ≥ m the image of A_k → A_n equals the image of A_m → A_n, which is word for word the explicit form of Stacks Definition 10.86.1 (Tag 0595). It holds because these images shrink as k grows, so 'the image from A_m lies inside every image from further up' is the same as 'all images from further up equal it'. Red-team checks: both directions are proved with no extra hypotheses; used to verify that the zero tower is Mittag-Leffler.

A tower whose terms are all finite sets is Mittag-Leffler: the images in a fixed term A_n form a decreasing family of finite subsets, which must stabilise; the proof applies the general criterion for inverse systems of sets with a finite image at each index. Red-team checks: statement and docstring agree; finiteness is used (the multiplication-by-2 tower on the infinite group ℤ is not Mittag-Leffler); the hypothesis could be weakened to Artinian terms, recorded separately as a generality note, not a correctness issue.

If every transition map A_{n+1} → A_n is surjective, the tower is Mittag-Leffler: all composite maps are then surjective, so every image is already all of A_n. This is the first case in Stacks Example 10.86.2. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is needed (the multiplication-by-2 tower on ℤ is not Mittag-Leffler); specialised to the identity tower on ℤ and combined with the main theorem to give vanishing lim¹.

For a Mittag-Leffler tower, the map from ∏A_n to itself sending (x_n) to (x_n − φ_n(x_{n+1})) is surjective: every family (c_n) can be written as c_n = x_n − φ_n(x_{n+1}). This is the vanishing of lim¹ in the two-term presentation of Stacks Lemma 15.88.1 (Tag 07KW), parts (2) and (3). Idea of proof: modulo the image of this map, finite telescoping sums of composite transitions move any family into the stable images B_n, and since the transitions map B_{n+1} onto B_n, a family with values in the B_n is solved by choosing x_{n+1} as a preimage step by step. Red-team checks: the hypothesis is needed (the multiplication-by-2 tower on ℤ has nonzero lim¹); restated with Stacks' explicit stabilisation condition and the explicit equation, and proved from it.

Says that a Mittag-Leffler tower of modules A₀ ← A₁ ← ⋯ over any ring has lim¹ = 0, where lim¹ is the cokernel of the map ∏A_n → ∏A_n, (x_n) ↦ (x_n − φ_n(x_{n+1})), and 'zero' is stated as the quotient having at most one element. This is Stacks Lemma 15.88.1 (Tag 07KW), part (3), with lim¹ in the presentation of part (2) of the same lemma, and the Mittag-Leffler condition of Stacks Definition 10.86.1 (Tag 0595). It holds because the shift map is surjective for such towers (the stable images form a subtower with surjective maps, on which the shift is onto, and telescoping sums reduce any family to that subtower modulo the image of the shift). Conventions: towers are indexed by the natural numbers as in Stacks, modules are left modules over an arbitrary ring, abelian groups being the case of ℤ. Red-team checks: lim¹ is by definition the cokernel of the shift (checked to hold definitionally); the hypothesis is needed (multiplication by 2 on ℤ ← ℤ ← ⋯ gives lim¹ ≅ ℤ₂/ℤ ≠ 0 in the library); the zero-map tower is Mittag-Leffler but not surjective and gets lim¹ = 0, so this is stronger than the surjective case; no Mathlib duplicate (pinned Mathlib has the Mittag-Leffler condition but no lim¹).

Correctly stated. It says: for a discrete subgroup Γ of PSL(2,ℝ) and determinant-one lifts A, B of elements of Γ with A parabolic (tr²A = 4, A ≠ ±1), unless B commutes with A in PSL(2,ℝ) (in a discrete group, equivalently B fixes the boundary fixed point of A), |tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1. This is the parabolic case of Jørgensen's inequality, where the term |tr²A − 4| vanishes, and is Shimizu's lemma in trace form: after conjugating A to z ↦ z + w, tr[A,B] − 2 = w²c² with c the lower-left entry of the conjugated B, and Shimizu's lemma gives |wc| ≥ 1. The constant is sharp: in the modular group with A = z ↦ z + 1 and B = z ↦ −1/z, tr[A,B] = 3 and equality holds (checked in Lean; it is also the sharpness example of Theorem 7 in F. Cejka's Heidelberg BA thesis). Red-team checks at ab0153c6: all hypotheses load-bearing; that compiled witness satisfies every hypothesis.

Correctly stated. It says: for a discrete subgroup Γ of PSL(2,ℝ) and determinant-one lifts A, B of elements of Γ, unless B conjugates the class of A to itself or to its inverse, |tr²A − 4| + |tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1. This is Jørgensen's inequality for Fuchsian groups as in F. Cejka's Heidelberg BA thesis on the Jørgensen inequality (Theorem 7: T, S in PSL(2,ℝ) generating a discrete non-elementary group satisfy |tr²T − 4| + |tr(TST⁻¹S⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1, best possible), and as Wikipedia states it for SL(2,ℂ): if A and B generate a non-elementary group, B cannot map the finite fixed-point set of A to itself, so the hypotheses here follow from the textbook ones, and the conclusion has the same constant 1. Proof: split on |tr A| < 2, = 2 and > 2 into the elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic cases; A = ±1 commutes with every B and so is excluded. Red-team checks at ab0153c6: both exceptional clauses load-bearing; compiled witnesses in the modular group, including equality (sum exactly 1) at A = z ↦ z + 1, B = z ↦ −1/z, so the constant is sharp; only the three standard axioms.

Correctly stated. It says: for a discrete subgroup Γ of PSL(2,ℝ) and determinant-one lifts A, B of elements of Γ with A elliptic (|tr A| < 2), unless B commutes with A in PSL(2,ℝ) (equivalently, B fixes the fixed point of A in the upper half-plane), |tr²A − 4| + |tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1. This is the elliptic case only, as its name and docstring say; the hyperbolic case and the statement for every element are its siblings ending in of_two_lt_abs_trace and with no suffix. It matches Jørgensen's inequality for discrete non-elementary pairs (F. Cejka's Heidelberg BA thesis on the Jørgensen inequality (Theorem 7: T, S in PSL(2,ℝ) generating a discrete non-elementary group satisfy |tr²T − 4| + |tr(TST⁻¹S⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1, best possible); Wikipedia), whose hypothesis implies the one here; both sides are unchanged by the signs of the lifts. Proof: with κ = (4 − tr²A)/2 and d the distance from z to Bz, the left side equals κ(1 + cosh d), which the geometric form bounds below by 1. Red-team checks at ab0153c6 (compiled): witness in the modular group with A = z ↦ −1/z and B = z ↦ z + 1, where tr[A,B] = 3 and the left side is 5; non-witness: for the elliptic A = (1 1; −1/100 99/100) and B = diag(2, 1/2) the left side is 0.0624 < 1, and the theorem then proves the group they generate is not discrete, so discreteness (in the quotient of the matrix topology) is a genuine hypothesis; every hypothesis load-bearing.

Correctly stated. It says: for a discrete subgroup Γ of PSL(2,ℝ) and determinant-one lifts A, B of elements of Γ with A hyperbolic (|tr A| > 2), unless B conjugates the class of A to itself or to its inverse (B fixes or swaps the two boundary fixed points of A), |tr²A − 4| + |tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1. This is the hyperbolic case of Jørgensen's inequality as in F. Cejka's Heidelberg BA thesis on the Jørgensen inequality (Theorem 7: T, S in PSL(2,ℝ) generating a discrete non-elementary group satisfy |tr²T − 4| + |tr(TST⁻¹S⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1, best possible) and on Wikipedia's page for SL(2,ℂ); a non-elementary pair never has B preserving the fixed-point pair of A, so this hypothesis is weaker than the textbook one. Proof: conjugate A to a dilation (both traces are conjugation- and sign-invariant) and apply the coordinate form. Red-team checks at ab0153c6: all hypotheses load-bearing; compiled witness in the modular group with A = (2 1; 1 1) (trace 3) and B = z ↦ z + 1; also checked in Lean that z ↦ −1/z conjugates this A to its inverse (it swaps the fixed points (1 ± √5)/2), so the exceptional clause correctly removes that pair.

Correctly stated. It says: if a discrete subgroup of PSL(2,ℝ) contains the dilation z ↦ eˢz and the class of a determinant-one matrix B = (a b; c d), and B conjugates the dilation neither to itself nor to its inverse, then 4 sinh²(s/2)(1 + |bc|) ≥ 1. This is Jørgensen's inequality for a hyperbolic element in diagonal form: for D = diag(e^{s/2}, e^{−s/2}) one has tr²D − 4 = 4 sinh²(s/2) and tr(DBD⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2 = −4 sinh²(s/2)·bc, so the left side is exactly |tr²D − 4| + |tr[D,B] − 2|. Jørgensen's proof: if the bound fails, the products bₙcₙ along the sequence Bₙ₊₁ = BₙDBₙ⁻¹ shrink geometrically, balanced conjugates of the Bₙ by powers of D converge to D, discreteness makes one equal to D, and running backwards shows B is diagonal or antidiagonal, i.e. B fixes or swaps 0 and ∞ (the excluded cases). Red-team checks at ab0153c6: every hypothesis load-bearing; the hypotheses are realised (the hyperbolic trace form, which has a compiled modular-group witness, constructs them after conjugation); s = 0 is excluded by the first exceptional clause; whole file elaborates in about 2 s.

Correctly stated. It says: if A lifts a nontrivial element of a discrete subgroup Γ of PSL(2,ℝ) that fixes a point z of the upper half-plane, every B in Γ not fixing z satisfies (4 − tr²A)·cosh²(d/2) ≥ 1, where d is the hyperbolic distance from z to Bz. This is the geometric form of Jørgensen's inequality for an elliptic element: by the displacement formula tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2 = ((4 − tr²A)/2)(cosh d − 1), the trace form's left side equals (4 − tr²A)(1 + cosh d)/2 = (4 − tr²A)cosh²(d/2); for a rotation through angle 2θ it reads 2|sin θ| cosh(d/2) ≥ 1, as the docstring says. Proof: if it fails, the displacements of z along Jørgensen's sequence Bₙ₊₁ = BₙABₙ⁻¹ strictly decrease, giving infinitely many elements of Γ that move z a bounded distance, which contradicts proper discontinuity. Red-team checks at ab0153c6: all five hypotheses load-bearing; compiled witness in the modular group with A = z ↦ −1/z (fixing i) and B = z ↦ z + 1.
